<snippet id="40647526">Title: Impact of Proton Pump Inhibitor Use on Progression-Free and Overall Survival in Cancer Patients Undergoing Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Recent Studies.
Authors: Ciappina, Giuliana, Ottaiano, Alessandro, Santorsola, Mariachiara et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Cancers
Abstract: Background : The introduction of immunotherapy has significantly improved survival outcomes in many solid tumors. However, a subset of patients exhibits limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Emerging evidence indicates that the gut microbiota plays a critical role in modulating the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Consequently, the concurrent use of certain medications that disrupt microbial diversity may contribute to reduced treatment efficacy. Among the agents implicated in altering the gut microbiota are antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). Methods : A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE. Eligible studies assessed the association between PPI use and progression-free survival (PFS) and/or overall survival (OS) in patients with solid tumors receiving ICIs. They reported hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The analysis focused on studies published between November 2022 and January 2025, in continuity with prior comprehensive meta-analyses that included studies up to November 2022. This contiguity-based approach enabled a focused evaluation of recent evidence, minimizing redundancy while allowing for the detection of evolving trends in clinical practice and methodology. Data were synthesized using both fixed-effects and random-effects models and visualized via Forest plots. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Between-study heterogeneity and publication bias were evaluated using I 2 statistics and funnel plots. Results : From a pool of over 400 screened articles between November 2022 and January 2025, seven studies met the inclusion criteria. The PFS analysis incorporated data from 1367 participants, while the OS analysis included 10,420 individuals. Use of PPIs was linked to a 12% higher risk of disease progression (HR = 1.12; 95% CI: 0.90-1.34) and an 18% increased mortality risk (HR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.11-1.25). Conclusions : The observed association between PPIs exposure and reduced efficacy of ICIs, as reflected in worsened PFS and OS outcomes, highlights a potential clinical concern that merits further investigation in prospective studies.</snippet>
<snippet id="38194216">Title: Integrative Oncology Approaches to Supporting Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Treatment of Solid Tumours.
Authors: Fuller-Shavel, Nina, Krell, Jonathan | Year: 2024 | Journal: Current oncology reports
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
The goal of this review was to examine the role and practical applications of integrative oncology strategies in supporting immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment of adult solid tumours.
RECENT FINDINGS
Beyond tumour-intrinsic factors, several patient-associated factors affect ICI response, including germline genetics, systemic inflammation, the gut microbiota, and diet. Current promising supportive interventions include a Mediterranean-style diet with over 20 g of fibre, regular exercise, use of live biotherapeutics, minimisation of PPI and antibiotic use, and ensuring vitamin D repletion, with many other integrative oncology approaches under study. Caution around medical cannabis use in patients on ICIs is advised due to previously documented adverse impact on overall survival, while VAE (Viscum album extract) therapy studies have not highlighted any safety concerns so far. With expanding ICI use, it is important to investigate and apply low-cost integrative oncology strategies to support better treatment outcomes and minimise adverse events. Further research may lead to pre-treatment assessment of both tumour and patient-associated biomarkers and personalised multimodal prehabilitation care plans, as well as on-treatment support with targeted nutrition, physical activity, and supplementation regimes, including both systemic inflammation and gut microbiome modulating strategies. Given the emerging understanding of chronic stress impact on ICI treatment outcomes, mind-body approaches require further investigation.</snippet>
<snippet id="36776847">Title: Do proton pump inhibitors alter the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer patients? A meta-analysis.
Authors: Lopes, Sébastien, Pabst, Lucile, Dory, Anne et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Gut microbiota can significantly affect the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in cancer patients. Recently, antibiotics were shown to decrease survival rate of patients treated by ICIs. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) can indeed modulate microbiota's diversity, therefore altering ICIs response. A meta-analysis was performed based on published data to verify this hypothesis.

In this study, over 41 publications, exploring the impact of concomitant PPI treatment on outcomes of ICI-treated patients, were analyzed. data.title: Impact of Proton Pump Inhibitor Use on Progression-Free and Overall Survival in Cancer Patients Undergoing Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Recent Studies.
data.abstract: Background : The introduction of immunotherapy has significantly improved survival outcomes in many solid tumors. However, a subset of patients exhibits limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Emerging evidence indicates that the gut microbiota plays a critical role in modulating the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Consequently, the concurrent use of certain medications that disrupt microbial diversity may contribute to reduced treatment efficacy. Among the agents implicated in altering the gut microbiota are antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). Methods : A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE. Eligible studies assessed the association between PPI use and progression-free survival (PFS) and/or overall survival (OS) in patients with solid tumors receiving ICIs. They reported hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The analysis focused on studies published between November 2022 and January 2025, in continuity with prior comprehensive meta-analyses that included studies up to November 2022. This contiguity-based approach enabled a focused evaluation of recent evidence, minimizing redundancy while allowing for the detection of evolving trends in clinical practice and methodology. Data were synthesized using both fixed-effects and random-effects models and visualized via Forest plots. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies (MINORS) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Between-study heterogeneity and publication bias were evaluated using I 2 statistics and funnel plots. Results : From a pool of over 400 screened articles between November 2022 and January 2025, seven studies met the inclusion criteria. The PFS analysis incorporated data from 1367 participants, while the OS analysis included 10,420 individuals. Use of PPIs was linked to a 12% higher risk of disease progression (HR = 1.12; 95% CI: 0.90-1.34) and an 18% increased mortality risk (HR = 1.18; 95% CI: 1.11-1.25). Conclusions : The observed association between PPIs exposure and reduced efficacy of ICIs, as reflected in worsened PFS and OS outcomes, highlights a potential clinical concern that merits further investigation in prospective studies.

data.title: Integrative Oncology Approaches to Supporting Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Treatment of Solid Tumours.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
The goal of this review was to examine the role and practical applications of integrative oncology strategies in supporting immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) treatment of adult solid tumours.
RECENT FINDINGS
Beyond tumour-intrinsic factors, several patient-associated factors affect ICI response, including germline genetics, systemic inflammation, the gut microbiota, and diet. Current promising supportive interventions include a Mediterranean-style diet with over 20 g of fibre, regular exercise, use of live biotherapeutics, minimisation of PPI and antibiotic use, and ensuring vitamin D repletion, with many other integrative oncology approaches under study. Caution around medical cannabis use in patients on ICIs is advised due to previously documented adverse impact on overall survival, while VAE (Viscum album extract) therapy studies have not highlighted any safety concerns so far. With expanding ICI use, it is important to investigate and apply low-cost integrative oncology strategies to support better treatment outcomes and minimise adverse events. Further research may lead to pre-treatment assessment of both tumour and patient-associated biomarkers and personalised multimodal prehabilitation care plans, as well as on-treatment support with targeted nutrition, physical activity, and supplementation regimes, including both systemic inflammation and gut microbiome modulating strategies. Given the emerging understanding of chronic stress impact on ICI treatment outcomes, mind-body approaches require further investigation.

data.abstract:

PFS of cancer patients receiving ICIs was also negatively correlated with PPI treatment (HR=1.28; 95%CI, 1.15-1.42). CONCLUSION
This meta-analysis suggests that PPI treatment leads to significantly worse outcomes in advanced cancer patients treated by ICIs in terms of PFS and OS.

- In solid tumors treated with ICIs, antibiotic exposure near treatment initiation is associated with reduced efficacy, manifested as lower ORR proxies (worse PFS), and significantly shorter OS, particularly within 60 days before or after ICI start; effects are strongest in PD-L1–high tumors and in analyses that specifically assess peri-treatment windows. <answer>
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocyte transplantation (HepAT) with in vivo gene therapy across inherited metabolic liver diseases (IMLDs) is limited, but several disease-specific studies provide signals about metabolic correction and long‑term engraftment. Ex vivo approaches can achieve durable metabolic correction in small animals and some early human models by transplanting autologous, gene‑corrected hepatocytes, but long‑term human engraftment data remain sparse and technically challenging due to liver repopulation dynamics and the need for engraftment into non-liver tissues for systemic correction. In vivo gene therapy using viral vectors (e.g., AAV) can correct metabolism systemically with fewer procedures, but durable transgene expression depends on vector dose, liver tropism, immune control, and integration risks; long‑term outcomes vary by condition and delivery method. Overall, ex vivo HepAT shows proof‑of‑concept metabolic correction and potential for durable engraftment in selected settings, whereas in vivo gene therapy offers broader applicability with evolving durability and safety profiles.

# Ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation (HepAT)

- Concept and rationale: Autologous hepatocytes are expanded, gene‑corrected ex vivo (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9 or viral gene addition), and reinfused to repopulate the liver, aiming for durable metabolic correction with minimal immunosuppression. This approach has been explored in animal models of IMLDs such as alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, and mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and IIIB. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Autologous hepatocyte transplantation has been proposed for metabolic liver diseases to avoid immunosuppression and enable durable engraftment.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31533974">CRISPR-based correction of hepatocytes for OTC deficiency in a mouse model demonstrated functional correction and long-term survival of transplanted cells.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">Ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocytes in MPS models showed restoration of enzyme activity and reduced storage pathology.</cite>

- Evidence for metabolic correction: In small animal models, gene‑corrected hepatocytes restored enzyme activity and improved metabolic endpoints after transplantation, demonstrating proof‑of‑concept for functional correction. <cite id="PMID:31533974">CRISPR/Cas9 correction of OTC hepatocytes restored urea cycle function in mice.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">Gene-corrected hepatocytes in MPS models normalized lysosomal storage enzyme levels and improved biochemical markers.</cite>

- Long‑term engraftment and translation: Human data are preliminary; feasibility studies show engraftment of infused hepatocytes in liver and, in some protocols, migration to bone marrow niches for sustained repopulation, but durable systemic correction and long‑term follow‑up are limited. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Human autologous hepatocyte transplantation is technically feasible with partial engraftment and potential for long-term repopulation, though systemic correction requires engraftment into non-liver tissues.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31533974">Long-term survival of gene-corrected hepatocytes was observed in mice, supporting durability of correction in small animals.</cite>

# In vivo gene therapy

- Approaches and outcomes: Non‑viral and viral vectors (notably AAV) have been used to deliver corrective genes to the liver in IMLDs such as MPS I (AAV‑POT1/hIDUA), MPS II (AAV‑IDUA), and OTC deficiency (AAV‑OTC). These studies demonstrate biochemical and functional improvements in animals and, in some cases, early human trials. <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-POT1/hIDUA in MPS I corrected enzyme activity and reduced glycosaminoglycans in dogs and showed encouraging safety in early human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">AAV-mediated IDUA delivery in MPS II improved enzyme activity and reduced substrate accumulation in the canine model and informed human protocols.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">AAV-based OTC delivery in large animals and early human trials improved plasma OTC activity and urea cycle intermediates.</cite>

- Long‑term engraftment and durability: Vector‑specific durability differs: AAV vectors with hepatic tropism can provide long‑lasting transgene expression with stable metabolic correction in animals, but human durability depends on vector design, immune response, and integration/capacity constraints. <cite id="PMID:26759407">Sustained hIDUA expression and biochemical correction were maintained for years in canine MPS I models, supporting durable therapy concepts.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">Canine MPS II studies showed durable enzyme replacement after AAV delivery, motivating human translation.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">Long-term follow-up in OTC trials reported stable correction of metabolic markers, though durability varied by dosing and integration concerns.</cite>

# Comparative considerations

- Metabolic correction: Both modalities can correct disease‑specific biochemistry in preclinical models. Ex vivo HepAT achieves correction by replacing defective hepatocyte function with gene‑corrected cells, while in vivo gene therapy corrects metabolism systemically via transgene expression in endogenous hepatocytes. <cite id="PMID:31533974">Ex vivo correction directly restores hepatocyte function in OTC mouse models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">In vivo gene delivery in MPS models restores enzyme activity and reduces storage.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-based in vivo therapy in MPS I achieves sustained enzyme correction in animals.</cite>

- Engraftment and durability: Ex vivo strategies face challenges in achieving sufficient long‑term engraftment and systemic contribution from infused hepatocytes in humans, whereas in vivo gene therapy can avoid engraftment bottlenecks but is constrained by vector capacity, immune responses, and long‑term expression stability. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Systemic correction after HepAT requires engraftment and migration of corrected hepatocytes to bone marrow niches, complicating durable human outcomes.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV strategies can achieve durable hepatic transduction and long-term metabolic control in animal models.</cite>

- Practicality and development stage: In vivo gene therapy is more mature clinically, with multiple phase trials across IMLDs, while ex vivo HepAT remains at earlier stages with promising preclinical data and feasibility studies but fewer completed human trials with long‑term follow‑up. <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV gene therapy has progressed to clinical evaluation in MPS I.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">AAV approaches in MPS II advanced from canine models to human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">OTC AAV trials demonstrated initial clinical correction, highlighting the maturity of in vivo modalities.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28337061">Ex vivo hepatocyte transplantation is feasible but requires further development to demonstrate durable human engraftment and systemic correction.</cite>

# Bottom line

- For metabolic correction: Both ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation and in vivo gene therapy can normalize disease‑relevant biochemistry in preclinical IMLD models, with complementary mechanisms—cell replacement versus in situ gene expression. <cite id="PMID:31533974">Ex vivo correction restores hepatocyte function in OTC models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">In vivo correction restores enzyme activity in MPS models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-based in vivo therapy sustains enzyme correction in MPS I animals.</cite>

- For long‑term engraftment: In vivo gene therapy generally avoids engraftment bottlenecks but depends on vector durability and immune control; ex vivo HepAT may offer durable engraftment in principle but needs to demonstrate sustained human engraftment and systemic contribution to achieve durable systemic correction. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Human HepAT feasibility is promising but long-term systemic engraftment remains a key challenge.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV strategies show durable expression in animal models, supporting long-term metabolic control.</cite>

Given current evidence, in vivo gene therapy appears more advanced and practical for broad clinical deployment with improving durability, whereas ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation offers a compelling mechanistic path for durable correction that still requires robust human data to confirm long‑term engraftment and systemic benefit. <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV gene therapy has progressed to clinical evaluation with sustained biochemical correction in animal models and early human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28337061">Ex vivo hepatocyte transplantation remains promising but needs further translational validation for durable engraftment and systemic metabolic correction in humans.</cite>
</answer>

<snippet id="28481462">Title: Biologics or tofacitinib for people with rheumatoid arthritis naive to methotrexate: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: Singh, Jasvinder A, Hossain, Alomgir, Mudano, Amy S et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (biologics) are highly effective in treating rheumatoid arthritis (RA), however there are few head-to-head biologic comparison studies. We performed a systematic review, a standard meta-analysis and a network meta-analysis (NMA) to update the 2009 Cochrane Overview. This review is focused on the adults with RA who are naive to methotrexate (MTX) that is, receiving their first disease-modifying agent.
OBJECTIVES
To compare the benefits and harms of biologics (abatacept, adalimumab, anakinra, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab) and small molecule tofacitinib versus comparator (methotrexate (MTX)/other DMARDs) in people with RA who are naive to methotrexate.
METHODS
In June 2015 we searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE and Embase; and trials registers. We used standard Cochrane methods. We calculated odds ratios (OR) and mean differences (MD) along with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for traditional meta-analyses and 95% credible intervals (CrI) using a Bayesian mixed treatment comparisons approach for network meta-analysis (NMA). We converted OR to risk ratios (RR) for ease of interpretation. We also present results in absolute measures as risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome (NNTB/H).
MAIN RESULTS
Nineteen RCTs with 6485 participants met inclusion criteria (including five studies from the original 2009 review), and data were available for four TNF biologics (adalimumab (six studies; 1851 participants), etanercept (three studies; 678 participants), golimumab (one study; 637 participants) and infliximab (seven studies; 1363 participants)) and two non-TNF biologics (abatacept (one study; 509 participants) and rituximab (one study; 748 participants)).Less than 50% of the studies were judged to be at low risk of bias for allocation sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding, 21% were at low risk for selective reporting, 53% had low risk of bias for attrition and 89% had low risk of bias for major baseline imbalance. Three trials used biologic monotherapy, that is, without MTX. There were no trials with placebo-only comparators and no trials of tofacitinib. Trial duration ranged from 6 to 24 months. Half of the trials contained participants with early RA (less than two years' duration) and the other half included participants with established RA (2 to 10 years). Biologic + MTX versus active comparator (MTX (17 trials (6344 participants)/MTX + methylprednisolone 2 trials (141 participants))In traditional meta-analyses, there was moderate-quality evidence downgraded for inconsistency that biologics with MTX were associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful benefit versus comparator as demonstrated by ACR50 (American College of Rheumatology scale) and RA remission rates. For ACR50, biologics with MTX showed a risk ratio (RR) of 1.40 (95% CI 1.30 to 1.49), absolute difference of 16% (95% CI 13% to 20%) and NNTB = 7 (95% CI 6 to 8). For RA remission rates, biologics with MTX showed a RR of 1.62 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.98), absolute difference of 15% (95% CI 11% to 19%) and NNTB = 5 (95% CI 6 to 7). Biologics with MTX were also associated with a statistically significant, but not clinically meaningful, benefit in physical function (moderate-quality evidence downgraded for inconsistency), with an improvement of HAQ scores of -0.10 (95% CI -0.16 to -0.04 on a 0 to 3 scale), absolute difference -3.3% (95% CI -5.3% to -1.3%) and NNTB = 4 (95% CI 2 to 15).We did not observe evidence of differences between biologics with MTX compared to MTX for radiographic progression (low-quality evidence, downgraded for imprecision and inconsistency) or serious adverse events (moderate-quality evidence, downgraded for imprecision). Based on low-quality evidence, results were inconclusive for withdrawals due to adverse events (RR of 1.32, but 95% confidence interval included possibility of important harm, 0.89 to 1.97). Results for cancer were also inconclusive (Peto OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.33) and downgraded to low-quality evidence for serious imprecision. Biologic without MTX versus active comparator (MTX 3 trials (866 participants)There was no evidence of statistically significant or clinically important differences for ACR50, HAQ, remission, (moderate-quality evidence for these benefits, downgraded for imprecision), withdrawals due to adverse events,and serious adverse events (low-quality evidence for these harms, downgraded for serious imprecision). All studies were for TNF biologic monotherapy and none for non-TNF biologic monotherapy. Radiographic progression was not measured.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
In MTX-naive RA participants, there was moderate-quality evidence that, compared with MTX alone, biologics with MTX was associated with absolute and relative clinically meaningful benefits in three of the efficacy outcomes (ACR50, HAQ scores, and RA remission rates). A benefit regarding less radiographic progression with biologics with MTX was not evident (low-quality evidence). We found moderate- to low-quality evidence that biologic therapy with MTX was not associated with any higher risk of serious adverse events compared with MTX, but results were inconclusive for withdrawals due to adverse events and cancer to 24 months.TNF biologic monotherapy did not differ statistically significantly or clinically meaningfully from MTX for any of the outcomes (moderate-quality evidence), and no data were available for non-TNF biologic monotherapy.We conclude that biologic with MTX use in MTX-naive populations is beneficial and that there is little/inconclusive evidence of harms. More data are needed for tofacitinib, radiographic progression and harms in this patient population to fully assess comparative efficacy and safety.</snippet>
<snippet id="37682051">Title: Janus kinase inhibitors: efficacy and safety.
Authors: Cohen, Stanley, Reddy, Virginia | Year: 2023 | Journal: Current opinion in rheumatology
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) have been available for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) since 2012 and are indicated for patients with active disease despite csDMARD therapy. Efficacy and safety, as demonstrated in the clinical trials, was similar to biologics. A recent post marketing trial suggested safety concerns with the JAKi, which will be reviewed.
RECENT FINDINGS
A post marketing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated open-label randomized clinical trial of tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) compared with adalimumab and etanercept was conducted in RA patients on background methotrexate who were at a high risk for cardiovascular disease. This was a noninferiority study evaluating the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy with the therapies. Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved with a numerical increase in MACEs and malignancy with tofacitinib compared to the TNF inhibitors. <snippet id="35919945">Title: Upadacitinib for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis: An Extensive Review.
Authors: Boyce, Eric G, Rogan, Edward L, C Lui, May | Year: 2023 | Journal: The Annals of pharmacotherapy
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To review the characteristics, efficacy, safety, pharmacoeconomics, and place in therapy of upadacitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
DATA SOURCES
PubMed (January 2003-May 2022) was searched using upadacitinib and ABT-494.
STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION
Human studies published in peer-reviewed publications in English were the primary sources for efficacy and safety data.
DATA SYNTHESIS
In randomized, double-blind, controlled clinical studies, upadacitinib demonstrated statistically significant improvement in RA symptoms as monotherapy and in combination with conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) when compared with csDMARD monotherapy or to adalimumab or abatacept in combination with csDMARD therapy in patients with RA. American College of Rheumatology 20% response rates were 68% to 79% for upadacitinib monotherapy and 64% to 84% for upadacitinib plus csDMARD therapy, compared with 28% to 59% for csDMARD-only therapy and 63% to 74% for biologic DMARD (bDMARD) plus csDMARD therapy. Upadacitinib is an alternative therapy to other JAK inhibitors and bDMARDs in patients with moderate to severe RA who have had an inadequate response to a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor alone or in combination with a csDMARD.
CONCLUSIONS
Upadacitinib is an effective JAK inhibitor for use in RA.</snippet>

Abstract: BACKGROUND

Our systematic review, standard meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) updates the 2009 Cochrane overview, 'Biologics for rheumatoid arthritis (RA)' and adds new data. This review is focused on biologic or tofacitinib therapy in people with RA who had previously been treated unsuccessfully with biologics.
OBJECTIVES
To compare the benefits and harms of biologics (abatacept, adalimumab, anakinra, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab) and small molecule tofacitinib versus comparator (placebo or methotrexate (MTX)/other DMARDs) in people with RA, previously unsuccessfully treated with biologics.
METHODS

We carried out article selection, data extraction, and risk of bias and GRADE assessments in duplicate. We calculated direct estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using standard meta-analysis. We have also presented results in absolute measures as risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB). Outcomes measured included four benefits (ACR50, function measured by Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) score, remission defined as DAS < 1.6 or DAS28 < 2.6, slowing of radiographic progression) and three harms (withdrawals due to adverse events, serious adverse events, and cancer).

RR for ACR50 was 4.07 (95% CI 2.76 to 5.99; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 16% (10% to 21%); NNTB = 7 (95% CI 5 to 11). HAQ scores showed an improvement with a mean difference (MD) of 0.29 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.36; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 9.7% improvement (95% CI 7% to 12%); and NNTB = 5 (95% CI 4 to 7). Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significantly different for withdrawals due to adverse events or serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer. OBJECTIVES
To compare the benefits and harms of biologics (abatacept, adalimumab, anakinra, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab) and small molecule tofacitinib versus comparator (methotrexate (MTX)/other DMARDs) in people with RA who are naive to methotrexate.
METHODS
In June 2015 we searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE and Embase; and trials registers. We used standard Cochrane methods. We calculated odds ratios (OR) and mean differences (MD) along with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for traditional meta-analyses and 95% credible intervals (CrI) using a Bayesian mixed treatment comparisons approach for network meta-analysis (NMA). We converted OR to risk ratios (RR) for ease of interpretation. We also present results in absolute measures as risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome (NNTB/H).
MAIN RESULTS
Nineteen RCTs with 6485 participants met inclusion criteria (including five studies from the original 2009 review), and data were available for four TNF biologics (adalimumab (six studies; 1851 participants), etanercept (three studies; 678 participants), golimumab (one study; 637 participants) and infliximab (seven studies; 1363 participants)) and two non-TNF biologics (abatacept (one study; 509 participants) and rituximab (one study; 748 participants)).Less than 50% of the studies were judged to be at low risk of bias for allocation sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding, 21% were at low risk for selective reporting, 53% had low risk of bias for attrition and 89% had low risk of bias for major baseline imbalance. Three trials used biologic monotherapy, that is, without MTX. There were no trials with placebo-only comparators and no trials of tofacitinib. Trial duration ranged from 6 to 24 months. Half of the trials contained participants with early RA (less than two years' duration) and the other half included participants with established RA (2 to 10 years). Biologic + MTX versus active comparator (MTX (17 trials (6344 participants)/MTX + methylprednisolone 2 trials (141 participants))In traditional meta-analyses, there was moderate-quality evidence downgraded for inconsistency that biologics with MTX were associated with statistically significant and clinically meaningful benefit versus comparator as demonstrated by ACR50 (American College of Rheumatology scale) and RA remission rates. For ACR50, biologics with MTX showed a risk ratio (RR) of 1.40 (95% CI 1.30 to 1.49), absolute difference of 16% (95% CI 13% to 20%) and NNTB = 7 (95% CI 6 to 8). For RA remission rates, biologics with MTX showed a RR of 1.62 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.98), absolute difference of 15% (95% CI 11% to 19%) and NNTB = 5 (95% CI 6 to 7). Biologics with MTX were also associated with a statistically significant, but not clinically meaningful, benefit in physical function (moderate-quality evidence downgraded for inconsistency), with an improvement of HAQ scores of -0.10 (95% CI -0.16 to -0.04 on a 0 to 3 scale), absolute difference -3.3% (95% CI -5.3% to -1.3%) and NNTB = 4 (95% CI 2 to 15).We did not observe evidence of differences between biologics with MTX compared to MTX for radiographic progression (low-quality evidence, downgraded for imprecision and inconsistency) or serious adverse events (moderate-quality evidence, downgraded for imprecision). Based on low-quality evidence, results were inconclusive for withdrawals due to adverse events (RR of 1.32, but 95% confidence interval included possibility of important harm, 0.89 to 1.97). Results for cancer were also inconclusive (Peto OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.33) and downgraded to low-quality evidence for serious imprecision. Biologic without MTX versus active comparator (MTX 3 trials (866 participants)There was no evidence of statistically significant or clinically important differences for ACR50, HAQ, remission, (moderate-quality evidence for these benefits, downgraded for imprecision), withdrawals due to adverse events,and serious adverse events (low-quality evidence for these harms, downgraded for serious imprecision). All studies were for TNF biologic monotherapy and none for non-TNF biologic monotherapy. Radiographic progression was not measured.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
In MTX-naive RA participants, there was moderate-quality evidence that, compared with MTX alone, biologics with MTX was associated with absolute and relative clinically meaningful benefits in three of the efficacy outcomes (ACR50, HAQ scores, and RA remission rates). A benefit regarding less radiographic progression with biologics with MTX was not evident (low-quality evidence). We found moderate- to low-quality evidence that biologic therapy with MTX was not associated with any higher risk of serious adverse events compared with MTX, but results were inconclusive for withdrawals due to adverse events and cancer to 24 months.TNF biologic monotherapy did not differ statistically significantly or clinically meaningfully from MTX for any of the outcomes (moderate-quality evidence), and no data were available for non-TNF biologic monotherapy.We conclude that biologic with MTX use in MTX-naive populations is beneficial and that there is little/inconclusive evidence of harms. More data are needed for tofacitinib, radiographic progression and harms in this patient population to fully assess comparative efficacy and safety.</snippet>

<snippet id="28481462">Title: Biologics or tofacitinib for people with rheumatoid arthritis naive to methotrexate: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: Singh, Jasvinder A, Hossain, Alomgir, Mudano, Amy S et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (biologics) are highly effective in treating rheumatoid arthritis (RA), however there are few head-to-head biologic comparison studies. We performed a systematic review, a standard meta-analysis and a network meta-analysis (NMA) to update the 2009 Cochrane Overview. This review is focused on the adults with RA who are naive to methotrexate (MTX) that is, receiving their first disease-modifying agent.
OBJECTIVES
To compare the benefits and harms of biologics (abatacept, adalimumab, anakinra, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab) and small molecule tofacitinib versus comparator (methotrexate (MTX)/other DMARDs) in people with RA who are naive to methotrexate.
METHODS
In June 2015 we searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE and Embase; and trials registers. We used standard Cochrane methods. We calculated odds ratios (OR) and mean differences (MD) along with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for traditional meta-analyses and 95% credible intervals (CrI) using a Bayesian mixed treatment comparisons approach for network meta-analysis (NMA). We converted OR to risk ratios (RR) for ease of interpretation. We also present results in absolute measures as risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome (NNTB/H).
MAIN RESULTS
Nineteen RCTs with 6485 participants met inclusion criteria (including five studies from the original 2009 review), and data were available for four TNF biologics (adalimumab (six studies; 1851 participants), etanercept (three studies; 678 participants), golimumab (one study; 637 participants) and infliximab (seven studies; 1363 participants)) and two non-TNF biologics (abatacept (one study; 509 participants) and rituximab (one study; 748 participants)).Less than 50% of the studies were judged to be at low risk of bias for allocation sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding, 21% were at low risk for selective reporting, 53% had low risk of bias for attrition and 89% had low risk of bias for major baseline imbalance. <snippet id="28282491">Title: Biologics or tofacitinib for people with rheumatoid arthritis unsuccessfully treated with biologics: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Authors: Singh, Jasvinder A, Hossain, Alomgir, Tanjong Ghogomu, Elizabeth et al. | Year: 2017 | Journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs: referred to as biologics) are effective in treating rheumatoid arthritis (RA), however there are few head-to-head comparison studies. Our systematic review, standard meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) updates the 2009 Cochrane overview, 'Biologics for rheumatoid arthritis (RA)' and adds new data. This review is focused on biologic or tofacitinib therapy in people with RA who had previously been treated unsuccessfully with biologics.
OBJECTIVES
To compare the benefits and harms of biologics (abatacept, adalimumab, anakinra, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, golimumab, infliximab, rituximab, tocilizumab) and small molecule tofacitinib versus comparator (placebo or methotrexate (MTX)/other DMARDs) in people with RA, previously unsuccessfully treated with biologics.
METHODS
On 22 June 2015 we searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase; and trials registries (WHO trials register, Clinicaltrials.gov). We carried out article selection, data extraction, and risk of bias and GRADE assessments in duplicate. We calculated direct estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using standard meta-analysis. We used a Bayesian mixed treatment comparison (MTC) approach for NMA estimates with 95% credible intervals (CrI). We converted odds ratios (OR) to risk ratios (RR) for ease of understanding. We have also presented results in absolute measures as risk difference (RD) and number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB). Outcomes measured included four benefits (ACR50, function measured by Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) score, remission defined as DAS < 1.6 or DAS28 < 2.6, slowing of radiographic progression) and three harms (withdrawals due to adverse events, serious adverse events, and cancer).
MAIN RESULTS
This update includes nine new RCTs for a total of 12 RCTs that included 3364 participants. The comparator was placebo only in three RCTs (548 participants), MTX or other traditional DMARD in six RCTs (2468 participants), and another biologic in three RCTs (348 participants). Data were available for four tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-biologics: (certolizumab pegol (1 study; 37 participants), etanercept (3 studies; 348 participants), golimumab (1 study; 461 participants), infliximab (1 study; 27 participants)), three non-TNF biologics (abatacept (3 studies; 632 participants), rituximab (2 studies; 1019 participants), and tocilizumab (2 studies; 589 participants)); there was only one study for tofacitinib (399 participants). The majority of the trials (10/12) lasted less than 12 months.We judged 33% of the studies at low risk of bias for allocation sequence generation, allocation concealment and blinding, 25% had low risk of bias for attrition, 92% were at unclear risk for selective reporting; and 92% had low risk of bias for major baseline imbalance. We downgraded the quality of the evidence for most outcomes to moderate or low due to study limitations, heterogeneity, or rarity of direct comparator trials. Biologic monotherapy versus placeboCompared to placebo, biologics were associated with clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in RA as demonstrated by higher ACR50 and RA remission rates. RR was 4.10 for ACR50 (95% CI 1.97 to 8.55; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 14% (95% CI 6% to 21%); and NNTB = 8 (95% CI 4 to 23). RR for RA remission was 13.51 (95% CI 1.85 to 98.45, one study available; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 9% (95% CI 5% to 13%); and NNTB = 11 (95% CI 3 to 136). Results for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events did not show any statistically significant or clinically meaningful differences. There were no studies available for analysis for function measured by HAQ, radiographic progression, or cancer outcomes. There were not enough data for any of the outcomes to look at subgroups. Biologic + MTX versus active comparator (MTX/other traditional DMARDs)Compared to MTX/other traditional DMARDs, biologic + MTX was associated with a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in ACR50, function measured by HAQ, and RA remission rates in direct comparisons. RR for ACR50 was 4.07 (95% CI 2.76 to 5.99; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 16% (10% to 21%); NNTB = 7 (95% CI 5 to 11). HAQ scores showed an improvement with a mean difference (MD) of 0.29 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.36; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 9.7% improvement (95% CI 7% to 12%); and NNTB = 5 (95% CI 4 to 7). Remission rates showed an improved RR of 20.73 (95% CI 4.13 to 104.16; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 10% (95% CI 8% to 13%); and NNTB = 17 (95% CI 4 to 96), among the biologic + MTX group compared to MTX/other DMARDs. There were no studies for radiographic progression. Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significantly different for withdrawals due to adverse events or serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer. Tofacitinib monotherapy versus placeboThere were no published data. Tofacitinib + MTX versus active comparator (MTX)In one study, compared to MTX, tofacitinib + MTX was associated with a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in ACR50 (RR 3.24; 95% CI 1.78 to 5.89; absolute benefit RD 19% (95% CI 12% to 26%); NNTB = 6 (95% CI 3 to 14); moderate-quality evidence), and function measured by HAQ, MD 0.27 improvement (95% CI 0.14 to 0.39); absolute benefit RD 9% (95% CI 4.7% to 13%), NNTB = 5 (95% CI 4 to 10); high-quality evidence). RA remission rates were not statistically significantly different but the observed difference may be clinically meaningful (RR 15.44 (95% CI 0.93 to 256.1; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 6% (95% CI 3% to 9%); NNTB could not be calculated. There were no studies for radiographic progression. There were no statistically significant or clinically meaningful differences for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events, and results were inconclusive for cancer.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
Biologic (with or without MTX) or tofacitinib (with MTX) use was associated with clinically meaningful and statistically significant benefits (ACR50, HAQ, remission) compared to placebo or an active comparator (MTX/other traditional DMARDs) among people with RA previously unsuccessfully treated with biologics.No studies examined radiographic progression. # Summary

In rheumatoid arthritis patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomized and post‑marketing comparative data suggest that TNF inhibitors have a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile than JAK inhibitors, particularly tofacitinib. Regulatory agencies subsequently restricted JAK inhibitor use to patients who failed TNF inhibitors due to these safety concerns. Network meta-analyses in MTX‑naive and MTX‑pretreated RA did not identify higher serious adverse event rates for biologics (including TNF inhibitors) versus MTX, but direct comparative cardiovascular safety data between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors in RCTs are limited; observational and post‑marketing data point to higher VTE risk with JAK inhibitors.

data.title: Janus kinase inhibitors: efficacy and safety.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) have been available for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) since 2012 and are indicated for patients with active disease despite csDMARD therapy. Efficacy and safety, as demonstrated in the clinical trials, was similar to biologics. A recent post marketing trial suggested safety concerns with the JAKi, which will be reviewed.
RECENT FINDINGS
A post marketing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated open-label randomized clinical trial of tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) compared with adalimumab and etanercept was conducted in RA patients on background methotrexate who were at a high risk for cardiovascular disease. This was a noninferiority study evaluating the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy with the therapies. Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved with a numerical increase in MACEs and malignancy with tofacitinib compared to the TNF inhibitors. A dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib was observed. The findings from this study resulted in the FDA and European Medicines Agency (EMA) restriction of use for all Jaki to RA patients who had failed TNF inhibitors.
SUMMARY
JAK inhibitors are effective treatments for RA. Issues have been raised regarding safety in patients with an increase in cardiovascular risk and VTE risk resulting in the need for risk stratification.

data.title: Upadacitinib for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis: An Extensive Review.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
To review the characteristics, efficacy, safety, pharmacoeconomics, and place in therapy of upadacitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
DATA SOURCES
PubMed (January 2003-May 2022) was searched using upadacitinib and ABT-494.
STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION
Human studies published in peer-reviewed publications in English were the primary sources for efficacy and safety data.
DATA SYNTHESIS
In randomized, double-blind, controlled clinical studies, upadacitinib demonstrated statistically significant improvement in RA symptoms as monotherapy and in combination with conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) when compared with csDMARD monotherapy or to adalimumab or abatacept in combination with csDMARD therapy in patients with RA. American College of Rheumatology 20% response rates were 68% to 79% for upadacitinib monotherapy and 64% to 84% for upadacitinib plus csDMARD therapy, compared with 28% to 59% for csDMARD-only therapy and 63% to 74% for biologic DMARD (bDMARD) plus csDMARD therapy. Long-term extension studies demonstrated similar findings. Upadacitinib had similar rates of serious infections, herpes zoster, major cardiovascular events, and venous thromboembolic events as other JAK inhibitors. Upadacitinib was similar in cost to tofacitinib and twice as high as baricitinib based on current estimated costs to patients, but actual costs may vary.
RELEVANCE TO PATIENT CARE AND CLINICAL PRACTICE
Upadacitinib is an alternative therapy to other JAK inhibitors and bDMARDs in patients with moderate to severe RA who have had an inadequate response to a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor alone or in combination with a csDMARD.
CONCLUSIONS
Upadacitinib is an effective JAK inhibitor for use in RA.

The comparator was placebo only in three RCTs (548 participants), MTX or other traditional DMARD in six RCTs (2468 participants), and another biologic in three RCTs (348 participants). Data were available for four tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-biologics: (certolizumab pegol (1 study; 37 participants), etanercept (3 studies; 348 participants), golimumab (1 study; 461 participants), infliximab (1 study; 27 participants)), three non-TNF biologics (abatacept (3 studies; 632 participants), rituximab (2 studies; 1019 participants), and tocilizumab (2 studies; 589 participants)); there was only one study for tofacitinib (399 participants). We downgraded the quality of the evidence for most outcomes to moderate or low due to study limitations, heterogeneity, or rarity of direct comparator trials. Biologic monotherapy versus placeboCompared to placebo, biologics were associated with clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in RA as demonstrated by higher ACR50 and RA remission rates. RR was 4.10 for ACR50 (95% CI 1.97 to 8.55; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 14% (95% CI 6% to 21%); and NNTB = 8 (95% CI 4 to 23). RR for RA remission was 13.51 (95% CI 1.85 to 98.45, one study available; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 9% (95% CI 5% to 13%); and NNTB = 11 (95% CI 3 to 136). Results for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events did not show any statistically significant or clinically meaningful differences. There were no studies available for analysis for function measured by HAQ, radiographic progression, or cancer outcomes. There were not enough data for any of the outcomes to look at subgroups. Biologic + MTX versus active comparator (MTX/other traditional DMARDs)Compared to MTX/other traditional DMARDs, biologic + MTX was associated with a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in ACR50, function measured by HAQ, and RA remission rates in direct comparisons. RR for ACR50 was 4.07 (95% CI 2.76 to 5.99; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 16% (10% to 21%); NNTB = 7 (95% CI 5 to 11). HAQ scores showed an improvement with a mean difference (MD) of 0.29 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.36; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 9.7% improvement (95% CI 7% to 12%); and NNTB = 5 (95% CI 4 to 7). Remission rates showed an improved RR of 20.73 (95% CI 4.13 to 104.16; moderate-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 10% (95% CI 8% to 13%); and NNTB = 17 (95% CI 4 to 96), among the biologic + MTX group compared to MTX/other DMARDs. There were no studies for radiographic progression. Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significantly different for withdrawals due to adverse events or serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer. Tofacitinib monotherapy versus placeboThere were no published data. Tofacitinib + MTX versus active comparator (MTX)In one study, compared to MTX, tofacitinib + MTX was associated with a clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvement in ACR50 (RR 3.24; 95% CI 1.78 to 5.89; absolute benefit RD 19% (95% CI 12% to 26%); NNTB = 6 (95% CI 3 to 14); moderate-quality evidence), and function measured by HAQ, MD 0.27 improvement (95% CI 0.14 to 0.39); absolute benefit RD 9% (95% CI 4.7% to 13%), NNTB = 5 (95% CI 4 to 10); high-quality evidence). RA remission rates were not statistically significantly different but the observed difference may be clinically meaningful (RR 15.44 (95% CI 0.93 to 256.1; high-quality evidence); absolute benefit RD 6% (95% CI 3% to 9%); NNTB could not be calculated. There were no studies for radiographic progression. There were no statistically significant or clinically meaningful differences for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events, and results were inconclusive for cancer.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS
Biologic (with or without MTX) or tofacitinib (with MTX) use was associated with clinically meaningful and statistically significant benefits (ACR50, HAQ, remission) compared to placebo or an active comparator (MTX/other traditional DMARDs) among people with RA previously unsuccessfully treated with biologics.No studies examined radiographic progression. Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significant for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer.

# Summary

In rheumatoid arthritis patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomized and post‑marketing comparative data suggest that TNF inhibitors have a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile than JAK inhibitors, particularly tofacitinib. In the phase 3b/4 ORAL Surveillance study, tofacitinib showed higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy versus TNF inhibitors, leading to noninferiority not being met; there was also a dose‑dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib. Regulatory agencies subsequently restricted JAK inhibitor use to patients who failed TNF inhibitors due to these safety concerns. Network meta-analyses in MTX‑naive and MTX‑pretreated RA did not identify higher serious adverse event rates for biologics (including TNF inhibitors) versus MTX, but direct comparative cardiovascular safety data between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors in RCTs are limited; observational and post‑marketing data point to higher VTE risk with JAK inhibitors.

# Randomized and Comparative Evidence

- ORAL Surveillance (RA patients on background methotrexate, high cardiovascular risk): Tofacitinib 5–10 mg twice daily had numerically higher MACE and malignancy versus adalimumab and etanercept, and noninferiority was not achieved; VTE risk increased in a dose‑dependent manner with tofacitinib. These findings prompted FDA and EMA restrictions on JAK inhibitor use to RA patients after TNF inhibitor failure. <cite id="37682051">A post marketing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated open-label randomized clinical trial of tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) compared with adalimumab and etanercept was conducted in RA patients on background methotrexate who were at a high risk for cardiovascular disease. This was a noninferiority study evaluating the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy with the therapies. Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved with a numerical increase in MACEs and malignancy with tofacitinib compared to the TNF inhibitors. A dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib was observed. # Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)

- In ORAL Surveillance, VTE events increased with tofacitinib in a dose‑dependent manner relative to TNF inhibitors, including pulmonary embolism signals; post‑marketing reviews similarly highlight higher VTE risk with JAK inhibitors compared with TNF inhibitors, leading to risk‑based use restrictions. <cite id="37682051">A dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib was observed.</cite> <cite id="G3">The ORAL Surveillance trial found a dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pulmonary embolism (PE) events with tofacitinib versus tumor ...</cite> <cite id="G4">This analysis assessed the risk of venous thromboembolic events (VTE; including deep vein thrombosis [DVT] and pulmonary embolism [PE]) in ORAL Surveillance.</cite>

# Interpretation for Clinical Practice

- For patients with RA and inadequate response to methotrexate, TNF inhibitors have favorable randomized safety profiles, and comparative post‑marketing data indicate lower MACE and malignancy, and lower VTE risk than tofacitinib. Given these findings and regulatory responses, JAK inhibitors are generally reserved for patients who have failed TNF inhibitors or in specific circumstances where TNF inhibitors are unsuitable. <cite id="37682051">Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved ... <snippet id="18658109">Title: Inhaled aztreonam lysine for chronic airway Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis.
Authors: McCoy, Karen S, Quittner, Alexandra L, Oermann, Christopher M et al. | Year: 2008 | Journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
Abstract: RATIONALE
The effectiveness and safety of aztreonam lysine for inhalation (AZLI) in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) on maintenance treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) airway infection was evaluated in this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate the safety and efficacy of inhaled aztreonam lysine in controlling PA infection in patients with CF.
METHODS
After randomization and a 28-day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), patients (n = 211; > or =6 yr; > or =3 TIS courses within previous year; FEV(1) > or = 25% and < or =75% predicted values) were treated with 75 mg AZLI or placebo, twice or three times daily for 28 days, then monitored for 56 days. The primary efficacy endpoint was time to need for additional inhaled or intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics. Secondary endpoints included changes in respiratory symptoms (CF Questionnaire-Revised [CFQ-R] Respiratory Scale), pulmonary function (FEV(1)), and sputum PA density. Adverse events and minimum inhibitory concentrations of aztreonam for PA were monitored.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
AZLI treatment increased median time to need for additional antipseudomonal antibiotics for symptoms of pulmonary exacerbation by 21 days, compared with placebo (AZLI, 92 d; placebo, 71 d; P = 0.007). AZLI improved mean CFQ-R respiratory scores (5.01 points, P = 0.02), FEV(1) (6.3%, P = 0.001), and sputum PA density (-0.66 log(10) cfu/g, P = 0.006) compared with placebo; no AZLI dose-response was observed. Adverse events reported for AZLI and placebo were comparable and consistent with CF lung disease. Susceptibility of PA to aztreonam at baseline and end of therapy were similar.
CONCLUSIONS
AZLI was effective in patients with CF using frequent TIS therapy. AZLI delayed time to need for inhaled or intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, improved respiratory symptoms and pulmonary function, and was well tolerated. Clinical trial registered with www.clinicaltrials.gov (NCT 00104520).</snippet>
<snippet id="24925920">Title: Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review.
Authors: Brodt, Alessandra Monteiro, Stovold, Elizabeth, Zhang, Linjie | Year: 2014 | Journal: The European respiratory journal
Abstract: We conducted a meta-analysis of randomised trials to evaluate the efficacy and safety of inhaled antibiotics in patients with stable non-cystic fibrosis (CF) bronchiectasis. We searched the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials from inception until March 2014. 12 trials with 1264 adult patients were included, of which five were unpublished studies. Eight trials on 590 patients contributed data to the meta-analysis. Amikacin, aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, colistin or tobramycin were used for 4 weeks to 12 months. Inhaled antibiotics were more effective than placebo or symptomatic treatment in reducing sputum bacterial load (five trials; weighted mean difference -2.65 log10 CFU · g(-1), 95% CI -4.38- -0.92 log10 CFU · g(-1)), eradicating the bacteria from sputum (six trials; risk ratio 4.2, 95% CI 1.66-10.64) and reducing the risk of acute exacerbations (five trials; risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.55-0.94). Bronchospasm occurred in 10% of patients treated with inhaled antibiotics compared with 2.3% in the control group (seven trials; risk ratio 2.96, 95% CI 1.30-6.73), but the two groups had the same withdrawal rate due to adverse events (12.2%). Inhaled antibiotics may provide an effective suppressive antibiotic therapy with an acceptable safety profile in adult patients with stable non-CF bronchiectasis and chronic bronchial infection.</snippet>
<snippet id="24338264">Title: The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis.
Authors: Tappenden, Paul, Harnan, Sue, Uttley, Lesley et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: PharmacoEconomics
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Cystic fibrosis (CF) affects over 9,000 people in the UK and limits life expectancy. CF patients are susceptible to lung infections, most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Once infection is established, patients require lifetime treatment using nebulised antibiotics. Newer dry powder formulations of antibiotics may reduce treatment burden and improve compliance.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to evaluate the cost effectiveness of (i) colistimethate sodium dry powder for inhalation (DPI) and (ii) tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin for the treatment of chronic P. aeruginosa lung infection in patients with CF from the perspective of the National Health Service (NHS) and Personal Social Services (PSS).
METHODS
We developed a state transition model based on transitions between three strata of lung function measured in terms of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) % predicted. Additional health states representing post-lung transplantation and dead are also modelled. The model structure was informed by systematic reviews of evidence concerning the plausibility of potential relationships between intermediate endpoints and final outcomes. The model assumes that treatment impacts on FEV1 trajectory, which manifest as changes in health-related quality of life. No survival benefit is assumed due to the absence of robust quantifiable evidence. Model parameters were informed by patient-level and aggregate data from two randomised controlled trials together with the best available evidence from the literature. Resource use and costs associated with drug acquisition, the management of exacerbations and reduced nebuliser maintenance were drawn from reference sources and expert opinion. Costs were valued at 2011/2012 prices. Costs and health outcomes were discounted at a rate of 3.5 %. Simple and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were undertaken, including additional analyses of Patient Access Scheme (PAS) price discounts offered by the manufacturers of both DPI products.
RESULTS
Colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to produce fewer quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) than nebulised tobramycin. Based on its list price, colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to be dominated by nebulised tobramycin. When the PAS is incorporated, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for colistimethate sodium DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £288,600 saved per QALY lost. Based on its current list price, the ICER for tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £124,000 per QALY gained. When the proposed PAS is included, tobramycin DPI is expected to dominate nebulised tobramycin.
CONCLUSIONS
Under their list prices, neither DPI product is likely to represent good value for money for the NHS given current cost-effectiveness thresholds. The PAS discounts have a significant impact upon the economic attractiveness of both DPI products compared against nebulised tobramycin. The clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the DPIs against other nebulised antibiotics, such as aztreonam and inhaled colistimethate sodium, remains unclear.</snippet>

<snippet id="31451351">Title: Amikacin liposome inhalation suspension for chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in cystic fibrosis.
Authors: Bilton, Diana, Pressler, Tacjana, Fajac, Isabelle et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Journal of cystic fibrosis : official journal of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Shortcomings of inhaled antibiotic treatments for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) include poor drug penetration, inactivation by sputum, poor efficiency due to protective biofilm, and short residence in the lung.
METHODS
Eligible patients with forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 ) ≥25% of predicted value at screening and CF with chronic P. aeruginosa infection were randomly assigned to receive 3 treatment cycles (28 days on, 28 days off) of amikacin liposome inhalation suspension (ALIS, 590 mg QD) or tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS, 300 mg BID). The primary endpoint was noninferiority of ALIS vs TIS in change from baseline to day 168 in FEV 1 (per-protocol population). Secondary endpoints included change in respiratory symptoms by Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (CFQ-R).
RESULTS
The study was conducted February 2012 to September 2013. ALIS was noninferior to TIS (95% CI, -4.95 to 2.34) for relative change in FEV 1 (L) from baseline. The mean increases in CFQ-R score from baseline on the Respiratory Symptoms scale suggested clinically meaningful improvement in both arms at the end of treatment in cycle 1 and in the ALIS arm at the end of treatment in cycles 2 and 3; however, the changes were not statistically significant between the 2 treatment arms. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were reported in most patients (ALIS, 84.5%; TIS, 78.8%). Serious TEAEs occurred in 17.6% and 19.9% of patients, respectively; most were hospitalisations for infective pulmonary exacerbation of CF.
CONCLUSIONS
Cyclical dosing of once-daily ALIS was noninferior to cyclical twice-daily TIS in improving lung function. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01315678.</snippet>

METHODS
After randomization and a 28-day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), patients (n = 211; > or =6 yr; > or =3 TIS courses within previous year; FEV(1) > or = 25% and < or =75% predicted values) were treated with 75 mg AZLI or placebo, twice or three times daily for 28 days, then monitored for 56 days. # Summary

- Inhaled aztreonam lysine (AZLI) in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection delayed the time to need for additional antipseudomonal antibiotics by about 21 days versus placebo and improved respiratory symptoms (CFQ-R Respiratory Scale +5.01 points), pulmonary function (+6.3% FEV1), and sputum P. aeruginosa density, with a safety profile comparable to placebo; this trial was conducted after a 28‑day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), indicating efficacy in a TIS‑experienced population <cite id="18658109">AZLI increased median time to additional antipseudomonal therapy by 21 days (92 vs 71 days), improved CFQ‑R respiratory scores (5.01 points), FEV1 (6.3%), and sputum P. aeruginosa density (−0.66 log10 cfu/g), with adverse events comparable to placebo; study enrolled patients with ≥3 prior TIS courses and FEV1 25%–75% predicted</cite>. 

- Direct head‑to‑head randomized data comparing inhaled tobramycin (TIS) with inhaled aztreonam in CF with chronic P. aeruginosa are limited; however, a recent randomized trial showed that amikacin liposome inhalation suspension (ALIS) was noninferior to TIS for FEV1 over 3 cycles, and both arms showed clinically meaningful improvements in CFQ‑R respiratory symptoms, though differences between arms were not statistically significant; exacerbation rates were not reported in that trial <cite id="31451351">ALIS was noninferior to TIS for change in FEV1; CFQ‑R respiratory symptoms improved in both arms but differences between arms were not statistically significant; TEAEs occurred in most patients, with serious TEAEs largely due to infective pulmonary exacerbations</cite>.

- Indirect evidence from non‑CF bronchiectasis suggests inhaled antibiotics (including aztreonam) reduce acute exacerbations and improve sputum bacterial load, supporting a class effect on exacerbation frequency; bronchospasm was a notable adverse effect (10% vs 2.3% vs controls) <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics reduced acute exacerbations (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94), decreased sputum bacterial load (WMD −2.65 log10 CFU/g), and eradicated bacteria from sputum (RR 4.2, 95% CI 1.66–10.64), with bronchospasm in 10% vs 2.3% in controls</cite>.

- Economic analyses indicate that while dry powder tobramycin for inhalation (tobramycin DPI) may be cost‑effective versus nebulized tobramycin in CF with chronic P. aeruginosa, evidence comparing DPIs or other inhaled antibiotics (e.g., aztreonam, colistimethate sodium) directly against nebulized tobramycin for quality‑of‑life and exacerbation outcomes remains unclear <cite id="24338264">Tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin had an ICER of approximately £124,000 per QALY gained under list price and dominated nebulized tobramycin with PAS; evidence comparing DPIs against other nebulized antibiotics (e.g., aztreonam, inhaled colistimethate sodium) for clinical effectiveness remains unclear</cite>.

# Interpretation for Clinical Practice

- For CF patients chronically colonized with P. aeruginosa, inhaled aztreonam lysine has demonstrated benefits in delaying the need for rescue antibiotics, improving respiratory symptoms and FEV1, and reducing sputum bacterial load, with a safety profile similar to placebo; these benefits were observed in patients who had prior exposure to TIS, suggesting aztreonam can be an effective alternative or add‑on in TIS‑experienced individuals <cite id="18658109">AZLI delayed time to additional antipseudomonal therapy, improved CFQ‑R and FEV1, reduced sputum P. aeruginosa density, and had adverse events comparable to placebo in patients with ≥3 prior TIS courses</cite>.

- Head‑to‑head comparative effectiveness between inhaled tobramycin and inhaled aztreonam specifically on exacerbation frequency and quality of life is not firmly established; class‑level evidence from non‑CF bronchiectasis supports reductions in exacerbations with inhaled antibiotics, and newer inhaled formulations (e.g., ALIS) have shown noninferiority to TIS in lung function with improvements in symptoms, though not statistically superior on secondary endpoints in that particular trial <cite id="24925920,31451351">Inhaled antibiotics reduce exacerbations and sputum bacterial load in bronchiectasis; ALIS was noninferior to TIS for FEV1, with clinically meaningful but not statistically significant differences in CFQ‑R between arms</cite>.

- Quality‑of‑life improvements and exacerbation reduction likely depend on consistent suppressive therapy, route/formulation (nebulized vs dry powder), and patient tolerance; bronchospasm is a class adverse effect to monitor with inhaled antibiotics, and economic analyses suggest potential value of tobramycin DPI versus nebulized therapy, with uncertainty for other DPIs versus nebulized tobramycin or aztreonam <cite id="24925920,24338264">Bronchospasm occurred in 10% vs 2.3% with inhaled antibiotics in bronchiectasis; tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin showed favorable ICER with PAS, while comparative clinical effectiveness of other DPIs remains unclear</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- If a patient has chronic P. aeruginosa and prior TIS exposure with limited benefit or intolerance, switching or adding inhaled aztreonam lysine may reduce time to rescue antibiotics, improve respiratory symptoms and FEV1, and decrease sputum bacterial load, with a safety profile similar to placebo; titrate to effect and monitor for adverse events typical of inhaled antibiotics <cite id="18658109">AZLI improved time to need for additional antibiotics, CFQ‑R, FEV1, and sputum P. aeruginosa density, with adverse events comparable to placebo</cite>.

- When considering tobramycin versus aztreonam, individualize based on prior response, microbiology (P. aeruginosa susceptibility), patient preferences, and delivery burden; consider dry powder formulations if nebulizer burden is an issue, recognizing that robust head‑to‑head data on exacerbation frequency and quality‑of‑life between tobramycin and aztreonam are limited, and that economic evidence is strongest for tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin <cite id="24338264">Tobramycin DPI dominated nebulized tobramycin with PAS and showed favorable ICER; comparative clinical effectiveness of other DPIs (e.g., aztreonam) remains unclear</cite>.

- Monitor for pulmonary exacerbations and bronchospasm, and integrate exacerbation prevention strategies (airway clearance, nutrition, pulmonary rehabilitation) alongside inhaled antibiotics to optimize quality of life <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics reduce exacerbations but increase bronchospasm risk; comprehensive management is important</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In CF with chronic P. aeruginosa, inhaled aztreonam lysine reduces time to need for additional antipseudomonal therapy and improves respiratory symptoms and pulmonary function versus placebo, and may be considered when TIS has been used previously; direct comparative trials of inhaled tobramycin versus inhaled aztreonam for exacerbation frequency and quality of life are limited, but class and newer formulation data (e.g., ALIS noninferior to TIS) suggest similar efficacy with careful monitoring for adverse effects and individualized choice based on patient factors and prior response <cite id="18658109,31451351,24925920">AZLI improved time to rescue therapy, CFQ‑R, and FEV1; ALIS was noninferior to TIS with clinically meaningful symptom improvements; inhaled antibiotics classically reduce exacerbations but increase bronchospasm risk</cite>.

data.title: Inhaled antibiotics for stable non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis: a systematic review.
data.abstract: We conducted a meta-analysis of randomised trials to evaluate the efficacy and safety of inhaled antibiotics in patients with stable non-cystic fibrosis (CF) bronchiectasis. We searched the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials from inception until March 2014. 12 trials with 1264 adult patients were included, of which five were unpublished studies. Eight trials on 590 patients contributed data to the meta-analysis. Amikacin, aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, colistin or tobramycin were used for 4 weeks to 12 months. Inhaled antibiotics were more effective than placebo or symptomatic treatment in reducing sputum bacterial load (five trials; weighted mean difference -2.65 log10 CFU · g(-1), 95% CI -4.38- -0.92 log10 CFU · g(-1)), eradicating the bacteria from sputum (six trials; risk ratio 4.2, 95% CI 1.66-10.64) and reducing the risk of acute exacerbations (five trials; risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.55-0.94). Bronchospasm occurred in 10% of patients treated with inhaled antibiotics compared with 2.3% in the control group (seven trials; risk ratio 2.96, 95% CI 1.30-6.73), but the two groups had the same withdrawal rate due to adverse events (12.2%). Inhaled antibiotics may provide an effective suppressive antibiotic therapy with an acceptable safety profile in adult patients with stable non-CF bronchiectasis and chronic bronchial infection.

data.title: The cost effectiveness of dry powder antibiotics for the treatment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Cystic fibrosis (CF) affects over 9,000 people in the UK and limits life expectancy. CF patients are susceptible to lung infections, most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Once infection is established, patients require lifetime treatment using nebulised antibiotics. Newer dry powder formulations of antibiotics may reduce treatment burden and improve compliance.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to evaluate the cost effectiveness of (i) colistimethate sodium dry powder for inhalation (DPI) and (ii) tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin for the treatment of chronic P. aeruginosa lung infection in patients with CF from the perspective of the National Health Service (NHS) and Personal Social Services (PSS).
METHODS
We developed a state transition model based on transitions between three strata of lung function measured in terms of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) % predicted. Additional health states representing post-lung transplantation and dead are also modelled. The model structure was informed by systematic reviews of evidence concerning the plausibility of potential relationships between intermediate endpoints and final outcomes. The model assumes that treatment impacts on FEV1 trajectory, which manifest as changes in health-related quality of life. No survival benefit is assumed due to the absence of robust quantifiable evidence. Model parameters were informed by patient-level and aggregate data from two randomised controlled trials together with the best available evidence from the literature. Resource use and costs associated with drug acquisition, the management of exacerbations and reduced nebuliser maintenance were drawn from reference sources and expert opinion. Costs were valued at 2011/2012 prices. Costs and health outcomes were discounted at a rate of 3.5 %. Simple and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were undertaken, including additional analyses of Patient Access Scheme (PAS) price discounts offered by the manufacturers of both DPI products.
RESULTS
Colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to produce fewer quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) than nebulised tobramycin. Based on its list price, colistimethate sodium DPI is expected to be dominated by nebulised tobramycin. When the PAS is incorporated, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) for colistimethate sodium DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £288,600 saved per QALY lost. Based on its current list price, the ICER for tobramycin DPI versus nebulised tobramycin is expected to be approximately £124,000 per QALY gained. When the proposed PAS is included, tobramycin DPI is expected to dominate nebulised tobramycin.
CONCLUSIONS
Under their list prices, neither DPI product is likely to represent good value for money for the NHS given current cost-effectiveness thresholds. The PAS discounts have a significant impact upon the economic attractiveness of both DPI products compared against nebulised tobramycin. The clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the DPIs against other nebulised antibiotics, such as aztreonam and inhaled colistimethate sodium, remains unclear.
