data.title: Clinical Activity of Ipilimumab Plus Nivolumab in Patients With Metastatic Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab has been approved for intermediate- and poor-risk metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC). However, the activity in non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC) is unknown.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Patients from Cleveland Clinic and the University of Texas Southwestern who had received ipilimumab plus nivolumab for metastatic nccRCC from October 2017 to May 2019 were retrospectively identified. Ipilimumab plus nivolumab was administered in accordance with the CHECKMATE 214 trial. Imaging was obtained at baseline and every 12 weeks. The baseline patient characteristics, objective response per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1, and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0, were analyzed.
RESULTS
Eighteen patients were identified. The median age was 59 years (range, 32-81 years), 77.8% were men, and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status was 0 (38%) or 1 (50%). The median treatment duration was 2.4 months (range, 0.7-12.3 months). The non-clear cell histologic types included 6 papillary, 5 chromophobe, 3 unclassified, 2 adenocarcinoma of renal origin, 1 translocation, and 1 medullary. Most had an intermediate (66%) or poor (22%) International Metastatic Database Consortium risk. The best objective response included 6 partial responses (PRs; 33.3%) and 3 with stable disease (16.7%). Of the patients with a PR, the median time to the best response was 3.0 months, and median duration of the PR was 4.3 months. The median progression-free survival was 7.1 months. All-grade TRAEs were noted in 11 patients (61.1%) and included colitis (22%), hepatotoxicity (16%), rash (11%), and fatigue (11%). Eleven patients (61%) had TRAEs requiring high-dose glucocorticoids (> 40 mg of prednisone equivalent daily).
CONCLUSIONS
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated objective responses and notable toxicity in patients with nccRCC.

data.title: Nationwide Real-World Outcomes of Trial Eligible and Trial Ineligible Patients With Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Treated With Nivolumab Plus Ipilimumab.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy in metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). However, patients who do not meet trial eligibility criteria constitute a large proportion of the real-world population, and their outcomes remain poorly described.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
This nationwide, retrospective cohort study included all Danish patients with mRCC who initiated nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NIVO/IPI) by May 5, 2022. Clinical data were obtained from electronic patient records. Outcomes included median progression-free survival (mPFS), median overall survival (mOS), and objective response rate (ORR), assessed by treating physicians. Patients were classified as trial-eligible or ineligible according to CheckMate 214 (CM214) key criteria. Survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods, and subgroups were explored.
RESULTS
A total of 464 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 33 months. In the total cohort, mPFS was 9 months, mOS 41 months, and ORR 43%, including 13% complete responses. Among 282 trial-eligible patients, outcomes were comparable to CM214 with mPFS 12 months and mOS 49 month, while 182 ineligible patients had inferior outcomes, with mPFS 6 months and mOS 26 months (both P < .001). The presence of brain metastases did not adversely affect OS, while patients with autoimmune disease demonstrated unexpectedly favorable outcomes. Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% in the total cohort, comparable to CM214.
CONCLUSION
This is the first nationwide real-world study evaluating NIVO/IPI outcomes in unselected mRCC. Trial-eligible patients achieved survival outcomes comparable to clinical trial results. Although ineligible patients derived less benefit, they still experienced meaningful clinical outcomes. These findings provide benchmark data for treatment of real-world mRCC populations in routine clinical practice.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

- First-line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo) improves overall survival (OS) versus sunitinib in intermediate/poor‑risk metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), but with higher immune‑related toxicity. In CheckMate 214, the doublet achieved a median OS that was not reached at 28.2–NR versus 26.0 months with sunitinib and had a favorable OS‑toxicity trade‑off compared with sunitinib, albeit with increased immune adverse events and lower PFS compared with single‑agent PD‑1 or with VEGF‑TKI combinations. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214, a randomized phase-3 trial, demonstrated improved overall survival (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab vs Sunitinib: median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months; hazard ratio 0.63) and better side effect profile and quality of life compared with Sunitinib, but with a considerable increase in immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="32800717">Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated objective responses and notable toxicity in patients with non-clear cell RCC, reflecting the immune-related adverse event profile characteristic of CTLA‑4‑targeted regimens</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world cohorts treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab show median PFS ~9–12 months and median OS ~41–49 months, with ~44% experiencing severe (grade ≥3) treatment‑related toxicity, consistent with trial‑expected toxicity</cite>.

- First-line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib [CheckMate 284] or nivo‑lenva‑t inib [CheckMate 9ER]) improves PFS and OS versus sunitinib and has lower toxicity than double‑checkpoint blockade. Network meta‑analysis comparing four immune first‑line regimens suggests lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab may offer the most favorable PFS and objective response rate, nivolumab‑cabozantinib may favor OS, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among these regimens. <cite id="34546767">A 2022 systematic review and network meta‑analysis of first‑line immune combinations in mRCC found: nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked best for OS, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked best for PFS and objective response rate, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ adverse events</cite>.

# Survival

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): CheckMate 214 showed a statistically significant OS benefit over sunitinib in IMDC intermediate/poor‑risk mRCC, with median OS not reached in the double‑immune arm at ~28.2–NR versus 26.0 months for sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 demonstrated improved overall survival (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab vs Sunitinib: median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months; hazard ratio 0.63)</cite>. Real‑world cohorts corroborate this OS advantage, with median OS around 41–49 months for ipi/nivo versus ~26–28 months for sunitinib in trials, though outcomes vary by patient selection. <cite id="41176489">Trial‑eligible patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab had median OS 49 months, close to CheckMate 214, while ineligible patients had shorter OS (26 months)</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib or nivo‑lenvatinib): Both CheckMate 284 (nivo‑cabozantinib) and CheckMate 9ER (nivo‑lenvatinib) demonstrated superior OS and PFS over sunitinib in first‑line mRCC. Network meta‑analysis indicates these regimens generally outperform double‑immune therapy in PFS and ORR, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS benefit among immune combinations. <cite id="34546767">Regarding OS, nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked first, followed by lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Regarding PFS and objective response rate, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked first, followed by nivolumab‑cabozantinib, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.

# Toxicity

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): Double‑checkpoint blockade has a higher rate of immune‑related adverse events and lower PFS compared with VEGF‑TKI combinations, but offers a favorable OS‑toxicity balance over sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 showed a considerable increase in immune-related adverse events with nivolumab‑ipilimumab compared with sunitinib, despite improved survival and quality of life</cite>. Real‑world cohorts report substantial grade ≥3 toxicity (≈40–44%) and characteristic toxicities such as colitis, hepatitis, rash, and endocrine disorders. <cite id="41176489">Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% of patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in a nationwide real‑world cohort</cite>. <cite id="32800717">Common treatment‑related adverse events included colitis, hepatotoxicity, rash, and fatigue, with many requiring high‑dose corticosteroids</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI: These regimens generally achieve lower toxicity than double‑checkpoint blockade, with better PFS and OS versus sunitinib. Network meta‑analysis suggests nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among the compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab and nivolumab‑cabozantinib prioritize PFS/ORR. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab ranked first for lowest grade 3+ adverse events, followed by pembrolizumab‑axitinib, nivolumab‑cabozantinib, and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation

- For metastatic renal cell carcinoma, first‑line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, or pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib) provide strong PFS/ORR benefits and OS improvements over sunitinib with lower toxicity than CTLA‑4‑containing regimens, making them favorable options in broader risk groups. <cite id="34546767">Lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab showed the most favorable PFS and ORR, and nivolumab‑cabozantinib showed favorable OS</cite>.

- PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 (nivo‑ipi) remains an effective option, particularly for intermediate/poor‑risk patients, with a clear OS advantage over sunitinib but higher immune‑related toxicity and lower PFS than VEGF‑TKI combinations. Careful patient selection and immune‑related adverse event monitoring are essential. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improved OS over sunitinib but increased immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world outcomes confirm meaningful survival benefit with substantial grade ≥3 toxicity in a sizable fraction of patients</cite>.

- Population differences (e.g., age, performance status, comorbidities) can influence observed survival and toxicity across regimens, and subgroup analyses may show heterogeneity in benefit. <cite id="34546767">Differences in follow-up duration, risk grouping, and nephrectomy rates may affect generalizability of comparative findings across trials</cite>. <cite id="39941888">In elderly or poor performance status patients, outcomes with ipi/nivo can mirror trial‑based toxicity and survival patterns, with worse OS and PFS in those with poor KPS</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Survival: PD‑1/PD‑L1 + VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, lenva‑t‑pembrolizumab) deliver robust PFS/ORR and OS gains over sunitinib, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS signal among immune regimens. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked best for OS; lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab best for PFS and ORR</cite>. PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (nivo‑ipi) also improves OS over sunitinib, with CheckMate 214 demonstrating a median OS advantage not reached in the double‑immune arm versus 26 months with sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab improved OS over sunitinib (median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months)</cite>.

- Toxicity: PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 regimens have higher immune‑related toxicity (≈40–44% grade ≥3) and lower PFS than VEGF‑TKI combinations, whereas PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKIs generally offer a more favorable toxicity profile and better PFS/ORR than double‑checkpoint blockade. <cite id="29587324">Double‑checkpoint therapy increased immune-related adverse events compared with sunitinib</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Severe toxicity (grade ≥3) occurred in 44% in real‑world nivo‑ipi practice</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab led in PFS/ORR</cite>.

Overall, for first‑line metastatic RCC, PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI therapy generally yields superior PFS and often better OS than sunitinib with lower toxicity than PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4, while PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 remains a high‑efficacy option with a more toxic profile that may be preferred in selected intermediate/poor‑risk patients. <cite id="34546767">Across immune combinations, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab favors PFS/ORR, nivolumab‑cabozantinib favors OS, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity</cite>. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improves OS over sunitinib but increases immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world nivolumab‑ipilimumab cohorts confirm meaningful survival benefit alongside substantial grade ≥3 toxicity</cite>.

<snippet id="22231479">Title: Efficacy and safety of rituximab in patients with active proliferative lupus nephritis: the Lupus Nephritis Assessment with Rituximab study.
Authors: Rovin, Brad H, Furie, Richard, Latinis, Kevin et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Arthritis and rheumatism
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the efficacy and safety of rituximab in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial in patients with lupus nephritis treated concomitantly with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and corticosteroids.
METHODS
Patients (n = 144) with class III or class IV lupus nephritis were randomized 1:1 to receive rituximab (1,000 mg) or placebo on days 1, 15, 168, and 182. The primary end point was renal response status at week 52.
RESULTS
Rituximab depleted peripheral CD19+ B cells in 71 of 72 patients. The overall (complete and partial) renal response rates were 45.8% among the 72 patients receiving placebo and 56.9% among the 72 patients receiving rituximab (P = 0.18); partial responses accounted for most of the difference. The primary end point (superior response rate with rituximab) was not achieved. Eight placebo-treated patients and no rituximab-treated patients required cyclophosphamide rescue therapy through week 52. Statistically significant improvements in serum complement C3, C4, and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) levels were observed among patients treated with rituximab. In both treatment groups, a reduction in anti-dsDNA levels greater than the median reduction was associated with reduced proteinuria. The rates of serious adverse events, including infections, were similar in both groups. Neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension occurred more frequently in the rituximab group.
CONCLUSION
Although rituximab therapy led to more responders and greater reductions in anti-dsDNA and C3/C4 levels, it did not improve clinical outcomes after 1 year of treatment. The combination of rituximab with MMF and corticosteroids did not result in any new or unexpected safety signals.</snippet>
<snippet id="29410944">Title: Clinical Outcomes Observed among Biopsy Proven Lupus Nephritis Patients Treated with Mycophenolate Mofetil as First-line Therapy.
Authors: Timlin, Homa, Magder, Laurence, Petri, Michelle | Year: 2017 | Journal: Cureus
Abstract: Background and objective The rate of end-stage renal disease from lupus nephritis has not declined, in spite of recent advances in therapeutics, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). To provide insight into rates of the clinical outcomes in current practice after biopsy-proven lupus nephritis, we used a prospective cohort of the patients with newly diagnosed lupus nephritis, treated with MMF and observed their outcomes. Method Twenty systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients who began mycophenolate mofetil shortly after a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of lupus nephritis were included in the analysis. There were five patients with class III, nine with class IV, four with class III-V, one with class IV-V and two with class V lupus nephritis. The initial dose of mycophenolate mofetil was 1000 mg twice daily. If no improvement was observed, the dose was increased to 1500 mg twice daily after one month. We estimated the survival function for the time until the urine protein/creatinine reached 0.50 grams or less, after starting MMF by using an approach that accommodated interval-censored data. We also evaluated the treatment response using five different sets of criteria for the response that have previously been used in the clinical trials. These included the Bristol Myers-Squibb (BMS), the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab (LUNAR ), the Aspreva Lupus Management Study (ALMS), and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study (ACCESS). Result We estimated that 52% of the SLE patients reached 0.50 grams of proteinuria within 51 days of starting mycophenolate mofetil (95% confidence interval 29%-74%) and 77% reached 0.50 grams or less within 260 days (95% confidence interval 57%-97%). The probability of response at 90 and 180 days was 5% and 33% (the Bristol Myers-Squibb), 26% and 57% (the American College of Rheumatology), and 11% and 28% (the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab, the Aspreva Lupus Management Study and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study). Conclusion The complete renal response ranged from 28% to 57% at six months in the routine clinical practice, mirroring the results in randomized clinical trials. Regardless of the response measures, the complete renal response was slow and, by most indices, reached in only a minority of the patients by the end of six months of the induction therapy. This indicates the urgent need for the faster and more effective lupus nephritis treatments.</snippet>

<snippet id="19369404">Title: Mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide for induction treatment of lupus nephritis.
Authors: Appel, Gerald B, Contreras, Gabriel, Dooley, Mary Anne et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN
Abstract: Recent studies have suggested that mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) may offer advantages over intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVC) for the treatment of lupus nephritis, but these therapies have not been compared in an international randomized, controlled trial. Here, we report the comparison of MMF and IVC as induction treatment for active lupus nephritis in a multinational, two-phase (induction and maintenance) study. We randomly assigned 370 patients with classes III through V lupus nephritis to open-label MMF (target dosage 3 g/d) or IVC (0.5 to 1.0 g/m(2) in monthly pulses) in a 24-wk induction study. Both groups received prednisone, tapered from a maximum starting dosage of 60 mg/d. The primary end point was a prespecified decrease in urine protein/creatinine ratio and stabilization or improvement in serum creatinine. Secondary end points included complete renal remission, systemic disease activity and damage, and safety. Overall, we did not detect a significantly different response rate between the two groups: 104 (56.2%) of 185 patients responded to MMF compared with 98 (53.0%) of 185 to IVC. Secondary end points were also similar between treatment groups. There were nine deaths in the MMF group and five in the IVC group. We did not detect significant differences between the MMF and IVC groups with regard to rates of adverse events, serious adverse events, or infections. Although most patients in both treatment groups experienced clinical improvement, the study did not meet its primary objective of showing that MMF was superior to IVC as induction treatment for lupus nephritis.</snippet>
<snippet id="25383558">Title: Multitarget therapy for induction treatment of lupus nephritis: a randomized trial.
Authors: Liu, Zhihong, Zhang, Haitao, Liu, Zhangsuo et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Annals of internal medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Treatment of lupus nephritis (LN) remains challenging.
OBJECTIVE
To assess the efficacy and safety of a multitarget therapy consisting of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and steroid compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide and steroid as induction therapy for LN.
DESIGN
24-week randomized, open-label, multicenter study. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00876616).
SETTING
26 renal centers in China.
PATIENTS
Adults (aged 18 to 65 years) with biopsy-proven LN.
INTERVENTION
Tacrolimus, 4 mg/d, and mycophenolate mofetil, 1.0 g/d, versus intravenous cyclophosphamide with a starting dose of 0.75 (adjusted to 0.5 to 1.0) g/m2 of body surface area every 4 weeks for 6 months. Both groups received 3 days of pulse methylprednisolone followed by a tapering course of oral prednisone therapy.
MEASUREMENTS
The primary end point was complete remission at 24 weeks. Secondary end points included overall response (complete and partial remission), time to overall response, and adverse events.
RESULTS
After 24 weeks of therapy, more patients in the multitarget group (45.9%) than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (25.6%) showed complete remission (difference, 20.3 percentage points [95% CI, 10.0 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001). The overall response incidence was higher in the multitarget group than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (83.5% vs. 63.0%; difference, 20.4 percentage points [CI, 10.3 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001), and the median time to overall response was shorter in the multitarget group (difference, -4.1 weeks [CI, -7.9 to -2.1 weeks]). Incidence of adverse events did not differ between the multitarget and intravenous cyclophosphamide groups (50.3% [91 of 181] vs. 52.5% [95 of 181]).
LIMITATION
The study was limited to 24 weeks of follow-up.
CONCLUSION
Multitarget therapy provides superior efficacy compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide as induction therapy for LN.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE

Authors: Stolyar, Liya, Lahita, Robert G, Panush, Richard S | Year: 2020 | Journal: Lupus

METHODS

Authors: Lee, Y H, Woo, J-H, Choi, S J et al. | Year: 2010 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the efficacies and toxicities of immunosuppressive treatments for lupus nephritis (LN) versus cyclophosphamide (CYC). A meta-analysis was performed to determine treatment efficacy and toxicity outcomes between mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and CYC induction therapies, between MMF and azathioprine (AZA) as maintenance therapies, and between low-dose intravenous (IV) CYC and high-dose IV CYC therapy. # Summary

In active lupus nephritis, a large international randomized trial (JASN 2009) directly compared mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 3 g/day with intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVC) 0.5–1.0 g/m2 monthly pulses for induction therapy. Overall response rates were similar (56.2% for MMF vs 53.0% for IVC), and secondary endpoints, including complete renal remission, systemic disease activity, and safety, were also comparable over 24 weeks of induction. Serious adverse events and infections occurred at similar rates, and the study did not demonstrate a superiority of MMF over IVC on the primary outcome of proteinuria reduction plus creatinine stability/improvement. However, a meta-analysis across randomized trials indicates that MMF is as effective as cyclophosphamide for induction but has a more favorable safety profile—particularly lower risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia—favoring MMF for patients concerned about fertility and hematologic toxicity. A separate randomized trial from China showed that a multitarget regimen (tacrolimus + MMF) outperformed IVC for complete remission at 24 weeks, but this does not change the head-to-head comparison between MMF and cyclophosphamide.

# Complete Renal Response

- In the MMF vs IVC induction trial, complete renal remission was similar between arms, with overall response rates of 56.2% (MMF) and 53.0% (IVC) over 24 weeks; the primary endpoint (proteinuria reduction plus creatinine stability/improvement) favored neither regimen. This suggests comparable induction efficacy for achieving complete renal response between MMF and cyclophosphamide in active lupus nephritis. <cite id="19369404">In the MMF versus cyclophosphamide induction trial, overall response rates were 56.2% with MMF and 53.0% with IVC, with no significant differences in secondary endpoints including complete renal remission, systemic disease activity, or safety</cite>.

- A systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs concluded that MMF was as effective as cyclophosphamide for induction in terms of complete and partial remission, reinforcing that renal response rates are broadly comparable between MMF and cyclophosphamide during induction. <cite id="20064907">Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found MMF did not increase complete or partial remission rates compared with cyclophosphamide during induction therapy</cite>.

# Fertility-Related and Hematologic Safety

- The same meta-analysis reported that MMF had lower relative risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia compared with cyclophosphamide, indicating a reduced burden of fertility-related adverse effects and hematologic toxicity with MMF. This is clinically important for women of childbearing age, where preserving fertility and minimizing ovarian toxicity is a priority. <cite id="20064907">MMF showed lower relative risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia than cyclophosphamide during induction therapy</cite>.

- The JASN trial also found no significant differences in overall adverse events or infections between MMF and cyclophosphamide, supporting comparable safety overall while MMF spares fertility and hematologic endpoints. <cite id="19369404">Rates of adverse events, serious adverse events, and infections were similar between MMF and cyclophosphamide in the 24-week induction study</cite>.

# Context and Alternatives

- While MMF and cyclophosphamide are standard induction options, newer combinations can improve remission rates. For example, a randomized trial of tacrolimus plus MMF versus cyclophosphamide showed higher complete remission (45.9% vs 25.6% at 24 weeks) and shorter time to response, though this compares a multitarget regimen to cyclophosphamide rather than directly to MMF. <cite id="25383558">Tacrolimus plus mycophenolate mofetil achieved higher complete remission (45.9% vs 25.6%) and faster time to response than intravenous cyclophosphamide in a 24-week randomized trial</cite>.

- For patients with active lupus nephritis requiring induction, MMF provides similar renal response rates to cyclophosphamide but with fewer fertility-related and hematologic toxicities, making it a reasonable choice when fertility preservation is a concern. <cite id="19369404,20064907">MMF and cyclophosphamide yield similar induction response rates, but MMF has lower risks of amenorrhea and leukopenia</cite>.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of rituximab in patients with active proliferative lupus nephritis: the Lupus Nephritis Assessment with Rituximab study.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the efficacy and safety of rituximab in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial in patients with lupus nephritis treated concomitantly with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and corticosteroids.
METHODS
Patients (n = 144) with class III or class IV lupus nephritis were randomized 1:1 to receive rituximab (1,000 mg) or placebo on days 1, 15, 168, and 182. The primary end point was renal response status at week 52.
RESULTS
Rituximab depleted peripheral CD19+ B cells in 71 of 72 patients. The overall (complete and partial) renal response rates were 45.8% among the 72 patients receiving placebo and 56.9% among the 72 patients receiving rituximab (P = 0.18); partial responses accounted for most of the difference. The primary end point (superior response rate with rituximab) was not achieved. Eight placebo-treated patients and no rituximab-treated patients required cyclophosphamide rescue therapy through week 52. Statistically significant improvements in serum complement C3, C4, and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) levels were observed among patients treated with rituximab. In both treatment groups, a reduction in anti-dsDNA levels greater than the median reduction was associated with reduced proteinuria. The rates of serious adverse events, including infections, were similar in both groups. Neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension occurred more frequently in the rituximab group.
CONCLUSION
Although rituximab therapy led to more responders and greater reductions in anti-dsDNA and C3/C4 levels, it did not improve clinical outcomes after 1 year of treatment. The combination of rituximab with MMF and corticosteroids did not result in any new or unexpected safety signals.

data.title: Clinical Outcomes Observed among Biopsy Proven Lupus Nephritis Patients Treated with Mycophenolate Mofetil as First-line Therapy.
data.abstract: Background and objective The rate of end-stage renal disease from lupus nephritis has not declined, in spite of recent advances in therapeutics, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). To provide insight into rates of the clinical outcomes in current practice after biopsy-proven lupus nephritis, we used a prospective cohort of the patients with newly diagnosed lupus nephritis, treated with MMF and observed their outcomes. Method Twenty systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients who began mycophenolate mofetil shortly after a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of lupus nephritis were included in the analysis. There were five patients with class III, nine with class IV, four with class III-V, one with class IV-V and two with class V lupus nephritis. The initial dose of mycophenolate mofetil was 1000 mg twice daily. If no improvement was observed, the dose was increased to 1500 mg twice daily after one month. We estimated the survival function for the time until the urine protein/creatinine reached 0.50 grams or less, after starting MMF by using an approach that accommodated interval-censored data. We also evaluated the treatment response using five different sets of criteria for the response that have previously been used in the clinical trials. These included the Bristol Myers-Squibb (BMS), the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab (LUNAR ), the Aspreva Lupus Management Study (ALMS), and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study (ACCESS). Result We estimated that 52% of the SLE patients reached 0.50 grams of proteinuria within 51 days of starting mycophenolate mofetil (95% confidence interval 29%-74%) and 77% reached 0.50 grams or less within 260 days (95% confidence interval 57%-97%). The probability of response at 90 and 180 days was 5% and 33% (the Bristol Myers-Squibb), 26% and 57% (the American College of Rheumatology), and 11% and 28% (the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab, the Aspreva Lupus Management Study and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study). Conclusion The complete renal response ranged from 28% to 57% at six months in the routine clinical practice, mirroring the results in randomized clinical trials. Regardless of the response measures, the complete renal response was slow and, by most indices, reached in only a minority of the patients by the end of six months of the induction therapy. This indicates the urgent need for the faster and more effective lupus nephritis treatments.

data.title: Mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide for induction treatment of lupus nephritis.
data.abstract: Recent studies have suggested that mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) may offer advantages over intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVC) for the treatment of lupus nephritis, but these therapies have not been compared in an international randomized, controlled trial. Here, we report the comparison of MMF and IVC as induction treatment for active lupus nephritis in a multinational, two-phase (induction and maintenance) study. We randomly assigned 370 patients with classes III through V lupus nephritis to open-label MMF (target dosage 3 g/d) or IVC (0.5 to 1.0 g/m(2) in monthly pulses) in a 24-wk induction study. Both groups received prednisone, tapered from a maximum starting dosage of 60 mg/d. The primary end point was a prespecified decrease in urine protein/creatinine ratio and stabilization or improvement in serum creatinine. Secondary end points included complete renal remission, systemic disease activity and damage, and safety. Overall, we did not detect a significantly different response rate between the two groups: 104 (56.2%) of 185 patients responded to MMF compared with 98 (53.0%) of 185 to IVC. Secondary end points were also similar between treatment groups. There were nine deaths in the MMF group and five in the IVC group. We did not detect significant differences between the MMF and IVC groups with regard to rates of adverse events, serious adverse events, or infections. Although most patients in both treatment groups experienced clinical improvement, the study did not meet its primary objective of showing that MMF was superior to IVC as induction treatment for lupus nephritis.

data.title: Multitarget therapy for induction treatment of lupus nephritis: a randomized trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Treatment of lupus nephritis (LN) remains challenging.
OBJECTIVE
To assess the efficacy and safety of a multitarget therapy consisting of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and steroid compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide and steroid as induction therapy for LN.
DESIGN
24-week randomized, open-label, multicenter study. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00876616).
SETTING
26 renal centers in China.
PATIENTS
Adults (aged 18 to 65 years) with biopsy-proven LN.
INTERVENTION
Tacrolimus, 4 mg/d, and mycophenolate mofetil, 1.0 g/d, versus intravenous cyclophosphamide with a starting dose of 0.75 (adjusted to 0.5 to 1.0) g/m2 of body surface area every 4 weeks for 6 months. Both groups received 3 days of pulse methylprednisolone followed by a tapering course of oral prednisone therapy.
MEASUREMENTS
The primary end point was complete remission at 24 weeks. Secondary end points included overall response (complete and partial remission), time to overall response, and adverse events.
RESULTS
After 24 weeks of therapy, more patients in the multitarget group (45.9%) than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (25.6%) showed complete remission (difference, 20.3 percentage points [95% CI, 10.0 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001). The overall response incidence was higher in the multitarget group than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (83.5% vs. 63.0%; difference, 20.4 percentage points [CI, 10.3 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001), and the median time to overall response was shorter in the multitarget group (difference, -4.1 weeks [CI, -7.9 to -2.1 weeks]). Incidence of adverse events did not differ between the multitarget and intravenous cyclophosphamide groups (50.3% [91 of 181] vs. 52.5% [95 of 181]).
LIMITATION
The study was limited to 24 weeks of follow-up.
CONCLUSION
Multitarget therapy provides superior efficacy compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide as induction therapy for LN.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE
National Basic Research Program of China, National Key Technology R&D Program.

Decompose the question: The user asks for a comparative assessment between levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) specifically for Parkinson’s disease with motor fluctuations, focusing on “off time” and quality of life (QoL). Key outcomes: change in off time (patient-reported and wearable/actigraph), dyskinesia, “on time without dyskinesia,” and QoL measures (e.g., UPDRS Part III, 39-item PDQ, SF-36). <snippet id="21351823">Title: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel for treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Fernandez, H H, Odin, P | Year: 2011 | Journal: Current medical research and opinion
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Levodopa is the mainstay of Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment, but is often eventually associated with disabling motor complications in patients with advanced PD. The inability of perorally administered levodopa to provide more physiologic continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) is a leading hypothesis to explain these complications.
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the cumulative efficacy and safety, and re-evaluate the role, of levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion in treatment of advanced PD patients experiencing levodopa-associated motor complications, through its purported mechanism for providing CDS.
METHODS
Literature searches in the MEDLINE/PubMed database were used to identify peer-reviewed publications examining the role of CDS in levodopa-associated motor complications and pharmacologic strategies for CDS, focusing on LCIG infusion for advanced PD patients.
RESULTS
LCIG, an aqueous gel, is continuously infused (daytime only or 24 h) via a portable pump and tube permanently inserted into the duodenum through percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). LCIG infusion provides stable levodopa plasma levels, which are significantly less variable than those with oral levodopa. Clinical trials indicate LCIG may significantly improve motor complications (reduction of time in 'off' and time in 'on with dyskinesias'), motor scores using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), non-motor symptomatology (Non-motor Symptom Scale) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in advanced PD patients. <snippet id="36414908">Title: Comparative Effectiveness of Device-Aided Therapies on Quality of Life and Off-Time in Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis.
Authors: Antonini, Angelo, Pahwa, Rajesh, Odin, Per et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: CNS drugs
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Research comparing levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI) for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) is lacking. This network meta-analysis (NMA) assessed the comparative effectiveness of LCIG, DBS, CSAI and best medical therapy (BMT) in reducing off-time and improving quality of life (QoL) in patients with advanced PD.
METHODS
A systematic literature review was conducted for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational and interventional studies from January 2003 to September 2019. Data extracted at baseline and 6 months were off-time, as reported by diary or Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part IV item 39, and QoL, as reported by Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39/PDQ-8). Bayesian NMA was performed to estimate pooled treatment effect sizes and to rank treatments in order of effectiveness.
RESULTS
A total of 22 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria (n = 2063 patients): four RCTs, and 16 single-armed, one 2-armed and one 3-armed prospective studies. Baseline mean age was between 55.5-70.9 years, duration of PD was 9.1-15.3 years, off-time ranged from 5.4 to 8.7 h/day in 9 studies, and PDQ scores ranged from 28.8 to 67.0 in 19 studies. There was no significant difference in the effects of LCIG and DBS, but DBS was ranked first for reduction in off-time, and LCIG was ranked first for improvement in QoL.

<snippet id="41415581">Title: Treatment strategies for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of efficacy, functionality, and drug accessibility with a focus on Latin America.
Authors: Arias-Carrión, Oscar, Ortega-Robles, Emmanuel | Year: 2025 | Journal: Frontiers in pharmacology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Motor fluctuations represent a major therapeutic challenge in Parkinson's disease, particularly among individuals on long-term levodopa therapy. Although diverse pharmacological and device-aided strategies are available, their comparative efficacy, functional benefits, and real-world accessibility-especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)-remain inadequately characterised.
METHODOLOGY
We conducted a systematic review of randomised controlled trials, comparative effectiveness studies, and high-quality observational cohorts evaluating pharmacological, surgical, and experimental interventions for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease. PubMed and Scopus were searched through 31 May 2025. Eligible studies enrolled adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations despite levodopa therapy and reported outcomes related to OFF/ON-time duration, functional disability (UPDRS-II), and health-related quality of life (PDQ-39 or EQ-5D). Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools, and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. In parallel, we conducted a comparative analysis of drug accessibility across nine Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico, Panama, and Peru) and the United States, assessing marketing authorisation status and Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)-adjusted prices per Defined Daily Dose (DDD).
RESULTS
Ninety-two studies met the inclusion criteria. High-certainty evidence supports the efficacy of extended-release levodopa (IPX066), opicapone, pramipexole, rotigotine, and safinamide in reducing OFF-time, although improvements in functional disability and quality of life were modest or inconsistent. Moderate-certainty evidence supports device-aided therapies, including levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa, and continuous apomorphine infusion, which achieved larger effects on OFF-time and functional outcomes. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the globus pallidus internus was adequate but limited by cost and availability in LMICs. The Latin American analysis revealed substantial cross-country disparities: the United States had the widest therapeutic portfolio (19 approved drugs) and generally lower PPP-adjusted prices for advanced formulations. In contrast, several newer therapies-such as IPX066, opicapone, istradefylline, and foslevodopa-foscarbidopa-were unavailable in most Latin American markets, and price differentials for controlled-release or add-on therapies were often several-fold higher after PPP adjustment.
CONCLUSION
While multiple pharmacological and device-based interventions effectively reduce OFF-time in Parkinson's disease, their real-world impact is constrained by uneven global access and affordability. The Latin American region exemplifies these disparities, with limited regulatory availability, heterogeneous pricing, and insufficient inclusion of novel agents in national formularies. Integrating efficacy evidence with accessibility analyses highlights the need for coordinated regional policies-centred on price regulation, health technology assessment, and equitable funding mechanisms-to ensure that advances in treatment translate into meaningful improvements in function and quality of life for patients with Parkinson's disease worldwide.</snippet>

<snippet id="38780079">Title: Levodopa infusion therapies for Parkinson disease.
Authors: Dean, Marissa N, Standaert, David G | Year: 2024 | Journal: Current opinion in neurology
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
to review recent progress in the development and use of continuous levodopa therapies in Parkinson disease (PD).
RECENT FINDINGS
Levodopa/Carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is a continuous levodopa therapy which is widely used in the United States, Europe and other countries and is effective at reducing 'off' time. Recent work has shown that LCIG can be useful in managing dyskinesias and can improve nonmotor symptoms and quality of life. Several studies have shown good long-term effectiveness of LCIG. Recent data support the cost-effectiveness of this treatment strategy. Subcutaneous (SC) delivery of levodopa is a newer strategy that avoids the need for a surgically placed gastric tube. Two different products enabling SC delivery of levodopa are in development: ND0612 and foslevodopa/foscarbidopa. Both have recently been shown to reduce 'off' time in randomized, double-blind trials. Adverse effects of SC levodopa are primarily related to skin reactions at the infusion site.
SUMMARY
Continuous levodopa therapies can be used to treat Parkinson disease motor fluctuations that cannot be managed with standard oral therapies. They may also improve nonmotor symptoms, and improve overall quality of life in patients with advanced PD.</snippet>
<snippet id="34018146">Title: The Long-Term Impact of Levodopa/Carbidopa Intestinal Gel on 'Off'-time in Patients with Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review.
Authors: Antonini, Angelo, Odin, Per, Pahwa, Rajesh et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Advances in therapy
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG; carbidopa/levodopa enteral suspension) has been widely used and studied for the treatment of motor fluctuations in levodopa-responsive patients with advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) when other treatments have not given satisfactory results. Reduction in 'off'-time is a common primary endpoint in studies of LCIG, and it is important to assess the durability of this response. This systematic literature review was conducted to qualitatively summarise the data on the long-term effects of LCIG therapy on 'off'-time.
METHODS
Studies were identified by searching PubMed, EMBASE and Ovid on 30 September 2019. Studies were included if they reported on patients with PD, had a sample size of ≥ 10, LCIG was an active intervention and 'off'-time was reported for ≥ 12 months after initiation of LCIG treatment. Randomised clinical trials, retrospective and prospective observational studies, and other interventional studies were included for selection. Data were collected on: 'off'-time (at pre-specified time periods and the end of follow-up), study characteristics, Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) II, III and IV total scores, dyskinesia duration, quality of life scores, non-motor symptoms and safety outcomes.
RESULTS
Twenty-seven studies were included in this review. The improvement in 'off'-time observed shortly after initiating LCIG was maintained and was statistically significant at the end of follow-up in 24 of 27 studies. 'Off'-time was reduced from baseline to end of follow-up by 38-84% and was accompanied by a clinically meaningful improvement in quality of life. Stratified analysis of 'off'-time demonstrated mean relative reductions of 47-82% at 3-6 months and up to 83% reduction at 3-5 years of follow-up. Most studies reported significant improvements in activities of daily living and motor complications. Most frequent adverse events were related to the procedure or the device.
CONCLUSION
In one of the largest qualitative syntheses of published LCIG studies, LCIG treatment was observed to provide a durable effect in reducing 'off'-time.

Abstract: Dyskinesias encompass a variety of different hyperkinetic phenomenologies, particularly chorea, dystonia, stereotypies, and akathisia. Based on the temporal pattern in relationship to levodopa dosing, LIDs are divided into "peak-dose dyskinesia," "diphasic dyskinesia," and "wearing off" or "off-period" dyskinesia, of which peak-dose dyskinesia is the most common, followed by off-period, and then diphasic dyskinesia. Treatment strategy includes identifying the kind of dyskinesia and tailoring treatment accordingly. Peak-dose dyskinesia is treated mainly by reducing individual doses of levodopa and adding amantadine and dopamine agonists, whereas off-period dystonia often responds to baclofen and botulinum toxin injections. Diphasic dyskinesias, occurring particularly in patients with young-onset PD, are the most difficult to treat. While fractionation of levodopa dosage is the most frequently utilized strategy, many patients require deep brain stimulation to control their troublesome motor fluctuations and LIDs. A variety of emerging (experimental) drugs currently in development promise to provide better control of LIDs and other levodopa-related complications in the near future.</snippet>

Authors: Wirdefeldt, Karin, Odin, Per, Nyholm, Dag | Year: 2016 | Journal: CNS drugs
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is available in several countries for the treatment of advanced levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease (PD) with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesia when other treatments have not given satisfactory results.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to summarize the present evidence base for LCIG therapy through a systematic review of the literature.
METHODS
Studies were identified from the PubMed and EMBASE databases up to 12 March 2016 using the following search terms: Parkinson disease, duodopa, levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, LCIG, l-dopa infusion, levodopa infusion, duodenal l-dopa infusion, and duodenal levodopa infusion. Data extraction focused on whether LCIG therapy improves motor and non-motor outcomes as well as quality of life in PD patients compared with conventional therapy, apomorphine infusion, or deep brain stimulation. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies, with or without a control group, that included more than ten patients were included. The quality of evidence that LCIG is effective in reducing fluctuating motor symptoms and improving quality of life is moderate. Quality of evidence for reduction of non-motor symptoms is very low. <snippet id="21351823">Title: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel for treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Fernandez, H H, Odin, P | Year: 2011 | Journal: Current medical research and opinion
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Levodopa is the mainstay of Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment, but is often eventually associated with disabling motor complications in patients with advanced PD. The inability of perorally administered levodopa to provide more physiologic continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) is a leading hypothesis to explain these complications.
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the cumulative efficacy and safety, and re-evaluate the role, of levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion in treatment of advanced PD patients experiencing levodopa-associated motor complications, through its purported mechanism for providing CDS.
METHODS
Literature searches in the MEDLINE/PubMed database were used to identify peer-reviewed publications examining the role of CDS in levodopa-associated motor complications and pharmacologic strategies for CDS, focusing on LCIG infusion for advanced PD patients.
RESULTS
LCIG, an aqueous gel, is continuously infused (daytime only or 24 h) via a portable pump and tube permanently inserted into the duodenum through percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). LCIG infusion provides stable levodopa plasma levels, which are significantly less variable than those with oral levodopa. Clinical trials indicate LCIG may significantly improve motor complications (reduction of time in 'off' and time in 'on with dyskinesias'), motor scores using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), non-motor symptomatology (Non-motor Symptom Scale) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in advanced PD patients. LCIG has demonstrated efficacy in reducing levodopa-associated motor complications in patients with advanced PD, and improving UPDRS and HRQOL scores. Because it involves PEG and its associated risks, LCIG is recommended for patients in whom motor fluctuations and dyskinesias are inadequately treated with traditional peroral medication. For these patients, LCIG can be a valuable alternative to deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when DBS is contraindicated. These conclusions are limited by the modest number and size of completed randomized, controlled trials of LCIG.</snippet>

# Summary

In Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations, both levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) improve off time and quality of life compared with best medical therapy, but head-to-head randomized evidence is limited. Network meta-analyses and systematic reviews suggest LCIG and DBS have broadly comparable effectiveness on motor outcomes, with DBS often ranking slightly higher for off-time reduction and LCIG ranking higher for quality-of-life gains at 6 months. LCIG reduces off time and increases on time without worsening troublesome dyskinesias, and improves health-related quality of life in randomized trials and observational follow-up. DBS has robust randomized evidence for reducing off time, dyskinesias, and improving activities of daily living and quality of life, with long-term observational data showing sustained benefits.

# Levodopa–carbidopa Intestinal Gel (LCIG)

- LCIG reduces off time and increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life in randomized controlled trials and subsequent open-label follow-up, supporting its role in advanced PD with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesias uncontrolled by other therapies. Safety concerns are mainly related to the intestinal infusion system and device-related complications. <cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces "off" time, increases "on" time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life in three RCTs (one double-blind), with long-term follow-ups confirming these findings; evidence quality for motor symptoms and QoL is moderate, while non-motor symptom reduction is very low; safety issues mainly involve the intestinal infusion system</cite>.
- Long-term systematic review data show durable reductions in off time (often by 47–82% at 3–6 months and up to 83% at 3–5 years) accompanied by clinically meaningful quality-of-life improvements. <cite id="34018146">In 27 studies, off-time improvements initiated after LCIG were maintained and statistically significant at end-of-follow-up in 24/27 studies, with 38–84% reductions in off time and concomitant meaningful quality-of-life gains; reductions reached 47–82% at 3–6 months and up to 83% at 3–5 years</cite>.
- Recent reviews emphasize that LCIG is effective at reducing off time and can manage dyskinesias and nonmotor symptoms, with growing evidence for long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. <cite id="38780079">Recent work shows LCIG can manage dyskinesias and improve nonmotor symptoms and quality of life; several studies show good long-term effectiveness and support cost-effectiveness</cite>.
- As an alternative or adjunct to DBS, LCIG is recommended for patients with inadequately controlled motor fluctuations and dyskinesias despite peroral therapy, particularly when DBS is contraindicated. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated, for patients with motor fluctuations and dyskinesias inadequately treated by oral medication</cite>.

# Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)

- Randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that DBS significantly reduces off time and dyskinesias, improves on-period motor function, activities of daily living, and quality of life, and allows levodopa dose reduction with fewer medication-induced complications. <cite id="24487826">Six RCTs (n=1,184) showed DBS significantly improves motor signs, functionality, and quality of life, with intense effects on reducing off-medication symptoms and improving on-medication functionality, plus levodopa-equivalent dose reduction and fewer complications</cite>.
- Long-term follow-up indicates sustained motor control improvements and signals that subthalamic DBS may delay certain late-stage disability milestones (e.g., psychosis, falls, institutionalization) and slightly prolong survival versus medically managed controls, although direct effects on underlying disease progression are unproven. <cite id="35560443">Observational and controlled follow-ups show sustained motor improvements; signals suggest subthalamic DBS may delay late-stage milestones and slightly prolong survival compared with matched medical management, likely attributable to sustained motor and medication side-effect improvements rather than direct disease modification</cite>.
- DBS is frequently considered when dyskinesias are severe and refractory to medical optimization. <cite id="27091215">Many patients with troublesome motor fluctuations and levodopa-induced dyskinesias require deep brain stimulation for control</cite>.

# Comparative Evidence: LCIG vs DBS

- Direct head-to-head randomized trials between LCIG and DBS are scarce; comparative effectiveness analyses suggest similar improvements in off time and quality of life versus best medical therapy, with nuanced differences in ranking. A 2022 network meta-analysis across 22 studies (n=2063) found both LCIG and DBS improved off time and quality of life more than continuous apomorphine infusion and best medical therapy at 6 months; there was no significant difference between LCIG and DBS on these outcomes, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked first for quality-of-life improvement. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS demonstrated significantly greater improvement in off-time and QoL at 6 months compared with CSAI and BMT; no significant difference was found between LCIG and DBS, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked first for QoL improvement</cite>.
- Earlier systematic reviews also note that LCIG’s evidence base—though growing—has fewer randomized trials than DBS, which has robust RCT support; LCIG remains a reasonable alternative when DBS is unsuitable. <cite id="27138916">Evidence for LCIG includes three RCTs with improvements in off time, on time, and QoL, but long-term data are limited</cite><cite id="21351823">Conclusions are limited by modest number and size of completed randomized controlled trials of LCIG, but it can serve as a valuable alternative to DBS when contraindicated</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with advanced PD and marked motor fluctuations and dyskinesias, LCIG can substantially reduce off time, preserve or improve on time without worsening dyskinesias, and improve quality of life, with durable benefits over months to years in observational cohorts; risks are mainly device- and infusion-related. <cite id="34018146">Off-time reductions are maintained and often large over 12+ months, accompanied by meaningful QoL gains</cite><cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces off time and improves QoL without increasing troublesome dyskinesias; safety concerns are device-related</cite>.
- DBS offers strong, randomized-trial-backed reductions in off time and dyskinesias, functional gains, and quality-of-life improvements, with long-term sustainability and potential to delay certain late-stage milestones; it is generally preferred when medically and surgically appropriate, but carries surgical risks and device-related complications. <cite id="24487826">DBS significantly improves motor signs, functionality, and QoL and reduces medication needs in RCTs</cite><cite id="35560443">Long-term observational data support sustained motor benefits and possible delay of late-stage milestones</cite>.
- Choice between LCIG and DBS should be individualized based on patient factors, comorbidities, preferences, access, and surgical feasibility; when DBS is unsuitable or contraindicated, LCIG is a viable alternative with comparable improvements in off time and quality of life in comparative analyses. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated</cite><cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS show broadly similar improvements in off time and QoL at 6 months, with nuanced differences favoring DBS for off-time and LCIG for QoL</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Both LCIG and DBS reduce off time and improve quality of life versus best medical therapy, with DBS having stronger randomized evidence and LCIG demonstrating durable, meaningful improvements with a minimally invasive infusion system. Direct head-to-head trials are limited; current comparative analyses suggest similar efficacy on motor outcomes, with DBS tending to rank higher for off-time reduction and LCIG for quality-of-life gains at mid-term follow-up. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS show significantly greater improvements in off time and QoL than apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months, with no significant difference between LCIG and DBS; DBS ranked first for off-time, LCIG for QoL</cite><cite id="24487826">DBS has robust RCT support for reducing off time, dyskinesias, and improving QoL and function</cite><cite id="34018146">LCIG provides durable off-time reduction and quality-of-life improvements over multi-year follow-up</cite>.

data.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Device-Aided Therapies on Quality of Life and Off-Time in Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Research comparing levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI) for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) is lacking. This network meta-analysis (NMA) assessed the comparative effectiveness of LCIG, DBS, CSAI and best medical therapy (BMT) in reducing off-time and improving quality of life (QoL) in patients with advanced PD.
METHODS
A systematic literature review was conducted for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational and interventional studies from January 2003 to September 2019. Data extracted at baseline and 6 months were off-time, as reported by diary or Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part IV item 39, and QoL, as reported by Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39/PDQ-8). Bayesian NMA was performed to estimate pooled treatment effect sizes and to rank treatments in order of effectiveness.
RESULTS
A total of 22 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria (n = 2063 patients): four RCTs, and 16 single-armed, one 2-armed and one 3-armed prospective studies. Baseline mean age was between 55.5-70.9 years, duration of PD was 9.1-15.3 years, off-time ranged from 5.4 to 8.7 h/day in 9 studies, and PDQ scores ranged from 28.8 to 67.0 in 19 studies. Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel and DBS demonstrated significantly greater improvement in off-time and QoL at 6 months compared with CSAI and BMT (p < 0.05). There was no significant difference in the effects of LCIG and DBS, but DBS was ranked first for reduction in off-time, and LCIG was ranked first for improvement in QoL.
CONCLUSIONS
This NMA found that LCIG and DBS were associated with superior improvement in off-time and PD-related QoL compared with CSAI and BMT at 6 months after treatment initiation. This comparative effectiveness research may assist providers, patients, and caregivers in the selection of the optimal device-aided therapy.

data.title: Treatment strategies for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of efficacy, functionality, and drug accessibility with a focus on Latin America.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Motor fluctuations represent a major therapeutic challenge in Parkinson's disease, particularly among individuals on long-term levodopa therapy. Although diverse pharmacological and device-aided strategies are available, their comparative efficacy, functional benefits, and real-world accessibility-especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)-remain inadequately characterised.
METHODOLOGY
We conducted a systematic review of randomised controlled trials, comparative effectiveness studies, and high-quality observational cohorts evaluating pharmacological, surgical, and experimental interventions for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease. PubMed and Scopus were searched through 31 May 2025. Eligible studies enrolled adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations despite levodopa therapy and reported outcomes related to OFF/ON-time duration, functional disability (UPDRS-II), and health-related quality of life (PDQ-39 or EQ-5D). Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools, and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. In parallel, we conducted a comparative analysis of drug accessibility across nine Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico, Panama, and Peru) and the United States, assessing marketing authorisation status and Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)-adjusted prices per Defined Daily Dose (DDD).
RESULTS
Ninety-two studies met the inclusion criteria. High-certainty evidence supports the efficacy of extended-release levodopa (IPX066), opicapone, pramipexole, rotigotine, and safinamide in reducing OFF-time, although improvements in functional disability and quality of life were modest or inconsistent. Moderate-certainty evidence supports device-aided therapies, including levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa, and continuous apomorphine infusion, which achieved larger effects on OFF-time and functional outcomes. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the globus pallidus internus was adequate but limited by cost and availability in LMICs. The Latin American analysis revealed substantial cross-country disparities: the United States had the widest therapeutic portfolio (19 approved drugs) and generally lower PPP-adjusted prices for advanced formulations. In contrast, several newer therapies-such as IPX066, opicapone, istradefylline, and foslevodopa-foscarbidopa-were unavailable in most Latin American markets, and price differentials for controlled-release or add-on therapies were often several-fold higher after PPP adjustment.
CONCLUSION
While multiple pharmacological and device-based interventions effectively reduce OFF-time in Parkinson's disease, their real-world impact is constrained by uneven global access and affordability. The Latin American region exemplifies these disparities, with limited regulatory availability, heterogeneous pricing, and insufficient inclusion of novel agents in national formularies. Integrating efficacy evidence with accessibility analyses highlights the need for coordinated regional policies-centred on price regulation, health technology assessment, and equitable funding mechanisms-to ensure that advances in treatment translate into meaningful improvements in function and quality of life for patients with Parkinson's disease worldwide.

data.title: Levodopa infusion therapies for Parkinson disease.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
to review recent progress in the development and use of continuous levodopa therapies in Parkinson disease (PD).
RECENT FINDINGS
Levodopa/Carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is a continuous levodopa therapy which is widely used in the United States, Europe and other countries and is effective at reducing 'off' time. Recent work has shown that LCIG can be useful in managing dyskinesias and can improve nonmotor symptoms and quality of life. Several studies have shown good long-term effectiveness of LCIG. Recent data support the cost-effectiveness of this treatment strategy. Subcutaneous (SC) delivery of levodopa is a newer strategy that avoids the need for a surgically placed gastric tube. Two different products enabling SC delivery of levodopa are in development: ND0612 and foslevodopa/foscarbidopa. Both have recently been shown to reduce 'off' time in randomized, double-blind trials. Adverse effects of SC levodopa are primarily related to skin reactions at the infusion site.
SUMMARY
Continuous levodopa therapies can be used to treat Parkinson disease motor fluctuations that cannot be managed with standard oral therapies. They may also improve nonmotor symptoms, and improve overall quality of life in patients with advanced PD.

data.title: The Long-Term Impact of Levodopa/Carbidopa Intestinal Gel on 'Off'-time in Patients with Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG; carbidopa/levodopa enteral suspension) has been widely used and studied for the treatment of motor fluctuations in levodopa-responsive patients with advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) when other treatments have not given satisfactory results. Reduction in 'off'-time is a common primary endpoint in studies of LCIG, and it is important to assess the durability of this response. This systematic literature review was conducted to qualitatively summarise the data on the long-term effects of LCIG therapy on 'off'-time.
METHODS
Studies were identified by searching PubMed, EMBASE and Ovid on 30 September 2019. Studies were included if they reported on patients with PD, had a sample size of ≥ 10, LCIG was an active intervention and 'off'-time was reported for ≥ 12 months after initiation of LCIG treatment. Randomised clinical trials, retrospective and prospective observational studies, and other interventional studies were included for selection. Data were collected on: 'off'-time (at pre-specified time periods and the end of follow-up), study characteristics, Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS) II, III and IV total scores, dyskinesia duration, quality of life scores, non-motor symptoms and safety outcomes.
RESULTS
Twenty-seven studies were included in this review. The improvement in 'off'-time observed shortly after initiating LCIG was maintained and was statistically significant at the end of follow-up in 24 of 27 studies. 'Off'-time was reduced from baseline to end of follow-up by 38-84% and was accompanied by a clinically meaningful improvement in quality of life. Stratified analysis of 'off'-time demonstrated mean relative reductions of 47-82% at 3-6 months and up to 83% reduction at 3-5 years of follow-up. Most studies reported significant improvements in activities of daily living and motor complications. Most frequent adverse events were related to the procedure or the device.
CONCLUSION
In one of the largest qualitative syntheses of published LCIG studies, LCIG treatment was observed to provide a durable effect in reducing 'off'-time.

data.title: Levodopa-Carbidopa Intestinal Gel in Patients with Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is available in several countries for the treatment of advanced levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease (PD) with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesia when other treatments have not given satisfactory results.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to summarize the present evidence base for LCIG therapy through a systematic review of the literature.
METHODS
Studies were identified from the PubMed and EMBASE databases up to 12 March 2016 using the following search terms: Parkinson disease, duodopa, levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, LCIG, l-dopa infusion, levodopa infusion, duodenal l-dopa infusion, and duodenal levodopa infusion. Data extraction focused on whether LCIG therapy improves motor and non-motor outcomes as well as quality of life in PD patients compared with conventional therapy, apomorphine infusion, or deep brain stimulation. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies, with or without a control group, that included more than ten patients were included. The search was limited to peer-reviewed articles published in full in the English language and involving humans.
RESULTS
Infusion of LCIG reduced "off" time, increased "on" time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improved quality of life in three RCTs (one double-blind). Open-label follow-ups confirm these findings. The data evaluating long-term efficacy and safety are still limited.
CONCLUSIONS
The quality of evidence that LCIG is effective in reducing fluctuating motor symptoms and improving quality of life is moderate. Quality of evidence for reduction of non-motor symptoms is very low. Safety issues mainly relate to the intestinal infusion system. LCIG might be a useful treatment option in PD patients with severe motor fluctuations.

data.title: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel for treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Levodopa is the mainstay of Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment, but is often eventually associated with disabling motor complications in patients with advanced PD. The inability of perorally administered levodopa to provide more physiologic continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) is a leading hypothesis to explain these complications.
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the cumulative efficacy and safety, and re-evaluate the role, of levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion in treatment of advanced PD patients experiencing levodopa-associated motor complications, through its purported mechanism for providing CDS.
METHODS
Literature searches in the MEDLINE/PubMed database were used to identify peer-reviewed publications examining the role of CDS in levodopa-associated motor complications and pharmacologic strategies for CDS, focusing on LCIG infusion for advanced PD patients.
RESULTS
LCIG, an aqueous gel, is continuously infused (daytime only or 24 h) via a portable pump and tube permanently inserted into the duodenum through percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). LCIG infusion provides stable levodopa plasma levels, which are significantly less variable than those with oral levodopa. Clinical trials indicate LCIG may significantly improve motor complications (reduction of time in 'off' and time in 'on with dyskinesias'), motor scores using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), non-motor symptomatology (Non-motor Symptom Scale) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in advanced PD patients. The adverse-event profile of LCIG is similar to that of oral levodopa, although technical problems with the infusion device have occurred in up to 70% of patients.
CONCLUSION
LCIG has demonstrated efficacy in reducing levodopa-associated motor complications in patients with advanced PD, and improving UPDRS and HRQOL scores. Because it involves PEG and its associated risks, LCIG is recommended for patients in whom motor fluctuations and dyskinesias are inadequately treated with traditional peroral medication. For these patients, LCIG can be a valuable alternative to deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when DBS is contraindicated. These conclusions are limited by the modest number and size of completed randomized, controlled trials of LCIG.

data.title: How Does Deep Brain Stimulation Change the Course of Parkinson's Disease?
data.abstract: A robust body of evidence from randomized controlled trials has established the efficacy of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in reducing off time and dyskinesias in levodopa-treated patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). These effects go along with improvements in on period motor function, activities of daily living, and quality of life. In addition, subthalamic DBS is effective in controlling drug-refractory PD tremor. Here, we review the available data from long-term observational and controlled follow-up studies in DBS-treated patients to re-examine the persistence of motor and quality of life benefits and evaluate the effects on disease progression, major disability milestones, and survival. Although there is consistent evidence from observational follow-up studies in DBS-treated patients over 5-10 years and beyond showing sustained improvement of motor control, the long-term impact of DBS on overall progression of disability in PD is less clear. Whether DBS reduces or delays the development of later motor and non-motor disability milestones in comparison to best medical management strategies is difficult to answer by uncontrolled observational follow-up, but there are signals from controlled long-term observational studies suggesting that subthalamic DBS may delay some of the late-stage disability milestones including psychosis, falls, and institutionalization, and also slightly prolongs survival compared with matched medically managed patients. These observations could be attributable to the sustained improvements in motor function and reduction in medication-induced side effects, whereas there is no clinical evidence of direct effects of DBS on the underlying disease progression. © 2022 The Authors. data.title: Deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
data.abstract: Until recent years there has been no evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the efficacy of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD). This review and meta-analysis of RCTs describes the efficacy of DBS in improving motor signs, functionality and quality of life of PD patients. Several electronic databases were consulted up to April 2013. RCTs that compared DBS plus medication versus medication (alone or plus sham DBS) in PD patients were included. Outcome measures were motor function, waking time on good functioning without troublesome dyskinesias, levodopa-equivalent dose reduction, medication-induced complications, activities of daily living, health-related quality of life, and neurocognitive and psychiatric effects. Six RCTs (n = 1,184) that compared DBS plus medication versus medication alone were included. The results show that DBS significantly improves patients' symptoms, functionality and quality of life. Effects sizes are intense for the reduction of motor signs and improvement of functionality in the off-medication phase, in addition to the reduction of the required medication dose and its associated complications. Moderate effects were observed in the case of motor signs and time in good functionality in the on-medication phase, in addition to the quality of life. Although the number of RCTs obtained is small, the total sample size is relatively large, confirming the efficacy of DBS in the control of motor signs and improvement of patients' functionality and quality of life. More controlled research is required on the neurocognitive and psychiatric effects of DBS.

data.title: Drug-Induced Dyskinesia, Part 1: Treatment of Levodopa-Induced Dyskinesia.
data.abstract: Dyskinesias encompass a variety of different hyperkinetic phenomenologies, particularly chorea, dystonia, stereotypies, and akathisia. Levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) is one of the main types of drug-induced dyskinesia, occurring in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) who have been treated with levodopa for long time, but this side effect may be encountered even within a few weeks or months after initiation of levodopa therapy. Based on the temporal pattern in relationship to levodopa dosing, LIDs are divided into "peak-dose dyskinesia," "diphasic dyskinesia," and "wearing off" or "off-period" dyskinesia, of which peak-dose dyskinesia is the most common, followed by off-period, and then diphasic dyskinesia. Treatment strategy includes identifying the kind of dyskinesia and tailoring treatment accordingly. Peak-dose dyskinesia is treated mainly by reducing individual doses of levodopa and adding amantadine and dopamine agonists, whereas off-period dystonia often responds to baclofen and botulinum toxin injections. Diphasic dyskinesias, occurring particularly in patients with young-onset PD, are the most difficult to treat. While fractionation of levodopa dosage is the most frequently utilized strategy, many patients require deep brain stimulation to control their troublesome motor fluctuations and LIDs. A variety of emerging (experimental) drugs currently in development promise to provide better control of LIDs and other levodopa-related complications in the near future.
