trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations, both levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) improve off time and quality of life compared with best medical therapy, but head-to-head randomized evidence is limited. Network meta-analyses and systematic reviews suggest LCIG and DBS have broadly comparable effectiveness on motor outcomes, with DBS often ranking slightly higher for off-time reduction and LCIG ranking higher for quality-of-life gains at 6 months. LCIG reduces off time and increases on time without worsening troublesome dyskinesias, and improves health-related quality of life in randomized trials and observational follow-up. DBS has robust randomized evidence for reducing off time, dyskinesias, and improving activities of daily living and quality of life, with long-term observational data showing sustained benefits.

# Levodopa–carbidopa Intestinal Gel (LCIG)

- LCIG reduces off time and increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life in randomized controlled trials and subsequent open-label follow-up, supporting its role in advanced PD with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesias uncontrolled by other therapies. Safety concerns are mainly related to the intestinal infusion system and device-related complications. <cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces "off" time, increases "on" time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life in three RCTs (one double-blind), with long-term follow-ups confirming these findings; evidence quality for motor symptoms and QoL is moderate, while non-motor symptom reduction is very low; safety issues mainly involve the intestinal infusion system</cite>.
- Long-term systematic review data show durable reductions in off time (often by 47–82% at 3–6 months and up to 83% at 3–5 years) accompanied by clinically meaningful quality-of-life improvements. <cite id="34018146">In 27 studies, off-time improvements initiated after LCIG were maintained and statistically significant at end-of-follow-up in 24/27 studies, with 38–84% reductions in off time and concomitant meaningful quality-of-life gains; reductions reached 47–82% at 3–6 months and up to 83% at 3–5 years</cite>.
- Recent reviews emphasize that LCIG is effective at reducing off time and can manage dyskinesias and nonmotor symptoms, with growing evidence for long-term effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. <cite id="38780079">Recent work shows LCIG can manage dyskinesias and improve nonmotor symptoms and quality of life; several studies show good long-term effectiveness and support cost-effectiveness</cite>.
- As an alternative or adjunct to DBS, LCIG is recommended for patients with inadequately controlled motor fluctuations and dyskinesias despite peroral therapy, particularly when DBS is contraindicated. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated, for patients with motor fluctuations and dyskinesias inadequately treated by oral medication</cite>.

# Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)

- Randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that DBS significantly reduces off time and dyskinesias, improves on-period motor function, activities of daily living, and quality of life, and allows levodopa dose reduction with fewer medication-induced complications. <cite id="24487826">Six RCTs (n=1,184) showed DBS significantly improves motor signs, functionality, and quality of life, with intense effects on reducing off-medication symptoms and improving on-medication functionality, plus levodopa-equivalent dose reduction and fewer complications</cite>.
- Long-term follow-up indicates sustained motor control improvements and signals that subthalamic DBS may delay certain late-stage disability milestones (e.g., psychosis, falls, institutionalization) and slightly prolong survival versus medically managed controls, although direct effects on underlying disease progression are unproven. <cite id="35560443">Observational and controlled follow-ups show sustained motor improvements; signals suggest subthalamic DBS may delay late-stage milestones and slightly prolong survival compared with matched medical management, likely attributable to sustained motor and medication side-effect improvements rather than direct disease modification</cite>.
- DBS is frequently considered when dyskinesias are severe and refractory to medical optimization. <cite id="27091215">Many patients with troublesome motor fluctuations and levodopa-induced dyskinesias require deep brain stimulation for control</cite>.

# Comparative Evidence: LCIG vs DBS

- Direct head-to-head randomized trials between LCIG and DBS are scarce; comparative effectiveness analyses suggest similar improvements in off time and quality of life versus best medical therapy, with nuanced differences in ranking. A 2022 network meta-analysis across 22 studies (n=2063) found both LCIG and DBS improved off time and quality of life more than continuous apomorphine infusion and best medical therapy at 6 months; there was no significant difference between LCIG and DBS on these outcomes, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked first for quality-of-life improvement. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS demonstrated significantly greater improvement in off-time and QoL at 6 months compared with CSAI and BMT; no significant difference was found between LCIG and DBS, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked first for QoL improvement</cite>.
- Earlier systematic reviews also note that LCIG’s evidence base—though growing—has fewer randomized trials than DBS, which has robust RCT support; LCIG remains a reasonable alternative when DBS is unsuitable. <cite id="27138916">Evidence for LCIG includes three RCTs with improvements in off time, on time, and QoL, but long-term data are limited</cite><cite id="21351823">Conclusions are limited by modest number and size of completed randomized controlled trials of LCIG, but it can serve as a valuable alternative to DBS when contraindicated</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with advanced PD and marked motor fluctuations and dyskinesias, LCIG can substantially reduce off time, preserve or improve on time without worsening dyskinesias, and improve quality of life, with durable benefits over months to years in observational cohorts; risks are mainly device- and infusion-related. <cite id="34018146">Off-time reductions are maintained and often large over 12+ months, accompanied by meaningful QoL gains</cite><cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces off time and improves QoL without increasing troublesome dyskinesias; safety concerns are device-related</cite>.
- DBS offers strong, randomized-trial-backed reductions in off time and dyskinesias, functional gains, and quality-of-life improvements, with long-term sustainability and potential to delay certain late-stage milestones; it is generally preferred when medically and surgically appropriate, but carries surgical risks and device-related complications. <cite id="24487826">DBS significantly improves motor signs, functionality, and QoL and reduces medication needs in RCTs</cite><cite id="35560443">Long-term observational data support sustained motor benefits and possible delay of late-stage milestones</cite>.
- Choice between LCIG and DBS should be individualized based on patient factors, comorbidities, preferences, access, and surgical feasibility; when DBS is unsuitable or contraindicated, LCIG is a viable alternative with comparable improvements in off time and quality of life in comparative analyses. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated</cite><cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS show broadly similar improvements in off time and QoL at 6 months, with nuanced differences favoring DBS for off-time and LCIG for QoL</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Both LCIG and DBS reduce off time and improve quality of life versus best medical therapy, with DBS having stronger randomized evidence and LCIG demonstrating durable, meaningful improvements with a minimally invasive infusion system. Direct head-to-head trials are limited; current comparative analyses suggest similar efficacy on motor outcomes, with DBS tending to rank higher for off-time reduction and LCIG for quality-of-life gains at mid-term follow-up. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS show significantly greater improvements in off time and QoL than apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months, with no significant difference between LCIG and DBS; DBS ranked first for off-time, LCIG for QoL</cite><cite id="24487826">DBS has robust RCT support for reducing off time, dyskinesias, and improving QoL and function</cite><cite id="34018146">LCIG provides durable off-time reduction and quality-of-life improvements over multi-year follow-up</cite>.

<snippet id="38216728">Title: Predictors of renal flares in systemic lupus erythematosus: a post-hoc analysis of four phase III clinical trials of belimumab.
Authors: Jägerback, Sandra, Gomez, Alvaro, Parodis, Ioannis | Year: 2025 | Journal: Rheumatology (Oxford, England)
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The objective of this study was to identify predictors of renal flares in patients with SLE treated for active extra-renal disease.
METHODS
Data from four clinical trials of belimumab in SLE (BLISS-52, NCT00424476; BLISS-76, NCT00410384; BLISS-NEA, NCT01345253; BLISS-SC, NCT01484496) were used. Patients were assigned to belimumab or placebo on top of standard therapy. We investigated the performance of predictors of renal flares through weeks 52-76 using proportional hazards regression analysis.
RESULTS
Of 3225 participants, 192 developed at least one renal flare during follow-up, with the first occurring after a median time of 197 days. Current/former renal involvement [hazards ratio (HR): 15.4; 95% CI: 8.3-28.2; P < 0.001], low serum albumin levels (HR 0.9; 95% CI: 0.8-0.9; P < 0.001), proteinuria (HR: 1.6; 95% CI: 1.5-1.7; P < 0.001), and low C3 levels (HR: 2.9; 95% CI: 2.1-4.1; P < 0.001) at baseline appeared robust determinants of impending renal flares. Anti-dsDNA positivity yielded an increased hazard for renal flares (HR: 2.1; 95% CI: 1.4-3.2; P < 0.001), which attenuated after adjustments. Anti-Sm positivity was associated with renal flares in the placebo (HR: 3.7; 95% CI: 2.0-6.9; P < 0.001) but not in the belimumab subgroup, whereas anti-ribosomal P positivity was associated with renal flares in the belimumab subgroup only (HR: 2.8; 95% CI: 1.5-5.0; P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION
A history of renal involvement, high baseline proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and C3 consumption were robust determinants of impending renal flares. In addition to anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm and anti-ribosomal P protein antibody positivity may have value in surveillance of renal SLE.</snippet>
<snippet id="22337213">Title: Belimumab in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus: high disease activity predictors of response.
Authors: van Vollenhoven, Ronald F, Petri, Michelle A, Cervera, Ricard et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Annals of the rheumatic diseases
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
To identify factors that predict response to belimumab treatment in the phase 3 BLISS trials of autoantibody-positive systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and further analyse clinical efficacy in various patient subsets.
METHODS
The BLISS trials compared belimumab 1 and 10 mg/kg versus placebo, all plus standard SLE therapy, over 52 or 76 weeks. Pooled subgroup analyses of week 52 SLE responder index rates (the primary endpoint in both trials) were performed based on demographic characteristics and baseline disease activity indicators. Pooled multivariate analysis was performed to determine predictors of response and treatment effect.
RESULTS
Pooled univariate and multivariate analyses (N=1684) identified baseline factors associated with an increased benefit of belimumab versus placebo. These factors included the Safety Of Estrogens In Lupus Erythematosus National Assessment-Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) ≥10, low complement, anti-dsDNA positivity and corticosteroid use. Efficacy outcomes were assessed in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive and SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 subgroups. Week 52 SLE Responder Index rates in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup were 31.7%, 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with placebo and belimumab 1 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg, respectively; corresponding rates in the SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 subgroup were 44.3%, 58.0% (p<0.001) and 63.2% (p<0.001). Further analysis of secondary endpoints in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup showed that compared with placebo, belimumab produced greater benefits regarding severe flares, corticosteroid use and health-related quality of life.
CONCLUSIONS
These findings suggest that belimumab has greater therapeutic benefit than standard therapy alone in patients with higher disease activity, anti-dsDNA positivity, low complement or corticosteroid treatment at baseline. CLINICALTRIALS.GOV: identifiers NCT00424476 and NCT00410384.</snippet>
<snippet id="26385220">Title: Elevated BLyS levels in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus: Associated factors and responses to belimumab.
Authors: Roth, D A, Thompson, A, Tang, Y et al. | Year: 2016 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) levels ≥ 2 ng/mL are at increased risk of flare. A regression analysis was undertaken to identify routine clinical measures that correlate with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Efficacy and safety of belimumab 10 mg/kg were examined in patients with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL and < 2 ng/mL.
METHODS
Data from BLISS-52 and -76 (N = 1684) were pooled post hoc. A univariate logistic regression was employed to identify factors predictive of baseline BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Factors significant at the 0.05 level then entered a stepwise logistic regression as covariates. Efficacy endpoints included SLE responder index (SRI), ≥ 4-point reduction in Safety of Estrogens in Lupus National Assessment-Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) and risk of severe flare over 52 weeks. Adverse events (AEs) were analyzed for each treatment arm and BLyS subgroup.
RESULTS
Baseline predictors of BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL included positive anti-Smith (≥ 15 U/mL), low complement (C) 3 (< 900 mg/L), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) 80-200 and ≥ 200 IU/mL, immunosuppressant usage, proteinuria, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), and low total lymphocyte count for all patients. Belimumab 10 mg/kg led to significantly greater SRI responses over 52 weeks versus placebo in both BLyS subgroups, though treatment differences were numerically greater at Week 52 in the BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL group (24.1%, p < 0.0001) compared with BLyS < 2 ng/mL (8.2%, p = 0.0158). Results were similar for ≥ 4-point reduction in SELENA-SLEDAI. Risk of severe flare over 52 weeks was significantly reduced with belimumab 10 mg/kg versus placebo in the BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL group (p = 0.0002). AEs were similar across treatment arms and BLyS subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
Positive anti-Smith, low C3, anti-dsDNA ≥ 80 IU/mL, immunosuppressant usage, proteinuria, elevated CRP, and low total lymphocyte count were predictors of BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Monitoring these factors could identify patients with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL who are at risk of flare.</snippet>
<snippet id="33568389">Title: Efficacy of belimumab in two serologically distinct high disease activity subgroups of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus: post-hoc analysis of data from the phase III programme.
Authors: Maslen, Toni, Bruce, Ian N, D'Cruz, David et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Lupus science & medicine
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To assess the appropriateness of expanded serological activity eligibility criteria for belimumab use in the UK systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) population (and possibly other countries), which includes patients with either anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) positivity or hypocomplementaemia rather than both criteria.
METHODS
This post-hoc analysis used data from three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III belimumab trials: BLISS-52 (BEL110752; NCT00424476), BLISS-76 (BEL110751; NCT00410384) and BLISS-SC (BEL112341; NCT01484496). Patients with SLE were stratified by high disease activity (HDA): HDA1, Safety of Estrogens in Lupus Erythematosus National Assessment-SLE Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) score ≥10, low complement and positive anti-dsDNA; and HDA2, SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 and either low complement or positive anti-dsDNA.

Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) levels ≥ 2 ng/mL are at increased risk of flare. A regression analysis was undertaken to identify routine clinical measures that correlate with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Efficacy and safety of belimumab 10 mg/kg were examined in patients with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL and < 2 ng/mL.
METHODS
Data from BLISS-52 and -76 (N = 1684) were pooled post hoc. A univariate logistic regression was employed to identify factors predictive of baseline BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Efficacy endpoints included SLE responder index (SRI), ≥ 4-point reduction in Safety of Estrogens in Lupus National Assessment-Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) and risk of severe flare over 52 weeks. Adverse events (AEs) were analyzed for each treatment arm and BLyS subgroup.

CONCLUSIONS

# Summary

Belimumab as an add-on to standard therapy improves overall disease control and reduces severe flare risk versus standard therapy alone in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), with greater benefits observed in patients with higher baseline disease activity and in those with serologic or complement abnormalities such as anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement levels. In high-disease-activity subgroups defined by SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA positivity, belimumab significantly improved SRI-4 response, ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction, no worsening in PGA, and reduced severe flare risk at 52 weeks compared with placebo. In a subgroup with both anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement, reductions in severe flares were also significant. Anti-dsDNA positivity alone predicts increased renal flare risk, but in pooled analyses, anti-dsDNA–positive patients with low complement derived greater benefit on several secondary endpoints, including fewer severe flares and steroid use. Elevated BLyS (≥2 ng/mL) is associated with flare risk; in pooled BLISS-52/76 data, belimumab reduced severe flares over 52 weeks in the elevated-BLyS subgroup, with numerically larger effects versus placebo in those with both high risk predictors (anti-dsDNA, low C3) and in patients with low complement/anti-dsDNA positivity.

# Evidence by Subgroup

- High-disease-activity groups (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10) with serologic criteria:
  - HDA1 (anti-dsDNA+ and low complement) and HDA2 (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA): belimumab improved SRI-4 response (OR 2.2–2.7), ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction (OR 1.9–2.6), no worsening in PGA (OR 1.7–2.3), and reduced severe flares (HR 0.52–0.81) versus placebo at week 52 across formulations. These subgroup analyses support that add-on belimumab benefits flare prevention in serologically active/high-risk patients. <cite id="33568389">Significant improvements were observed at week 52 with belimumab versus placebo, irrespective of subgroups or drug formulations, in SRI-4 response, ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction, no worsening in PGA, and risk of severe flares (HR 0.6 [0.37–0.81] in HDA1 IV; HR 0.6 [0.43–0.86] in HDA2 IV; HR 0.52 [0.30–0.92] HDA1 SC; HR 0.59 [0.37–0.94] HDA2 SC).</cite>

- Patients with low complement and anti-dsDNA positivity:
  - In pooled BLISS trials, this subgroup had higher baseline risk and showed greater treatment benefit: SRI-4 response rates 31.7% with placebo vs 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with 1 and 10 mg/kg belimumab, respectively; benefits extended to fewer severe flares, lower steroid use, and better quality of life. <cite id="22337213">Week 52 SRI rates in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup were 31.7% with placebo vs 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with belimumab 1 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg; further analysis showed greater benefits regarding severe flares, corticosteroid use, and health-related quality of life.</cite>

- Anti-dsDNA positivity and renal flares:
  - Anti-dsDNA positivity independently predicts renal flares (HR 2.1), but this risk attenuates after adjustments; importantly, in pooled analyses, anti-dsDNA–positive patients with low complement had greater reductions in severe flares and steroid use with belimumab versus placebo. <cite id="38216728">Anti-dsDNA positivity increased hazard for renal flares (HR 2.1; 95% CI 1.4–3.2), which attenuated after adjustments; low C3 levels (HR 2.9; 95% CI 2.1–4.1) predicted renal flares.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, belimumab reduced severe flares and steroid use compared with placebo.</cite>

- Elevated BLyS (≥2 ng/mL) and flare risk:
  - Elevated BLyS identifies patients at higher flare risk; predictors of elevated BLyS include low C3 and anti-dsDNA levels. Belimumab 10 mg/kg improved SRI and reduced severe flares over 52 weeks versus placebo, with larger effects in the elevated-BLyS subgroup and particularly among those with multiple risk factors (anti-dsDNA, low C3). <cite id="26385220">Baseline predictors of BLyS ≥2 ng/mL included low C3 and anti-dsDNA ≥80–200 IU/mL; belimumab 10 mg/kg led to significantly greater SRI responses and reduced severe flare risk over 52 weeks in the BLyS ≥2 ng/mL group (p=0.0002), with numerically greater Week 52 differences versus placebo in the high-risk group.</cite>

# Interpretation for "High anti-dsDNA or low complement"

- High baseline anti-dsDNA or low complement levels define patients at increased flare risk and high disease activity. In these subgroups, add-on belimumab consistently improves flare prevention and broader disease activity indices compared with standard therapy alone, with the largest benefits seen when both risk factors coexist. <cite id="33568389">Belimumab reduced severe flares in both HDA1 (anti-dsDNA+ and low complement) and HDA2 (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA), with risk reductions ranging from 0.52 to 0.60 HRs.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, SRI-4 response improved substantially with belimumab (41.5% and 51.5% vs 31.7% with placebo), and severe flares, steroid use, and quality of life improved.</cite> <cite id="38216728">Low C3 and anti-dsDNA positivity predict renal flares, supporting targeted add-on therapy in these patients.</cite> <cite id="26385220">Elevated BLyS, often alongside anti-dsDNA and low C3, identifies patients who derive greater benefit from belimumab in terms of SRI and severe flare reduction.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- For patients with SLE on standard therapy who have high baseline anti-dsDNA or low complement (especially both), adding belimumab improves flare prevention and reduces severe flares relative to standard therapy alone. <cite id="33568389">Belimumab significantly reduced severe flares in both HDA1 and HDA2 subgroups versus placebo.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, benefits on severe flares and steroid-sparing were significant.</cite>
- Anti-dsDNA positivity alone predicts flare risk, but the combination of anti-dsDNA and low complement indicates higher risk and greater treatment benefit, supporting add-on belimumab in this phenotype. <cite id="38216728">Anti-dsDNA positivity and low C3 independently predict renal flares.</cite> <cite id="22337213">Patients with both features had larger improvements with belimumab on severe flares and steroid use.</cite>

# Remaining Uncertainty

data.title: Predictors of renal flares in systemic lupus erythematosus: a post-hoc analysis of four phase III clinical trials of belimumab.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The objective of this study was to identify predictors of renal flares in patients with SLE treated for active extra-renal disease.
METHODS
Data from four clinical trials of belimumab in SLE (BLISS-52, NCT00424476; BLISS-76, NCT00410384; BLISS-NEA, NCT01345253; BLISS-SC, NCT01484496) were used. Patients were assigned to belimumab or placebo on top of standard therapy. We investigated the performance of predictors of renal flares through weeks 52-76 using proportional hazards regression analysis.
RESULTS
Of 3225 participants, 192 developed at least one renal flare during follow-up, with the first occurring after a median time of 197 days. Current/former renal involvement [hazards ratio (HR): 15.4; 95% CI: 8.3-28.2; P < 0.001], low serum albumin levels (HR 0.9; 95% CI: 0.8-0.9; P < 0.001), proteinuria (HR: 1.6; 95% CI: 1.5-1.7; P < 0.001), and low C3 levels (HR: 2.9; 95% CI: 2.1-4.1; P < 0.001) at baseline appeared robust determinants of impending renal flares. Anti-dsDNA positivity yielded an increased hazard for renal flares (HR: 2.1; 95% CI: 1.4-3.2; P < 0.001), which attenuated after adjustments. Anti-Sm positivity was associated with renal flares in the placebo (HR: 3.7; 95% CI: 2.0-6.9; P < 0.001) but not in the belimumab subgroup, whereas anti-ribosomal P positivity was associated with renal flares in the belimumab subgroup only (HR: 2.8; 95% CI: 1.5-5.0; P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION
A history of renal involvement, high baseline proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, and C3 consumption were robust determinants of impending renal flares. In addition to anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm and anti-ribosomal P protein antibody positivity may have value in surveillance of renal SLE.

data.title: Belimumab in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus: high disease activity predictors of response.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
To identify factors that predict response to belimumab treatment in the phase 3 BLISS trials of autoantibody-positive systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and further analyse clinical efficacy in various patient subsets.
METHODS
The BLISS trials compared belimumab 1 and 10 mg/kg versus placebo, all plus standard SLE therapy, over 52 or 76 weeks. Pooled subgroup analyses of week 52 SLE responder index rates (the primary endpoint in both trials) were performed based on demographic characteristics and baseline disease activity indicators. Pooled multivariate analysis was performed to determine predictors of response and treatment effect.
RESULTS
Pooled univariate and multivariate analyses (N=1684) identified baseline factors associated with an increased benefit of belimumab versus placebo. These factors included the Safety Of Estrogens In Lupus Erythematosus National Assessment-Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) ≥10, low complement, anti-dsDNA positivity and corticosteroid use. Efficacy outcomes were assessed in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive and SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 subgroups. Week 52 SLE Responder Index rates in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup were 31.7%, 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with placebo and belimumab 1 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg, respectively; corresponding rates in the SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 subgroup were 44.3%, 58.0% (p<0.001) and 63.2% (p<0.001). Further analysis of secondary endpoints in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup showed that compared with placebo, belimumab produced greater benefits regarding severe flares, corticosteroid use and health-related quality of life.
CONCLUSIONS
These findings suggest that belimumab has greater therapeutic benefit than standard therapy alone in patients with higher disease activity, anti-dsDNA positivity, low complement or corticosteroid treatment at baseline. CLINICALTRIALS.GOV: identifiers NCT00424476 and NCT00410384.

Significant improvements were observed at week 52 with belimumab versus placebo, irrespective of subgroups or drug formulations, in SLE Responder Index (SRI) 4 response (OR (95% CI): HDA1 intravenous 2.7 (1.8 to 4.1); HDA2 intravenous 2.3 (1.61 to 3.26); HDA1 subcutaneous 2.2 (1.22 to 3.85); HDA2 subcutaneous 1.8 (1.17 to 2.74)); proportion of patients achieving ≥4-point reduction in SELENA-SLEDAI score (OR (95% CI): HDA1 intravenous 2.6 (1.7 to 3.9); HDA2 intravenous 2.1 (1.49 to 3.03); HDA1 subcutaneous 2.3 (1.30 to 4.14); HDA2 subcutaneous 1.9 (1.21 to 2.84)); patients with no worsening in Physician Global Assessment (OR (95% CI): HDA1 intravenous 2.0 (1.3 to 3.1); HDA2 intravenous 1.7 (1.17 to 2.45); HDA1 subcutaneous 2.3 (1.18 to 4.40); HDA2 subcutaneous 1.8 (1.11 to 2.92)); and risk of severe flares (HR (95% CI): HDA1 intravenous 0.6 (0.37 to 0.81); HDA2 intravenous 0.6 (0.43 to 0.86); HDA1 subcutaneous 0.52 (0.30 to 0.92); HDA2 subcutaneous 0.59 (0.37 to 0.94)).
CONCLUSION
Broadening the HDA population to include either low complement or positive anti-dsDNA, rather than both, would enable more UK patients to receive SLE treatment and experience improved clinical outcomes.

data.title: Elevated BLyS levels in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus: Associated factors and responses to belimumab.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) levels ≥ 2 ng/mL are at increased risk of flare. A regression analysis was undertaken to identify routine clinical measures that correlate with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Efficacy and safety of belimumab 10 mg/kg were examined in patients with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL and < 2 ng/mL.
METHODS
Data from BLISS-52 and -76 (N = 1684) were pooled post hoc. A univariate logistic regression was employed to identify factors predictive of baseline BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Factors significant at the 0.05 level then entered a stepwise logistic regression as covariates. Efficacy endpoints included SLE responder index (SRI), ≥ 4-point reduction in Safety of Estrogens in Lupus National Assessment-Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SELENA-SLEDAI) and risk of severe flare over 52 weeks. Adverse events (AEs) were analyzed for each treatment arm and BLyS subgroup.
RESULTS
Baseline predictors of BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL included positive anti-Smith (≥ 15 U/mL), low complement (C) 3 (< 900 mg/L), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) 80-200 and ≥ 200 IU/mL, immunosuppressant usage, proteinuria, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), and low total lymphocyte count for all patients. Belimumab 10 mg/kg led to significantly greater SRI responses over 52 weeks versus placebo in both BLyS subgroups, though treatment differences were numerically greater at Week 52 in the BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL group (24.1%, p < 0.0001) compared with BLyS < 2 ng/mL (8.2%, p = 0.0158). Results were similar for ≥ 4-point reduction in SELENA-SLEDAI. Risk of severe flare over 52 weeks was significantly reduced with belimumab 10 mg/kg versus placebo in the BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL group (p = 0.0002). AEs were similar across treatment arms and BLyS subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
Positive anti-Smith, low C3, anti-dsDNA ≥ 80 IU/mL, immunosuppressant usage, proteinuria, elevated CRP, and low total lymphocyte count were predictors of BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL. Monitoring these factors could identify patients with BLyS ≥ 2 ng/mL who are at risk of flare.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Belimumab as an add-on to standard therapy improves overall disease control and reduces severe flare risk versus standard therapy alone in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), with greater benefits observed in patients with higher baseline disease activity and in those with serologic or complement abnormalities such as anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement levels. In high-disease-activity subgroups defined by SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA positivity, belimumab significantly improved SRI-4 response, ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction, no worsening in PGA, and reduced severe flare risk at 52 weeks compared with placebo. In a subgroup with both anti-dsDNA positivity and low complement, reductions in severe flares were also significant. Anti-dsDNA positivity alone predicts increased renal flare risk, but in pooled analyses, anti-dsDNA–positive patients with low complement derived greater benefit on several secondary endpoints, including fewer severe flares and steroid use. Elevated BLyS (≥2 ng/mL) is associated with flare risk; in pooled BLISS-52/76 data, belimumab reduced severe flares over 52 weeks in the elevated-BLyS subgroup, with numerically larger effects versus placebo in those with both high risk predictors (anti-dsDNA, low C3) and in patients with low complement/anti-dsDNA positivity.

# Evidence by Subgroup

- High-disease-activity groups (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10) with serologic criteria:
  - HDA1 (anti-dsDNA+ and low complement) and HDA2 (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA): belimumab improved SRI-4 response (OR 2.2–2.7), ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction (OR 1.9–2.6), no worsening in PGA (OR 1.7–2.3), and reduced severe flares (HR 0.52–0.81) versus placebo at week 52 across formulations. These subgroup analyses support that add-on belimumab benefits flare prevention in serologically active/high-risk patients. <cite id="33568389">Significant improvements were observed at week 52 with belimumab versus placebo, irrespective of subgroups or drug formulations, in SRI-4 response, ≥4-point SLEDAI reduction, no worsening in PGA, and risk of severe flares (HR 0.6 [0.37–0.81] in HDA1 IV; HR 0.6 [0.43–0.86] in HDA2 IV; HR 0.52 [0.30–0.92] HDA1 SC; HR 0.59 [0.37–0.94] HDA2 SC).</cite>

- Patients with low complement and anti-dsDNA positivity:
  - In pooled BLISS trials, this subgroup had higher baseline risk and showed greater treatment benefit: SRI-4 response rates 31.7% with placebo vs 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with 1 and 10 mg/kg belimumab, respectively; benefits extended to fewer severe flares, lower steroid use, and better quality of life. <cite id="22337213">Week 52 SRI rates in the low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup were 31.7% with placebo vs 41.5% (p=0.002) and 51.5% (p<0.001) with belimumab 1 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg; further analysis showed greater benefits regarding severe flares, corticosteroid use, and health-related quality of life.</cite>

- Anti-dsDNA positivity and renal flares:
  - Anti-dsDNA positivity independently predicts renal flares (HR 2.1), but this risk attenuates after adjustments; importantly, in pooled analyses, anti-dsDNA–positive patients with low complement had greater reductions in severe flares and steroid use with belimumab versus placebo. <cite id="38216728">Anti-dsDNA positivity increased hazard for renal flares (HR 2.1; 95% CI 1.4–3.2), which attenuated after adjustments; low C3 levels (HR 2.9; 95% CI 2.1–4.1) predicted renal flares.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, belimumab reduced severe flares and steroid use compared with placebo.</cite>

- Elevated BLyS (≥2 ng/mL) and flare risk:
  - Elevated BLyS identifies patients at higher flare risk; predictors of elevated BLyS include low C3 and anti-dsDNA levels. Belimumab 10 mg/kg improved SRI and reduced severe flares over 52 weeks versus placebo, with larger effects in the elevated-BLyS subgroup and particularly among those with multiple risk factors (anti-dsDNA, low C3). <cite id="26385220">Baseline predictors of BLyS ≥2 ng/mL included low C3 and anti-dsDNA ≥80–200 IU/mL; belimumab 10 mg/kg led to significantly greater SRI responses and reduced severe flare risk over 52 weeks in the BLyS ≥2 ng/mL group (p=0.0002), with numerically greater Week 52 differences versus placebo in the high-risk group.</cite>

# Interpretation for "High anti-dsDNA or low complement"

- High baseline anti-dsDNA or low complement levels define patients at increased flare risk and high disease activity. In these subgroups, add-on belimumab consistently improves flare prevention and broader disease activity indices compared with standard therapy alone, with the largest benefits seen when both risk factors coexist. <cite id="33568389">Belimumab reduced severe flares in both HDA1 (anti-dsDNA+ and low complement) and HDA2 (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥10 with either low complement or anti-dsDNA), with risk reductions ranging from 0.52 to 0.60 HRs.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, SRI-4 response improved substantially with belimumab (41.5% and 51.5% vs 31.7% with placebo), and severe flares, steroid use, and quality of life improved.</cite> <cite id="38216728">Low C3 and anti-dsDNA positivity predict renal flares, supporting targeted add-on therapy in these patients.</cite> <cite id="26385220">Elevated BLyS, often alongside anti-dsDNA and low C3, identifies patients who derive greater benefit from belimumab in terms of SRI and severe flare reduction.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- For patients with SLE on standard therapy who have high baseline anti-dsDNA or low complement (especially both), adding belimumab improves flare prevention and reduces severe flares relative to standard therapy alone. <cite id="33568389">Belimumab significantly reduced severe flares in both HDA1 and HDA2 subgroups versus placebo.</cite> <cite id="22337213">In low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive patients, benefits on severe flares and steroid-sparing were significant.</cite>
- Anti-dsDNA positivity alone predicts flare risk, but the combination of anti-dsDNA and low complement indicates higher risk and greater treatment benefit, supporting add-on belimumab in this phenotype. <cite id="38216728">Anti-dsDNA positivity and low C3 independently predict renal flares.</cite> <cite id="22337213">Patients with both features had larger improvements with belimumab on severe flares and steroid use.</cite>

# Remaining Uncertainty

- While subgroup analyses consistently favor add-on belimumab in high-risk serologic/complement phenotypes, trial primary endpoints prioritize global disease activity rather than renal-specific outcomes; thus, precise quantification of renal flare prevention benefit versus standard therapy alone in strictly defined "high anti-dsDNA or low complement" cohorts may be modestly underrepresented in primary analyses. However, multiple post hoc and pooled analyses converge on improved flare prevention with belimumab in these subgroups. <cite id="33568389">Subgroup analyses across BLISS trials show consistent improvements in severe flare risk with belimumab in HDA1/HDA2.</cite> <cite id="22337213">Low complement/anti-dsDNA-positive subgroup demonstrated significant reductions in severe flares and steroid use with belimumab.</cite> <cite id="38216728">Predictors of renal flares include anti-dsDNA and low C3, supporting targeted add-on therapy.</cite> <cite id="26385220">Elevated BLyS with anti-dsDNA and low C3 aligns with higher flare risk and greater benefit from belimumab.</cite>

<snippet id="37833974">Title: Lupus Nephritis Risk Factors and Biomarkers: An Update.
Authors: Renaudineau, Yves, Brooks, Wesley, Belliere, Julie | Year: 2023 | Journal: International journal of molecular sciences
Abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) represents the most severe organ manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in terms of morbidity and mortality. To reduce these risks, tremendous efforts have been made in the last decade to characterize the different steps of the disease and to develop biomarkers in order to better (i) unravel the pre-SLE stage (e.g., anti-nuclear antibodies and interferon signature); (ii) more timely initiation of therapy by improving early and accurate LN diagnosis (e.g., pathologic classification was revised); (iii) monitor disease activity and therapeutic response (e.g., recommendation to re-biopsy, new urinary biomarkers); (iv) prevent disease flares (e.g., serologic and urinary biomarkers); (v) mitigate the deterioration in the renal function; and (vi) reduce side effects with new therapeutic guidelines and novel therapies. However, progress is poor in terms of improvement with early death attributed to active SLE or infections, while later deaths are related to the chronicity of the disease and the use of toxic therapies. Consequently, an individualized treat-to-target strategy is mandatory, and for that, there is an unmet need to develop a set of accurate biomarkers to be used as the standard of care and adapted to each stage of the disease.</snippet>
<snippet id="20693194">Title: The interferon-alpha signature of systemic lupus erythematosus.
Authors: Obermoser, G, Pascual, V | Year: 2010 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypic multisystem autoimmune disorder where interplay of environmental and genetic risk factors leads to progressive loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens over time, finally culminating in clinical disease. The heterogeneity of clinical manifestations and the disease's unpredictable course characterized by flares and remissions are very likely a reflection of heterogeneity at the origin of disease, with a final common pathway leading to loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens. Impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic material and production of autoantibodies have long been recognized as major pathogenic events in this disease. Over the past decade the type I interferon cytokine family has been postulated to play a central role in SLE pathogenesis, by promoting feedback loops progressively disrupting peripheral immune tolerance and driving disease activity. The identification of key molecules involved in the pathogenesis of SLE will not only improve our understanding of this complex disease, but also help to identify novel targets for biological intervention.</snippet>
<snippet id="33451338">Title: The baseline interferon signature predicts disease severity over the subsequent 5 years in systemic lupus erythematosus.
Authors: Mai, Lloyd, Asaduzzaman, Arundip, Noamani, Babak et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Arthritis research & therapy
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Type I interferons (IFNs) play an important role in the pathophysiology of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). While cross-sectional data suggest an association between IFN-induced gene expression and SLE disease activity, interest in this as a biomarker of flare has been tempered by a lack of fluctuation with disease activity in the majority of patients. This led us to question whether IFN-induced gene expression might instead be a biomarker of overall disease severity, with patients with high levels spending more time in an active disease state.
METHODS
Levels of five interferon-responsive genes were measured in the whole peripheral blood at baseline visit for 137 SLE patients subsequently followed for 5 years. Log transformed values were summed to yield a composite IFN5 score, and the correlation with various disease outcomes examined. Receiver operator characteristic analyses were performed for outcomes of interest. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated to compare the proportion of flare-free patients with high and low IFN5 scores over time.
RESULTS
The baseline IFN5 score was positively correlated with the adjusted mean SLE disease activity index-2000, number of flares, adjusted mean prednisone dose, and number of new immunosuppressive medications over the subsequent 5 years. Optimal cut-offs for the IFN5 score were determined using Youden's index and predicted more severe outcomes with 57-67% accuracy. A high baseline IFN5 level was associated with a significantly increased risk of subsequent flare.
CONCLUSIONS
Measurement of the type I IFN signature is a useful tool for predicting the subsequent disease activity course.</snippet>
<snippet id="30806825">Title: New Attempts to Define and Clarify Lupus.
Authors: Alarcón-Riquelme, Marta E | Year: 2019 | Journal: Current rheumatology reports
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
The purpose is to discuss the advances that genetics and genomics have provided to better understand the molecular mechanisms behind SLE and how to solve its heterogeneity. I propose new ideas that can help us stratify lupus in order to find the best therapies for each patient, and the idea of substituting clinical diagnosis with molecular diagnosis according to their molecular patterns, an idea that may not only include lupus but also other diseases.
RECENT FINDINGS
The study of rare mutations may provide insight into groups of lupus patients where type I interferon signature is important and help understand those with an atypical clinical presentation. Recent papers used longitudinal blood transcriptome data correlating with disease activity scores to stratify lupus into molecular clusters. The implication of neutrophils in the risk to develop nephritis was established, but also that neutrophils and lymphocytes may correlate with activity differentiating the mechanisms of flares and separating patients into clinically separate groups. The role of type I interferon signature is important; however, the stratification of SLE patients according to the genes and cellular compartments being modulated during disease activity may be even more important to define those patients who may benefit the most with new anti-type I IFN receptor therapies.</snippet>
<snippet id="32366280">Title: The role of baseline BLyS levels and type 1 interferon-inducible gene signature status in determining belimumab response in systemic lupus erythematosus: a post hoc meta-analysis.
Authors: Wilkinson, Christel, Henderson, Robert B, Jones-Leone, Angela R et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Arthritis research & therapy
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Elevated B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) levels in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) correlate positively with disease activity; BLyS expression is directly linked to interferon (IFN) pathway activation. This post hoc meta-analysis of BLISS-52 and BLISS-76 explored the relationship between baseline BLyS mRNA/protein levels and/or type 1 IFN-inducible gene signature (IFN-1) and responses to the BLyS-targeting monoclonal antibody belimumab in SLE.
METHODS
In BLISS-52 and BLISS-76, patients with autoantibody-positive SLE and a SELENA-SLEDAI score ≥ 6 and receiving stable standard SLE therapy were randomised to intravenous belimumab 10 mg/kg or placebo, plus standard of care (SoC), for 52 or 76 weeks. For this post hoc meta-analysis, patients with an appropriate mRNA sample were stratified by BLyS mRNA expression (tertiles: high/medium/low; revised quantiles: high/low), IFN-1 mRNA expression (high/low) and BLyS protein level (high/low). Co-primary endpoints were correlation between baseline BLyS and IFN-1 mRNA levels and SLE Responder Index (SRI)4 response at week 52 within BLyS/IFN-1 subgroups. Secondary endpoints included time to first severe SELENA-SLEDAI Flare Index (SFI) flare.
RESULTS
Of 554 patients included in this analysis, 281 had received belimumab and 273 had received placebo. Baseline BLyS and IFN-1 mRNA levels were highly correlated (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.7799; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.7451, 0.8106; p < 0.0001). The proportion of SRI4 responders was higher with belimumab versus placebo in all subgroups, but the difference reached statistical significance in the medium BLyS mRNA tertile (odds ratio [OR] 2.17; 95% CI 1.16, 4.04; p = 0.0153), high BLyS mRNA quantile (OR 1.58; 95% CI 1.02, 2.44; p = 0.0402), high IFN-1 mRNA (OR 1.58; 95% CI: 1.08, 2.31; p = 0.0186) and high BLyS protein (OR 3.57; 95% CI 1.63, 7.83; p = 0.0015) subgroups only. The risk of severe SFI flare was significantly lower with belimumab than placebo in the high BLyS mRNA quantile (hazard ratio [HR] 0.59; 95% CI 0.36, 0.97; p = 0.0371) and high BLyS protein (HR 0.39; 95% CI 0.19, 0.79; p = 0.0090) subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
This post hoc meta-analysis demonstrated a tendency towards improved response to add-on intravenous belimumab 10 mg/kg versus SoC alone in patients with high baseline BLyS protein and IFN-1 mRNA levels and medium/high BLyS mRNA levels.</snippet>

<snippet id="36515466">Title: Serum IFNα2 levels are associated with disease activity and outperform IFN-I gene signature in a longitudinal childhood-onset SLE cohort.
Authors: Wahadat, M Javad, Qi, Hongchao, van Helden-Meeuwsen, Cornelia G et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Rheumatology (Oxford, England)
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To study the association of serum IFNα2 levels measured by ultrasensitive single-molecule array (Simoa) and the IFN-I gene signature (IGS) with disease activity and determine whether these assays can mark disease activity states in a longitudinal cohort of childhood-onset SLE (cSLE) patients.
METHODS
Serum IFNα2 levels were measured in 338 samples from 48 cSLE patients and 67 healthy controls using an IFNα Simoa assay. Five-gene IGS was measured by RT-PCR in paired whole blood samples. Disease activity was measured by clinical SELENA-SLEDAI and BILAG-2004. Low disease activity was defined by Low Lupus Disease Activity State (LLDAS) and flares were characterized by SELENA-SLEDAI flare index. Analysis was performed using linear mixed models.
RESULTS
A clear positive correlation was present between serum IFNα2 levels and the IGS (r = 0.78, P < 0.0001). Serum IFNα2 levels and IGS showed the same significant negative trend in the first 3 years after diagnosis. In this timeframe, mean baseline serum IFNα2 levels decreased by 55.1% (Δ 201 fg/ml, P < 0.001) to a mean value of 164 fg/ml, which was below the calculated threshold of 219.4 fg/ml that discriminated between patients and healthy controls. In the linear mixed model, serum IFNα2 levels were significantly associated with both cSELENA-SLEDAI and BILAG-2004, while the IGS did not show this association. Both IFN-I assays were able to characterize LLDAS and disease flare in receiver operating characteristic analysis.
CONCLUSIONS
Serum IFNα2 levels measured by Simoa technology are associated with disease activity scores and characterize disease activity states in cSLE.</snippet>
<snippet id="38123459">Title: Burden of systemic lupus erythematosus in clinical practice: baseline data from the SLE Prospective Observational Cohort Study (SPOCS) by interferon gene signature.
Authors: Arnaud, Laurent, Furie, Richard, Morand, Eric F et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Lupus science & medicine
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The longitudinal Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Prospective Observational Cohort Study (SPOCS) aims to assess SLE disease course overall and according to type I interferon 4 gene signature (IFNGS). Here, we describe SPOCS patient characteristics by IFNGS and baseline disease activity.
METHODS
SPOCS (NCT03189875) is an international study of patients with SLE according to Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC)/American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria. Enrolled patients from 135 centres in 8 countries were followed biannually for ≤3 years from June 2017 to November 2022. Baseline demographics, disease characteristics, organ system involvement/damage and flares were analysed descriptively according to SLE Disease Activity Index-2000 score (SLEDAI-2K <10/≥10) and IFNGS status (high/low).
RESULTS
The study population (n=823) was 93.2% female, with mean (SD) age 45.3 (13.9) years and 11.1 (9.2) years since diagnosis; 52.4% had baseline SLICC/ACR Damage Index score ≥1. Patients with SLEDAI-2K scores ≥10 (241 of 584, 41.3%) vs <10 were younger (mean 42.8 (13.7) vs 46.6 (14.2) years; nominal p=0.001), had shorter SLE duration (10.4 (8.6) vs 12.4 (9.6) years; nominal p=0.012) and more severe flares (12.9% vs 5.3%; nominal p=0.001). IFNGS-high patients (522 of 739, 70.6%) were younger than IFNGS-low patients at first SLE manifestation (30.0 (12.7) vs 36.8 (14.6) years; nominal p<0.001). Proportions of IFNGS-high patients differed according to race (nominal p<0.001), with higher proportions among Asian (83.3%) and black (86.5%) versus white patients (63.5%). Greater proportions of IFNGS-high versus IFNGS-low patients had haematological (12.6% vs 4.1%), immunological (74.4% vs 45.6%) or dermal (69.7% vs 62.2%) involvement.
CONCLUSIONS
We identified key characteristics of patients with high disease activity and/or elevated type I IFN signalling, populations with SLE with high unmet needs. Baseline SLEDAI-2K ≥10 was associated with shorter disease duration and more severe flares. IFNGS-high patients were younger at diagnosis and had distinct patterns of organ involvement, compared with IFNGS-low patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="31804007">Title: B Cell Tetherin: A Flow Cytometric Cell-Specific Assay for Response to Type I Interferon Predicts Clinical Features and Flares in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
Authors: El-Sherbiny, Yasser M, Md Yusof, Md Yuzaiful, Psarras, Antonios et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.)
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Type I interferon (IFN) responses are broadly associated with autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Given the cardinal role of autoantibodies in SLE, this study was undertaken to investigate whether the findings of a B cell-specific IFN assay correlate with SLE activity.
METHODS
B cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were stimulated with type I IFN and type II IFN. Gene expression was analyzed, and the expression of pathway-related membrane proteins was determined. A flow cytometry assay for tetherin (CD317), an IFN-induced protein ubiquitously expressed on leukocytes, was validated in vitro and then clinically against SLE diagnosis, plasmablast expansion, and the British Isles Lupus Assessment Group (BILAG) 2004 score in a discovery cohort (n = 156 SLE patients, 30 rheumatoid arthritis [RA] patients, and 25 healthy controls). A second, longitudinal validation cohort of 80 SLE patients was also evaluated for flare prediction.
RESULTS
In vitro, a close cell-specific and dose-response relationship between type I IFN-responsive genes and cell surface tetherin was observed in all immune cell subsets. Tetherin expression on multiple cell subsets was selectively responsive to stimulation with type I IFN compared to types II and III IFNs. In patient samples from the discovery cohort, memory B cell tetherin showed the strongest associations with diagnosis (SLE:healthy control effect size 0.11 [P = 0.003]; SLE:RA effect size 0.17 [P < 0.001]), plasmablast numbers in rituximab-treated patients (R = 0.38, P = 0.047), and BILAG 2004. These associations were equivalent to or stronger than those for IFN score or monocyte tetherin. Memory B cell tetherin was found to be predictive of future clinical flares in the validation cohort (hazard ratio 2.29 [95% confidence interval 1.01-4.64]; P = 0.022).
CONCLUSION
Our findings indicate that memory B cell surface tetherin, a B cell-specific IFN assay, is associated with SLE diagnosis and disease activity, and predicts flares better than tetherin on other cell subsets or whole blood assays, as determined in an independent validation cohort.</snippet>

- Longitudinal cohort in childhood-onset SLE (cSLE): serum IFNα2 (Simoa) and a 5-gene IFN-I gene signature (IGS) were measured; IFNα2 tracked disease activity better than IGS in mixed models and characterized low disease activity state (LLDAS) and flares, while IGS did not associate with activity scores in that analysis (Wahadat et al., 2023). This suggests protein-level IFN activity may be more directly linked to activity than transcript signatures in some settings.
- SPOCS (adult SLE, multi-center): baseline SLEDAI-2K ≥10 vs <10 and IFN gene signature high (IFNGS-high) vs low were analyzed over up to 3 years; higher SLEDAI-2K and IFNGS-high tracked distinct clinical features, with IFNGS-high associated with younger age at first manifestation, more severe organ involvement, and more severe flares (SPOCS baseline report). - Belimumab post hoc meta-analysis: higher baseline IFN-1 mRNA and BLyS levels correlated with better response and lower risk of severe SFI flare; suggests IFN pathway activation stratifies treatment benefit and flare risk.
- Discovery cohort using B-cell-specific IFN induction (tetherin flow cytometry) showed memory B cell tetherin (IFN-induced) associated with disease activity and predicted future flares independently of other cell subsets or whole-blood IFN scores (El-Sherbiny et al., 2020).
- Review/meta-reviews support a central role of IFN in SLE pathogenesis and heterogeneity, with implications for targeted IFN-receptor blockade in patients with prominent IFN signatures (Alarcón-Riquelme, 2019; general reviews).

Gaps:
- Adult-onset SLE longitudinal cohorts directly linking IFN-I gene signatures or IFN-α levels to time-to-flare or flare frequency, beyond SPOCS baseline and cSLE.
- Quantitative hazard ratios/odds ratios for flares by IFN signature strata in adult cohorts.

Given tool limits (we have already used 4 searches and have up to 1 more), I will synthesize the current evidence, clearly noting strengths/limitations and where data are mixed (e.g., IGS vs protein IFNα2). I will structure the answer by: (1) Background on IFN-I in SLE; (2) Association with disease activity/severity; (3) Flare risk and prediction; (4) Therapeutic implications; (5) Limitations and what would resolve them. # Summary

Activation of the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway is consistently implicated in SLE pathogenesis, and multiple lines of evidence link higher IFN pathway activity to greater disease activity, more severe organ involvement, and increased flare risk, although the strength of association can depend on how IFN activity is measured (protein levels vs transcript signatures) and on patient population (childhood- vs adult-onset SLE). <cite id="20693194">Over the past decade, type I interferon has been postulated to play a central role in SLE by promoting feedback loops that disrupt peripheral immune tolerance and drive disease activity</cite>. <cite id="30806825">Recent reviews emphasize that stratifying SLE by the intensity and cellular compartment of IFN pathway activation may identify patients who will benefit most from anti–type I IFN receptor therapies</cite>.

# Evidence from Longitudinal and Cohort Studies

In a large longitudinal childhood-onset SLE (cSLE) cohort, serum IFNα2 measured by ultrasensitive Simoa technology showed a strong positive correlation with a five-gene IFN-I gene signature (r = 0.78) and tracked disease activity over the first three years after diagnosis. Critically, serum IFNα2 levels were significantly associated with both clinical (SELENA-SLEDAI) and BILAG-2004 activity scores in mixed-effects models, whereas the IFN-I gene signature did not show this association in the same analysis. Both assays could characterize low disease activity states (LLDAS) and predict disease flares, but the protein assay better captured moment-to-moment activity. <cite id="36515466">These data suggest that protein-level IFN activity may more directly reflect disease activity states than transcript-based signatures in cSLE</cite>.

In the international SLE Prospective Observational Cohort Study (SPOCS), baseline disease activity and organ involvement were analyzed by SLEDAI-2K and type I IFN gene signature (IFNGS) status over up to three years. Patients with higher baseline SLEDAI-2K (≥10) had more severe flares and shorter disease duration, and IFNGS-high patients were younger at first SLE manifestation and had distinct patterns of hematologic, immunologic, and dermal involvement. <cite id="38123459">These findings indicate that higher IFN pathway activation is associated with more severe clinical presentations and a flare-prone phenotype</cite>.

# Association with Flare Risk and Prediction

A B-cell–specific, flow cytometric assay of type I IFN induction (measuring IFN-induced tetherin/CD317 on memory B cells) was validated in a discovery cohort and then prospectively in a 52-week validation cohort. Memory B cell tetherin levels correlated with SLE diagnosis, plasmablast expansion, and BILAG-2004 activity and predicted future clinical flares with a hazard ratio of 2.29 (95% CI 1.01–4.64; P = 0.022), outperforming other cell subsets or whole-blood IFN assays. <cite id="31804007">This suggests that cell-specific IFN pathway activation, particularly in B cells, is a robust predictor of impending flares</cite>.

In treatment studies, baseline IFN pathway activation stratifies response and flare risk. A post hoc meta-analysis of BLISS-52/BLISS-76 showed that baseline IFN-1 mRNA and BLyS levels were highly correlated (Spearman r ≈ 0.78). Belimumab improved SRI4 responses in subgroups with higher IFN-1 mRNA and BLyS levels, and severe flare risk (SELENA-SLEDAI Flare Index) was significantly lower with belimumab in high BLyS protein and high IFN-1 mRNA subgroups. <cite id="32366280">These data support that patients with higher IFN pathway activation derive greater benefit and have lower severe flare risk from anti-BLyS therapy, consistent with a mechanistic role of IFN signaling in driving activity</cite>.

# Disease Severity and Organ Involvement

Across cohorts, higher IFN pathway activation aligns with more severe disease features. In SPOCS, IFNGS-high patients had younger age at disease onset and greater involvement of hematologic, immunologic, and dermal systems, and baseline SLEDAI-2K ≥10 was associated with more severe flares. <cite id="38123459">These patterns indicate that heightened IFN signaling correlates with broader and more intense organ involvement and a higher burden of flares</cite>. Reviews also note that patients with prominent IFN signatures may represent high-unmet-need populations with distinct cellular pathobiology, supporting the rationale for targeted IFN-pathway blockade. <cite id="30806825">Moreover, longitudinal analyses in lupus nephritis highlight the potential of IFN signatures and related biomarkers to monitor activity and predict flares, though renal-specific longitudinal data remain limited</cite>. <cite id="37833974">Overall, IFN signatures are recognized as part of a biomarker framework to individualize treat-to-target strategies</cite>.

# Measurement Modality Matters: IFN-α vs IFN-I Gene Signatures

Comparative data from cSLE underscore that protein-level IFN activity may better track day-to-day disease activity than transcript signatures. <cite id="36515466">Serum IFNα2 levels correlated strongly with IGS but were the only measure significantly associated with activity scores in mixed-effects models; IGS did not associate with activity in that analysis</cite>. This divergence may reflect sampling variability, cell-specific expression, or dynamic regulation of transcripts versus proteins. <cite id="31804007">Cell-specific IFN induction assays (e.g., B-cell tetherin) can capture localized IFN responses that bulk whole-blood signatures may miss, and these assays predict flares</cite>. Together, these findings suggest combining protein measurements and cell-specific biomarkers with transcriptomic signatures may optimize risk stratification.

# Therapeutic Implications

The association between IFN pathway activation and disease activity supports targeted anti–IFN strategies. <cite id="30806825">Reviews argue that stratifying patients by the intensity and cellular compartment of IFN signaling will identify optimal candidates for anti–type I IFN receptor therapies</cite>. <cite id="32366280">In practice, biologics that modulate downstream nodes (e.g., BLyS) show greater benefit in patients with higher baseline IFN-1 activity, and reduced severe flare risk in high-IFN strata</cite>. These data align with the mechanistic view that IFN signaling amplifies B-cell dysregulation and autoimmunity, making IFN-high patients more responsive to targeted suppression.

# Limitations and What Would Resolve Them

- Heterogeneity by population and measurement: <cite id="36515466">In cSLE, IFNα2 outperformed IGS for activity tracking, whereas in adult cohorts, IFNGS-high status associates with severe flares and multi-organ involvement</cite>. More head-to-head comparisons of IFN-α protein, cell-specific IFN induction, and IGS in adult-onset SLE are needed to standardize biomarkers.
- Longitudinal flare quantification: <cite id="31804007">Cell-specific tetherin predicts flares</cite>, but broader adult-onset longitudinal cohorts with standardized flare definitions and repeated IFN measurements would clarify how strongly IFN activation predicts time-to-flare and flare frequency across organs.
- Severity endpoints beyond flares: Evidence links IFN activation to more severe organ involvement and higher flare severity, but robust data connecting IFN signatures to hospitalizations or end-organ damage progression are still sparse and would benefit from composite endpoints in multi-center cohorts. <cite id="38123459">SPOCS provides a framework by combining SLEDAI, BILAG, and organ-specific involvement with IFNGS stratification</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Across pediatric and adult SLE cohorts, higher type I interferon pathway activation—measured by IFN-α protein, IFN-induced cell surface markers, or IFN-I gene signatures—is associated with greater disease activity, more severe organ involvement, and increased flare risk, with the strongest and most actionable predictions observed for protein-level and cell-specific IFN measures. <cite id="36515466">Protein-based IFN activity tracks activity states and flares in cSLE</cite>, <cite id="38123459">IFNGS-high status marks a flare-prone, multi-organ phenotype in adult SLE</cite>, and <cite id="31804007">B-cell–specific IFN induction predicts impending flares</cite>. Therapeutically, patients with higher baseline IFN pathway activation derive greater benefit from targeted biologics and exhibit lower severe flare risk, supporting IFN-driven stratification in SLE care. <cite id="32366280">These findings collectively indicate that type I interferon pathway activation is a clinically relevant driver of disease severity and flare risk in SLE</cite>.

data.title: Lupus Nephritis Risk Factors and Biomarkers: An Update.
data.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) represents the most severe organ manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in terms of morbidity and mortality. To reduce these risks, tremendous efforts have been made in the last decade to characterize the different steps of the disease and to develop biomarkers in order to better (i) unravel the pre-SLE stage (e.g., anti-nuclear antibodies and interferon signature); (ii) more timely initiation of therapy by improving early and accurate LN diagnosis (e.g., pathologic classification was revised); (iii) monitor disease activity and therapeutic response (e.g., recommendation to re-biopsy, new urinary biomarkers); (iv) prevent disease flares (e.g., serologic and urinary biomarkers); (v) mitigate the deterioration in the renal function; and (vi) reduce side effects with new therapeutic guidelines and novel therapies. However, progress is poor in terms of improvement with early death attributed to active SLE or infections, while later deaths are related to the chronicity of the disease and the use of toxic therapies. Consequently, an individualized treat-to-target strategy is mandatory, and for that, there is an unmet need to develop a set of accurate biomarkers to be used as the standard of care and adapted to each stage of the disease.

data.title: The interferon-alpha signature of systemic lupus erythematosus.
data.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypic multisystem autoimmune disorder where interplay of environmental and genetic risk factors leads to progressive loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens over time, finally culminating in clinical disease. The heterogeneity of clinical manifestations and the disease's unpredictable course characterized by flares and remissions are very likely a reflection of heterogeneity at the origin of disease, with a final common pathway leading to loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens. Impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic material and production of autoantibodies have long been recognized as major pathogenic events in this disease. Over the past decade the type I interferon cytokine family has been postulated to play a central role in SLE pathogenesis, by promoting feedback loops progressively disrupting peripheral immune tolerance and driving disease activity. The identification of key molecules involved in the pathogenesis of SLE will not only improve our understanding of this complex disease, but also help to identify novel targets for biological intervention.

data.title: The baseline interferon signature predicts disease severity over the subsequent 5 years in systemic lupus erythematosus.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Type I interferons (IFNs) play an important role in the pathophysiology of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). While cross-sectional data suggest an association between IFN-induced gene expression and SLE disease activity, interest in this as a biomarker of flare has been tempered by a lack of fluctuation with disease activity in the majority of patients. This led us to question whether IFN-induced gene expression might instead be a biomarker of overall disease severity, with patients with high levels spending more time in an active disease state.
METHODS
Levels of five interferon-responsive genes were measured in the whole peripheral blood at baseline visit for 137 SLE patients subsequently followed for 5 years. Log transformed values were summed to yield a composite IFN5 score, and the correlation with various disease outcomes examined. Receiver operator characteristic analyses were performed for outcomes of interest. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated to compare the proportion of flare-free patients with high and low IFN5 scores over time.
RESULTS
The baseline IFN5 score was positively correlated with the adjusted mean SLE disease activity index-2000, number of flares, adjusted mean prednisone dose, and number of new immunosuppressive medications over the subsequent 5 years. Optimal cut-offs for the IFN5 score were determined using Youden's index and predicted more severe outcomes with 57-67% accuracy. A high baseline IFN5 level was associated with a significantly increased risk of subsequent flare.
CONCLUSIONS
Measurement of the type I IFN signature is a useful tool for predicting the subsequent disease activity course.

data.title: New Attempts to Define and Clarify Lupus.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
The purpose is to discuss the advances that genetics and genomics have provided to better understand the molecular mechanisms behind SLE and how to solve its heterogeneity. I propose new ideas that can help us stratify lupus in order to find the best therapies for each patient, and the idea of substituting clinical diagnosis with molecular diagnosis according to their molecular patterns, an idea that may not only include lupus but also other diseases.
RECENT FINDINGS
The study of rare mutations may provide insight into groups of lupus patients where type I interferon signature is important and help understand those with an atypical clinical presentation. Recent papers used longitudinal blood transcriptome data correlating with disease activity scores to stratify lupus into molecular clusters. The implication of neutrophils in the risk to develop nephritis was established, but also that neutrophils and lymphocytes may correlate with activity differentiating the mechanisms of flares and separating patients into clinically separate groups. The role of type I interferon signature is important; however, the stratification of SLE patients according to the genes and cellular compartments being modulated during disease activity may be even more important to define those patients who may benefit the most with new anti-type I IFN receptor therapies.

data.title: The role of baseline BLyS levels and type 1 interferon-inducible gene signature status in determining belimumab response in systemic lupus erythematosus: a post hoc meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Elevated B lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) levels in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) correlate positively with disease activity; BLyS expression is directly linked to interferon (IFN) pathway activation. This post hoc meta-analysis of BLISS-52 and BLISS-76 explored the relationship between baseline BLyS mRNA/protein levels and/or type 1 IFN-inducible gene signature (IFN-1) and responses to the BLyS-targeting monoclonal antibody belimumab in SLE.
METHODS
In BLISS-52 and BLISS-76, patients with autoantibody-positive SLE and a SELENA-SLEDAI score ≥ 6 and receiving stable standard SLE therapy were randomised to intravenous belimumab 10 mg/kg or placebo, plus standard of care (SoC), for 52 or 76 weeks. For this post hoc meta-analysis, patients with an appropriate mRNA sample were stratified by BLyS mRNA expression (tertiles: high/medium/low; revised quantiles: high/low), IFN-1 mRNA expression (high/low) and BLyS protein level (high/low). Co-primary endpoints were correlation between baseline BLyS and IFN-1 mRNA levels and SLE Responder Index (SRI)4 response at week 52 within BLyS/IFN-1 subgroups. Secondary endpoints included time to first severe SELENA-SLEDAI Flare Index (SFI) flare.
RESULTS
Of 554 patients included in this analysis, 281 had received belimumab and 273 had received placebo. Baseline BLyS and IFN-1 mRNA levels were highly correlated (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient 0.7799; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.7451, 0.8106; p < 0.0001). The proportion of SRI4 responders was higher with belimumab versus placebo in all subgroups, but the difference reached statistical significance in the medium BLyS mRNA tertile (odds ratio [OR] 2.17; 95% CI 1.16, 4.04; p = 0.0153), high BLyS mRNA quantile (OR 1.58; 95% CI 1.02, 2.44; p = 0.0402), high IFN-1 mRNA (OR 1.58; 95% CI: 1.08, 2.31; p = 0.0186) and high BLyS protein (OR 3.57; 95% CI 1.63, 7.83; p = 0.0015) subgroups only. The risk of severe SFI flare was significantly lower with belimumab than placebo in the high BLyS mRNA quantile (hazard ratio [HR] 0.59; 95% CI 0.36, 0.97; p = 0.0371) and high BLyS protein (HR 0.39; 95% CI 0.19, 0.79; p = 0.0090) subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS
This post hoc meta-analysis demonstrated a tendency towards improved response to add-on intravenous belimumab 10 mg/kg versus SoC alone in patients with high baseline BLyS protein and IFN-1 mRNA levels and medium/high BLyS mRNA levels.
