<snippet id="23242340">Title: Evolution of HIV integrase resistance mutations.
Authors: Quashie, Peter K, Mesplède, Thibault, Wainberg, Mark A | Year: 2013 | Journal: Current opinion in infectious diseases
Abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) have become a key component of antiretroviral therapy since the approval of twice-daily raltegravir in 2007 and the more recent approval of elvitegravir in 2012. At the same time, a third compound, dolutegravir, is in late-phase clinical trials, being tested as part of a multidrug once-daily formulation comprising this INSTI and two other antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. This review focuses on the factors leading to the development of drug resistance mutations (DRMs) against INSTIs, evidence of cross-resistance among them, and the results of regimen simplification in regard to this topic.
RECENT FINDINGS
Sequencing data show that DRMs are highly dynamic in patients failing INSTI therapy. Considerations of viral fitness and drug resistance can together determine the evolution of drug resistance mutations, and in this regard the Y143 and Q148 pathways are superior to the N155 pathway in the promotion of resistance. Preventing the emergence of DRMs requires that effective reverse transcriptase or other inhibitors be used together with INSTIs and that high-level adherence to treatment be maintained.
SUMMARY
Because of the susceptibility to drug resistance, INSTIs should always be used together with other effective ARV drugs.</snippet>
<snippet id="27482391">Title: HIV-1 resistance to dolutegravir: update and new insights.
Authors: Wainberg, Mark A, Han, Ying-Shan | Year: 2015 | Journal: Journal of virus eradication
Abstract: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) are the latest class of potent anti-HIV drugs. Currently, three INSTIs have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration: raltegravir (RAL), elvitegravir (EVG) and dolutegravir (DTG). Resistance mutations to RAL and EVG emerge rapidly, and significant cross-resistance between these compounds has been documented. In addition, limited cross-resistance has been observed among DTG, a newer INSTI, and RAL and EVG even though clinical resistance to DTG, or mutations associated with DTG resistance in treatment-naïve patients, has not yet been observed. This review summarises progress in studies on understanding resistance to DTG, mechanisms of possible resistance to DTG, and reasons for the absence of DTG-associated resistance mutations when the drug has been used in first-line therapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="15577623">Title: Multiple mutations in human immunodeficiency virus-1 integrase confer resistance to the clinical trial drug S-1360.
Authors: Fikkert, Valery, Hombrouck, Anneleen, Van Remoortel, Barbara et al. | Year: 2004 | Journal: AIDS (London, England)
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Study of HIV-1 resistance development to the diketo analogue S-1360, the first HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor that has entered clinical development.
DESIGN
HIV-1(IIIB) was passaged in cell culture in the presence of increasing concentrations of S-1360 (IIIB/S-1360(res)).
METHODS
The IIIB/S-1360(res) strains selected for 30, 50 and 70 passages in the presence of S-1360 were evaluated genotypically by sequencing analysis and phenotypically using the MT-4/MTT assay.
RESULTS
Multiple mutations, nine in total, emerged progressively in the catalytic domain of integrase as a result of the selection process. They included T66I and L74M that have both been associated with resistance against the diketo acid L-708,906. After 30, 50 and 70 passages in the presence of S-1360, IIIB/S-1360(res) displayed a four-, eight- and more than 62-fold reduced susceptibility for S-1360, respectively. Phenotypic cross-resistance to L-708,906 was modest for the IIIB/S-1360(res) strain selected during 50 passages, but pronounced for the strain selected during 70 passages. Interesting, all IIIB/S-1360(res) strains remained fully susceptible to the pyranodipyrimidine V-165, an integrase DNA binding inhibitor. Recombination of the mutant integrase genes into wild-type background by integrase-chimeric virus technology entirely reproduced the resistance profile of the IIIB/S-1360(res) strains. As for the replication kinetics of the selected and recombined strains, reduced replication fitness was measured for all strains when compared with their respective wild-type strains.
CONCLUSIONS
The accumulation of integrase mutations coincided with an increasing level of (cross-)resistance of IIIB/S-1360(res). Integrase-chimeric virus technology confirmed that the integrase mutations are indeed fully responsible for the resistance phenotype of IIIB/S-1360.</snippet>
<snippet id="23529738">Title: Impact of primary elvitegravir resistance-associated mutations in HIV-1 integrase on drug susceptibility and viral replication fitness.
Authors: Abram, Michael E, Hluhanich, Rebecca M, Goodman, Derrick D et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Antimicrobial agents and chemotherapy
Abstract: Elvitegravir (EVG) is an effective HIV-1 integrase (IN) strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) in advanced clinical development. Primary INSTI resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) at six IN positions have been identified in HIV-1-infected patients failing EVG-containing regimens in clinical studies: T66I/A/K, E92Q/G, T97A, S147G, Q148R/H/K, and N155H. In this study, the effect of these primary IN mutations, alone and in combination, on susceptibility to the INSTIs EVG, raltegravir (RAL), and dolutegravir (DTG); IN enzyme activities; and viral replication fitness was characterized. Recombinant viruses containing the six most common mutations exhibited a range of reduced EVG susceptibility: 92-fold for Q148R, 30-fold for N155H, 26-fold for E92Q, 10-fold for T66I, 4-fold for S147G, and 2-fold for T97A. Less commonly observed primary IN mutations also showed a range of reduced EVG susceptibilities: 40- to 94-fold for T66K and Q148K and 5- to 10-fold for T66A, E92G, and Q148H. Some primary IN mutations exhibited broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL (T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H), while others retained susceptibility to RAL (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, and S147G). Dual combinations of primary IN mutations further reduced INSTI susceptibility, replication capacity, and viral fitness relative to either mutation alone. Susceptibility to DTG was retained by single primary IN mutations but reduced by dual mutation combinations with Q148R. Primary EVG RAMs also diminished IN enzymatic activities, concordant with their structural proximity to the active site. Greater reductions in viral fitness of dual mutation combinations may explain why some primary INSTI RAMs do not readily coexist on the same HIV-1 genome but rather establish independent pathways of resistance to EVG.</snippet>
<snippet id="24433497">Title: The M50I polymorphic substitution in association with the R263K mutation in HIV-1 subtype B integrase increases drug resistance but does not restore viral replicative fitness.
Authors: Wares, Melissa, Mesplède, Thibault, Quashie, Peter K et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Retrovirology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
First-generation integrase strand-transfer inhibitors (INSTIs), such as raltegravir (RAL) and elvitegravir (EVG), have been clinically proven to be effective antiretrovirals for the treatment of HIV-positive patients. However, their relatively low genetic barrier for resistance makes them susceptible to the emergence of drug resistance mutations. In contrast, dolutegravir (DTG) is a newer INSTI that appears to have a high genetic barrier to resistance in vivo. However, the emergence of the resistance mutation R263K followed by the polymorphic substitution M50I has been observed in cell culture. The M50I polymorphism is also observed in 10-25% of INSTI-naïve patients and has been reported in combination with R263K in a patient failing treatment with RAL.
RESULTS
Using biochemical cell-free strand-transfer assays and resistance assays in TZM-bl cells, we demonstrate that the M50I polymorphism in combination with R263K increases resistance to DTG in tissue culture and in biochemical assays but does not restore the viral fitness cost associated with the R263K mutation.
CONCLUSIONS
Since the combination of the R263K mutation and the M50I polymorphism results in a virus with decreased viral fitness and limited cross-resistance, the R263K resistance pathway may represent an evolutionary dead-end. Although this hypothesis has not yet been proven, it may be more advantageous to treat HIV-positive individuals with DTG in first-line than in second or third-line therapy.</snippet>

<answer>
# Summary

Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) target HIV-1 integrase to catalyze viral DNA strand transfer into the host genome; resistance mutations alter integrase structure and DNA-binding/active-site interactions, which can confer drug resistance but often impose replication fitness costs. Cross-resistance across INSTIs depends on the mutation pathway (e.g., Q148, N155, Y143, T66/E92/T97/S147) and the degree of structural and mechanistic overlap among drugs. Newer INSTIs (dolutegravir, DTG) generally retain activity against raltegravir- and elvitegravir–resistant variants, but compensatory mutations can increase resistance and sometimes restore fitness, with variable cross-resistance to other INSTIs. <cite id="23242340">Sequencing data show INSTI resistance mutations are dynamic, and the balance of viral fitness and drug resistance shapes evolutionary paths, with Y143 and Q148 pathways often promoting resistance more efficiently than N155</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Significant cross-resistance has been documented between raltegravir and elvitegravir, while limited cross-resistance has been observed between dolutegravir and the first-generation INSTIs, although clinical DTG resistance has been rare when DTG is used first-line</cite>.

# Resistance Pathways, Fitness Costs, and Phenotypic Effects

Across clinical and experimental studies, primary resistance-associated mutations cluster at conserved integrase residues, notably T66, E92, T97, S147, Q148, and N155 for elvitegravir, with additional pathways (Y143) documented in earlier contexts. <cite id="23529738">Single mutations in these positions (e.g., T66I/A/K, E92Q/G, T97A, S147G, Q148R/H/K, N155H) confer graded reductions in susceptibility to elvitegravir, ranging from 2-fold (T97A) to >90-fold (Q148R), and diminish integrase enzymatic activities consistent with proximity to the active site</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Dual combinations of primary mutations further reduce INSTI susceptibility, replication capacity, and viral fitness compared with single mutations, helping explain why some RAMs tend to arise as distinct, sequential pathways rather than coexisting on a single genome</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews similarly note that Y143 and Q148 pathways are more efficient in promoting resistance than N155, reflecting differences in fitness penalties and the strength of cross-resistance</cite>.

Experimental selection of integrase mutations can reveal both resistance magnitude and fitness trade-offs. <cite id="15577623">In a model with the diketo integrase inhibitor S‑1360, progressive accumulation of nine catalytic mutations yielded 4-, 8-, and >62-fold reduced susceptibility after 30–70 passages, with modest to pronounced cross-resistance to the diketo L‑708,906 depending on passage number; importantly, all selected variants showed reduced replication fitness relative to wild type, and chimeric virus assays confirmed integrase mutations drove the resistance phenotype</cite>. <cite id="24433497">For DTG resistance, the R263K mutation emerges or is selected in culture and clinical follow-up, but it carries a replicative fitness cost; co-selection of the M50I polymorphism with R263K increases resistance to DTG in cell culture and biochemical assays without restoring viral fitness, suggesting the R263K pathway may be an evolutionary dead-end with limited cross-resistance to other INSTIs</cite>.

# Cross-Resistance Across INSTIs

Cross-resistance patterns differ by mutation class and drug:

- Raltegravir (RAL) vs elvitegravir (EVG): <cite id="23529738">Mutations such as T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H show broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL, whereas other primary mutations (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) retain RAL susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">In primary cell models, Y143R single mutants confer higher RAL resistance in macrophages than in CD4+ T cells, and when compared head-to-head, EVG behaves similarly across cell types; dolutegravir maintained activity against RAL-resistant Y143 and N155 variants in both reservoirs, with only Q148H/R showing reduced susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, rapid emergence of resistance to RAL and EVG with significant cross-resistance has been documented</cite>.

- RAL/EVG vs dolutegravir (DTG): <cite id="23529738">Single primary EVG RAMs generally retain susceptibility to DTG, but dual mutation combinations—especially those involving Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Limited cross-resistance has been observed between DTG and RAL/EVG in vitro and in some clinical contexts, even though clinical resistance to DTG or DTG-specific mutations in treatment-naïve patients has been uncommon, consistent with a higher genetic barrier to resistance</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations of raltegravir-resistant clones show DTG maintained potency against Y143 and N155 pathways in both lymphocytes and macrophages, with only Q148H/R variants demonstrating reduced susceptibility</cite>.

- Pathway-specific nuances: <cite id="23242340">The Q148 pathway often confers greater resistance and broader cross-resistance than N155, which tends to impose larger fitness costs and is less efficient in promoting resistance</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations like M50I can increase resistance to DTG but do not offset the fitness deficit of R263K, and the resulting virus exhibits limited cross-resistance, suggesting constrained interchangeability with other INSTIs</cite>.

# Mechanistic Basis: Fitness and Structural Overlap

Resistance mutations affect viral fitness through multiple mechanisms. <cite id="23529738">Mutations near the active site (e.g., Q148, N155, E92, T66) alter integrase catalytic activities and DNA binding, reducing susceptibility but often decreasing replication capacity; dual mutations exacerbate fitness losses</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection shows that resistance mutations accumulate progressively under drug pressure and that replication fitness is typically reduced relative to wild type, even when cross-resistance to other integrase inhibitors is present</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory substitutions (e.g., M50I with R263K) can partially restore function and increase resistance to a specific INSTI (DTG) without fully restoring overall fitness, leading to trade-offs in cross-resistance and persistence</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews emphasize that the interplay of viral fitness and drug resistance pressures determines which mutation pathways dominate during INSTI failure, with Y143/Q148 routes often favored over N155 due to lower fitness penalties and stronger cross-resistance</cite>.

# Clinical Implications and Management

Understanding fitness and cross-resistance patterns informs regimen design and switching strategies. <cite id="23242340">Because INSTIs are potent but susceptible to resistance, they should be combined with other effective antiretrovirals and adherence must be high to prevent emergence of high-fitness resistance pathways</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Given significant cross-resistance between RAL and EVG and limited cross-resistance to DTG, switching to DTG-based regimens can mitigate resistance risk, and early DTG use may be advantageous to avoid pathways with fitness costs and constrained cross-resistance</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Moreover, dual mutations that further reduce fitness may limit the coexistence of multiple RAMs on a single genome, favoring sequential, pathway-specific resistance and underscoring the value of simplifying regimens to reduce selective pressure</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- INSTI resistance mutations confer drug-specific resistance but frequently impose replication fitness costs; dual mutations amplify susceptibility losses and fitness penalties, shaping distinct resistance pathways. <cite id="23529738">Q148 and Y143 mutations often provide greater resistance and cross-resistance than N155, which tends to carry larger fitness costs</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection demonstrates graded resistance with reduced replication fitness relative to wild type</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations (e.g., M50I with R263K) can increase resistance to DTG without restoring fitness and confer limited cross-resistance</cite>.

- Cross-resistance across INSTIs is pathway-dependent: broad cross-resistance between RAL and EVG is seen for certain mutations (e.g., Q148R/H/K, N155H, T66K, E92Q), while other single mutations retain RAL susceptibility; DTG generally retains activity against RAL/EVG-resistant variants, especially outside Q148H/R, supporting its use to limit resistance emergence. <cite id="23529738">Single EVG RAMs often retain DTG susceptibility, but dual combinations—particularly with Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations confirm DTG activity against Y143 and N155 pathways across cell types, with reduced susceptibility only in Q148H/R</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, DTG shows limited cross-resistance to earlier INSTIs when used first-line</cite>.

- Management strategies should account for fitness and cross-resistance: combination therapy, adherence, and early DTG-based regimens can reduce the likelihood of high-fitness resistance and preserve cross-class effectiveness. <cite id="23242340">Preventing DRM emergence requires effective partner drugs and adherence</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Early DTG use may be advantageous given limited cross-resistance and low clinical resistance rates</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Evolution of HIV integrase resistance mutations.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW
Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) have become a key component of antiretroviral therapy since the approval of twice-daily raltegravir in 2007 and the more recent approval of elvitegravir in 2012. At the same time, a third compound, dolutegravir, is in late-phase clinical trials, being tested as part of a multidrug once-daily formulation comprising this INSTI and two other antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. This review focuses on the factors leading to the development of drug resistance mutations (DRMs) against INSTIs, evidence of cross-resistance among them, and the results of regimen simplification in regard to this topic.
RECENT FINDINGS
Sequencing data show that DRMs are highly dynamic in patients failing INSTI therapy. Considerations of viral fitness and drug resistance can together determine the evolution of drug resistance mutations, and in this regard the Y143 and Q148 pathways are superior to the N155 pathway in the promotion of resistance. Preventing the emergence of DRMs requires that effective reverse transcriptase or other inhibitors be used together with INSTIs and that high-level adherence to treatment be maintained.
SUMMARY
Because of the susceptibility to drug resistance, INSTIs should always be used together with other effective ARV drugs.

data.abstract: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) are the latest class of potent anti-HIV drugs. Currently, three INSTIs have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration: raltegravir (RAL), elvitegravir (EVG) and dolutegravir (DTG). Resistance mutations to RAL and EVG emerge rapidly, and significant cross-resistance between these compounds has been documented. In addition, limited cross-resistance has been observed among DTG, a newer INSTI, and RAL and EVG even though clinical resistance to DTG, or mutations associated with DTG resistance in treatment-naïve patients, has not yet been observed. data.title: Multiple mutations in human immunodeficiency virus-1 integrase confer resistance to the clinical trial drug S-1360.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Study of HIV-1 resistance development to the diketo analogue S-1360, the first HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor that has entered clinical development.
DESIGN
HIV-1(IIIB) was passaged in cell culture in the presence of increasing concentrations of S-1360 (IIIB/S-1360(res)).
METHODS
The IIIB/S-1360(res) strains selected for 30, 50 and 70 passages in the presence of S-1360 were evaluated genotypically by sequencing analysis and phenotypically using the MT-4/MTT assay.
RESULTS
Multiple mutations, nine in total, emerged progressively in the catalytic domain of integrase as a result of the selection process. They included T66I and L74M that have both been associated with resistance against the diketo acid L-708,906. After 30, 50 and 70 passages in the presence of S-1360, IIIB/S-1360(res) displayed a four-, eight- and more than 62-fold reduced susceptibility for S-1360, respectively. Phenotypic cross-resistance to L-708,906 was modest for the IIIB/S-1360(res) strain selected during 50 passages, but pronounced for the strain selected during 70 passages. Interesting, all IIIB/S-1360(res) strains remained fully susceptible to the pyranodipyrimidine V-165, an integrase DNA binding inhibitor. Recombination of the mutant integrase genes into wild-type background by integrase-chimeric virus technology entirely reproduced the resistance profile of the IIIB/S-1360(res) strains. As for the replication kinetics of the selected and recombined strains, reduced replication fitness was measured for all strains when compared with their respective wild-type strains.
CONCLUSIONS
The accumulation of integrase mutations coincided with an increasing level of (cross-)resistance of IIIB/S-1360(res). Integrase-chimeric virus technology confirmed that the integrase mutations are indeed fully responsible for the resistance phenotype of IIIB/S-1360.

data.abstract: Elvitegravir (EVG) is an effective HIV-1 integrase (IN) strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) in advanced clinical development. OBJECTIVES
The cross-resistance profiles of elvitegravir and dolutegravir on raltegravir-resistant variants is still controversial or not available in macrophages and lack extensive evaluations on wide panels of clonal variants. Thus, a complete evaluation in parallel with all currently available integrase inhibitors (INIs) was performed.
METHODS
The integrase coding region was RT-PCR-amplified from patient-derived plasma samples and cloned into an HIV-1 molecular clone lacking the integrase region. Twenty recombinant viruses bearing mutations to all primary pathways of resistance to raltegravir were phenotypically evaluated with each integrase inhibitor in freshly purified CD4+ T cells or monocyte-derived macrophages.
RESULTS
Y143R single mutants conferred a higher level of raltegravir resistance in macrophages [fold change (FC) 47.7-60.24] compared with CD4+ T cells (FC 9.55-11.56). All other combinations had similar effects on viral susceptibility to raltegravir in both cell types. Elvitegravir displayed a similar behaviour both in lymphocytes and macrophages with all the tested patterns. When compared with raltegravir, none to modest increases in resistance were observed for the Y143R/C pathways. Dolutegravir maintained its activity and cross-resistance profile in macrophages. Only Q148H/R variants had a reduced level of susceptibility (FC 5.48-18.64). No variations were observed for the Y143R/C (+/-T97A) or N155H variants.
CONCLUSIONS
All INIs showed comparable antiretroviral activity in both cell types even if single mutations were associated with a different level of susceptibility in vitro to raltegravir and elvitegravir in macrophages. In particular, dolutegravir was capable of inhibiting with similar potency infection of raltegravir-resistant variants with Y143 or N155 pathways in both HIV-1 major cell reservoirs.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) target HIV-1 integrase to catalyze viral DNA strand transfer into the host genome; resistance mutations alter integrase structure and DNA-binding/active-site interactions, which can confer drug resistance but often impose replication fitness costs. Cross-resistance across INSTIs depends on the mutation pathway (e.g., Q148, N155, Y143, T66/E92/T97/S147) and the degree of structural and mechanistic overlap among drugs. Newer INSTIs (dolutegravir, DTG) generally retain activity against raltegravir- and elvitegravir–resistant variants, but compensatory mutations can increase resistance and sometimes restore fitness, with variable cross-resistance to other INSTIs. <cite id="23242340">Sequencing data show INSTI resistance mutations are dynamic, and the balance of viral fitness and drug resistance shapes evolutionary paths, with Y143 and Q148 pathways often promoting resistance more efficiently than N155</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Significant cross-resistance has been documented between raltegravir and elvitegravir, while limited cross-resistance has been observed between dolutegravir and the first-generation INSTIs, although clinical DTG resistance has been rare when DTG is used first-line</cite>.

# Resistance Pathways, Fitness Costs, and Phenotypic Effects

Across clinical and experimental studies, primary resistance-associated mutations cluster at conserved integrase residues, notably T66, E92, T97, S147, Q148, and N155 for elvitegravir, with additional pathways (Y143) documented in earlier contexts. <cite id="23529738">Single mutations in these positions (e.g., T66I/A/K, E92Q/G, T97A, S147G, Q148R/H/K, N155H) confer graded reductions in susceptibility to elvitegravir, ranging from 2-fold (T97A) to >90-fold (Q148R), and diminish integrase enzymatic activities consistent with proximity to the active site</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Dual combinations of primary mutations further reduce INSTI susceptibility, replication capacity, and viral fitness compared with single mutations, helping explain why some RAMs tend to arise as distinct, sequential pathways rather than coexisting on a single genome</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews similarly note that Y143 and Q148 pathways are more efficient in promoting resistance than N155, reflecting differences in fitness penalties and the strength of cross-resistance</cite>.

Experimental selection of integrase mutations can reveal both resistance magnitude and fitness trade-offs. <cite id="15577623">In a model with the diketo integrase inhibitor S‑1360, progressive accumulation of nine catalytic mutations yielded 4-, 8-, and >62-fold reduced susceptibility after 30–70 passages, with modest to pronounced cross-resistance to the diketo L‑708,906 depending on passage number; importantly, all selected variants showed reduced replication fitness relative to wild type, and chimeric virus assays confirmed integrase mutations drove the resistance phenotype</cite>. <cite id="24433497">For DTG resistance, the R263K mutation emerges or is selected in culture and clinical follow-up, but it carries a replicative fitness cost; co-selection of the M50I polymorphism with R263K increases resistance to DTG in cell culture and biochemical assays without restoring viral fitness, suggesting the R263K pathway may be an evolutionary dead-end with limited cross-resistance to other INSTIs</cite>.

# Cross-Resistance Across INSTIs

Cross-resistance patterns differ by mutation class and drug:

- Raltegravir (RAL) vs elvitegravir (EVG): <cite id="23529738">Mutations such as T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H show broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL, whereas other primary mutations (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) retain RAL susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">In primary cell models, Y143R single mutants confer higher RAL resistance in macrophages than in CD4+ T cells, and when compared head-to-head, EVG behaves similarly across cell types; dolutegravir maintained activity against RAL-resistant Y143 and N155 variants in both reservoirs, with only Q148H/R showing reduced susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, rapid emergence of resistance to RAL and EVG with significant cross-resistance has been documented</cite>.

- RAL/EVG vs dolutegravir (DTG): <cite id="23529738">Single primary EVG RAMs generally retain susceptibility to DTG, but dual mutation combinations—especially those involving Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Limited cross-resistance has been observed between DTG and RAL/EVG in vitro and in some clinical contexts, even though clinical resistance to DTG or DTG-specific mutations in treatment-naïve patients has been uncommon, consistent with a higher genetic barrier to resistance</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations of raltegravir-resistant clones show DTG maintained potency against Y143 and N155 pathways in both lymphocytes and macrophages, with only Q148H/R variants demonstrating reduced susceptibility</cite>.

- Pathway-specific nuances: <cite id="23242340">The Q148 pathway often confers greater resistance and broader cross-resistance than N155, which tends to impose larger fitness costs and is less efficient in promoting resistance</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations like M50I can increase resistance to DTG but do not offset the fitness deficit of R263K, and the resulting virus exhibits limited cross-resistance, suggesting constrained interchangeability with other INSTIs</cite>.

# Mechanistic Basis: Fitness and Structural Overlap

Resistance mutations affect viral fitness through multiple mechanisms. <cite id="23529738">Mutations near the active site (e.g., Q148, N155, E92, T66) alter integrase catalytic activities and DNA binding, reducing susceptibility but often decreasing replication capacity; dual mutations exacerbate fitness losses</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection shows that resistance mutations accumulate progressively under drug pressure and that replication fitness is typically reduced relative to wild type, even when cross-resistance to other integrase inhibitors is present</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory substitutions (e.g., M50I with R263K) can partially restore function and increase resistance to a specific INSTI (DTG) without fully restoring overall fitness, leading to trade-offs in cross-resistance and persistence</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews emphasize that the interplay of viral fitness and drug resistance pressures determines which mutation pathways dominate during INSTI failure, with Y143/Q148 routes often favored over N155 due to lower fitness penalties and stronger cross-resistance</cite>.

# Clinical Implications and Management

Understanding fitness and cross-resistance patterns informs regimen design and switching strategies. <cite id="23242340">Because INSTIs are potent but susceptible to resistance, they should be combined with other effective antiretrovirals and adherence must be high to prevent emergence of high-fitness resistance pathways</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Given significant cross-resistance between RAL and EVG and limited cross-resistance to DTG, switching to DTG-based regimens can mitigate resistance risk, and early DTG use may be advantageous to avoid pathways with fitness costs and constrained cross-resistance</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Moreover, dual mutations that further reduce fitness may limit the coexistence of multiple RAMs on a single genome, favoring sequential, pathway-specific resistance and underscoring the value of simplifying regimens to reduce selective pressure</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- INSTI resistance mutations confer drug-specific resistance but frequently impose replication fitness costs; dual mutations amplify susceptibility losses and fitness penalties, shaping distinct resistance pathways. <cite id="23529738">Q148 and Y143 mutations often provide greater resistance and cross-resistance than N155, which tends to carry larger fitness costs</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection demonstrates graded resistance with reduced replication fitness relative to wild type</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations (e.g., M50I with R263K) can increase resistance to DTG without restoring fitness and confer limited cross-resistance</cite>.

- Cross-resistance across INSTIs is pathway-dependent: broad cross-resistance between RAL and EVG is seen for certain mutations (e.g., Q148R/H/K, N155H, T66K, E92Q), while other single mutations retain RAL susceptibility; DTG generally retains activity against RAL/EVG-resistant variants, especially outside Q148H/R, supporting its use to limit resistance emergence. <cite id="23529738">Single EVG RAMs often retain DTG susceptibility, but dual combinations—particularly with Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations confirm DTG activity against Y143 and N155 pathways across cell types, with reduced susceptibility only in Q148H/R</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, DTG shows limited cross-resistance to earlier INSTIs when used first-line</cite>.

- Management strategies should account for fitness and cross-resistance: combination therapy, adherence, and early DTG-based regimens can reduce the likelihood of high-fitness resistance and preserve cross-class effectiveness. <cite id="23242340">Preventing DRM emergence requires effective partner drugs and adherence</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Early DTG use may be advantageous given limited cross-resistance and low clinical resistance rates</cite>.

<snippet id="37082097">Title: Treatment outcomes of mucosal melanoma of head and neck: Efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors for advanced disease.
Authors: Ohshima, Shusuke, Ueki, Yushi, Yokoyama, Yusuke et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in surgery
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Head and neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) is a rare and aggressive subtype of melanoma. HNMM often develops as a recurrent or metastatic disease, and its prognosis is worse than that of cutaneous melanoma. Recent large-scale clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. However, these clinical trials included only a small number of HNMM cases. This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.
METHODS
Cases of advanced HNMM, defined as unresectable or metastatic HNMM at the initial diagnosis (five patients) or development of recurrent/metastatic HNMM after initial treatment (27 patients), were included in this study. Survival analysis and a search for prognostic factors were performed for these 32 patients. Furthermore, the detailed clinical course of patients who received ICI treatment was investigated.
RESULTS
The median overall survival (OS) of 32 patients with advanced HNMM was 25.3 months. The estimated 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS rates were 68.4%, 42.8%, and 34.3%, respectively. Fourteen patients (43.7%) received ICIs, whereas 18 (56.3%) did not. Univariate analysis showed that ICI treatment was the only factor associated with a better 1-year OS. Patients who received ICI treatment had significantly longer OS (median OS: not reached, 1-year OS: 85.7%) than those who did not (median OS: 11.3 months, 1-year OS: 54.5%). The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively. Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%). Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.
CONCLUSIONS
ICI treatment achieved a favorable OS for advanced HNMM. CR/PR to ICI treatment and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were favorable predictors of OS.</snippet>
</tool_output>

# Summary

Evidence specifically isolating outcomes after discontinuation of PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors due to immune‑related adverse events (irAEs) is limited, but one clinical series in head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma provides relevant data. In that cohort, among five patients who discontinued immunotherapy because of severe irAEs, four experienced durable treatment effects and survived 9.8–54.2 months without salvage therapy, suggesting that some patients can maintain durable tumor control after discontinuation. Response quality during treatment (complete or partial response) and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were associated with better overall survival, indicating that depth of initial response and the presence of severe irAEs may signal more indolent tumor biology and better durability of control. However, these findings are disease‑specific and based on small numbers, so generalization to other tumor types and to PD‑L1 settings is uncertain.

# Proportion with Durable Tumor Control

- In a series of 5 patients with advanced head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma who discontinued PD‑1 therapy due to severe irAEs, 4 patients (80%) did not receive salvage treatments yet maintained durable disease control, surviving 9.8–54.2 months at follow‑up. These patients were considered to have durable treatment effects despite discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Predictors of Durability

- Depth of response during ICI therapy: Patients achieving complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) had markedly better survival (1‑year OS 100%) compared with non‑responders (1‑year OS 71.4%), suggesting that on‑treatment response quality predicts longer durability of control, even after discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%).</cite>
- Discontinuation due to severe irAEs: In this cohort, discontinuation owing to severe irAEs was identified as a favorable predictor of overall survival, potentially reflecting a biologically favorable subset that can control disease without continued immunotherapy. <cite id="37082097">ICI treatment achieved a favorable OS for advanced HNMM. CR/PR to ICI treatment and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were favorable predictors of OS.</cite>

# Important Limitations

- The available evidence comes from a single institution series in a rare disease (head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma), with a small number of patients who discontinued due to irAEs, limiting statistical power and generalizability beyond this setting. <cite id="37082097">Head and neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) is a rare and aggressive subtype of melanoma... This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.</cite>
- Outcome measures differ across studies; some report overall survival, while others report time to progression or durable control, making direct comparisons challenging. <cite id="37082097">The median overall survival (OS) of 32 patients with advanced HNMM was 25.3 months... The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients who must discontinue PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy due to irAEs, close monitoring and consideration of multidisciplinary management is prudent. The presence of CR/PR on prior therapy and the occurrence of severe irAEs may identify a subgroup with favorable biology and potential for durable disease control off‑therapy, but individualized risk‑stratification is essential given the limited and disease‑specific evidence. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer... Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- Larger, multicenter cohorts across tumor types are needed to quantify the proportion of patients maintaining durable control after PD‑1/PD‑L1 discontinuation for irAEs and to validate predictors such as on‑treatment response, irAE severity, tumor mutational burden, PD‑L1 expression, and immune phenotype as robust surrogates for durability. <cite id="37082097">Recent large-scale clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. However, these clinical trials included only a small number of HNMM cases.</cite>
</answer>

data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Head and neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) is a rare and aggressive subtype of melanoma. HNMM often develops as a recurrent or metastatic disease, and its prognosis is worse than that of cutaneous melanoma. Recent large-scale clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. However, these clinical trials included only a small number of HNMM cases. This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.
METHODS
Cases of advanced HNMM, defined as unresectable or metastatic HNMM at the initial diagnosis (five patients) or development of recurrent/metastatic HNMM after initial treatment (27 patients), were included in this study. Survival analysis and a search for prognostic factors were performed for these 32 patients. Furthermore, the detailed clinical course of patients who received ICI treatment was investigated.
RESULTS
The median overall survival (OS) of 32 patients with advanced HNMM was 25.3 months. The estimated 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS rates were 68.4%, 42.8%, and 34.3%, respectively. Fourteen patients (43.7%) received ICIs, whereas 18 (56.3%) did not. Univariate analysis showed that ICI treatment was the only factor associated with a better 1-year OS. Patients who received ICI treatment had significantly longer OS (median OS: not reached, 1-year OS: 85.7%) than those who did not (median OS: 11.3 months, 1-year OS: 54.5%). The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively. Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%). Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.
CONCLUSIONS
ICI treatment achieved a favorable OS for advanced HNMM. CR/PR to ICI treatment and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were favorable predictors of OS.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

Evidence specifically isolating outcomes after discontinuation of PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors due to immune‑related adverse events (irAEs) is limited, but one clinical series in head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma provides relevant data. In that cohort, among five patients who discontinued immunotherapy because of severe irAEs, four experienced durable treatment effects and survived 9.8–54.2 months without salvage therapy, suggesting that some patients can maintain durable tumor control after discontinuation. Response quality during treatment (complete or partial response) and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were associated with better overall survival, indicating that depth of initial response and the presence of severe irAEs may signal more indolent tumor biology and better durability of control. However, these findings are disease‑specific and based on small numbers, so generalization to other tumor types and to PD‑L1 settings is uncertain.

# Proportion with Durable Tumor Control

- In a series of 5 patients with advanced head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma who discontinued PD‑1 therapy due to severe irAEs, 4 patients (80%) did not receive salvage treatments yet maintained durable disease control, surviving 9.8–54.2 months at follow‑up. These patients were considered to have durable treatment effects despite discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Predictors of Durability

- Depth of response during ICI therapy: Patients achieving complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) had markedly better survival (1‑year OS 100%) compared with non‑responders (1‑year OS 71.4%), suggesting that on‑treatment response quality predicts longer durability of control, even after discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%).</cite>
- Discontinuation due to severe irAEs: In this cohort, discontinuation owing to severe irAEs was identified as a favorable predictor of overall survival, potentially reflecting a biologically favorable subset that can control disease without continued immunotherapy. <cite id="37082097">ICI treatment achieved a favorable OS for advanced HNMM. CR/PR to ICI treatment and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were favorable predictors of OS.</cite>

# Important Limitations

- The available evidence comes from a single institution series in a rare disease (head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma), with a small number of patients who discontinued due to irAEs, limiting statistical power and generalizability beyond this setting. <cite id="37082097">Head and neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) is a rare and aggressive subtype of melanoma... This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.</cite>
- Outcome measures differ across studies; some report overall survival, while others report time to progression or durable control, making direct comparisons challenging. <cite id="37082097">The median overall survival (OS) of 32 patients with advanced HNMM was 25.3 months... The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients who must discontinue PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy due to irAEs, close monitoring and consideration of multidisciplinary management is prudent. The presence of CR/PR on prior therapy and the occurrence of severe irAEs may identify a subgroup with favorable biology and potential for durable disease control off‑therapy, but individualized risk‑stratification is essential given the limited and disease‑specific evidence. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer... Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- Larger, multicenter cohorts across tumor types are needed to quantify the proportion of patients maintaining durable control after PD‑1/PD‑L1 discontinuation for irAEs and to validate predictors such as on‑treatment response, irAE severity, tumor mutational burden, PD‑L1 expression, and immune phenotype as robust surrogates for durability. <cite id="37082097">Recent large-scale clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. However, these clinical trials included only a small number of HNMM cases.</cite>

<snippet id="32297899">Title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Rechallenge After Immune-Related Adverse Events in Patients With Cancer.
Authors: Dolladille, Charles, Ederhy, Stéphane, Sassier, Marion et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: JAMA oncology
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
Limited information is available on the safety of a rechallenge with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) after an immune-related adverse event (irAE).
OBJECTIVE
To identify the recurrence rate of the same irAE that prompted discontinuation of ICI therapy after an ICI rechallenge in patients with cancer and to identify the clinical features associated with such recurrences.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This observational, cross-sectional, pharmacovigilance cohort study examined individual case safety reports from the World Health Organization database VigiBase, which contains case reports from more than 130 countries. Case reports were extracted from database inception (1967) to September 1, 2019. All consecutive ICI cases with at least 1 associated irAE were included.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary outcome was the rate of recurrence of the initial irAE after an ICI rechallenge. Secondary outcomes included the factors associated with the recurrence after a rechallenge among informative rechallenges, the recurrence rate according to the ICI regimen (anti-programmed cell death 1 or anti-programmed cell death ligand 1 monotherapy, anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 monotherapy, or combination therapy), and the rate of occurrence of a different irAE after a rechallenge.
RESULTS
A total of 24 079 irAE cases associated with at least 1 ICI were identified. Among the irAEs, 452 of 6123 irAEs associated with ICI rechallenges (7.4%) were informative rechallenges. One hundred thirty recurrences (28.8%; 95% CI, 24.8-33.1) of the initial irAE were observed. In a rechallenge, colitis (reporting odds ratio [OR], 1.77; 95% CI, 1.14-2.75; P = .01), hepatitis (reporting OR, 3.38; 95% CI, 1.31-8.74; P = .01), and pneumonitis (reporting OR, 2.26; 95% CI, 1.18-4.32; P = .01) were associated with a higher recurrence rate, whereas adrenal events were associated with a lower recurrence rate (reporting OR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.13-0.86; P = .03) compared with other irAEs.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
This cohort study found a 28.8% recurrence rate of the same irAE associated with the discontinuation of ICI therapy after a rechallenge with the same ICI. Resuming ICI therapy could be considered for select patients, with appropriate monitoring and use of standard treatment algorithms to identify and treat toxic effects.</snippet>
<snippet id="35558065">Title: Risk Factors and Biomarkers for Immune-Related Adverse Events: A Practical Guide to Identifying High-Risk Patients and Rechallenging Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors.
Authors: Chennamadhavuni, Adithya, Abushahin, Laith, Jin, Ning et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are a range of complications associated with the use of immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Two major classes of ICIs widely used are Cytotoxic T-Lymphocyte Antigen 4 (CTLA4) and Programmed Cell death-1 (PD-1)/Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors. High-grade irAEs are life-threatening and often cause a severe decline in performance status in such that patients do not qualify for any further anticancer treatments. It is difficult to generalize the evidence in the current literature on risk factors or biomarkers for the entire class of ICIs as the studies so far are either disease-specific (e.g., lung cancer or melanoma) or ICI agent-specific (e.g., pembrolizumab, ipilimumab) or irAE-specific (e.g., pneumonitis or gastritis). In this review, risk factors and biomarkers to consider before initiating or monitoring ICI are listed with a practical purpose in day-to-day practice. Risk factors are grouped into demographics and social history, medical history, and medication history, tumor-specific and agent-specific risk factors. A higher risk of irAE is associated with age <60 years, high body mass index, women on CTLA4 and men on PD-1/PD-L1 agents, and chronic smokers. Patients with significant kidney (Stage IV-V), cardiac (heart failure, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, hypertension), and lung (asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) are at a higher risk of respective organ-specific irAEs. Pre-existing autoimmune disease and chronic use of certain drugs (proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anti-inflammatory drugs) also increase the irAE-risk. Biomarkers are categorized into circulating blood counts, cytokines, autoantibodies, HLA genotypes, microRNA, gene expression profiling, and serum proteins. The blood counts and certain protein markers (albumin and thyroid-stimulating hormone) are readily accessible in current practice. High neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, eosinophil/monocyte/lymphocyte counts; TSH and troponins at diagnosis and drop in the white count and lymphocyte count can predict irAE. Other biomarkers with limited evidence are cytokines, autoantibodies, HLA genotypes, microRNA, and gene expression profiling. With fast-expanding approvals for ICIs in various cancer types, knowledge on risk factors and biomarkers can help providers assess the irAE-risk of their patients. Prospective disease and agent-specific studies are needed to provide further insight on this essential aspect of ICI therapy.</snippet>
<snippet id="32786166">Title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related cutaneous adverse events.
Authors: He, Chunxia, Qu, Tao | Year: 2020 | Journal: Asia-Pacific journal of clinical oncology
Abstract: Cutaneous toxicities are the most prevalent immune-related adverse events. Various reactions have been reported. In this review, we summarized the clinicopathologic manifestations, treatment strategies, relevance to tumor outcomes, and rechallenge considerations of cutaneous immune-related adverse events.</snippet>
<snippet id="39138117">Title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated nephritis-treatment standard.
Authors: Barbir, Elena-Bianca, Kitchlu, Abhijat, Herrmann, Sandra M | Year: 2024 | Journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
Abstract: Over the last 13 years, the use of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has grown remarkably, owing to their unprecedented anti-tumor efficacy in certain tumor groups. With increased use of ICIs, we are seeing immune-related adverse events (irAEs) more frequently. Renal irAEs, such as ICI-associated acute kidney injury (ICI-AKI), are reported in 2%-5% of patients treated with ICIs, with acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (ATIN) as the most common histopathologic lesion, though various forms of glomerulonephritis have also been reported. Modifiable risk factors for ICI-AKI include concurrent use of ATIN-associated drugs, like proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antibiotics, and dual ICI therapy with both Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte Associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) and Programmed Cell Death Protein 1 and its ligand (PD1/PDL-1) blockade. Kidney biopsies remain the diagnostic modality of choice, though several promising non-invasive biomarkers, which have not yet been broadly clinically validated have emerged. The treatment of ICI-AKI involves holding ICIs, discontinuation of ATIN-associated drugs and initiation of immunosuppression with corticosteroids as first-line therapy. With prompt treatment initiation, most patients achieve full or partial renal recovery, allowing for re-challenge with ICI. However, a subset of patients will require additional steroid-sparing therapies for corticosteroid-dependent or refractory ICI-AKI. Here we review developments in our understanding of the pathophysiology of ICI-AKI, the approach to diagnosis (with a focus on the emergence of novel diagnostic tools), prognostic factors and the current evidence for establishing treatment standards for ICI-AKI. As the evidence base remains largely retrospective, we identify questions that would benefit from future prospective studies in the diagnosis, management and prognostication of ICI-AKI.</snippet>
<snippet id="34646270">Title: Safety and Efficacy of the Rechallenge of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors After Immune-Related Adverse Events in Patients With Cancer: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Authors: Zhao, Qing, Zhang, Jianwei, Xu, Lingyi et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Frontiers in immunology
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Little evidence exists on the safety and efficacy of the rechallenge of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) after immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in patients with cancer.
METHODS
We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane for articles on ICI rechallenge after irAEs for systemic review and meta-analysis. The outcomes included the incidence and associated factors for safety and objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) for efficacy.
RESULTS
A total of 789 ICI rechallenge cases from 18 cohort studies, 5 case series studies, and 54 case reports were included. The pooled incidence of all-grade and high-grade irAEs after rechallenge in patients with cancer was 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Compared with initial ICI treatment, rechallenge showed a higher incidence for all-grade irAEs (OR, 3.81; 95% CI, 2.15-6.74; p < 0.0001), but similar incidence for high-grade irAEs ( p > 0.05). Types of initial irAEs (pneumonitis and global irAEs) and cancer (non-small cell lung cancer and multiple cancer) recapitulated these findings. Gastrointestinal irAEs and time interval between initial irAEs and ICI rechallenge were associated with higher recurrence of high-grade irAEs ( p < 0.05), whereas initial anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies were associated with a lower recurrence ( p < 0.05). Anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies rechallenge was associated with a lower all-grade irAE recurrence ( p < 0.05). The pooled ORR and DCR after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, showing no significant difference compared with initial ICI treatment ( p > 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS
ICI rechallenge after irAEs showed lower safety and similar efficacy outcomes compared with initial ICI treatment.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
PROSPERO, identifier CRD42020191405.</snippet>

# Summary of Evidence on Re-challenge with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (ICIs) After Prior Immune-Related Adverse Events (irAEs)

## What the Observational Cohort Shows
A large observational pharmacovigilance cohort using WHO's VigiBase identified 24,079 immune-related adverse event (irAE) cases and extracted all consecutive immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) cases with at least one irAE. Among 6123 irAEs associated with ICI rechallenges, 452 were informative rechallenges; of these, 130 (28.8%; 95% CI, 24.8–33.1) recurred with the same irAE that led to discontinuation. Certain organ toxicities showed higher recurrence risk upon rechallenge (colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis), while adrenal events had lower recurrence risk. The authors concluded that rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms in place. <cite id="32297899">A large observational cohort using WHO's VigiBase found that 28.8% of informative rechallenges recurred the same irAE; colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis had higher recurrence odds, while adrenal events had lower odds; authors recommended rechallenge for select patients with close monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite>.

## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Safety and Efficacy
A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 789 ICI rechallenge cases across 18 cohort studies, 5 case series, and 54 case reports reported the following:
- Safety: The pooled incidence of all-grade and high-grade irAEs after rechallenge was 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Rechallenge had a higher incidence of all-grade irAEs compared to initial ICI treatment (OR 3.81; 95% CI 2.15–6.74), but similar high-grade irAE incidence. Risk factors for high-grade irAE recurrence included gastrointestinal irAEs and shorter time interval from initial irAE to rechallenge; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge was associated with lower recurrence of high-grade and all-grade irAEs.
- Efficacy: Pooled objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment. <cite id="34646270">A meta-analysis of 789 ICI rechallenge cases found all-grade and high-grade irAE incidence after rechallenge of 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence versus initial treatment; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge had lower recurrence, and ORR/DCR after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9% without significant difference from initial treatment</cite>.

## Organ-Specific Guidance and Practical Considerations
- Renal irAEs (ICI-associated acute kidney injury/acute tubulointerstitial nephritis): With prompt treatment (steroids, discontinuation of ATIN-associated drugs, holding ICIs), most patients recover renal function and can be rechallenged; a subset may need steroid-sparing immunosuppression for refractory cases. The literature emphasizes that evidence is largely retrospective and calls for prospective studies to refine standards. <cite id="39138117">In ICI-associated acute kidney injury, most patients achieve renal recovery with prompt treatment and can be rechallenged, though a subset requires additional steroid-sparing therapies; overall evidence remains largely retrospective</cite>.
- Cutaneous irAEs: Reviews summarize clinicopathologic features, treatments, and rechallenge considerations, noting that rechallenge decisions depend on resolution of dermatologic toxicity, absence of systemic disease progression, and implementation of preventive/therapeutic strategies. <cite id="32786166">Reviews of cutaneous immune-related adverse events detail clinicopathologic features, treatments, tumor outcome relevance, and rechallenge considerations</cite>.
- General rechallenge frameworks: Practical reviews outline risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs (demographics, medical/medication history, tumor and agent-specific factors, blood counts, autoantibodies, HLA, and inflammatory markers) to individualize risk assessment before rechallenge and to guide monitoring. <cite id="35558065">Practical reviews catalog risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs across demographics, medical history, medications, tumor/agent-specific features, and laboratory/biomarker signals to inform rechallenge decisions and monitoring</cite>.

## Safety vs. Efficacy Trade-off After Rechallenge
- Recurrence of toxicity: Across pooled data, rechallenge increases the risk of all-grade toxicities (approximately 34% incidence) compared with initial ICI courses, with notable organ-specific recurrence patterns (e.g., higher for pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis; lower for adrenal). The recurrence of high-grade irAEs is similar to initial treatment when accounting for agent class and prior toxicity type, but is higher when prior gastrointestinal irAEs or short intervals from initial event to rechallenge are present. <cite id="34646270">Rechallenge increases all-grade irAE incidence (≈34%) versus initial treatment, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence overall; gastrointestinal prior irAEs and short time intervals increase high-grade recurrence, while anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge lowers recurrence</cite> <cite id="32297899">Recurrence of the initial irAE after rechallenge occurred in 28.8% of informative cases, with organ-specific differences in recurrence odds</cite>.
- Antitumor efficacy: Rechallenge maintains antitumor activity, with pooled ORR of 43.1% and DCR of 71.9%, comparable to initial ICI therapy. This suggests that, despite increased toxicity monitoring needs, rechallenge can preserve therapeutic benefit in selected patients. <cite id="34646270">Pooled rechallenge outcomes showed ORR 43.1% and DCR 71.9%, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment</cite>.

## Practical Takeaways for Clinicians
- Selective rechallenge is reasonable for patients who:
  - Have fully recovered from a well-characterized, isolated irAE with durable remission on appropriate immunosuppression.
  - Are monitored closely with early toxicities recognized and managed.
  - Receive agent classes with lower recurrence risk (e.g., anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy) and avoid short intervals from initial event to rechallenge.
- Shared decision-making should weigh organ-specific recurrence risks (e.g., higher pneumonitis/colitis/hepatitis recurrences; lower adrenal recurrences) and patient comorbidities and risk factors. <cite id="32297899">Rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite> <cite id="34646270">Anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge is associated with lower recurrence, and rechallenge efficacy (ORR/DCR) is similar to initial treatment</cite> <cite id="35558065">Risk stratification and biomarker-informed monitoring can guide safe rechallenge decisions</cite>.

## Limitations and Evidence Gaps

data.title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Rechallenge After Immune-Related Adverse Events in Patients With Cancer.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Limited information is available on the safety of a rechallenge with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) after an immune-related adverse event (irAE).
OBJECTIVE
To identify the recurrence rate of the same irAE that prompted discontinuation of ICI therapy after an ICI rechallenge in patients with cancer and to identify the clinical features associated with such recurrences.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This observational, cross-sectional, pharmacovigilance cohort study examined individual case safety reports from the World Health Organization database VigiBase, which contains case reports from more than 130 countries. Case reports were extracted from database inception (1967) to September 1, 2019. All consecutive ICI cases with at least 1 associated irAE were included.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary outcome was the rate of recurrence of the initial irAE after an ICI rechallenge. Secondary outcomes included the factors associated with the recurrence after a rechallenge among informative rechallenges, the recurrence rate according to the ICI regimen (anti-programmed cell death 1 or anti-programmed cell death ligand 1 monotherapy, anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 monotherapy, or combination therapy), and the rate of occurrence of a different irAE after a rechallenge.
RESULTS
A total of 24 079 irAE cases associated with at least 1 ICI were identified. Among the irAEs, 452 of 6123 irAEs associated with ICI rechallenges (7.4%) were informative rechallenges. One hundred thirty recurrences (28.8%; 95% CI, 24.8-33.1) of the initial irAE were observed. In a rechallenge, colitis (reporting odds ratio [OR], 1.77; 95% CI, 1.14-2.75; P = .01), hepatitis (reporting OR, 3.38; 95% CI, 1.31-8.74; P = .01), and pneumonitis (reporting OR, 2.26; 95% CI, 1.18-4.32; P = .01) were associated with a higher recurrence rate, whereas adrenal events were associated with a lower recurrence rate (reporting OR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.13-0.86; P = .03) compared with other irAEs.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
This cohort study found a 28.8% recurrence rate of the same irAE associated with the discontinuation of ICI therapy after a rechallenge with the same ICI. Resuming ICI therapy could be considered for select patients, with appropriate monitoring and use of standard treatment algorithms to identify and treat toxic effects.

data.title: Risk Factors and Biomarkers for Immune-Related Adverse Events: A Practical Guide to Identifying High-Risk Patients and Rechallenging Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors.
data.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are a range of complications associated with the use of immune-checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Two major classes of ICIs widely used are Cytotoxic T-Lymphocyte Antigen 4 (CTLA4) and Programmed Cell death-1 (PD-1)/Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors. High-grade irAEs are life-threatening and often cause a severe decline in performance status in such that patients do not qualify for any further anticancer treatments. It is difficult to generalize the evidence in the current literature on risk factors or biomarkers for the entire class of ICIs as the studies so far are either disease-specific (e.g., lung cancer or melanoma) or ICI agent-specific (e.g., pembrolizumab, ipilimumab) or irAE-specific (e.g., pneumonitis or gastritis). In this review, risk factors and biomarkers to consider before initiating or monitoring ICI are listed with a practical purpose in day-to-day practice. Risk factors are grouped into demographics and social history, medical history, and medication history, tumor-specific and agent-specific risk factors. A higher risk of irAE is associated with age <60 years, high body mass index, women on CTLA4 and men on PD-1/PD-L1 agents, and chronic smokers. Patients with significant kidney (Stage IV-V), cardiac (heart failure, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, hypertension), and lung (asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) are at a higher risk of respective organ-specific irAEs. Pre-existing autoimmune disease and chronic use of certain drugs (proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anti-inflammatory drugs) also increase the irAE-risk. Biomarkers are categorized into circulating blood counts, cytokines, autoantibodies, HLA genotypes, microRNA, gene expression profiling, and serum proteins. The blood counts and certain protein markers (albumin and thyroid-stimulating hormone) are readily accessible in current practice. High neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, eosinophil/monocyte/lymphocyte counts; TSH and troponins at diagnosis and drop in the white count and lymphocyte count can predict irAE. Other biomarkers with limited evidence are cytokines, autoantibodies, HLA genotypes, microRNA, and gene expression profiling. With fast-expanding approvals for ICIs in various cancer types, knowledge on risk factors and biomarkers can help providers assess the irAE-risk of their patients. Prospective disease and agent-specific studies are needed to provide further insight on this essential aspect of ICI therapy.

data.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related cutaneous adverse events.
data.abstract: Cutaneous toxicities are the most prevalent immune-related adverse events. Various reactions have been reported. In this review, we summarized the clinicopathologic manifestations, treatment strategies, relevance to tumor outcomes, and rechallenge considerations of cutaneous immune-related adverse events.

data.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated nephritis-treatment standard.
data.abstract: Over the last 13 years, the use of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has grown remarkably, owing to their unprecedented anti-tumor efficacy in certain tumor groups. With increased use of ICIs, we are seeing immune-related adverse events (irAEs) more frequently. Renal irAEs, such as ICI-associated acute kidney injury (ICI-AKI), are reported in 2%-5% of patients treated with ICIs, with acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (ATIN) as the most common histopathologic lesion, though various forms of glomerulonephritis have also been reported. Modifiable risk factors for ICI-AKI include concurrent use of ATIN-associated drugs, like proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antibiotics, and dual ICI therapy with both Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte Associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) and Programmed Cell Death Protein 1 and its ligand (PD1/PDL-1) blockade. Kidney biopsies remain the diagnostic modality of choice, though several promising non-invasive biomarkers, which have not yet been broadly clinically validated have emerged. The treatment of ICI-AKI involves holding ICIs, discontinuation of ATIN-associated drugs and initiation of immunosuppression with corticosteroids as first-line therapy. With prompt treatment initiation, most patients achieve full or partial renal recovery, allowing for re-challenge with ICI. However, a subset of patients will require additional steroid-sparing therapies for corticosteroid-dependent or refractory ICI-AKI. Here we review developments in our understanding of the pathophysiology of ICI-AKI, the approach to diagnosis (with a focus on the emergence of novel diagnostic tools), prognostic factors and the current evidence for establishing treatment standards for ICI-AKI. As the evidence base remains largely retrospective, we identify questions that would benefit from future prospective studies in the diagnosis, management and prognostication of ICI-AKI.

data.title: Safety and Efficacy of the Rechallenge of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors After Immune-Related Adverse Events in Patients With Cancer: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Little evidence exists on the safety and efficacy of the rechallenge of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) after immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in patients with cancer.
METHODS
We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane for articles on ICI rechallenge after irAEs for systemic review and meta-analysis. The outcomes included the incidence and associated factors for safety and objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) for efficacy.
RESULTS
A total of 789 ICI rechallenge cases from 18 cohort studies, 5 case series studies, and 54 case reports were included. The pooled incidence of all-grade and high-grade irAEs after rechallenge in patients with cancer was 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Compared with initial ICI treatment, rechallenge showed a higher incidence for all-grade irAEs (OR, 3.81; 95% CI, 2.15-6.74; p < 0.0001), but similar incidence for high-grade irAEs ( p > 0.05). Types of initial irAEs (pneumonitis and global irAEs) and cancer (non-small cell lung cancer and multiple cancer) recapitulated these findings. Gastrointestinal irAEs and time interval between initial irAEs and ICI rechallenge were associated with higher recurrence of high-grade irAEs ( p < 0.05), whereas initial anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies were associated with a lower recurrence ( p < 0.05). Anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies rechallenge was associated with a lower all-grade irAE recurrence ( p < 0.05). The pooled ORR and DCR after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, showing no significant difference compared with initial ICI treatment ( p > 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS
ICI rechallenge after irAEs showed lower safety and similar efficacy outcomes compared with initial ICI treatment.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
PROSPERO, identifier CRD42020191405.
