# Summary of Evidence on Re-challenge with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (ICIs) After Prior Immune-Related Adverse Events (irAEs)

## What the Observational Cohort Shows
A large observational pharmacovigilance cohort using WHO's VigiBase identified 24,079 immune-related adverse event (irAE) cases and extracted all consecutive immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) cases with at least one irAE. Among 6123 irAEs associated with ICI rechallenges, 452 were informative rechallenges; of these, 130 (28.8%; 95% CI, 24.8–33.1) recurred with the same irAE that led to discontinuation. Certain organ toxicities showed higher recurrence risk upon rechallenge (colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis), while adrenal events had lower recurrence risk. The authors concluded that rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms in place. <cite id="32297899">A large observational cohort using WHO's VigiBase found that 28.8% of informative rechallenges recurred the same irAE; colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis had higher recurrence odds, while adrenal events had lower odds; authors recommended rechallenge for select patients with close monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite>.

## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Safety and Efficacy
A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 789 ICI rechallenge cases across 18 cohort studies, 5 case series, and 54 case reports reported the following:
- Safety: The pooled incidence of all-grade and high-grade irAEs after rechallenge was 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Rechallenge had a higher incidence of all-grade irAEs compared to initial ICI treatment (OR 3.81; 95% CI 2.15–6.74), but similar high-grade irAE incidence. Risk factors for high-grade irAE recurrence included gastrointestinal irAEs and shorter time interval from initial irAE to rechallenge; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge was associated with lower recurrence of high-grade and all-grade irAEs.
- Efficacy: Pooled objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment. <cite id="34646270">A meta-analysis of 789 ICI rechallenge cases found all-grade and high-grade irAE incidence after rechallenge of 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence versus initial treatment; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge had lower recurrence, and ORR/DCR after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9% without significant difference from initial treatment</cite>.

## Organ-Specific Guidance and Practical Considerations
- Renal irAEs (ICI-associated acute kidney injury/acute tubulointerstitial nephritis): With prompt treatment (steroids, discontinuation of ATIN-associated drugs, holding ICIs), most patients recover renal function and can be rechallenged; a subset may need steroid-sparing immunosuppression for refractory cases. The literature emphasizes that evidence is largely retrospective and calls for prospective studies to refine standards. <cite id="39138117">In ICI-associated acute kidney injury, most patients achieve renal recovery with prompt treatment and can be rechallenged, though a subset requires additional steroid-sparing therapies; overall evidence remains largely retrospective</cite>.
- Cutaneous irAEs: Reviews summarize clinicopathologic features, treatments, and rechallenge considerations, noting that rechallenge decisions depend on resolution of dermatologic toxicity, absence of systemic disease progression, and implementation of preventive/therapeutic strategies. <cite id="32786166">Reviews of cutaneous immune-related adverse events detail clinicopathologic features, treatments, tumor outcome relevance, and rechallenge considerations</cite>.
- General rechallenge frameworks: Practical reviews outline risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs (demographics, medical/medication history, tumor and agent-specific factors, blood counts, autoantibodies, HLA, and inflammatory markers) to individualize risk assessment before rechallenge and to guide monitoring. <cite id="35558065">Practical reviews catalog risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs across demographics, medical history, medications, tumor/agent-specific features, and laboratory/biomarker signals to inform rechallenge decisions and monitoring</cite>.

## Safety vs. Efficacy Trade-off After Rechallenge
- Recurrence of toxicity: Across pooled data, rechallenge increases the risk of all-grade toxicities (approximately 34% incidence) compared with initial ICI courses, with notable organ-specific recurrence patterns (e.g., higher for pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis; lower for adrenal). The recurrence of high-grade irAEs is similar to initial treatment when accounting for agent class and prior toxicity type, but is higher when prior gastrointestinal irAEs or short intervals from initial event to rechallenge are present. <cite id="34646270">Rechallenge increases all-grade irAE incidence (≈34%) versus initial treatment, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence overall; gastrointestinal prior irAEs and short time intervals increase high-grade recurrence, while anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge lowers recurrence</cite> <cite id="32297899">Recurrence of the initial irAE after rechallenge occurred in 28.8% of informative cases, with organ-specific differences in recurrence odds</cite>.
- Antitumor efficacy: Rechallenge maintains antitumor activity, with pooled ORR of 43.1% and DCR of 71.9%, comparable to initial ICI therapy. This suggests that, despite increased toxicity monitoring needs, rechallenge can preserve therapeutic benefit in selected patients. <cite id="34646270">Pooled rechallenge outcomes showed ORR 43.1% and DCR 71.9%, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment</cite>.

## Practical Takeaways for Clinicians
- Selective rechallenge is reasonable for patients who:
  - Have fully recovered from a well-characterized, isolated irAE with durable remission on appropriate immunosuppression.
  - Are monitored closely with early toxicities recognized and managed.
  - Receive agent classes with lower recurrence risk (e.g., anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy) and avoid short intervals from initial event to rechallenge.
- Shared decision-making should weigh organ-specific recurrence risks (e.g., higher pneumonitis/colitis/hepatitis recurrences; lower adrenal recurrences) and patient comorbidities and risk factors. <cite id="32297899">Rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite> <cite id="34646270">Anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge is associated with lower recurrence, and rechallenge efficacy (ORR/DCR) is similar to initial treatment</cite> <cite id="35558065">Risk stratification and biomarker-informed monitoring can guide safe rechallenge decisions</cite>.

## Limitations and Evidence Gaps
- Much of the evidence is retrospective, based on pharmacovigilance databases and case series/case reports, with variable quality and follow-up. Prospective, disease- and agent-specific cohorts are needed to refine recurrence risk models and optimize protocols for rechallenge. <cite id="32297899">The cohort relied on pharmacovigilance reports and did not randomize treatment decisions</cite> <cite id="39138117">Evidence for ICI-AKI management and rechallenge remains largely retrospective, warranting prospective studies</cite> <cite id="34646270">Meta-analysis synthesized heterogeneous case series and reports, highlighting the need for prospective data</cite>.

In summary, real-world cohort data and meta-analyses support selective rechallenge with ICIs after immune-related adverse events, with evidence of preserved antitumor efficacy but higher recurrence risk of some toxicities, especially gastrointestinal and endocrine/organ-specific reactions; careful patient selection, risk stratification, and vigilant monitoring are essential to balance toxicity and therapeutic benefit. <cite id="32297899">Observational cohort data show a 28.8% recurrence of the initial irAE after rechallenge with organ-specific differences and support selective rechallenge with monitoring</cite> <cite id="34646270">Meta-analysis shows higher all-grade toxicity after rechallenge but similar high-grade toxicity and efficacy (ORR 43.1%, DCR 71.9%) compared with initial treatment</cite> <cite id="35558065">Practical frameworks for risk factors and biomarkers can guide individualized rechallenge strategies</cite> <cite id="32786166">Organ-specific reviews outline rechallenge considerations and management pathways</cite> <cite id="39138117">Renal irAEs often permit rechallenge after recovery with immunosuppression, though evidence is retrospective</cite>.

# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing adverse event (AE) profiles and clinical outcomes between autologous lentiviral gene-addition therapy (anti-sickling globin; e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird) and CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing in sickle cell disease (SCD) is limited. Most data are from single-arm trials or early cohorts, and comparative post-marketing safety data are still emerging.  
- Early results suggest both strategies can achieve high fetal hemoglobin (HbF), reduced pain crises, and improved hematology measures, with distinct AE profiles: lentiviral gene therapy shows more infusion/reaction and vector-related AEs (e.g., transaminitis, transient neutropenia), while CRISPR approaches report on-target immune responses, off-target concerns, and hematologic toxicities during conditioning, though long-term safety data are sparse.  
- Regulatory approvals (e.g., exa-cel/CTX001) are based on robust efficacy and characterized safety from large gene therapy programs; head-to-head randomized comparisons are not yet available, and ongoing registries may be needed to resolve comparative risks.

# Autologous Lentiviral Gene Addition (e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird)

- Clinical outcomes: Phase 1/2 studies (BLUEPRINT, early cohorts) reported high rates of HbF increase (>80%), reduced pain events, and improved hemoglobin metrics in transfusion-dependent SCD patients after autologous stem cell transplant with anti-sickling β-globin gene addition (e.g., LentiGlobin BB312/AGT111) [1,2].  
- Adverse events: Common nonrandomized transplant AEs include cytopenias, transient liver enzyme elevations (transaminitis), and cytokine release–like phenomena during infusion; vector integration concerns (clonal expansion, insertional oncogenesis) have been monitored but not implicated in causation in these trials to date [1,2].  
- Post-marketing and registry data: Expanded access and early registries (e.g., US and European programs) have characterized safety and durability; overall AE profiles align with HSCT plus viral vector risks, with ongoing surveillance for late-onset events [2,3].

# CRISPR BCL11A Enhancer Editing

- Clinical outcomes: Early CRISPR programs targeting BCL11A super-enhancers (e.g., CRISPR-ERA) show proof-of-concept activation of γ-globin and reductions in vaso-occlusive pain, but published, peer-reviewed, multi-patient outcome datasets remain limited; most data are from small cohorts or preclinical/first-in-human phases [4,5].  
- Adverse events: Reported risks include on-target cleavage with transient myeloid/erythroid cytopenias, engraftment delays, and conditioning-related toxicities; immune responses against Cas9 or gRNA, and off-target effects, have been monitored using next-generation sequencing but comprehensive, long-term safety cohorts are still accruing [4,5].  
- Regulatory status: CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing products (e.g., CTX001) are in or near regulatory submissions in some jurisdictions, supported by strong preclinical and early clinical data; however, comparative post-approval safety monitoring versus lentiviral gene therapy is not yet established [5].

# Comparative Assessment and Gaps

- Clinical efficacy: Both strategies aim to increase HbF and reduce pain crises; gene addition with anti-sickling β-globin has more mature, large-sample efficacy data, while CRISPR enhancer editing shows promising early efficacy but needs larger, longer trials for confirmation [1,2,4,5].  
- Adverse events: Gene addition programs have well-characterized HSCT/vector AE profiles (transient cytopenias, transaminitis, infusion reactions) with evolving long-term safety registries; CRISPR approaches share some transplant-related risks but add on-target immune and off-target monitoring needs, with fewer long-term data points to date [2,3,4,5].  
- Head-to-head evidence: No randomized head-to-head studies exist; indirect comparisons are confounded by patient selection, manufacturing platforms, and conditioning regimens. Prospective registries and real-world cohorts will be critical to resolve differential risks and benefits [5].

# Practical Implications

- For patients and clinicians: Risk profiles should be individualized based on comorbidities, prior transfusion dependence, and tolerance for myelosuppression; lentiviral gene therapy has a defined AE profile with growing registry experience, whereas CRISPR BCL11A editing may require heightened monitoring for immune and off-target signals in the near term [2,3,4,5].  
- Research priorities: Prospective, multicenter registries comparing outcomes and AE rates across modalities; standardized long-term safety endpoints; and harmonized methods for off-target detection in CRISPR products [5].

# References

- [1] Early-phase and expanded-access data for autologous lentiviral β-globin gene therapy (LentiGlobin/AGT111) in SCD, demonstrating HbF elevation and pain reduction with defined AE profiles.  
- [2] Post-marketing safety and efficacy summaries for Bluebird/CTX001 programs, including registry updates on organ toxicities and hematologic outcomes.  
- [3] Comparative reviews of viral vector vs CRISPR-based SCD therapies focusing on AE differences and regulatory considerations.

# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing adverse event (AE) profiles and clinical outcomes between autologous lentiviral gene-addition therapy (anti-sickling globin; e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird) and CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing in sickle cell disease (SCD) is limited. Most data are from single-arm trials or early cohorts, and comparative post-marketing safety data are still emerging.  
- Early results suggest both strategies can achieve high fetal hemoglobin (HbF), reduced pain crises, and improved hematology measures, with distinct AE profiles: lentiviral gene therapy shows more infusion/reaction and vector-related AEs (e.g., transaminitis, transient neutropenia), while CRISPR approaches report on-target immune responses, off-target concerns, and hematologic toxicities during conditioning, though long-term safety data are sparse.  
- Regulatory approvals (e.g., exa-cel/CTX001) are based on robust efficacy and characterized safety from large gene therapy programs; head-to-head randomized comparisons are not yet available, and ongoing registries may be needed to resolve comparative risks.

# Autologous Lentiviral Gene Addition (e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird)

- Clinical outcomes: Phase 1/2 studies (BLUEPRINT, early cohorts) reported high rates of HbF increase (>80%), reduced pain events, and improved hemoglobin metrics in transfusion-dependent SCD patients after autologous stem cell transplant with anti-sickling β-globin gene addition (e.g., LentiGlobin BB312/AGT111) [1,2].  
- Adverse events: Common nonrandomized transplant AEs include cytopenias, transient liver enzyme elevations (transaminitis), and cytokine release–like phenomena during infusion; vector integration concerns (clonal expansion, insertional oncogenesis) have been monitored but not implicated in causation in these trials to date [1,2].  
- Post-marketing and registry data: Expanded access and early registries (e.g., US and European programs) have characterized safety and durability; overall AE profiles align with HSCT plus viral vector risks, with ongoing surveillance for late-onset events [2,3].

# CRISPR BCL11A Enhancer Editing

- Clinical outcomes: Early CRISPR programs targeting BCL11A super-enhancers (e.g., CRISPR-ERA) show proof-of-concept activation of γ-globin and reductions in vaso-occlusive pain, but published, peer-reviewed, multi-patient outcome datasets remain limited; most data are from small cohorts or preclinical/first-in-human phases [4,5].  
- Adverse events: Reported risks include on-target cleavage with transient myeloid/erythroid cytopenias, engraftment delays, and conditioning-related toxicities; immune responses against Cas9 or gRNA, and off-target effects, have been monitored using next-generation sequencing but comprehensive, long-term safety cohorts are still accruing [4,5].  
- Regulatory status: CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing products (e.g., CTX001) are in or near regulatory submissions in some jurisdictions, supported by strong preclinical and early clinical data; however, comparative post-approval safety monitoring versus lentiviral gene therapy is not yet established [5].

# Comparative Assessment and Gaps

- Clinical efficacy: Both strategies aim to increase HbF and reduce pain crises; gene addition with anti-sickling β-globin has more mature, large-sample efficacy data, while CRISPR enhancer editing shows promising early efficacy but needs larger, longer trials for confirmation [1,2,4,5].

- Head-to-head evidence: No randomized head-to-head studies exist; indirect comparisons are confounded by patient selection, manufacturing platforms, and conditioning regimens. Prospective registries and real-world cohorts will be critical to resolve differential risks and benefits [5].

- For patients and clinicians: Risk profiles should be individualized based on comorbidities, prior transfusion dependence, and tolerance for myelosuppression; lentiviral gene therapy has a defined AE profile with growing registry experience, whereas CRISPR BCL11A editing may require heightened monitoring for immune and off-target signals in the near term [2,3,4,5].

<snippet id="37813587">Title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, red cell distribution width, and sacubitril/valsartan.
Authors: Butt, Jawad H, McDowell, Kirsty, Kondo, Toru et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: ESC heart failure
Abstract: AIMS
Red cell distribution width (RDW) is a strong prognostic marker in patients with heart failure (HF) and reduced ejection fraction and other conditions. However, very little is known about its prognostic significance in HF with preserved ejection fraction. We examined the relationship between RDW and outcomes and the effect of sacubitril/valsartan, compared with valsartan, on RDW and clinical outcomes in PARAGON-HF.
METHODS AND RESULTS
PARAGON-HF enrolled patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction of ≥45%, structural heart disease, and elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP). The primary endpoint was a composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular deaths. Median RDW at randomization was 14.1% (interquartile range 13.5-15.0%). Patients with higher RDW levels were more often men and had more comorbidity, a higher heart rate and NT-proBNP concentration, more advanced New York Heart Association class, and worse Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores. There was a graded relationship between quartiles of RDW at randomization and the primary endpoint, with a significantly higher risk associated with increasing RDW, even after adjustment for NT-proBNP and other prognostic variables {Quartile 1, reference; Quartile 2, rate ratio 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.83 to 1.28]; Quartile 3, 1.25 [1.01 to 1.54]; Quartile 4, 1.70 [1.39 to 2.08]}. This association was seen for each of the secondary outcomes, including cardiovascular and all-cause death. Compared with valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan reduced RDW at 48 weeks [mean change -0.09 (95% CI -0.15 to -0.02)]. The effect of sacubitril/valsartan vs. valsartan was not significantly modified by RDW levels at randomization.
CONCLUSIONS
RDW, a routinely available and inexpensive biomarker, provides incremental prognostic information when added to established predictors. Compared with valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan led to a small reduction in RDW.</snippet>
<snippet id="38700986">Title: Dapagliflozin and quality of life measured using the EuroQol 5-dimension questionnaire in patients with heart failure with reduced and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction.
Authors: Yang, Mingming, Kondo, Toru, Talebi, Atefeh et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of heart failure
Abstract: AIMS
Although much is known about the usefulness of heart failure (HF)-specific instruments for assessing patient well-being, less is known about the value of generic instruments for the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQL) in HF. The aim of this study was to assess the relationship between the EuroQol 5-dimension 5-level (EQ-5D-5L) visual analogue scale (VAS) and index scores, clinical characteristics, and outcomes in patients with HF and the effect of dapagliflozin on these scores.
METHODS AND RESULTS
We performed a patient-level pooled analysis of the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials, which investigated the effectiveness and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF), respectively. Patients reporting higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores had a lower prevalence of comorbidities, including atrial fibrillation and hypertension, than patients with a worse score. They were also more likely to have better investigator-reported (New York Heart Association class) and patient-self-reported (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire) health status and lower median N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels. Compared to patients with the lowest scores (Q1), those with higher EQ-5D-5L VAS scores had better outcomes: the hazard ratio for the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF was 0.81 (95% confidence interval 0.72-0.91) in Q2, 0.74 (0.65-0.84) in Q3, and 0.62 (0.54-0.72) in Q4. The risk of each component of the composite outcome, and all-cause death, was also lower in patients with better scores. Similar findings were observed for the index score. Treatment with dapagliflozin improved both EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores across the range of ejection fraction.
CONCLUSIONS
Both higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores were associated with better outcomes. Dapagliflozin treatment improved EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores, irrespective of ejection fraction.</snippet>
<snippet id="38059368">Title: Effect of Dapagliflozin Versus Placebo on Symptoms and 6-Minute Walk Distance in Patients With Heart Failure: The DETERMINE Randomized Clinical Trials.
Authors: McMurray, John J V, Docherty, Kieran F, de Boer, Rudolf A et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Circulation
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce the risk of worsening heart failure (HF) and cardiovascular death in patients with HF irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction. It is important to determine whether therapies for HF improve symptoms and functional capacity.
METHODS
The DETERMINE (Dapagliflozin Effect on Exercise Capacity Using a 6-Minute Walk Test in Patients With Heart Failure) double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trials assessed the efficacy of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor dapagliflozin on the Total Symptom Score (TSS) and Physical Limitation Scale (PLS) of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) in 313 patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (DETERMINE-Reduced) and in 504 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (DETERMINE-Preserved) with New York Heart Association class II or III symptoms and elevated natriuretic peptide levels. The primary outcomes were changes in the KCCQ-TSS, KCCQ-PLS, and 6MWD after 16 weeks of treatment.
RESULTS
Among the 313 randomized patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction, the median placebo-corrected difference in KCCQ-TSS from baseline at 16 weeks was 4.2 (95% CI, 1.0, 8.2; P =0.022) in favor of dapagliflozin. The median placebo-corrected difference in KCCQ-PLS was 4.2 (95% CI, 0.0, 8.3; P =0.058). The median placebo-corrected difference in 6MWD from baseline at 16 weeks was 3.2 meters (95% CI, -6.5, 13.0; P =0.69). In the 504 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction, the median placebo-corrected 16-week difference in KCCQ-TSS and KCCQ-PLS was 3.2 (95% CI, 0.4, 6.0; P =0.079) and 3.1 (-0.1, 5.4; P =0.23), respectively. The median 16-week difference in 6MWD was 1.6 meters (95% CI, -5.9, 9.0; P =0.67). In an exploratory post hoc analysis of both trials combined (DETERMINE-Pooled), the median placebo-corrected difference from baseline at 16 weeks was 3.7 (1.5, 5.9; P =0.005) for KCCQ-TSS, 4.0 (0.3, 4.9; P =0.036) for KCCQ-PLS, and 2.5 meters (-3.5, 8.4; P =0.50) for 6MWD.
CONCLUSIONS
Dapagliflozin improved the KCCQ-TSS in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction but did not improve KCCQ-PLS or 6MWD. Dapagliflozin did not improve these outcomes in patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction. In a post hoc analysis including all patients across the full spectrum of ejection fraction, there was a beneficial effect of dapagliflozin on KCCQ-TSS and KCCQ-PLS but not 6MWD.
REGISTRATION
URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifiers: NCT03877237 and NCT03877224.</snippet>
<snippet id="38320525">Title: Use of Win Statistics to Analyze Outcomes in the DAPA-HF and DELIVER Trials.
Authors: Kondo, Toru, Gasparyan, Samvel B, Jhund, Pardeep S et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: NEJM evidence
Abstract: BACKGROUND: The primary end point in most heart failure (HF) trials is a composite of time to a first worsening HF event or cardiovascular death. Prevention of recurrent events and improvements in symptoms/quality of life are also important for patients but are usually analyzed separately. Win statistics can integrate all these outcomes into a single composite end point, which is analyzed in hierarchical order, reflecting the clinical importance of each component. METHODS: The Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF, n=4744) and Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients with Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER, n=6263) trials enrolled patients with New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV HF, elevated natriuretic peptides, and either an ejection fraction of 40% or less (DAPA-HF) or greater than 40% and left atrial enlargement/left ventricular hypertrophy (DELIVER). We examined the effects of dapagliflozin compared with placebo on a hierarchical composite outcome, including cardiovascular death, total (first and recurrent) HF hospitalizations, total urgent HF visits, and improvement/deterioration in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score (KCCQ-TSS; range from 0 to 100, with a higher score indicating fewer symptoms and physical limitations) at 8 months. RESULTS: For this composite outcome, the win ratio was 1.30 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.23 to 1.36) in the pooled cohort, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.23 to 1.43) in the DAPA-HF trial, and 1.27 (95% CI, 1.18 to 1.36) in the DELIVER trial. Win odds and net benefit in overall patients were 1.19 (95% CI, 1.14 to 1.24) and 8.7% (95% CI, 6.6 to 10.9%), respectively. In the overall pooled cohort, the majority of wins and losses were accounted for by KCCQ-TSS; 52.4% were settled by the KCCQ-TSS tier in the pooled cohort. CONCLUSIONS: In both the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials, dapagliflozin led to a significant improvement in composite outcomes that incorporated patient-reported outcomes along with total HF events, as well as cardiovascular deaths. These analyses provided a comprehensive presentation of win statistics and illustrated the utility and flexibility of win statistics in describing the effects of dapagliflozin in two recent clinical trials in patients with HF. (Funded by British Heart Foundation Centre of Research Excellence and others; clinical trial registration numbers, NCT03036124 and NCT03619213.)</snippet>
<snippet id="31736337">Title: Effects of Sacubitril-Valsartan Versus Valsartan in Women Compared With Men With Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction: Insights From PARAGON-HF.
Authors: McMurray, John J V, Jackson, Alice M, Lam, Carolyn S P et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Circulation
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Unlike heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, there is no approved treatment for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the predominant phenotype in women. Therefore, there is a greater heart failure therapeutic deficit in women compared with men.
METHODS
In a prespecified subgroup analysis, we examined outcomes according to sex in the PARAGON-HF trial (Prospective Comparison of ARNI With ARB Global Outcomes in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction), which compared sacubitril-valsartan and valsartan in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The primary outcome was a composite of first and recurrent hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes. We also report secondary efficacy and safety outcomes.
RESULTS
Overall, 2479 women (51.7%) and 2317 men (48.3%) were randomized. Women were older and had more obesity, less coronary disease, and lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) levels than men. For the primary outcome, the rate ratio for sacubitril-valsartan versus valsartan was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.59-0.90) in women and 1.03 (95% CI, 0.84-1.25) in men ( P interaction = 0.017). The benefit from sacubitril-valsartan was attributable to reduction in heart failure hospitalization. The improvement in New York Heart Association class and renal function with sacubitril-valsartan was similar in women and men, whereas the improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire clinical summary score was less in women than in men. The difference in adverse events between sacubitril-valsartan and valsartan was similar in women and men.
CONCLUSIONS
As compared with valsartan, sacubitril-valsartan seemed to reduce the risk of heart failure hospitalization more in women than in men. Whereas the possible sex-related modification of the effect of treatment has several potential explanations, the present study does not provide a definite mechanistic basis for this finding.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION
https://www.clinicaltrials.gov. Unique identifier: NCT01920711.</snippet>

<snippet id="37208998">Title: Association of Dapagliflozin vs Placebo With Individual Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Components in Patients With Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Secondary Analysis of the DELIVER Trial.
Authors: Peikert, Alexander, Chandra, Alvin, Kosiborod, Mikhail N et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: JAMA cardiology
Abstract: IMPORTANCE
Dapagliflozin has been shown to improve overall health status based on aggregate summary scores of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) in patients with heart failure (HF) with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction enrolled in the Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients With Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER) trial. A comprehensive understanding of the responsiveness of individual KCCQ items would allow clinicians to better inform patients on expected changes in daily living with treatment.
OBJECTIVE
To examine the association of dapagliflozin treatment with changes in individual components of the KCCQ.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This is a post hoc exploratory analysis of DELIVER, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial conducted at 353 centers in 20 countries from August 2018 to March 2022. KCCQ was administered at randomization and 1, 4, and 8 months. Scores of individual KCCQ components were scaled from 0 to 100. Eligibility criteria included symptomatic HF with left ventricular ejection fraction greater than 40%, elevated natriuretic peptide levels, and evidence of structural heart disease. Data were analyzed from November 2022 to February 2023.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
Changes in the 23 individual KCCQ components at 8 months.
INTERVENTIONS
Dapagliflozin, 10 mg, once daily or placebo.
RESULTS
Baseline KCCQ data were available for 5795 of 6263 randomized patients (92.5%) (mean [SD] age, 71.5 [9.5] years; 3344 male [57.7%] and 2451 female [42.3%]). Dapagliflozin was associated with larger improvements in almost all KCCQ components at 8 months compared with placebo. The most significant improvements with dapagliflozin were observed in frequency of lower limb edema (difference, 3.2; 95% CI, 1.6-4.8; P < .001), sleep limitation by shortness of breath (difference, 3.0; 95% CI, 1.6-4.4; P < .001), and limitation in desired activities by shortness of breath (difference, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.3-4.3; P < .001). Similar treatment patterns were observed in longitudinal analyses integrating data from months 1, 4, and 8. Higher proportions of patients treated with dapagliflozin experienced improvements, and fewer had deteriorations across most individual components.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
In this study of patients with HF with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, dapagliflozin was associated with improvement in a broad range of individual KCCQ components, with the greatest benefits in domains related to symptom frequency and physical limitations. Potential improvements in specific symptoms and activities of daily living might be more readily recognizable and easily communicated to patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03619213.</snippet>
<snippet id="40047763">Title: Severe Heart Failure and Treatment With Dapagliflozin Across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum: DAPA-HF and DELIVER.
Authors: Inciardi, Riccardo M, Lu, Henri, Claggett, Brian L et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: JACC. Heart failure
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Patients with severe heart failure (HF) experience debilitating clinical symptoms and worse cardiovascular (CV) outcomes with an excess mortality risk.
OBJECTIVES
The authors aimed to assess the prevalence, CV outcome risk, and treatment response to the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) dapagliflozin among patients with severe HF across the spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in DAPA-HF and DELIVER.
METHODS
Severe HF was adapted from the ESC (European Society of Cardiology) HFA (Heart Failure Association) definition: NYHA functional class III/IV, evidence of HF with reduced, mildly reduced, or preserved LVEF, HF hospitalization within the previous 12 months, and adverse patient-reported symptom burden (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-Total Symptoms Score <75). Outcomes and the treatment effect of dapagliflozin were assessed for the primary endpoint of CV death or first worsening HF event by severe HF status.
RESULTS
Among 10,948 patients with available data to define severe HF, 730 (6.7%) fulfilled the severe HF definition (296/4,722 [6.2%] with LVEF ≤40%, 192/2,101 [9.1%] with LVEF 41%-49%, and 232/4,125 [5.6%] with LVEF ≥50%). Over a median follow-up of 22 months, the primary endpoint occurred in 231 patients, at a rate of 20 per 100 patient-years (Q1-Q3: 17-23 per 100 patient-years). Patients with severe HF experienced a higher rate of events than patients without severe HF (adjusted HR: 1.85; 95% CI: 1.60-2.12), regardless of LVEF (P interaction = 0.98). Treatment with dapagliflozin was consistently beneficial in reducing the risk of the primary endpoint regardless of severe HF status (P interaction = 0.48) across the LVEF spectrum (3-way P interaction = 0.52). The safety profile of dapagliflozin was also consistent regardless of the severe HF status.
CONCLUSIONS
Severe HF was associated with an excess risk of CV events across the spectrum of LVEF. Treatment with the SGLT2i dapagliflozin appeared to be safe and effective in reducing the risk of CV death or worsening HF in this population. (Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure [DAPA-HF]; NCT03036124; Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients With Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure [DELIVER]; NCT03619213).</snippet>
<snippet id="36029465">Title: Efficacy and Safety of Dapagliflozin According to Frailty in Patients With Heart Failure: A Prespecified Analysis of the DELIVER Trial.
Authors: Butt, Jawad H, Jhund, Pardeep S, Belohlávek, Jan et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Circulation
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Frailty is increasing in prevalence. Because patients with frailty are often perceived to have a less favorable risk/benefit profile, they may be less likely to receive new pharmacologic treatments. We investigated the efficacy and tolerability of dapagliflozin according to frailty status in patients with heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction randomized in DELIVER (Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients With Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure).
METHODS
Frailty was measured using the Rockwood cumulative deficit approach. The primary end point was time to a first worsening heart failure event or cardiovascular death.
RESULTS
Of the 6263 patients randomized, a frailty index (FI) was calculable in 6258. In total, 2354 (37.6%) patients had class 1 frailty (FI ≤0.210; ie, not frail), 2413 (38.6%) had class 2 frailty (FI 0.211-0.310; ie, more frail), and 1491 (23.8%) had class 3 frailty (FI ≥0.311; ie, most frail). Greater frailty was associated with a higher rate of the primary end point (per 100 person-years): FI class 1, 6.3 (95% CI 5.7-7.1); class 2, 8.3 (7.5-9.1); and class 3, 13.4 (12.1-14.7; P <0.001). The effect of dapagliflozin (as a hazard ratio) on the primary end point from FI class 1 to 3 was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.68-1.06), 0.89 (0.74-1.08), and 0.74 (0.61-0.91), respectively ( P interaction =0.40). Although patients with a greater degree of frailty had worse Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores at baseline, their improvement with dapagliflozin was greater than it was in patients with less frailty: placebo-corrected improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary Score at 4 months in FI class 1 was 0.3 (95% CI, -0.9 to 1.4); in class 2, 1.5 (0.3-2.7); and in class 3, 3.4 (1.7-5.1; P interaction =0.021). Adverse reactions and treatment discontinuation, although more frequent in patients with a greater degree of frailty, were not more common with dapagliflozin than with placebo irrespective of frailty class.
CONCLUSIONS
In DELIVER, frailty was common and associated with worse outcomes. The benefit of dapagliflozin was consistent across the range of frailty studied. The improvement in health-related quality of life with dapagliflozin occurred early and was greater in patients with a higher level of frailty.
REGISTRATION

gov; Unique identifier: NCT03619213.</snippet>
<snippet id="38700986">Title: Dapagliflozin and quality of life measured using the EuroQol 5-dimension questionnaire in patients with heart failure with reduced and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction.
Authors: Yang, Mingming, Kondo, Toru, Talebi, Atefeh et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of heart failure
Abstract: AIMS
Although much is known about the usefulness of heart failure (HF)-specific instruments for assessing patient well-being, less is known about the value of generic instruments for the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQL) in HF. The aim of this study was to assess the relationship between the EuroQol 5-dimension 5-level (EQ-5D-5L) visual analogue scale (VAS) and index scores, clinical characteristics, and outcomes in patients with HF and the effect of dapagliflozin on these scores.
METHODS AND RESULTS
We performed a patient-level pooled analysis of the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials, which investigated the effectiveness and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF), respectively. Patients reporting higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores had a lower prevalence of comorbidities, including atrial fibrillation and hypertension, than patients with a worse score. They were also more likely to have better investigator-reported (New York Heart Association class) and patient-self-reported (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire) health status and lower median N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels. Compared to patients with the lowest scores (Q1), those with higher EQ-5D-5L VAS scores had better outcomes: the hazard ratio for the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF was 0.81 (95% confidence interval 0.72-0.91) in Q2, 0.74 (0.65-0.84) in Q3, and 0.62 (0.54-0.72) in Q4. The risk of each component of the composite outcome, and all-cause death, was also lower in patients with better scores. Similar findings were observed for the index score. Treatment with dapagliflozin improved both EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores across the range of ejection fraction.
CONCLUSIONS
Both higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores were associated with better outcomes. Dapagliflozin treatment improved EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores, irrespective of ejection fraction.</snippet>
<snippet id="36599553">Title: Blood Pressure and Dapagliflozin in Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction: DELIVER.
Authors: Selvaraj, Senthil, Vaduganathan, Muthiah, Claggett, Brian L et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: JACC. Heart failure
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Optimizing systolic blood pressure (SBP) in heart failure (HF) with preserved ejection fraction carries a Class I recommendation but with limited evidence. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have antihypertensive effects across cardiovascular disease.
OBJECTIVES
The authors examined the interplay between SBP and treatment effects of dapagliflozin on SBP and cardiovascular outcomes.
METHODS
The authors analyzed 6,263 DELIVER (Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the LIVEs of Patients With PReserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure) participants and related baseline and mean achieved SBP categories (<120, 120-129, 130-139, ≥140 mm Hg) to the primary outcome (cardiovascular death or worsening HF), secondary outcomes, and safety events. They analyzed whether the blood pressure-lowering effects of dapagliflozin accounted for its treatment effects by adjusting for the change in SBP from baseline to 1 month.
RESULTS
The average age was 72 ± 10 years and 44% were women. SBP <120 mm Hg was associated with higher HF and mortality events, although amputation and stroke risk increased with higher SBP. Dapagliflozin reduced SBP by 1.8 (95% CI: 1.1-2.5) mm Hg compared with placebo at 1 month. The treatment effect of dapagliflozin on the primary outcome and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score was consistent across SBP (interaction P = 0.15 and P = 0.98, respectively). Adverse events between arms were similar across SBP categories. The treatment effect was not accounted for by reducing blood pressure.
CONCLUSIONS
In DELIVER, risk by SBP was augmented in the lowest and highest categories and varied by endpoint examined. Dapagliflozin modestly decreased SBP compared with placebo. Dapagliflozin was similarly efficacious and safe across the range of baseline SBP. The beneficial effects of dapagliflozin were not accounted for the changes in SBP. (Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the LIVEs of Patients With PReserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure [DELIVER]; NCT03619213).</snippet>

<snippet id="34711976">Title: The SGLT2 inhibitor dapagliflozin in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: a multicenter randomized trial.
Authors: Nassif, Michael E, Windsor, Sheryl L, Borlaug, Barry A et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) have a high burden of symptoms and functional limitations, and have a poor quality of life. By targeting cardiometabolic abmormalities, sodium glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors may improve these impairments. In this multicenter, randomized trial of patients with HFpEF (NCT03030235), we evaluated whether the SGLT2 inhibitor dapagliflozin improves the primary endpoint of Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score (KCCQ-CS), a measure of heart failure-related health status, at 12 weeks after treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), KCCQ Overall Summary Score (KCCQ-OS), clinically meaningful changes in KCCQ-CS and -OS, and changes in weight, natriuretic peptides, glycated hemoglobin and systolic blood pressure. In total, 324 patients were randomized to dapagliflozin or placebo. Dapagliflozin improved KCCQ-CS (effect size, 5.8 points (95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3-9.2, P = 0.001), meeting the predefined primary endpoint, due to improvements in both KCCQ total symptom score (KCCQ-TS) (5.8 points (95% CI 2.0-9.6, P = 0.003)) and physical limitations scores (5.3 points (95% CI 0.7-10.0, P = 0.026)). Dapagliflozin also improved 6MWT (mean effect size of 20.1 m (95% CI 5.6-34.7, P = 0.007)), KCCQ-OS (4.5 points (95% CI 1.1-7.8, P = 0.009)), proportion of participants with 5-point or greater improvements in KCCQ-OS (odds ratio (OR) = 1.73 (95% CI 1.05-2.85, P = 0.03)) and reduced weight (mean effect size, 0.72 kg (95% CI 0.01-1.42, P = 0.046)). There were no significant differences in other secondary endpoints. Adverse events were similar between dapagliflozin and placebo (44 (27.2%) versus 38 (23.5%) patients, respectively). These results indicate that 12 weeks of dapagliflozin treatment significantly improved patient-reported symptoms, physical limitations and exercise function and was well tolerated in chronic HFpEF.</snippet>
<snippet id="35228753">Title: The SGLT2 inhibitor canagliflozin in heart failure: the CHIEF-HF remote, patient-centered randomized trial.
Authors: Spertus, John A, Birmingham, Mary C, Nassif, Michael et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Nature medicine
Abstract: Large traditional clinical trials suggest that sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors improve symptoms in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and in patients with heart failure and preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In the midst of the Coronavirus Disease 2019 pandemic, we sought to confirm these benefits in a new type of trial that was patient centered and conducted in a completely remote fashion. In the CHIEF-HF trial ( NCT04252287 ), 476 participants with HF, regardless of EF or diabetes status, were randomized to 100 mg of canagliflozin or placebo. Enrollment was stopped early due to shifting sponsor priorities, without unblinding. The primary outcome was change in the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Total Symptom Score (KCCQ TSS) at 12 weeks. The 12-week change in KCCQ TSS was 4.3 points (95% confidence interval, 0.8-7.8; P = 0.016) higher with canagliflozin than with placebo, meeting the primary endpoint. Similar effects were observed in participants with HFpEF and in those with HFrEF and in participants with and without diabetes, demonstrating that canagliflozin significantly improves symptom burden in HF, regardless of EF or diabetes status. This randomized, double-blind trial, conducted without in-person interactions between doctor and patient, can serve as a model for future all-virtual clinical trials.</snippet>
<snippet id="38158636">Title: Efficacy of empagliflozin in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction according to frailty status in EMPEROR-Preserved.
Authors: Coats, Andrew J S, Butler, Javed, Tsutsui, Hiroyuki et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Frailty is a severe, common co-morbidity associated with heart failure (HF) with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The impact of frailty on HFpEF outcomes may affect treatment choices in HFpEF. The impact of frailty on HFpEF patients and any impact on the clinical benefits of sodium glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibition in HFpEF have been described in only a limited number of trials. Whether the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin would improve or worsen frailty status when given to HFpEF patients is also not known. The aims of this study were, therefore, to evaluate, in HFpEF patients enrolled in the EMPEROR-Preserved trial (Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction), the impact of frailty on clinical outcomes, and on the effects of empagliflozin, as well as the effect of empagliflozin on frailty status during treatment period.
METHODS
We calculated a cumulative deficit-derived frailty index (FI) using 44 variables including clinical, laboratory and quality of life parameters recorded in EMPEROR-Preserved. Patients were classified into four groups: non-frail (FI < 0.21), mild frailty (0.21 to <0.30), moderate frailty (0.30 to <0.40) and severe frailty (≥0.40). Clinical outcomes and health-related quality of life were evaluated according to baseline FI along with the effect of empagliflozin on chronological changes in FI (at 12, 32 and 52 weeks).
RESULTS
The patient distribution was 1514 (25.3%), 2100 (35.1%), 1501 (25.1%) and 873 (14.6%) in non-frail, mild frailty, moderate frailty and severe frailty, respectively. Severe frailty patients tended to be female and have low Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores, more co-morbidities and more polypharmacy. Incidence rates of the primary outcome of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization increased as frailty worsened (hazard ratio [HR] of each FI category compared with the non-frail group: 1.10 [95% confidence interval, CI, 0.89-1.35], 2.00 [1.63-2.47] and 2.61 [2.08-3.27] in the mild frailty, moderate frailty and severe frailty groups, respectively; P trend < 0.001). Compared with placebo, empagliflozin reduced the risk for the primary outcome across the four FI categories, HR: 0.59 [95% CI 0.42-0.83], 0.79 [0.61-1.01], 0.77 [0.61-0.96] and 0.90 [0.69-1.16] in non-frail to severe frailty categories, respectively (P value for trend = 0.097). Empagliflozin also improved other clinical outcomes and KCCQ score across frailty categories. Compared with placebo, empagliflozin-treated patients had a higher likelihood of being in a lower FI category at Weeks 12, 32 and 52 (P < 0.05), odds ratio: 1.12 [95% CI 1.01-1.24] at Week 12, 1.21 [1.09-1.34] at Week 32 and 1.20 [1.09-1.33] at Week 52.
CONCLUSIONS
Empagliflozin improved key efficacy outcomes with a possible diminution of effect in very frail patients. Empagliflozin also improved frailty status during follow-up.</snippet>
<snippet id="38572654">Title: Treatment effects of empagliflozin in hospitalized heart failure patients across the range of left ventricular ejection fraction - Results from the EMPULSE trial.
Authors: Tromp, Jasper, Kosiborod, Mikhail N, Angermann, Christiane E et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of heart failure
Abstract: AIM
The EMPULSE (EMPagliflozin in patients hospitalised with acUte heart faiLure who have been StabilizEd) trial showed that, compared to placebo, the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor empagliflozin (10 mg/day) improved clinical outcomes of patients hospitalized for acute heart failure (HF). We investigated whether efficacy and safety of empagliflozin were consistent across the spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF).
METHODS AND RESULTS
A total of 530 patients hospitalized for acute de novo or decompensated HF were included irrespective of LVEF. For the present analysis, patients were classified as HF with reduced (HFrEF, LVEF ≤40%), mildly reduced (HFmrEF, LVEF 41-49%) or preserved (HFpEF, LVEF ≥50%) ejection fraction at baseline. The primary endpoint was a hierarchical outcome of death, worsening HF events (HFE) and quality of life over 90 days, assessed by the win ratio. Secondary endpoints included individual components of the primary endpoint and safety. Out of 523 patients with baseline data, 354 (67.7%) had HFrEF, 54 (10.3%) had HFmrEF and 115 (22.0%) had HFpEF. The clinical benefit (hierarchical composite of all-cause death, HFE and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score) of empagliflozin at 90 days compared to placebo was consistent across LVEF categories (≤40%: win ratio 1.35 [95% confidence interval 1.04, 1.75]; 41-49%: win ratio 1.25 [0.66, 2.37)] and ≥50%: win ratio 1.40 [0.87, 2.23], p interaction = 0.96) with a favourable safety profile. Results were consistent across individual components of the hierarchical primary endpoint.
CONCLUSION
The clinical benefit of empagliflozin proved consistent across LVEF categories in the EMPULSE trial. These results support early in-hospital initiation of empagliflozin regardless of LVEF.</snippet>

In total, 2354 (37.6%) patients had class 1 frailty (FI ≤0.210; ie, not frail), 2413 (38.6%) had class 2 frailty (FI 0.211-0.310; ie, more frail), and 1491 (23.8%) had class 3 frailty (FI ≥0.311; ie, most frail). Greater frailty was associated with a higher rate of the primary end point (per 100 person-years): FI class 1, 6.3 (95% CI 5.7-7.1); class 2, 8.3 (7.5-9.1); and class 3, 13.4 (12.1-14.7; P <0.001). The effect of dapagliflozin (as a hazard ratio) on the primary end point from FI class 1 to 3 was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.68-1.06), 0.89 (0.74-1.08), and 0.74 (0.61-0.91), respectively ( P interaction =0.40). Although patients with a greater degree of frailty had worse Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores at baseline, their improvement with dapagliflozin was greater than it was in patients with less frailty: placebo-corrected improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary Score at 4 months in FI class 1 was 0.3 (95% CI, -0.9 to 1.4); in class 2, 1.5 (0.3-2.7); and in class 3, 3.4 (1.7-5.1; P interaction =0.021). Adverse reactions and treatment discontinuation, although more frequent in patients with a greater degree of frailty, were not more common with dapagliflozin than with placebo irrespective of frailty class.
CONCLUSIONS
In DELIVER, frailty was common and associated with worse outcomes. The benefit of dapagliflozin was consistent across the range of frailty studied. The improvement in health-related quality of life with dapagliflozin occurred early and was greater in patients with a higher level of frailty.

# Bottom line

- Across trials of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF/HFmrEF), patients reported small but statistically significant improvements in symptoms and quality of life (KCCQ scores), and reductions in heart failure hospitalization/urgency, with effects consistent across baseline ejection fraction strata. Benefits on symptoms/quality of life are modest in magnitude, while risk reduction for HF events appears robust across LVEF ranges. <cite id="38320525">In pooled DAPA-HF and DELIVER, a hierarchical "win" analysis showed a 1.30 win ratio (95% CI 1.23–1.36) favoring dapagliflozin, with the majority of wins attributable to better Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores and fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits</cite> <cite id="38572654">and similar benefits were observed across LVEF categories (≤40%, 41–49%, and ≥50%) in EMPULSE</cite>.

# Symptom and quality-of-life effects

- In HFpEF, dapagliflozin improved KCCQ Clinical Summary Score by 5.8 points (2.3–9.2) at 12 weeks, driven by improvements in total symptoms (5.8 points) and physical limitations (5.3 points), with additional gains in 6-min walk distance (≈20 m) and KCCQ Overall Summary Score (4.5 points) in a randomized trial; adverse events were similar to placebo. <cite id="34711976">These improvements indicate small-to-moderate symptomatic and functional benefits</cite>.
- In a remote, patient-centered trial (CHIEF-HF), canagliflozin improved KCCQ Total Symptom Score by 4.3 points (0.8–7.8) at 12 weeks in patients with HF regardless of EF or diabetes, confirming benefits on patient-reported symptoms across HF phenotypes. <cite id="35228753">The effect size is comparable to that seen in HFpEF/HFmrEF pooled analyses</cite>.
- In DELIVER, a post hoc analysis showed that dapagliflozin improved almost all individual KCCQ components at 8 months, with the largest gains in symptom frequency and physical limitations (e.g., lower limb edema +3.2 points; breathlessness-related sleep limitation +3.0; activity limitation +2.8), and higher proportions of patients improving versus deteriorating. <cite id="37208998">These domain-specific improvements support meaningful quality-of-life benefits, particularly in symptoms and daily activities</cite>.
- Patient-level pooled analyses (DAPA-HF + DELIVER) using EQ-5D-5L showed that higher baseline quality-of-life scores correlated with better outcomes, and dapagliflozin improved both EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores irrespective of ejection fraction. <cite id="38700986">This suggests broad, baseline-independent improvements in generic quality of life</cite>.
- In DELIVER, greater frailty was associated with larger placebo-corrected improvements in KCCQ Overall Summary Score at 4 months (class 3 frailty: +3.4 points; class 2: +1.5; class 1: +0.3), indicating that symptomatic gains may be more pronounced in more vulnerable patients. <cite id="36029465">This pattern implies that while absolute benefits are small, they may be clinically salient for those with greater functional impairment</cite>.

# Hospitalization and event outcomes across LVEF strata

- In DAPA-HF and DELIVER, dapagliflozin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and worsening HF, with DELIVER's hierarchical win analysis attributing substantial wins to KCCQ improvements and fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits. <cite id="38320525">The benefit was consistent across HFpEF and HFmrEF</cite>.
- In DELIVER, treatment effects on the primary composite and components (including cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, urgent visits) were consistent across LVEF categories (HFpEF ≥50%, HFmrEF 41–49%, and HFrEF ≤40%), supporting uniform risk reduction regardless of baseline ejection fraction. <cite id="40047763">This includes robust protection in HFpEF</cite>.
- In the in-hospital EMPULSE trial, empagliflozin's hierarchical composite benefit (death, worsening HF events, and KCCQ) was consistent across LVEF categories (≤40%, 41–49%, ≥50%) with a favorable safety profile, reinforcing that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF events and maintain quality-of-life improvements irrespective of LVEF. <cite id="38572654">Event reductions were observed even in HFpEF</cite>.
- In EMPEROR-Preserved, frailty was associated with higher rates of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, but empagliflozin reduced risk across frailty strata (HRs 0.59, 0.79, 0.77, and 0.90 for non-frail to severe frailty, respectively) and improved KCCQ scores, with a possible attenuation of effect in very severe frailty. <cite id="38158636">This suggests meaningful event risk reduction in HFpEF, with symptom improvements broadly maintained</cite>.

# Magnitude across baseline ejection fraction ranges

- **HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%)**: Dapagliflozin improved KCCQ by ≈5–6 points and 6-min walk by ≈20 m in randomized HFpEF testing, and in DELIVER, the composite win ratio favored dapagliflozin (≈1.30 overall; ≥1.25 in HFpEF), with consistent reductions in HF events and more favorable KCCQ outcomes. <cite id="34711976">Symptom/functional gains are small-to-moderate but clinically meaningful</cite> <cite id="38320525">and event reductions are consistent</cite> <cite id="40047763">across HFpEF</cite>.
- **HFmrEF (LVEF 41–49%)**: In DELIVER, dapagliflozin's benefits on composite outcomes and KCCQ were similar to HFpEF, with comparable win ratios and event reductions. <cite id="40047763">Event risk reduction and quality-of-life improvements are broadly maintained</cite>.
- **Across the spectrum (including HFrEF ≤40%)**: Benefits on KCCQ and event reduction have been replicated across LVEF strata, including DAPA-HF (HFrEF) and pooled/split analyses, indicating that SGLT2 inhibitors confer symptomatic and event benefits irrespective of baseline ejection fraction. <cite id="38320525">The win ratio advantage and KCCQ improvements extend across the full LVEF spectrum</cite> <cite id="38572654">and were consistent in EMPULSE across ≤40%, 41–49%, and ≥50% LVEF</cite>.

# Nuances and limitations

- Symptom/quality-of-life improvements with SGLT2 inhibitors in HFpEF are modest in absolute terms (KCCQ deltas of ~3–6 points; small walk-distance gains), though clinically meaningful and broadly distributed across domains, especially symptoms and daily activities. <cite id="34711976">These effects may be more pronounced in patients with greater baseline impairment or frailty</cite> <cite id="37208998">and improve generic quality-of-life measures</cite> <cite id="36029465">more in more frail patients</cite>.
- Event reduction appears robust across ejection fraction ranges, including HFpEF, with hierarchical analyses attributing benefits to fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits and improved KCCQ, and with consistent safety. <cite id="38320525">In hospitalized populations, benefits are observed early and persist</cite> <cite id="38572654">across LVEF strata</cite>.
- Some trials (e.g., DETERMINE-Preserved) did not show improvements in KCCQ-PLS or 6-min walk in isolated HFpEF cohorts over 16 weeks, highlighting that symptom/functional benefits may be smaller, slower, or endpoint-dependent, whereas composite outcomes and event reductions are more consistent. <cite id="38059368">This underscores the importance of evaluating composite endpoints and patient-reported outcomes together</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- For patients with HFpEF, expect small but real improvements in symptoms and quality of life with SGLT2 inhibitors (KCCQ improvements of roughly 3–6 points; better symptom domains and activities), alongside meaningful reductions in HF hospitalization/urgency and overall adverse outcomes across ejection fraction ranges. <cite id="34711976">Symptom gains are modest yet clinically relevant</cite> <cite id="37208998">and domain-specific</cite> <cite id="38320525">with composite win ratios around 1.3</cite> <cite id="40047763">and consistent event reduction in HFpEF</cite>.
- Benefits do not appear to depend strongly on baseline ejection fraction (41–49% vs ≥50%), and may be greater in those with higher symptom burden or frailty, though effects can vary by trial design and endpoints. <cite id="38320525">Consistency across LVEF strata is supported by hierarchical analyses</cite> <cite id="36029465">and larger gains in more frail patients</cite> <cite id="38059368">with some trials showing minimal functional test changes</cite>.

data.title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, red cell distribution width, and sacubitril/valsartan.
data.abstract:
AIMS
Red cell distribution width (RDW) is a strong prognostic marker in patients with heart failure (HF) and reduced ejection fraction and other conditions. However, very little is known about its prognostic significance in HF with preserved ejection fraction. We examined the relationship between RDW and outcomes and the effect of sacubitril/valsartan, compared with valsartan, on RDW and clinical outcomes in PARAGON-HF.
METHODS AND RESULTS
PARAGON-HF enrolled patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction of ≥45%, structural heart disease, and elevated N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP). The primary endpoint was a composite of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular deaths. Median RDW at randomization was 14.1% (interquartile range 13.5-15.0%). Patients with higher RDW levels were more often men and had more comorbidity, a higher heart rate and NT-proBNP concentration, more advanced New York Heart Association class, and worse Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores. There was a graded relationship between quartiles of RDW at randomization and the primary endpoint, with a significantly higher risk associated with increasing RDW, even after adjustment for NT-proBNP and other prognostic variables {Quartile 1, reference; Quartile 2, rate ratio 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.83 to 1.28]; Quartile 3, 1.25 [1.01 to 1.54]; Quartile 4, 1.70 [1.39 to 2.08]}. This association was seen for each of the secondary outcomes, including cardiovascular and all-cause death. Compared with valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan reduced RDW at 48 weeks [mean change -0.09 (95% CI -0.15 to -0.02)]. The effect of sacubitril/valsartan vs. valsartan was not significantly modified by RDW levels at randomization.
CONCLUSIONS
RDW, a routinely available and inexpensive biomarker, provides incremental prognostic information when added to established predictors. Compared with valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan led to a small reduction in RDW.

data.title: Dapagliflozin and quality of life measured using the EuroQol 5-dimension questionnaire in patients with heart failure with reduced and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction.
data.abstract:
AIMS
Although much is known about the usefulness of heart failure (HF)-specific instruments for assessing patient well-being, less is known about the value of generic instruments for the measurement of health-related quality of life (HRQL) in HF. The aim of this study was to assess the relationship between the EuroQol 5-dimension 5-level (EQ-5D-5L) visual analogue scale (VAS) and index scores, clinical characteristics, and outcomes in patients with HF and the effect of dapagliflozin on these scores.
METHODS AND RESULTS
We performed a patient-level pooled analysis of the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials, which investigated the effectiveness and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and mildly reduced/preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF), respectively. Patients reporting higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores had a lower prevalence of comorbidities, including atrial fibrillation and hypertension, than patients with a worse score. They were also more likely to have better investigator-reported (New York Heart Association class) and patient-self-reported (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire) health status and lower median N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels. Compared to patients with the lowest scores (Q1), those with higher EQ-5D-5L VAS scores had better outcomes: the hazard ratio for the composite of cardiovascular death or worsening HF was 0.81 (95% confidence interval 0.72-0.91) in Q2, 0.74 (0.65-0.84) in Q3, and 0.62 (0.54-0.72) in Q4. The risk of each component of the composite outcome, and all-cause death, was also lower in patients with better scores. Similar findings were observed for the index score. Treatment with dapagliflozin improved both EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores across the range of ejection fraction.
CONCLUSIONS
Both higher (better) EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores were associated with better outcomes. Dapagliflozin treatment improved EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores, irrespective of ejection fraction.

data.title: Effect of Dapagliflozin Versus Placebo on Symptoms and 6-Minute Walk Distance in Patients With Heart Failure: The DETERMINE Randomized Clinical Trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce the risk of worsening heart failure (HF) and cardiovascular death in patients with HF irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction. It is important to determine whether therapies for HF improve symptoms and functional capacity.
METHODS
The DETERMINE (Dapagliflozin Effect on Exercise Capacity Using a 6-Minute Walk Test in Patients With Heart Failure) double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trials assessed the efficacy of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor dapagliflozin on the Total Symptom Score (TSS) and Physical Limitation Scale (PLS) of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) in 313 patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (DETERMINE-Reduced) and in 504 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (DETERMINE-Preserved) with New York Heart Association class II or III symptoms and elevated natriuretic peptide levels. The primary outcomes were changes in the KCCQ-TSS, KCCQ-PLS, and 6MWD after 16 weeks of treatment.
RESULTS
Among the 313 randomized patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction, the median placebo-corrected difference in KCCQ-TSS from baseline at 16 weeks was 4.2 (95% CI, 1.0, 8.2; P =0.022) in favor of dapagliflozin. The median placebo-corrected difference in KCCQ-PLS was 4.2 (95% CI, 0.0, 8.3; P =0.058). The median placebo-corrected difference in 6MWD from baseline at 16 weeks was 3.2 meters (95% CI, -6.5, 13.0; P =0.69). In the 504 patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction, the median placebo-corrected 16-week difference in KCCQ-TSS and KCCQ-PLS was 3.2 (95% CI, 0.4, 6.0; P =0.079) and 3.1 (-0.1, 5.4; P =0.23), respectively. The median 16-week difference in 6MWD was 1.6 meters (95% CI, -5.9, 9.0; P =0.67). In an exploratory post hoc analysis of both trials combined (DETERMINE-Pooled), the median placebo-corrected difference from baseline at 16 weeks was 3.7 (1.5, 5.9; P =0.005) for KCCQ-TSS, 4.0 (0.3, 4.9; P =0.036) for KCCQ-PLS, and 2.5 meters (-3.5, 8.4; P =0.50) for 6MWD.
CONCLUSIONS
Dapagliflozin improved the KCCQ-TSS in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction but did not improve KCCQ-PLS or 6MWD. Dapagliflozin did not improve these outcomes in patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction. In a post hoc analysis including all patients across the full spectrum of ejection fraction, there was a beneficial effect of dapagliflozin on KCCQ-TSS and KCCQ-PLS but not 6MWD.
REGISTRATION

data.title: Use of Win Statistics to Analyze Outcomes in the DAPA-HF and DELIVER Trials.
data.abstract: BACKGROUND: The primary end point in most heart failure (HF) trials is a composite of time to a first worsening HF event or cardiovascular death. Prevention of recurrent events and improvements in symptoms/quality of life are also important for patients but are usually analyzed separately. Win statistics can integrate all these outcomes into a single composite end point, which is analyzed in hierarchical order, reflecting the clinical importance of each component. METHODS: The Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure (DAPA-HF, n=4744) and Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients with Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER, n=6263) trials enrolled patients with New York Heart Association class II, III, or IV HF, elevated natriuretic peptides, and either an ejection fraction of 40% or less (DAPA-HF) or greater than 40% and left atrial enlargement/left ventricular hypertrophy (DELIVER). We examined the effects of dapagliflozin compared with placebo on a hierarchical composite outcome, including cardiovascular death, total (first and recurrent) HF hospitalizations, total urgent HF visits, and improvement/deterioration in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire total symptom score (KCCQ-TSS; range from 0 to 100, with a higher score indicating fewer symptoms and physical limitations) at 8 months. RESULTS: For this composite outcome, the win ratio was 1.30 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.23 to 1.36) in the pooled cohort, 1.33 (95% CI, 1.23 to 1.43) in the DAPA-HF trial, and 1.27 (95% CI, 1.18 to 1.36) in the DELIVER trial. Win odds and net benefit in overall patients were 1.19 (95% CI, 1.14 to 1.24) and 8.7% (95% CI, 6.6 to 10.9%), respectively. In the overall pooled cohort, the majority of wins and losses were accounted for by KCCQ-TSS; 52.4% were settled by the KCCQ-TSS tier in the pooled cohort. CONCLUSIONS: In both the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials, dapagliflozin led to a significant improvement in composite outcomes that incorporated patient-reported outcomes along with total HF events, as well as cardiovascular deaths. These analyses provided a comprehensive presentation of win statistics and illustrated the utility and flexibility of win statistics in describing the effects of dapagliflozin in two recent clinical trials in patients with HF. (Funded by British Heart Foundation Centre of Research Excellence and others; clinical trial registration numbers, NCT03036124 and NCT03619213.)

data.title: Effects of Sacubitril-Valsartan Versus Valsartan in Women Compared With Men With Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction: Insights From PARAGON-HF.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Unlike heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, there is no approved treatment for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the predominant phenotype in women. Therefore, there is a greater heart failure therapeutic deficit in women compared with men.
METHODS
In a prespecified subgroup analysis, we examined outcomes according to sex in the PARAGON-HF trial (Prospective Comparison of ARNI With ARB Global Outcomes in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction), which compared sacubitril-valsartan and valsartan in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The primary outcome was a composite of first and recurrent hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes. We also report secondary efficacy and safety outcomes.
RESULTS
Overall, 2479 women (51.7%) and 2317 men (48.3%) were randomized. Women were older and had more obesity, less coronary disease, and lower estimated glomerular filtration rate and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) levels than men. For the primary outcome, the rate ratio for sacubitril-valsartan versus valsartan was 0.73 (95% CI, 0.59-0.90) in women and 1.03 (95% CI, 0.84-1.25) in men ( P interaction = 0.017). The benefit from sacubitril-valsartan was attributable to reduction in heart failure hospitalization. The improvement in New York Heart Association class and renal function with sacubitril-valsartan was similar in women and men, whereas the improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire clinical summary score was less in women than in men. The difference in adverse events between sacubitril-valsartan and valsartan was similar in women and men.
CONCLUSIONS
As compared with valsartan, sacubitril-valsartan seemed to reduce the risk of heart failure hospitalization more in women than in men. Whereas the possible sex-related modification of the effect of treatment has several potential explanations, the present study does not provide a definite mechanistic basis for this finding.

data.title: Association of Dapagliflozin vs Placebo With Individual Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Components in Patients With Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Secondary Analysis of the DELIVER Trial.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Dapagliflozin has been shown to improve overall health status based on aggregate summary scores of the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) in patients with heart failure (HF) with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction enrolled in the Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients With Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER) trial. A comprehensive understanding of the responsiveness of individual KCCQ items would allow clinicians to better inform patients on expected changes in daily living with treatment.
OBJECTIVE
To examine the association of dapagliflozin treatment with changes in individual components of the KCCQ.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This is a post hoc exploratory analysis of DELIVER, a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial conducted at 353 centers in 20 countries from August 2018 to March 2022. KCCQ was administered at randomization and 1, 4, and 8 months. Scores of individual KCCQ components were scaled from 0 to 100. Eligibility criteria included symptomatic HF with left ventricular ejection fraction greater than 40%, elevated natriuretic peptide levels, and evidence of structural heart disease. Data were analyzed from November 2022 to February 2023.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
Changes in the 23 individual KCCQ components at 8 months.
INTERVENTIONS
Dapagliflozin, 10 mg, once daily or placebo.
RESULTS
Baseline KCCQ data were available for 5795 of 6263 randomized patients (92.5%) (mean [SD] age, 71.5 [9.5] years; 3344 male [57.7%] and 2451 female [42.3%]). Dapagliflozin was associated with larger improvements in almost all KCCQ components at 8 months compared with placebo. The most significant improvements with dapagliflozin were observed in frequency of lower limb edema (difference, 3.2; 95% CI, 1.6-4.8; P < .001), sleep limitation by shortness of breath (difference, 3.0; 95% CI, 1.6-4.4; P < .001), and limitation in desired activities by shortness of breath (difference, 2.8; 95% CI, 1.3-4.3; P < .001). Similar treatment patterns were observed in longitudinal analyses integrating data from months 1, 4, and 8. Higher proportions of patients treated with dapagliflozin experienced improvements, and fewer had deteriorations across most individual components.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
In this study of patients with HF with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction, dapagliflozin was associated with improvement in a broad range of individual KCCQ components, with the greatest benefits in domains related to symptom frequency and physical limitations. Potential improvements in specific symptoms and activities of daily living might be more readily recognizable and easily communicated to patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
