ACTRN12613000935730.

data.title: Intermittent Fasting and Obesity-Related Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review of Meta-analyses of Randomized Clinical Trials.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Several meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the many health benefits of intermittent fasting (IF). However, there has been little synthesis of the strength and quality of this evidence in aggregate to date.
OBJECTIVE
To grade the evidence from published meta-analyses of RCTs that assessed the associations of IF (zero-calorie alternate-day fasting, modified alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet, and time-restricted eating) with obesity-related health outcomes.
EVIDENCE REVIEW
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane database of systematic reviews were searched from database inception to January 12, 2021. Data analysis was conducted from April 2021 through July 2021. Meta-analyses of RCTs investigating effects of IF in adults were included. The effect sizes of IF were recalculated using a random-effects model. We assessed the quality of evidence per association by applying the GRADE criteria (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) as high, moderate, low, and very low.
FINDINGS
A total of 11 meta-analyses comprising 130 RCTs (median [IQR] sample size, 38 [24-69] participants; median [IQR] follow-up period, 3 [2-5] months) were included describing 104 unique associations of different types of IF with obesity-related health outcomes (median [IQR] studies per association, 4 [3-5]). There were 28 statistically significant associations (27%) that demonstrated the beneficial outcomes for body mass index, body weight, fat mass, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, total cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance, and blood pressure. IF was found to be associated with reduced fat-free mass. One significant association (1%) supported by high-quality evidence was modified alternate-day fasting for 1 to 2 months, which was associated with moderate reduction in body mass index in healthy adults and adults with overweight, obesity, or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease compared with regular diet. Six associations (6%) were supported by moderate quality evidence. The remaining associations found to be significant were supported by very low (75 associations [72%]) to low (22 associations [21%]) quality evidence.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
In this umbrella review, we found beneficial associations of IF with anthropometric and cardiometabolic outcomes supported by moderate to high quality of evidence, which supports the role of IF, especially modified alternate-day fasting, as a weight loss approach for adults with overweight or obesity. More clinical trials with long-term follow-up are needed to investigate the effects of IF on clinical outcomes such as cardiovascular events and mortality.

data.title: Effects of a 12-Week Mediterranean-Type Time-Restricted Feeding Protocol in Patients With Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: A Randomised Controlled Trial-The 'CHRONO-NAFLD Project'.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The Mediterranean diet (MD) is considered the best dietary approach for patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Recently, time-restricted feeding (TRF) has gained attention for its lifestyle compatibility and health benefits.
AIMS
This study aimed to compare the effects of a hypocaloric MD with a 10-h TRF protocol to an unrestricted MD in MASLD patients with overweight/obesity and evaluate differences between early and late TRF.
METHODS
This 12-week randomised controlled trial in MASLD patients with overweight/obesity consisted of three groups, all following a hypocaloric Mediterranean-type diet. The control group had no eating time restrictions. The early TRF (eTRF) and late TRF (lTRF) groups had a 10-h eating window, from 8 AM to 6 PM and from 12 PM to 10 PM, respectively. Various health parameters were measured. Compliance was tracked via food diaries, and an 8-week follow-up occurred post-intervention.
RESULTS
Fifty-nine MASLD individuals (27 males; 52.9 years; body mass index 32.1 kg/m 2 ) completed the trial (control, n = 19; eTRF, n = 20; lTRF, n = 20). All groups showed significant 12-week reductions in body weight, anthropometry and blood pressure. Glycated haemoglobin A 1c and insulin resistance, as measured by the Matsuda index, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and fasting glucose-to-insulin ratio, improved in the eTRF group at 12 weeks.
CONCLUSIONS
This study corroborates the efficacy of MD in ameliorating cardiometabolic risk factors such as body weight and blood pressure in MASLD patients. The combination with an eTRF protocol may improve glycaemic control (NCT05866744).
TRIAL REGISTRATION
The study is registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05866744).

data.title: A 5:2 Intermittent Fasting Meal Replacement Diet and Glycemic Control for Adults With Diabetes: The EARLY Randomized Clinical Trial.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
An intermittent fasting plan consisting of 2 nonconsecutive fasting days and 5 days of habitual intake per week and meal replacement diet (5:2 MR) could provide additional benefits to patients with type 2 diabetes.
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the effect of the 5:2 MR on glycemic control among patients with early type 2 diabetes compared with metformin and empagliflozin.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
The EARLY (Exploration of Treatment of Newly Diagnosed Overweight/Obese Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus) study is a randomized, open-label, active parallel-controlled clinical trial conducted between November 13, 2020, and December 29, 2022, in 9 centers across China. A total of 509 eligible patients underwent screening, out of which 405 were randomly assigned to 3 groups and included in the intention-to-treat analysis.
INTERVENTIONS
Patients were randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive either metformin, empagliflozin, or 5:2 MR. The treatment was 16 weeks, with an 8-week follow-up.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary end point was the change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level from baseline to 16 weeks. Secondary end points included changes in body weight, anthropometric measurements, and biochemical parameters.
RESULTS
Of the 405 randomized participants (265 men [65.4%]; mean [SD] age, 45.5 [11.0] years; mean [SD] body mass index, 29.5 [4.1]; and mean [SD] HbA1c level, 7.9% [0.6%]), 332 completed the 16-week treatment. From baseline to week 16, participants in the 5:2 MR group showed the greatest reduction in HbA1c (least-squares mean [LSM], -1.9% [SE, 0.2%]), significantly greater than patients receiving metformin (LSM, -1.6% [SE, 0.2%]; adjusted LSM difference, -0.3% [95% CI, -0.4% to -0.1%]) and empagliflozin (LSM, -1.5% [SE, 0.2%]; adjusted LSM difference, -0.4% [95% CI, -0.6% to -0.2%]). At week 16, the mean weight loss in the 5:2 MR group (LSM, -9.7 kg [SE, 2.2 kg]) was greater than that in the metformin group (LSM, -5.5 kg [SE, 2.3 kg]) and empagliflozin group (LSM, -5.8 kg [SE, 2.3 kg]).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
This randomized clinical trial of Chinese adults with overweight or obesity and with early type 2 diabetes found that 5:2 MR could improve glycemic outcomes and weight loss in the short term compared with metformin or empagliflozin, making it a promising initial intervention and early management for type 2 diabetes.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2000040656.

data.title: Effect of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Time-restricted eating (TRE) has become increasingly popular, yet longer-term randomized clinical trials have not evaluated its efficacy and safety in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D).
OBJECTIVE
To determine whether TRE is more effective for weight reduction and glycemic control than daily calorie restriction (CR) or a control condition in adults with T2D.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This 6-month, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial was performed between January 25, 2022, and April 1, 2023, at the University of Illinois Chicago. Participants were aged 18 to 80 years with obesity and T2D. Data analysis was based on intention to treat.
INTERVENTIONS
Participants were randomized to 1 of 3 groups: 8-hour TRE (eating 12 to 8 pm only, without calorie counting), CR (25% energy restriction daily), or control.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary outcome measure was change in body weight by month 6. Secondary outcomes included changes in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and metabolic risk factors.
RESULTS
Seventy-five participants were enrolled with a mean (SD) age of 55 (12) years. The mean (SD) body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) was 39 (7) and the mean (SD) HbA1c level was 8.1% (1.6%). A total of 53 participants (71%) were women. One participant (1%) was Asian, 30 (40%) were Hispanic White, 40 (53%) were non-Hispanic Black, and 4 (5%) were non-Hispanic White. Participants in the TRE group were adherent with their eating window on a mean (SD) of 6.1 (0.8) days per week, and 17 (68%) in the CR group were adherent with their prescribed calorie goals over 6 months. The mean (SD) reduction in energy intake was -313 (509) kcal/d for TRE, -197 (426) kcal/d for CR, and -16 (439) kcal/d for controls. By month 6, body weight decreased significantly in the TRE group (-3.56% [95% CI, -5.92% to -1.20%]; P = .004) but not the CR group (-1.78% [95% CI, -3.67% to 0.11%]; P = .06), relative to controls. Levels of HbA1c decreased in the TRE (-0.91% [95% CI, -1.61% to -0.20%]) and CR (-0.94% [95% CI, -1.59% to -0.30%]) groups, relative to controls, with no differences between the TRE and CR groups. Time in euglycemic range, medication effect score, blood pressure, and plasma lipid levels did not differ among groups. No serious adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
This randomized clinical trial found that a TRE diet strategy without calorie counting was effective for weight loss and lowering of HbA1c levels compared with daily calorie counting in a sample of adults with T2D. These findings will need to be confirmed by larger RCTs with longer follow-up.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05225337.

data.title: Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To assess the effect of intermittent fasting diets, with continuous energy restriction or unrestricted (ad-libitum) diets on intermediate cardiometabolic outcomes from randomised clinical trials.
DESIGN
Systematic review and network meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES
Medline, Embase, and central databases from inception to 14 November 2024.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES
Randomised clinical trials comparing the association of intermittent fasting diets (alternate day fasting, time restricted eating, and whole day fasting), continuous energy restriction, and ad-libitum diets were included.
MAIN OUTCOMES
Outcomes included body weight (primary) and measures of anthropometry, glucose metabolism, lipid profiles, blood pressure, C-reactive protein, and markers of liver disease.
DATA SYNTHESIS
A network meta-analysis based on a frequentist framework was performed with data expressed as mean difference with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using grading of recommendations assessment, development, and evaluation (GRADE).
RESULTS
99 randomised clinical trials involving 6582 adults of varying health conditions (720 healthy, 5862 existing health conditions) were identified. All intermittent fasting and continuous energy restriction diet strategies reduced body weight when compared with ad-libitum diet. Compared with continuous energy restriction, alternate day fasting was the only form of intermittent fasting diet strategy to show benefit in body weight reduction (mean difference -1.29 kg (95% CI -1.99 to -0.59), moderate certainty of evidence). Additionally, alternate day fasting showed a trivial reduction in body weight compared with both time restricted eating and whole day fasting (mean difference -1.69 kg (-2.49 to -0.88) and -1.05 kg (-1.90 to -0.19), respectively, both with moderate certainty of evidence). Estimates were similar among trials with less than 24 weeks follow-up (n=76); however, moderate-to-long-term trials (≥24 weeks, n=17) only showed benefits in weight reduction in diet strategies compared with ad-libitum. Furthermore, in comparisons between intermittent fasting strategies, alternate day fasting lowered total cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-high density lipoprotein compared with time restricted eating. Compared with whole day fasting, however, time restricted eating resulted in a small increase in total cholesterol, low density lipoprotein cholesterol, and non-high density lipoprotein cholesterol. No differences were noted between intermittent fasting, continuous energy restriction, and ad-libitum diets for HbA 1c and high density lipoprotein.
CONCLUSIONS
Minor differences were noted between some intermittent fasting diets and continuous energy restriction, with some benefit of weight loss with alternate day fasting in shorter duration trials. The current evidence provides some indication that intermittent fasting diets have similar benefits to continuous energy restriction for weight loss and cardiometabolic risk factors. Longer duration trials are needed to further substantiate these findings.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05309057.

data.title: Comparing the effects of time-restricted eating on glycaemic control in people with type 2 diabetes with standard dietetic practice: A randomised controlled trial.
data.abstract:
AIMS
To test the efficacy of time-restricted eating (TRE) in comparison to dietitian-led individualised dietary guidance to improve HbA1c in people with Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
METHODS
In a parallel groups design, 51 adults (35-65 y) with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and overweight/obesity (HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol), BMI ≥25-≤40 kg/m 2 ) commenced a six-month intervention. Following baseline, participants were randomised to TRE (1000-1900 h) or DIET (individualised dietetic guidance) with four consultations over four months. Changes in HbA1c (primary), body composition, and self-reported adherence (secondary) were analysed using linear mixed models. A non-inferiority margin of 0.3% (4 mmol/mol) HbA1c was set a priori.
RESULTS
Forty-three participants (56 ± 8 y, BMI: 33 ± 5 kg/m 2 , HbA1c: 7.6 ± 0.8%) completed the intervention. HbA1c was reduced (P=0.002; TRE: -0.4% (-5 mmol/mol), DIET: -0.3% (-4 mmol/mol)) with no group or interaction effects; TRE was non-inferior to DIET (-0.11%, 95%CI: -0.50% to 0.28%). Body mass reduced in both groups (TRE: -1.7 kg; DIET: -1.2 kg) via ∼900 kJ/d spontaneous energy reduction (P<0.001). Self-reported adherence was higher in TRE versus DIET (P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS
When individualised dietary guidance is not available, effective, and/or suitable, TRE may be an alternative dietary strategy to improve glycaemic control in people with Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

data.title: Randomized Controlled Feasibility Trial of Late 8-Hour Time-Restricted Eating for Adolescents With Type 2 Diabetes.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
No trial to date has tested the effects of late time-restricted eating (lTRE) on glycemic control or body composition in adolescents with type 2 diabetes (T2D).
OBJECTIVE
The objective of the current study was to examine the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of lTRE compared to a prolonged eating window in adolescents with T2D.
DESIGN
A 12-week, randomized, controlled, feasibility study of lTRE compared to control in adolescents with obesity and new onset T2D was conducted.
PARTICIPANTS/SETTING
Eligible participants were 13-21 years old; with a diagnosis of T2D, on metformin monotherapy, recruited from Children's Hospital Los Angeles, between January 2021 and December of 2022. From 36 eligible participants, 27 were enrolled (75% recruitment rate; age: 16.5 ± 1.7 years, HbA1c: 6.6 ± 0.9%, 22/27 [81%] Hispanic, 17/27 [63%] female, 23/27 [85%] public insurance; all p-values >.05), and 23 of 27 completed the protocol.
INTERVENTION
Participants wore a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) daily and were randomized to one of two meal-timing schedules for 12-weeks: (1) lTRE (eating all food between 12:00 PM and 20:00 PM without calorie counting or recommended daily caloric intake) or (2) Control (eating over a period of 12 or more hours per day).
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
Study recruitment, retention and adherence to intervention arms were captured to operationalize feasibility. Glucose control (HbA1c), weight loss (%BMI p95 ), total body fat mass on DEXA, sleep, and dietary intake were explored as secondary outcomes.
STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
Analyses were based on the intention to treat (ITT) population. Between-group differences in clinical outcomes were assessed using mixed-effects longitudinal regression models.
RESULTS
Overall adherence to the 8-hr lTRE was 6.2 ± 1.1 d/wk and Control was 5.9 ± 0.9 d/wk. Participants assigned to lTRE indicated that limiting their eating window did not negatively affect their daily functioning and no adverse events were reported. In this pilot study, lTRE led to a reduction in %BMI p95 (-3.4%-95%CI: -6.1, -0.7, p = 0.02), HbA1c (-0.4%, 95%CI: -0.9, -0.01, p = .06), and ALT (-31.1 U/L, 95%CI: -60, -2, p = .05) within the group. There was no significant difference observed between lTRE and control across these measures (all p > .05). The lTRE group had a -271.4 (95% CI, -565.2, 5.2) kcal/day energy reduction compared to a +293.2 (95% CI: 30.4, 552.7) kcal/day increase in Control (p = .01). There were no significant changes observed in sleep or eating behaviors over the study period between groups.
CONCLUSIONS
Recruitment and retention rates suggest a trial of lTRE in adolescents with T2D was feasible. lTRE was seen as acceptable by participants and adherence was high. A revised intervention, building on the successful elements of this pilot alongside adapting implementations strategies to augment adherence and engagement, should therefore be considered.

data.title: Intermittent Fasting and Obesity-Related Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review of Meta-analyses of Randomized Clinical Trials.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Several meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the many health benefits of intermittent fasting (IF). However, there has been little synthesis of the strength and quality of this evidence in aggregate to date.
OBJECTIVE
To grade the evidence from published meta-analyses of RCTs that assessed the associations of IF (zero-calorie alternate-day fasting, modified alternate-day fasting, the 5:2 diet, and time-restricted eating) with obesity-related health outcomes.
EVIDENCE REVIEW
PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane database of systematic reviews were searched from database inception to January 12, 2021. Data analysis was conducted from April 2021 through July 2021. Meta-analyses of RCTs investigating effects of IF in adults were included. The effect sizes of IF were recalculated using a random-effects model. We assessed the quality of evidence per association by applying the GRADE criteria (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) as high, moderate, low, and very low.
FINDINGS
A total of 11 meta-analyses comprising 130 RCTs (median [IQR] sample size, 38 [24-69] participants; median [IQR] follow-up period, 3 [2-5] months) were included describing 104 unique associations of different types of IF with obesity-related health outcomes (median [IQR] studies per association, 4 [3-5]). There were 28 statistically significant associations (27%) that demonstrated the beneficial outcomes for body mass index, body weight, fat mass, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, total cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance, and blood pressure. IF was found to be associated with reduced fat-free mass. One significant association (1%) supported by high-quality evidence was modified alternate-day fasting for 1 to 2 months, which was associated with moderate reduction in body mass index in healthy adults and adults with overweight, obesity, or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease compared with regular diet. Six associations (6%) were supported by moderate quality evidence. The remaining associations found to be significant were supported by very low (75 associations [72%]) to low (22 associations [21%]) quality evidence.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
In this umbrella review, we found beneficial associations of IF with anthropometric and cardiometabolic outcomes supported by moderate to high quality of evidence, which supports the role of IF, especially modified alternate-day fasting, as a weight loss approach for adults with overweight or obesity. More clinical trials with long-term follow-up are needed to investigate the effects of IF on clinical outcomes such as cardiovascular events and mortality.

data.title: Effects of a 12-Week Mediterranean-Type Time-Restricted Feeding Protocol in Patients With Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: A Randomised Controlled Trial-The 'CHRONO-NAFLD Project'.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The Mediterranean diet (MD) is considered the best dietary approach for patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Recently, time-restricted feeding (TRF) has gained attention for its lifestyle compatibility and health benefits.
AIMS
This study aimed to compare the effects of a hypocaloric MD with a 10-h TRF protocol to an unrestricted MD in MASLD patients with overweight/obesity and evaluate differences between early and late TRF.
METHODS
This 12-week randomised controlled trial in MASLD patients with overweight/obesity consisted of three groups, all following a hypocaloric Mediterranean-type diet. The control group had no eating time restrictions. The early TRF (eTRF) and late TRF (lTRF) groups had a 10-h eating window, from 8 AM to 6 PM and from 12 PM to 10 PM, respectively. Various health parameters were measured. Compliance was tracked via food diaries, and an 8-week follow-up occurred post-intervention.
RESULTS
Fifty-nine MASLD individuals (27 males; 52.9 years; body mass index 32.1 kg/m 2 ) completed the trial (control, n = 19; eTRF, n = 20; lTRF, n = 20). All groups showed significant 12-week reductions in body weight, anthropometry and blood pressure. Glycated haemoglobin A 1c and insulin resistance, as measured by the Matsuda index, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance and fasting glucose-to-insulin ratio, improved in the eTRF group at 12 weeks.
CONCLUSIONS
This study corroborates the efficacy of MD in ameliorating cardiometabolic risk factors such as body weight and blood pressure in MASLD patients. The combination with an eTRF protocol may improve glycaemic control (NCT05866744).
TRIAL REGISTRATION
The study is registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05866744).

trajectory.final_answer:
# Bottom line

- In adults with type 2 diabetes, time‑restricted eating (TRE) produces modest improvements in glycemic control and weight comparable to or better than daily calorie restriction over 6 months, but head‑to‑head evidence versus usual care varies by study and duration; benefits on HbA1c are generally small to moderate and accompanied by lifestyle‑compatible adherence and low adverse event rates. <cite id="37889487">In a 6‑month randomized clinical trial in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, an 8‑hour TRE window (eating 12:00–20:00) reduced body weight by 3.56% versus 1.78% with daily calorie restriction, lowered HbA1c by ~0.9% in both TRE and CR arms versus control, with no significant difference between TRE and CR, no serious adverse events, and good adherence to the eating window</cite> <cite id="38904963">A randomized trial in early type 2 diabetes found a 5:2 meal‑replacement intermittent fasting regimen reduced HbA1c by ~1.9% over 16 weeks, outperforming metformin and empagliflozin in short‑term glycemic control and weight loss</cite> <cite id="39414086">In a 6‑month randomized trial comparing TRE (1000–1900 h) with individualized dietetic guidance, HbA1c fell by ~0.4% in both groups (TRE non‑inferior to dietetics), with higher adherence to TRE</cite> <cite id="39464252">A 12‑week randomized feasibility trial in adolescents with new‑onset type 2 diabetes showed high acceptability of late TRE, a small within‑group HbA1c reduction, and no serious adverse events</cite>. Evidence syntheses suggest intermittent fasting strategies, including TRE, have weight and cardiometabolic benefits broadly similar to continuous energy restriction, with some advantages for total weight loss in shorter trials, but longer‑term outcomes remain uncertain. <cite id="40533200">A 2025 network meta‑analysis of 99 randomized trials (n=6582) found all intermittent fasting and continuous energy restriction strategies reduced body weight versus ad‑libitum diets, with alternate‑day fasting showing additional weight benefit versus continuous restriction; TRE and alternate‑day fasting modestly reduced total and LDL cholesterol compared with time‑restricted eating in some comparisons, while HbA1c differences versus continuous restriction were negligible</cite>.

- For hepatic steatosis (NAFLD/MASLD), TRE reduces intrahepatic triglyceride content over months but appears to offer no advantage over daily calorie restriction when caloric intake is matched; however, some controlled trials without matched energy intake show greater steatosis reduction with TRE/TRF. <cite id="36930148">In a 12‑month randomized trial in adults with obesity and NAFLD, TRE (8:00–16:00) reduced IHTG by ~8% at 6 and 12 months, comparable to daily calorie restriction, with similar reductions in liver stiffness, body weight, and metabolic risk factors</cite> <cite id="36549296">In a 3‑month randomized trial in NAFLD with obesity, alternate‑day fasting reduced IHTG by ~2.3% versus control, and combining ADF with aerobic exercise reduced IHTG by ~5.5%, while TRE alone reduced IHTG by ~2.3% without additional benefit from exercise</cite> <cite id="38068729">A randomized crossover trial in NAFLD found time‑restricted fasting (16 hours/day) significantly decreased hepatic steatosis, waist circumference, and BMI versus standard care despite no overall change in caloric intake</cite> <cite id="40017349">In MASLD patients with overweight/obesity, a 12‑week hypocaloric Mediterranean‑type diet with a 10‑hour early TRE window (8:00–18:00) improved HbA1c and insulin resistance indices at 12 weeks relative to control, while an unrestricted diet improved blood pressure and weight across all groups</cite>. Umbrella reviews support intermittent fasting (including TRE) as a weight‑loss approach with moderate‑quality evidence for cardiometabolic benefits, but emphasize the need for longer trials on clinical outcomes. <cite id="34919135">An umbrella review graded intermittent fasting (including TRE) as associated with improvements in BMI, body weight, lipids, fasting glucose/insulin, and HOMA‑IR, with one high‑quality finding for modified alternate‑day fasting on BMI in people with NAFLD versus regular diet; most other associations were low‑to‑moderate quality</cite>.

# Glycemic control in type 2 diabetes

Across randomized controlled trials, TRE and other intermittent fasting strategies improve HbA1c modestly in adults with type 2 diabetes, often alongside weight loss and lifestyle‑compatible adherence. In the 6‑month JAMA Network Open trial, TRE lowered HbA1c by ~0.9% versus control, similar to daily calorie restriction, indicating that energy reduction, not just meal timing, drives glycemic benefits. <cite id="37889487">In that study, TRE participants reduced energy intake by ~313 kcal/day without calorie counting, while CR reduced by ~197 kcal/day; both TRE and CR outperformed control on HbA1c, but TRE was not superior to CR</cite>. In contrast, the EARLY trial showed a more pronounced short‑term HbA1c reduction with a 5:2 meal‑replacement regimen than with metformin or empagliflozin, suggesting that structured meal replacement within TRE can enhance glycemic effects. <cite id="38904963">The 5:2 meal‑replacement group achieved an HbA1c reduction of ~1.9% at 16 weeks, exceeding metformin (~1.6%) and empagliflozin (~1.5%), with greater weight loss</cite>. For patients unable to access dietetic care, TRE can be a practical alternative with non‑inferior HbA1c reduction and higher adherence, though effects are small to moderate. <cite id="39414086">In a 6‑month randomized trial, TRE and individualized dietetics each reduced HbA1c by ~0.4% (TRE non‑inferior), with TRE showing higher self‑reported adherence</cite>. In adolescents with new‑onset T2D, late TRE was feasible and acceptable with signals of improved glycemia and liver enzymes within the small pilot sample. <cite id="39464252">A 12‑week randomized feasibility study reported high adherence to a late 8‑hour eating window, no adverse events, and within‑group improvements in %BMI‑p95, HbA1c, and ALT</cite>.

Synthesis across trials indicates that intermittent fasting strategies, including TRE, produce weight and glycemic improvements broadly comparable to continuous energy restriction when calories are reduced, with some evidence of superior total weight loss in shorter trials and potential small advantages in lipid profiles in specific comparisons. <cite id="40533200">A 2025 network meta‑analysis across 99 RCTs found intermittent fasting and continuous restriction both reduced body weight versus ad‑libitum diets, with alternate‑day fasting showing an additional advantage; in comparisons among fasting strategies, alternate‑day fasting lowered total and LDL cholesterol more than TRE, while TRE slightly increased these lipids versus whole‑day fasting; HbA1c differences between intermittent fasting and continuous restriction were minimal</cite>.

# Hepatic steatosis (NAFLD/MASLD)

When caloric intake is controlled or matched, TRE reduces hepatic fat similar to daily calorie restriction, suggesting that energy reduction is the primary driver of steatosis improvement. <cite id="36930148">In the 12‑month TREATY‑FLD trial, TRE and daily calorie restriction each reduced IHTG by ~8% at 6 months and ~7–9% at 12 months, with comparable improvements in liver stiffness, body weight, and metabolic risk factors</cite>. Adding exercise to intermittent fasting can amplify benefits on hepatic fat beyond fasting alone in some settings, though results may vary by protocol. <cite id="36549296">In a 3‑month randomized trial, combining alternate‑day fasting with moderate‑intensity aerobic exercise reduced IHTG by ~5.5% versus ~2.3% with fasting alone and greater reductions than control, while fasting plus exercise did not significantly outperform exercise alone on IHTG</cite>. Trials that do not enforce energy restriction still report steatosis improvements with TRE/TRF, indicating meal timing may confer independent benefits in some contexts. <cite id="38068729">A randomized crossover trial in NAFLD found 16‑hour daily time‑restricted fasting reduced hepatic steatosis, waist, and BMI versus standard care despite no overall change in caloric intake</cite>. In MASLD, pairing a hypocaloric Mediterranean‑type diet with early TRE improved glycemic and insulin‑resistance markers relative to an unrestricted Mediterranean diet, supporting the additive value of time restriction on metabolic outcomes. <cite id="40017349">A 12‑week randomized controlled trial in MASLD showed that an early 10‑hour TRE window improved HbA1c and insulin resistance indices in the eTRF arm, while all groups reduced weight and blood pressure</cite>.

# Practical considerations and limitations

- TRE's glycemic and hepatic benefits are largely mediated by reduced energy intake and lifestyle changes; when total calories are matched, TRE does not appear to outperform daily calorie restriction for steatosis or HbA1c. <cite id="36930148">In TREATY‑FLD, TRE and daily calorie restriction produced similar reductions in IHTG and metabolic risk factors</cite> <cite id="37889487">In the JAMA trial, TRE and CR both lowered HbA1c similarly versus control</cite>. 
- Some trials show TRE is easier to adhere to than individualized dietetic counseling, which can be beneficial in resource‑limited settings, but effects on HbA1c are small to moderate and may not surpass pharmacologic therapies over short horizons. <cite id="39414086">TRE was non‑inferior to dietetic guidance on HbA1c with higher adherence</cite> <cite id="38904963">A 5:2 meal‑replacement regimen outperformed metformin and empagliflozin in short‑term HbA1c reduction</cite>.
- Evidence for long‑term clinical outcomes (cardiovascular events, mortality) and durability of glycemic control with TRE is limited; most benefits are observed over months in controlled settings. <cite id="37889487">The 6‑month JAMA trial called for confirmation in larger RCTs with longer follow‑up</cite> <cite id="40533200">The 2025 network meta‑analysis emphasized the need for longer trials to validate clinical impact</cite>.

# Conclusion

Current randomized evidence indicates that TRE can improve glycemic control and hepatic steatosis in adults with type 2 diabetes or NAFLD/MASLD, largely by facilitating energy restriction and lifestyle change. When total calories are controlled, TRE does not consistently outperform daily calorie restriction for steatosis or HbA1c, suggesting that meal timing complements—but does not replace—overall caloric intake. TRE is generally feasible, acceptable, and safe, with small to moderate improvements in HbA1c and weight, and signals of improved insulin sensitivity and hepatic fat when combined with hypocaloric diets and, in some studies, exercise. However, high‑quality, longer‑duration trials are needed to confirm sustained glycemic and hepatic benefits and to define optimal protocols (window timing, flexibility, and integration with medical therapy). <cite id="37889487">TRE reduced HbA1c and weight versus control in adults with type 2 diabetes over 6 months without serious adverse events</cite> <cite id="36930148">In NAFLD, TRE reduced IHTG comparably to daily calorie restriction with improvements in liver stiffness and metabolic risk factors</cite> <cite id="38068729">Time‑restricted fasting improved steatosis and anthropometry versus standard care in NAFLD without calorie restriction</cite> <cite id="40533200">Intermittent fasting strategies show weight and cardiometabolic benefits broadly similar to continuous restriction, with some differences among specific IF modalities and limited evidence on long‑term clinical outcomes</cite>.

Abstract: BACKGROUND

Osimertinib demonstrated central nervous system activity in patients with brain metastasis; however, its efficacy against other distant metastatic organs, including bone and liver, remains unclear. Therefore, we retrospectively analyzed the clinical efficacy of osimertinib in these patients in comparison to other EGFR-TKIs.

Furthermore, the ORR of osimertinib in patients with liver metastases was significantly attenuated, and the effectiveness was similar to 1 st - or 2 nd -generation EGFR-TKIs.
CONCLUSION
Osimertinib provided better clinical benefits than 1 st - and 2 nd -generation EGFR-TKIs for patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC, particularly those with brain or bone metastases and exon 19 deletion; however, its efficacy against liver metastasis was remarkably attenuated. New therapeutic developments for patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC with liver metastases are needed.</snippet>

# Summary

- First-line osimertinib provides longer progression-free survival (PFS) and similar or better overall survival (OS) compared with first- or second-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) in EGFR-mutant metastatic non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with the largest advantages seen in patients with brain metastases or bone metastases and in those with exon 19 deletions. In contrast, in patients with liver metastasis, osimertinib's PFS advantage is lost, and its efficacy is similar to first- or second-generation TKIs. Osimertinib also shows superior central nervous system (CNS) control, including activity against brain metastases, whereas activity against liver metastases is limited. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain or bone metastasis and exon 19 deletion than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs, but its efficacy against liver metastasis was markedly attenuated, with similar effectiveness to first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs in that subgroup</cite>.

# Progression-Free Survival (PFS)

- In patients with brain or bone metastases and in those with exon 19 deletions, osimertinib was associated with significantly longer PFS than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain or bone metastasis and exon 19 deletion compared with the other EGFR-TKIs</cite>.
- In patients with liver metastasis, the PFS benefit of osimertinib versus first- or second-generation TKIs was not significant. <cite id="35698083">In liver metastases, the PFS of osimertinib was not significantly different among the three EGFR-TKI groups</cite>.
- Independent adverse prognostic factors for PFS included liver metastasis and the L858R mutation. <cite id="35698083">Liver metastasis and L858R mutation were independently associated with shorter PFS</cite>.

# Overall Survival (OS)

- For patients without liver metastasis, OS was substantially longer with osimertinib compared with first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs, whereas in those with liver metastasis, OS was shorter and not reached in the osimertinib arm in the comparison subgroup. <cite id="35698083">PFS and OS in patients with liver metastases were significantly shorter with osimertinib compared with those without liver metastases (PFS 7.4 vs 19.7 months; OS 12.1 months vs not reached), suggesting a survival disadvantage in this subgroup</cite>.
- Overall, across all metastatic sites, multivariable analysis indicated better outcomes with osimertinib in the absence of high-risk features like liver metastasis. <cite id="35698083">Most distant metastases, including brain and bone, were unrelated to therapeutic efficacy in multivariable analyses, with liver metastasis independently linked to shorter PFS</cite>.

# Central Nervous System (CNS) Control

- Osimertinib demonstrates notable activity against brain metastases, with superior PFS and clinical benefit in patients with central nervous system involvement compared with earlier-generation EGFR-TKIs. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain metastasis than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs</cite>.
- In contrast, osimertinib shows limited efficacy against liver metastasis, which is a different organ metastatic site with distinct biology and response patterns. <cite id="35698083">Its efficacy against liver metastasis was remarkably attenuated, with outcomes similar to first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For first-line therapy in EGFR-mutant metastatic NSCLC, osimertinib is generally preferred due to improved PFS and CNS control, particularly when brain or bone metastases are present or when the driver mutation is exon 19 deletion. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided better clinical benefits than first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs for patients with brain or bone metastases and exon 19 deletion</cite>.
- Patients with liver metastasis may derive less benefit from osimertinib in terms of PFS, and alternative strategies or combination approaches may be warranted in this subgroup. <cite id="35698083">New therapeutic developments are needed for patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC and liver metastases, as osimertinib's efficacy is attenuated in this setting</cite>.

# Limitations

- The evidence above is based on a retrospective multicenter analysis comparing historical cohorts of first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs with contemporary osimertinib-treated patients, which may introduce selection bias and confounding factors. Prospective head-to-head trials (e.g., FLAURA) would further clarify the magnitude of PFS and OS benefits and CNS response rates with first-line osimertinib versus earlier-generation TKIs. <cite id="35698083">The study was a retrospective analysis across five medical institutions comparing gefitinib/erlotinib, afatinib, and osimertinib</cite>.

Osimertinib also shows superior central nervous system (CNS) control, including activity against brain metastases, whereas activity against liver metastases is limited. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain or bone metastasis and exon 19 deletion than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs, but its efficacy against liver metastasis was markedly attenuated, with similar effectiveness to first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs in that subgroup</cite>.

# Progression-Free Survival (PFS)

- In patients with brain or bone metastases and in those with exon 19 deletions, osimertinib was associated with significantly longer PFS than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain or bone metastasis and exon 19 deletion compared with the other EGFR-TKIs</cite>.
- In patients with liver metastasis, the PFS benefit of osimertinib versus first- or second-generation TKIs was not significant. <cite id="35698083">In liver metastases, the PFS of osimertinib was not significantly different among the three EGFR-TKI groups</cite>.
- Independent adverse prognostic factors for PFS included liver metastasis and the L858R mutation. <cite id="35698083">Liver metastasis and L858R mutation were independently associated with shorter PFS</cite>.

# Overall Survival (OS)

- For patients without liver metastasis, OS was substantially longer with osimertinib compared with first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs, whereas in those with liver metastasis, OS was shorter and not reached in the osimertinib arm in the comparison subgroup. <cite id="35698083">PFS and OS in patients with liver metastases were significantly shorter with osimertinib compared with those without liver metastases (PFS 7.4 vs 19.7 months; OS 12.1 months vs not reached), suggesting a survival disadvantage in this subgroup</cite>.

# Central Nervous System (CNS) Control

- Osimertinib demonstrates notable activity against brain metastases, with superior PFS and clinical benefit in patients with central nervous system involvement compared with earlier-generation EGFR-TKIs. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided significantly longer PFS in patients with brain metastasis than first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs</cite>.
- In contrast, osimertinib shows limited efficacy against liver metastasis, which is a different organ metastatic site with distinct biology and response patterns. <cite id="35698083">Its efficacy against liver metastasis was remarkably attenuated, with outcomes similar to first- or second-generation EGFR-TKIs</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For first-line therapy in EGFR-mutant metastatic NSCLC, osimertinib is generally preferred due to improved PFS and CNS control, particularly when brain or bone metastases are present or when the driver mutation is exon 19 deletion. <cite id="35698083">Osimertinib provided better clinical benefits than first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs for patients with brain or bone metastases and exon 19 deletion</cite>.
- Patients with liver metastasis may derive less benefit from osimertinib in terms of PFS, and alternative strategies or combination approaches may be warranted in this subgroup. <cite id="35698083">New therapeutic developments are needed for patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC and liver metastases, as osimertinib's efficacy is attenuated in this setting</cite>.

# Limitations

- The evidence above is based on a retrospective multicenter analysis comparing historical cohorts of first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs with contemporary osimertinib-treated patients, which may introduce selection bias and confounding factors. Prospective head-to-head trials (e.g., FLAURA) would further clarify the magnitude of PFS and OS benefits and CNS response rates with first-line osimertinib versus earlier-generation TKIs. <cite id="35698083">The study was a retrospective analysis across five medical institutions comparing gefitinib/erlotinib, afatinib, and osimertinib</cite>.

<snippet id="34500451">Title: Parkinson's Disease and Gut Microbiota.
Authors: Hirayama, Masaaki, Ohno, Kinji | Year: 2021 | Journal: Annals of nutrition & metabolism
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Parkinson's disease (PD) is caused by abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein fibrils, called the Lewy bodies, in the central nervous system. Accumulating knowledge points to the notion that α-synuclein fibrils start from the dorsal vagal nucleus and ascend to the locus ceruleus and the substantia nigra (SN). Even in healthy elderly subjects without motor or cognitive impairment, α-synuclein fibrils are frequently observed in the brain and sometimes in the intestinal neural plexus. Enteroendocrine cells have a direct synapse to the vagal afferents, and the vagal nucleus has synaptic pathways to the SN and the striatum. Intestinal bacteria are likely to be involved in the formation of intestinal α-synuclein fibrils.
SUMMARY
A nonparametric meta-analysis of intestinal microbiota in PD in 5 countries, as well as scrutinization of the other reports from the other countries, indicates that mucin-degrading Akkermansia is increased in PD and that short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria are decreased in PD. Both dysbiosis should increase the intestinal permeability, which subsequently facilitates exposure of the intestinal neural plexus to toxins like lipopolysaccharide and pesticide, which should lead to abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein fibrils. Decreased SCFA also downregulates regulatory T cells and fails to suppress neuronal inflammation. Key Messages: Therapeutic intervention may be able to be established against these mechanisms. Additional biochemical, cellular, and animal studies are required to further dissect the direct association between intestinal microbiota and PD.</snippet>
<snippet id="36376318">Title: Metagenomics of Parkinson's disease implicates the gut microbiome in multiple disease mechanisms.
Authors: Wallen, Zachary D, Demirkan, Ayse, Twa, Guy et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Nature communications
Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) may start in the gut and spread to the brain. To investigate the role of gut microbiome, we conducted a large-scale study, at high taxonomic resolution, using uniform standardized methods from start to end. We enrolled 490 PD and 234 control individuals, conducted deep shotgun sequencing of fecal DNA, followed by metagenome-wide association studies requiring significance by two methods (ANCOM-BC and MaAsLin2) to declare disease association, network analysis to identify polymicrobial clusters, and functional profiling. Here we show that over 30% of species, genes and pathways tested have altered abundances in PD, depicting a widespread dysbiosis. PD-associated species form polymicrobial clusters that grow or shrink together, and some compete. PD microbiome is disease permissive, evidenced by overabundance of pathogens and immunogenic components, dysregulated neuroactive signaling, preponderance of molecules that induce alpha-synuclein pathology, and over-production of toxicants; with the reduction in anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective factors limiting the capacity to recover. Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases. Authors: Munoz-Pinto, Mário F, Candeias, Emanuel, Melo-Marques, Inês et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Molecular neurodegeneration
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In Parkinson's patients, intestinal dysbiosis can occur years before clinical diagnosis, implicating the gut and its microbiota in the disease. Recent evidence suggests the gut microbiota may trigger body-first Parkinson Disease (PD), yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aims to elucidate how a dysbiotic microbiome through intestinal immune alterations triggers PD-related neurodegeneration.

To determine the impact of gut dysbiosis on the development and progression of PD pathology, wild-type male C57BL/6 mice were transplanted with fecal material from PD patients and age-matched healthy donors to challenge the gut-immune-brain axis.

Piperine (PIP) the main alkaloid of P. longum, exists neuroprotective effects on various animal models of Parkinson's disease (PD). Nevertheless, the underlying mechanism, particularly the role of PIP in promoting gut-brain autophagy for α-Synuclein (α-Syn) degradation in PD, remains incompletely understood.

Behavioral experiments were conducted to assess the impact of PIP on 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-induced PD rats. The intestinal microbiome composition and intestinal metabolites were analyzed by metagenomics and GC-MS/MS. The auto-phagosomes were visualized by transmission electron microscopy. Immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, and western blotting were performed to assess the levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), α-Syn, LC3II/LC3I, p62, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in both the SN and colon of the rats. This effect could be inhibited by the autophagy inhibitor bafilomycin A1 and the PI3K agonist 740 Y-P.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings suggested that PIP could protect neurons by activating autophagy to degrade α-Syn in the SN and colon, which were related to the suppression of PIP on the activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.</snippet>

# Summary of human evidence linking gut microbiome alterations to Parkinson’s disease (PD) via inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms

## Overview
Human observational and translational studies increasingly implicate the gut microbiome in PD pathogenesis through two complementary mechanisms: (1) inflammatory and barrier dysfunction pathways that may promote α‑synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation, and (2) direct involvement of microbiome-derived factors that induce or propagate α‑synuclein pathology. Converging evidence from meta-analyses, metagenomics, and human–mouse fecal transfer models supports these mechanisms, while also highlighting important gaps and confounders.

## Microbiome dysbiosis, inflammation, and barrier dysfunction in PD
A cross-cohort meta-analysis across multiple countries reported increased abundance of mucin-degrading Akkermansia and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria in PD, consistent with increased intestinal permeability and chronic low-grade inflammation. The authors propose that mucin degradation and reduced SCFAs facilitate exposure to microbial toxins (e.g., LPS) and environmental pesticides in the intestinal neural plexus, which can trigger abnormal α‑synuclein fibrillation; decreased SCFAs are also linked to reduced regulatory T cells and impaired suppression of neuronal inflammation, reinforcing a pro-inflammatory milieu that could promote PD pathophysiology. These findings align with the “gut–brain–immune axis” model in which microbiome-driven inflammation and barrier defects may seed or exacerbate neurodegeneration. <cite id="34500451">A nonparametric meta-analysis of intestinal microbiota in PD indicates increased Akkermansia and decreased SCFA-producing bacteria, with mechanistic implications for increased intestinal permeability, exposure to toxins like lipopolysaccharide and pesticide, and abnormal α-synuclein fibrils; decreased SCFAs are proposed to downregulate regulatory T cells and fail to suppress neuronal inflammation</cite>.

A large-scale, high-resolution metagenomics study (n = 490 PD, 234 controls) demonstrated widespread dysbiosis, with over 30% of species, genes, and pathways altered in PD. The PD microbiome exhibited features of being “disease permissive,” including overabundance of pathogens and immunogenic components, dysregulated neuroactive signaling, and a preponderance of molecules that induce α‑synuclein pathology, alongside reduced anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective factors. Network analyses identified polymicrobial clusters that co-fluctuate, suggesting community-level interactions that may drive inflammatory and proteopathic changes relevant to PD. This work provides broad human evidence that gut microbial composition and function are intertwined with inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms in PD. <cite id="36376318">In a study of 490 PD and 234 control individuals, over 30% of species, genes, and pathways had altered abundances in PD, depicting widespread dysbiosis; PD-associated species formed polymicrobial clusters, and the PD microbiome showed overabundance of pathogens and immunogenic components, dysregulated neuroactive signaling, and a preponderance of molecules that induce alpha-synuclein pathology, with reduced anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective factors</cite>.

A recent review synthesizes clinical, mechanistic, and therapeutic studies, emphasizing that non-motor gastrointestinal symptoms often precede motor manifestations and that the microbiota–gut–brain axis can influence CNS physiology via neural, endocrine, and immune pathways. It collates human evidence for microbial changes in PD and proposes mechanisms by which gut bacteria may mediate disease, including immune activation and neuroinflammation, while also discussing the promise of microbiome-targeted therapies. <cite id="38098067">Reviews highlight that intestinal issues can precede motor symptoms in PD and that gut microbiota are strongly associated with PD, summarizing microbial changes, mechanisms via the microbiota–gut–brain axis, and therapeutic implications</cite>.

## Human–mouse fecal transfer evidence connecting dysbiosis to inflammatory and α‑synuclein pathology
Translational studies using patient-derived fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) into germ-free mice provide causal evidence that PD-associated dysbiosis can trigger systemic inflammation, barrier disruption, and α‑synuclein propagation. In a mouse model receiving PD patient fecal material, donor microbiota induced midbrain tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)–positive cell loss and motor deficits. FMT was associated with ileal remodeling, decreased Th17 cells, increased gut inflammation and barrier disruption, elevated circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, blood–brain barrier leakage, and mesencephalic IL‑17 and IgG, consistent with systemic immune activation. Critically, α‑synuclein aggregates spread caudorostrally in the enteric nervous system, causing mitochondrial fragmentation, which activated neuronal innate immune responses and microglial activation, linking gut immune alterations to neuroinflammation and α‑synuclein propagation. These findings support a gut–immune–brain cascade wherein dysbiotic communities and immune shifts (e.g., Th17 loss) promote inflammation and facilitate α‑synuclein pathology dissemination. <cite id="39449004">In mice transplanted with fecal material from PD patients, patient-derived microbiota caused midbrain TH+ cell loss and motor dysfunction; ileal remodeling with decreased Th17 homeostatic cells led to increased gut inflammation, barrier disruption, and systemic cytokines; blood–brain barrier leakage and mesencephalic IL-17 were observed, and alpha-synuclein aggregates spread caudo-rostrally, causing mitochondrial fragmentation, neuronal innate immune activation, and microglial activation</cite>.

Complementary mechanistic work in PD models shows that modulating gut–brain autophagy can reduce α‑synuclein burden in both gut and brain compartments. In 6‑hydroxydopamine–induced PD rats, piperine increased colonic and substantia nigra autophagy markers (LC3II/LC3I ratio, p62 degradation) and reduced α‑synuclein aggregation, paralleling improvements in motor and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Pharmacologic and genetic manipulations confirmed that these effects depended on PI3K/AKT/mTOR–mediated autophagy, and in vitro studies in α‑synuclein–overexpressing cells showed that autophagy inhibition or pathway activation altered α‑syn clearance. While this study is preclinical, it supports the concept that enhancing gut–brain autophagy can degrade α‑synuclein and mitigate inflammation-associated toxicity, aligning with human observations of dysbiosis and inflammatory signaling. <cite id="38158101">In 6-OHDA-induced PD rats, piperine improved autonomic and gastrointestinal dysfunction and reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation; LC3II/LC3I increased and p62 degraded in both substantia nigra and colon, with phosphorylation changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR; these effects depended on autophagy and were confirmed in A53T-alpha-syn–overexpressing cells</cite>.

## Evidence for microbiome-derived induction of α‑synuclein pathology
Human metagenomics indicates that the PD microbiome is enriched for immunogenic components and molecules that induce α‑synuclein pathology, suggesting a direct role for microbial metabolites, toxins, or structural proteins in promoting proteopathic seeding. The identification of polymicrobial clusters that co-vary across species and pathways supports the idea that community-level dysbiosis, rather than single-organism effects alone, drives α‑synuclein–related changes via inflammatory and metabolic outputs. <cite id="36376318">The PD microbiome showed a preponderance of molecules that induce alpha-synuclein pathology and over-production of toxicants, with polymicrobial clusters that grow or shrink together, implicating community-level dysbiosis in disease mechanisms</cite>.

## Clinical correlates and immune activation markers
Clinical reviews and cohort analyses emphasize that gut-first PD and intestinal symptoms preceding motor signs are consistent with microbiome–immune–neuro interactions. Proposed human mechanisms include increased intestinal permeability, endotoxemia, and systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines that could activate microglia and astrocytes and contribute to Lewy body formation. The convergence of decreased SCFA producers and increased mucin degraders in PD points to reduced anti-inflammatory signaling and heightened epithelial exposure to microbial products, both of which could foster α‑synuclein aggregation. <cite id="34500451">Intestinal bacteria are implicated in the formation of intestinal alpha-synuclein fibrils, with increased mucin-degrading Akkermansia and decreased SCFA producers linked to increased permeability, exposure to toxins, and downregulation of regulatory T cells that suppress neuronal inflammation</cite>. <cite id="38098067">Clinical observations of intestinal issues preceding motor symptoms and strong associations between gut microbiota and PD support microbiota–gut–brain immune pathways in PD</cite>.

## Limitations and gaps
- Many human studies are cross-sectional and confounders (age, diet, medication, comorbidities) are difficult to control; longitudinal preclinical FMT studies are needed to establish temporality and causality in humans. <cite id="34500451">The review calls for additional biochemical, cellular, and animal studies to further dissect direct associations between intestinal microbiota and PD</cite>.
- While FMT mouse models robustly demonstrate inflammatory and α‑synuclein propagation phenotypes, direct human α‑synuclein seeding assays from fecal material remain technically challenging and ethically constrained; however, convergent metagenomic signals of immunogenicity and proteopathic molecules strengthen the inference of microbial involvement. <cite id="36376318">Metagenomics identifies immunogenic components and alpha-synuclein–inducing molecules in PD microbiomes, providing a foundation for testable hypotheses but requiring further human mechanistic validation</cite>.

## Bottom line
Human studies provide converging evidence that PD-associated gut dysbiosis promotes inflammation and barrier dysfunction, enriches for immunogenic and α‑synuclein–inducing microbial factors, and can, when transferred to mice, trigger systemic inflammatory cascades and α‑synuclein propagation to the brain. These data support gut microbiome alterations as contributors to PD pathogenesis via inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms, while emphasizing the need for longitudinal human studies and mechanistic validations to delineate causality and therapeutic targets. <cite id="34500451">Human meta-analytic and mechanistic reviews support increased permeability, inflammation, and α-synuclein aggregation linked to microbiome changes</cite> <cite id="36376318">Large-scale metagenomics shows widespread dysbiosis, immunogenicity, and alpha-synuclein–inducing molecules in PD microbiomes</cite> <cite id="39449004">FMT mouse models demonstrate that PD patient microbiota induce gut inflammation, barrier disruption, systemic cytokines, BBB leakage, and alpha-synuclein propagation with neuroinflammation</cite> <cite id="38098067">Clinical and mechanistic reviews synthesize microbiota–gut–brain immune pathways and early gut symptoms in PD</cite>.
</answer>

The pathway-related inhibitor and agonist were used to verify the autophagy mechanism in the SH-SY5Y cells overexpressing A53T mutant α-Syn (A53T-α-Syn).
RESULTS
PIP improved autonomic movement and gastrointestinal dysfunctions, reduced α-Syn aggregation and attenuated the loss of dopaminergic neurons in 6-OHDA-induced PD rats. After oral administration of PIP, the radio of LC3II/LC3I increased and the expression of p62 was degraded, as well as the phosphorylation levels of PI3K, AKT and mTOR decreased in the SN and colon of rats. The effect of PIP on reducing A53T-α-Syn through the activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR-mediated autophagy pathway was further confirmed in A53T-α-Syn transgenic SH-SY5Y cells. This effect could be inhibited by the autophagy inhibitor bafilomycin A1 and the PI3K agonist 740 Y-P.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings suggested that PIP could protect neurons by activating autophagy to degrade α-Syn in the SN and colon, which were related to the suppression of PIP on the activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway.

# Summary of human evidence linking gut microbiome alterations to Parkinson’s disease (PD) via inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms

## Overview
Human observational and translational studies increasingly implicate the gut microbiome in PD pathogenesis through two complementary mechanisms: (1) inflammatory and barrier dysfunction pathways that may promote α‑synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation, and (2) direct involvement of microbiome-derived factors that induce or propagate α‑synuclein pathology. Converging evidence from meta-analyses, metagenomics, and human–mouse fecal transfer models supports these mechanisms, while also highlighting important gaps and confounders.

## Microbiome dysbiosis, inflammation, and barrier dysfunction in PD
A cross-cohort meta-analysis across multiple countries reported increased abundance of mucin-degrading Akkermansia and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria in PD, consistent with increased intestinal permeability and chronic low-grade inflammation. The authors propose that mucin degradation and reduced SCFAs facilitate exposure to microbial toxins (e.g., LPS) and environmental pesticides in the intestinal neural plexus, which can trigger abnormal α‑synuclein fibrillation; decreased SCFAs are also linked to reduced regulatory T cells and impaired suppression of neuronal inflammation, reinforcing a pro-inflammatory milieu that could promote PD pathophysiology. These findings align with the “gut–brain–immune axis” model in which microbiome-driven inflammation and barrier defects may seed or exacerbate neurodegeneration. <cite id="34500451">A nonparametric meta-analysis of intestinal microbiota in PD indicates increased Akkermansia and decreased SCFA-producing bacteria, with mechanistic implications for increased intestinal permeability, exposure to toxins like lipopolysaccharide and pesticide, and abnormal α-synuclein fibrils; decreased SCFAs are proposed to downregulate regulatory T cells and fail to suppress neuronal inflammation</cite>.

A large-scale, high-resolution metagenomics study (n = 490 PD, 234 controls) demonstrated widespread dysbiosis, with over 30% of species, genes, and pathways altered in PD. The PD microbiome exhibited features of being “disease permissive,” including overabundance of pathogens and immunogenic components, dysregulated neuroactive signaling, and a preponderance of molecules that induce α‑synuclein pathology, alongside reduced anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective factors. Network analyses identified polymicrobial clusters that co-fluctuate, suggesting community-level interactions that may drive inflammatory and proteopathic changes relevant to PD. This work provides broad human evidence that gut microbial composition and function are intertwined with inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms in PD. <cite id="36376318">In a study of 490 PD and 234 control individuals, over 30% of species, genes, and pathways had altered abundances in PD, depicting widespread dysbiosis; PD-associated species formed polymicrobial clusters, and the PD microbiome showed overabundance of pathogens and immunogenic components, dysregulated neuroactive signaling, and a preponderance of molecules that induce alpha-synuclein pathology, with reduced anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective factors</cite>.

A recent review synthesizes clinical, mechanistic, and therapeutic studies, emphasizing that non-motor gastrointestinal symptoms often precede motor manifestations and that the microbiota–gut–brain axis can influence CNS physiology via neural, endocrine, and immune pathways. It collates human evidence for microbial changes in PD and proposes mechanisms by which gut bacteria may mediate disease, including immune activation and neuroinflammation, while also discussing the promise of microbiome-targeted therapies. <cite id="38098067">Reviews highlight that intestinal issues can precede motor symptoms in PD and that gut microbiota are strongly associated with PD, summarizing microbial changes, mechanisms via the microbiota–gut–brain axis, and therapeutic implications</cite>.

## Human–mouse fecal transfer evidence connecting dysbiosis to inflammatory and α‑synuclein pathology
Translational studies using patient-derived fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) into germ-free mice provide causal evidence that PD-associated dysbiosis can trigger systemic inflammation, barrier disruption, and α‑synuclein propagation. In a mouse model receiving PD patient fecal material, donor microbiota induced midbrain tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)–positive cell loss and motor deficits. FMT was associated with ileal remodeling, decreased Th17 cells, increased gut inflammation and barrier disruption, elevated circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, blood–brain barrier leakage, and mesencephalic IL‑17 and IgG, consistent with systemic immune activation. Critically, α‑synuclein aggregates spread caudorostrally in the enteric nervous system, causing mitochondrial fragmentation, which activated neuronal innate immune responses and microglial activation, linking gut immune alterations to neuroinflammation and α‑synuclein propagation. These findings support a gut–immune–brain cascade wherein dysbiotic communities and immune shifts (e.g., Th17 loss) promote inflammation and facilitate α‑synuclein pathology dissemination. <cite id="39449004">In mice transplanted with fecal material from PD patients, patient-derived microbiota caused midbrain TH+ cell loss and motor dysfunction; ileal remodeling with decreased Th17 homeostatic cells led to increased gut inflammation, barrier disruption, and systemic cytokines; blood–brain barrier leakage and mesencephalic IL-17 were observed, and alpha-synuclein aggregates spread caudo-rostrally, causing mitochondrial fragmentation, neuronal innate immune activation, and microglial activation</cite>.

Complementary mechanistic work in PD models shows that modulating gut–brain autophagy can reduce α‑synuclein burden in both gut and brain compartments. In 6‑hydroxydopamine–induced PD rats, piperine increased colonic and substantia nigra autophagy markers (LC3II/LC3I ratio, p62 degradation) and reduced α‑synuclein aggregation, paralleling improvements in motor and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Pharmacologic and genetic manipulations confirmed that these effects depended on PI3K/AKT/mTOR–mediated autophagy, and in vitro studies in α‑synuclein–overexpressing cells showed that autophagy inhibition or pathway activation altered α‑syn clearance. While this study is preclinical, it supports the concept that enhancing gut–brain autophagy can degrade α‑synuclein and mitigate inflammation-associated toxicity, aligning with human observations of dysbiosis and inflammatory signaling. <cite id="38158101">In 6-OHDA-induced PD rats, piperine improved autonomic and gastrointestinal dysfunction and reduced alpha-synuclein aggregation; LC3II/LC3I increased and p62 degraded in both substantia nigra and colon, with phosphorylation changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR; these effects depended on autophagy and were confirmed in A53T-alpha-syn–overexpressing cells</cite>.

## Evidence for microbiome-derived induction of α‑synuclein pathology
Human metagenomics indicates that the PD microbiome is enriched for immunogenic components and molecules that induce α‑synuclein pathology, suggesting a direct role for microbial metabolites, toxins, or structural proteins in promoting proteopathic seeding. The identification of polymicrobial clusters that co-vary across species and pathways supports the idea that community-level dysbiosis, rather than single-organism effects alone, drives α‑synuclein–related changes via inflammatory and metabolic outputs. <cite id="36376318">The PD microbiome showed a preponderance of molecules that induce alpha-synuclein pathology and over-production of toxicants, with polymicrobial clusters that grow or shrink together, implicating community-level dysbiosis in disease mechanisms</cite>.

## Clinical correlates and immune activation markers
Clinical reviews and cohort analyses emphasize that gut-first PD and intestinal symptoms preceding motor signs are consistent with microbiome–immune–neuro interactions. Proposed human mechanisms include increased intestinal permeability, endotoxemia, and systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines that could activate microglia and astrocytes and contribute to Lewy body formation. The convergence of decreased SCFA producers and increased mucin degraders in PD points to reduced anti-inflammatory signaling and heightened epithelial exposure to microbial products, both of which could foster α‑synuclein aggregation. <cite id="34500451">Intestinal bacteria are implicated in the formation of intestinal alpha-synuclein fibrils, with increased mucin-degrading Akkermansia and decreased SCFA producers linked to increased permeability, exposure to toxins, and downregulation of regulatory T cells that suppress neuronal inflammation</cite>. <cite id="38098067">Clinical observations of intestinal issues preceding motor symptoms and strong associations between gut microbiota and PD support microbiota–gut–brain immune pathways in PD</cite>.

## Limitations and gaps
- Many human studies are cross-sectional and confounders (age, diet, medication, comorbidities) are difficult to control; longitudinal preclinical FMT studies are needed to establish temporality and causality in humans. <cite id="34500451">The review calls for additional biochemical, cellular, and animal studies to further dissect direct associations between intestinal microbiota and PD</cite>.
- While FMT mouse models robustly demonstrate inflammatory and α‑synuclein propagation phenotypes, direct human α‑synuclein seeding assays from fecal material remain technically challenging and ethically constrained; however, convergent metagenomic signals of immunogenicity and proteopathic molecules strengthen the inference of microbial involvement. <cite id="36376318">Metagenomics identifies immunogenic components and alpha-synuclein–inducing molecules in PD microbiomes, providing a foundation for testable hypotheses but requiring further human mechanistic validation</cite>.

## Bottom line
Human studies provide converging evidence that PD-associated gut dysbiosis promotes inflammation and barrier dysfunction, enriches for immunogenic and α‑synuclein–inducing microbial factors, and can, when transferred to mice, trigger systemic inflammatory cascades and α‑synuclein propagation to the brain. These data support gut microbiome alterations as contributors to PD pathogenesis via inflammatory and α‑synuclein–related mechanisms, while emphasizing the need for longitudinal human studies and mechanistic validations to delineate causality and therapeutic targets. <cite id="34500451">Human meta-analytic and mechanistic reviews support increased permeability, inflammation, and α-synuclein aggregation linked to microbiome changes</cite> <cite id="36376318">Large-scale metagenomics shows widespread dysbiosis, immunogenicity, and alpha-synuclein–inducing molecules in PD microbiomes</cite> <cite id="39449004">FMT mouse models demonstrate that PD patient microbiota induce gut inflammation, barrier disruption, systemic cytokines, BBB leakage, and alpha-synuclein propagation with neuroinflammation</cite> <cite id="38098067">Clinical and mechanistic reviews synthesize microbiota–gut–brain immune pathways and early gut symptoms in PD</cite>.
