<snippet id="25192851">Title: Oral teriflunomide for patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis (TOPIC): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
Authors: Miller, Aaron E, Wolinsky, Jerry S, Kappos, Ludwig et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: The Lancet. Neurology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Teriflunomide is a once-daily oral immunomodulator approved for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of teriflunomide in patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis.
METHODS
In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, we enrolled patients aged 18-55 years with clinically isolated syndrome (defined as a neurological event consistent with demyelination, starting within 90 days of randomisation, and two or more T2-weighted MRI lesions ≥3 mm in diameter) from 112 centres (mostly hospitals) in 20 countries. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) in a double-blind manner (by an interactive voice response system) to once-daily oral teriflunomide 14 mg, teriflunomide 7 mg, or placebo, for up to 108 weeks. Patients, staff administering the interventions, and outcome assessors were masked to treatment assignment. The primary endpoint was time to relapse (a new neurological abnormality separated by ≥30 days from a preceding clinical event, present for ≥24 h in the absence of fever or known infection), which defined conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis. The key secondary endpoint was time to relapse or new gadolinium-enhancing or T2 lesions on MRI, whichever occurred first. The primary outcome was analysed for the modified intention-to-treat population; safety analyses included all randomised patients who were exposed to the study drug, as treated. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00622700.
FINDINGS
Between Feb 13, 2008, and Aug 22, 2012, 618 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to teriflunomide 14 mg (n=216), teriflunomide 7 mg (n=205), or placebo (n=197). Two patients in each of the teriflunomide groups did not receive the study drug, so the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 214 patients in the teriflunomide 14 mg group, 203 in the teriflunomide 7 mg group, and 197 in the placebo group. Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio [HR] 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271). Teriflunomide reduced the risk of relapse or a new MRI lesion compared with placebo at the 14 mg dose (HR 0·651 [95% CI 0·515-0·822]; p=0·0003) and at the 7 mg dose (0·686 [0·540-0·871]; p=0·0020). During the study, six patients who were randomly assigned to placebo accidently also received teriflunomide at some point: four received 7 mg and two received 14 mg. Therefore, the safety population comprised 216 patients on teriflunomide 14 mg, 207 on teriflunomide 7 mg, and 191 on placebo. Adverse events that occurred in at least 10% of patients in either teriflunomide group and with an incidence that was at least 2% higher than that with placebo were increased alanine aminotransferase (40 [19%] of 216 patients in the 14 mg group, 36 [17%] of 207 in the 7 mg group vs 27 [14%] of 191 in the placebo group), hair thinning (25 [12%] and 12 [6%] vs 15 [8%]), diarrhoea (23 [11%] and 28 [14%] vs 12 [6%]), paraesthesia (22 [10%] and 11 [5%] vs 10 [5%]), and upper respiratory tract infection (20 [9%] and 23 [11%] vs 14 [7%]). The most common serious adverse event was an increase in alanine aminotransferase (four [2%] and five [2%] vs three [2%]).
INTERPRETATION
TOPIC is to our knowledge the first study to report benefits of an available oral disease-modifying therapy in patients with early multiple sclerosis. These results extend the stages of multiple sclerosis in which teriflunomide shows a beneficial effect.

Genzyme, a Sanofi company.</snippet>

Abstract: BACKGROUND
CLASSIC-MS explored long-term outcomes of patients treated with cladribine tablets.
OBJECTIVE
Assess long-term efficacy in patients previously enrolled in ORACLE-MS, a Phase III parent trial.
METHODS
ORACLE-MS included patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (FCDE or clinically isolated syndrome) who received ⩾1 course of cladribine tablets or placebo. With a median follow-up time of 9.5 years, CLASSIC-MS assessed conversion rates to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), time-to-conversion, relapse rates, long-term mobility/disability status and subsequent disease-modifying therapy (DMT) use.
RESULTS
Of 227 patients from the ORACLE-MS cohort of 616, 68.7% were exposed to cladribine tablets and 31.3% were never exposed. Of the exposed patients at risk, 51.5% converted to CDMS with a median conversion time of 8.4 (95% confidence interval (CI): 5.4-not estimable) years, versus 80.6%, median time 0.8 (95% CI: 0.3-2.4) years, for never exposed. Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.
CONCLUSIONS
Proportionally, more FCDE patients exposed to cladribine tablets experienced delayed conversion to CDMS and fewer relapses and were less likely to use a wheelchair or ambulatory device than never-exposed patients, at 9.5 years (median).</snippet>

data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive inflammatory disease of the central nervous system that results in neurological dysfunction and disability. data.title: Long-term clinical outcomes in patients with CIS treated with interferon beta-1b: results from the 15-year follow up of the BENEFIT trial.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) treatment intervention with immunomodulating therapy at early disease stage improves short term clinical outcomes. The objective of this study is to describe the long-term outcomes and healthcare utilization of patients with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) included in the Betaferon®/Betaseron® in Newly Emerging MS for Initial Treatment (BENEFIT) randomized, parallel group trial. In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later. Of 468 patients, 261 (55.8%) were enrolled into BENEFIT 15 (161 [55.1%] from the early, 100 [56.8%] from the delayed treatment arm). In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group (p = 0.1008). Overall, 25 patients (9.6%; 9.9% early, 9.0% delayed) converted to secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. Disability remained low and stable with no significant difference between groups in Expanded Disability Status Scale score or MRI metrics. Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task-3 scores were better in the early treatment group (p = 0.0036 for treatment effect over 15 years). 66.3% of patients were still employed at Year 15 versus 74.7% at baseline. In conclusion, results 15 years from initial randomization support long-term benefits of early treatment with IFNB-1b.

data.title: Early treatment in multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: There is now a consensus that early treatment of patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is desirable, mainly because early treatment may delay the accumulation of disability, but also because disease-modifying treatments seem to be more effective when started early in the course of the disease. In particular, all current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome. The evidence for this comes from extensive experience in randomised controlled Phase III clinical trials. While many patients presenting a clinically isolated syndrome are at high risk of experiencing a second attack, early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment. Some of these trials have completed five years of follow-up. While the evidence for early intervention is stronger than ever, it is worthwhile to consider its relevance to everyday clinical practice. In particular, it is important to determine which patients are the best candidates for early therapy and to evaluate the anticipated risks and benefits of choosing a given therapy for a given patient.

data.title: Effects of early treatment with glatiramer acetate in patients with clinically isolated syndrome.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The placebo-controlled phase of the PreCISe study showed that glatiramer acetate delayed onset of clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome and brain lesions on MRI.
OBJECTIVE
To compare the effects of early versus delayed glatiramer acetate treatment in the open-label phase of PreCISe.
METHODS
Patients with a clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of MS with unifocal manifestation and ≥2 T2-weighted brain lesions were randomized to receive glatiramer acetate 20 mg/d (early-treatment, n=198) or placebo (delayed-treatment, n=211) for 36 months or until conversion to CDMS, followed by open-label glatiramer acetate treatment for two years.
RESULTS
Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%, p=0.0209), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%, <0.0001) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%, p=0.0005) versus delayed treatment. Adverse events were consistent with the established safety profile of glatiramer acetate.
CONCLUSIONS
Effects of early glatiramer acetate treatment on the rate of conversion to CDMS and on MRI measures of disease activity and lesion burden support initiating glatiramer acetate treatment soon after the first clinical symptoms suggestive of MS and continuing treatment to sustain benefits.

data.title: Magnetic resonance imaging predictors of conversion to multiple sclerosis in the BENEFIT study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Several studies have confirmed the predictive value of baseline and follow-up magnetic resonance (MR) imaging variables for conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), depending on the population, follow-up duration, and treatment intervention. However, the timing of follow-up imaging and the effect of treatment intervention on the predictive value of baseline MR imaging variables require further elucidation.
OBJECTIVES
To assess the prognostic value of baseline MR imaging variables for conversion to CDMS over 3 years and whether this was affected by treatment intervention and (2) to assess the increased risk for conversion posed by dissemination in time on follow-up MR imaging.
DESIGN
Cohort study.
SETTING
Multicenter randomized clinical trial.
PATIENTS
Four hundred sixty-eight patients with a clinically isolated syndrome who had an initial clinical demyelinating event within the past 60 days who received early treatment (3 years of interferon beta-1b) or delayed treatment (placebo first, followed by > or =1 year of interferon beta-1b). Intervention Magnetic resonance imaging. Main Outcome Measure Time to CDMS.
RESULTS
The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%. Barkhof criteria with the strongest prognostic value were the presence at baseline of at least 9 T2-weighted lesions (hazard ratio [HR], 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15-2.33; P = .006) and at least 3 periventricular lesions (1.66; 1.14-2.41; P = .009). No specific advantage was noted in using a fixed cutoff of at least 3 Barkhof criteria (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.95-1.79; P = .10). The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention (P > or = .20 for all). Dissemination in time resulted in increased risk for CDMS only in patients without dissemination in space at baseline and was most informative at the 9-month MR imaging (HR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.26-5.87; P = .01).
CONCLUSIONS
The modified Barkhof criteria showed moderate predictive value for conversion to CDMS, although all patients had received interferon beta-1b therapy for at least 1 year. The predictive value was unaffected by treatment intervention. Follow-up MR imaging was most informative after 9 months in patients without dissemination in space at baseline.

data.title: What do we currently know about the clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of multiple sclerosis? An update.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, demyelinating, not fully understood disease of the central nervous system. The first demyelinating clinical episode is called clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) suggestive of MS. Although the most common manifestations of CIS are long tracts dysfunction and unilateral optic neuritis, it can also include isolated brainstem syndromes, cerebellar involvement, and polysymptomatic clinical image. Recently, the frequency of CIS diagnosis has decreased due to the more sensitive and less specific 2017 McDonald criteria compared with the revisions from 2010. Not all patients with CIS develop MS. The risk of conversion can be estimated based on many predictive factors including epidemiological, ethnical, clinical, biochemical, radiological, immunogenetic, and other markers. The management of CIS is nowadays widely discussed among clinicians and neuroscientists. To date, interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies relying on large groups of patients with the first demyelinating event. All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS and might be used routinely in the future. The goal of this article is to explore the most relevant topics regarding CIS as well as to provide the most recent information in the field. The review presents CIS definition, classification, clinical image, predictive factors, and management. What is more, this is one of very few reviews summarizing the topic in the light of the 2017 McDonald criteria.

data.title: Long-term outcomes with teriflunomide in patients with clinically isolated syndrome: Results of the TOPIC extension study ★★ .
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In the phase 3 TOPIC study, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse determining conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome, versus placebo. We assessed clinical and safety outcomes associated with extended teriflunomide treatment in the TOPIC extension study.
METHODS
Patients who completed the TOPIC core study (including those still on study at early termination) or converted to CDMS after at least 24 weeks in the core study were eligible to participate in the extension. The primary efficacy endpoint in the extension was time to conversion to CDMS.
RESULTS
Risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS was 47.1% lower in patients treated with teriflunomide 14 mg during the core and extension studies compared with patients treated with placebo during the core study and teriflunomide 14 mg during the extension. The incidence of adverse events was 75.8% and 81.9% for 7 and 14 mg teriflunomide, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
Reduced risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS in patients with early MS receiving teriflunomide 14 mg in the core study remained throughout the extension supporting the benefits of early treatment. No new safety signals were observed for teriflunomide 7 or 14 mg.

data.title: Oral teriflunomide for patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis (TOPIC): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Teriflunomide is a once-daily oral immunomodulator approved for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of teriflunomide in patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis.
METHODS
In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, we enrolled patients aged 18-55 years with clinically isolated syndrome (defined as a neurological event consistent with demyelination, starting within 90 days of randomisation, and two or more T2-weighted MRI lesions ≥3 mm in diameter) from 112 centres (mostly hospitals) in 20 countries. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) in a double-blind manner (by an interactive voice response system) to once-daily oral teriflunomide 14 mg, teriflunomide 7 mg, or placebo, for up to 108 weeks. Patients, staff administering the interventions, and outcome assessors were masked to treatment assignment. The primary endpoint was time to relapse (a new neurological abnormality separated by ≥30 days from a preceding clinical event, present for ≥24 h in the absence of fever or known infection), which defined conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis. The key secondary endpoint was time to relapse or new gadolinium-enhancing or T2 lesions on MRI, whichever occurred first. The primary outcome was analysed for the modified intention-to-treat population; safety analyses included all randomised patients who were exposed to the study drug, as treated. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00622700.
FINDINGS
Between Feb 13, 2008, and Aug 22, 2012, 618 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to teriflunomide 14 mg (n=216), teriflunomide 7 mg (n=205), or placebo (n=197). Two patients in each of the teriflunomide groups did not receive the study drug, so the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 214 patients in the teriflunomide 14 mg group, 203 in the teriflunomide 7 mg group, and 197 in the placebo group. Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio [HR] 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271). Teriflunomide reduced the risk of relapse or a new MRI lesion compared with placebo at the 14 mg dose (HR 0·651 [95% CI 0·515-0·822]; p=0·0003) and at the 7 mg dose (0·686 [0·540-0·871]; p=0·0020). During the study, six patients who were randomly assigned to placebo accidently also received teriflunomide at some point: four received 7 mg and two received 14 mg. Therefore, the safety population comprised 216 patients on teriflunomide 14 mg, 207 on teriflunomide 7 mg, and 191 on placebo. Adverse events that occurred in at least 10% of patients in either teriflunomide group and with an incidence that was at least 2% higher than that with placebo were increased alanine aminotransferase (40 [19%] of 216 patients in the 14 mg group, 36 [17%] of 207 in the 7 mg group vs 27 [14%] of 191 in the placebo group), hair thinning (25 [12%] and 12 [6%] vs 15 [8%]), diarrhoea (23 [11%] and 28 [14%] vs 12 [6%]), paraesthesia (22 [10%] and 11 [5%] vs 10 [5%]), and upper respiratory tract infection (20 [9%] and 23 [11%] vs 14 [7%]). The most common serious adverse event was an increase in alanine aminotransferase (four [2%] and five [2%] vs three [2%]).
INTERPRETATION
TOPIC is to our knowledge the first study to report benefits of an available oral disease-modifying therapy in patients with early multiple sclerosis. These results extend the stages of multiple sclerosis in which teriflunomide shows a beneficial effect.
FUNDING
Genzyme, a Sanofi company.

data.title: Long-term follow-up of patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (clinically isolated syndrome) who received cladribine tablets in CLASSIC-MS: Findings for the ORACLE-MS cohort.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
CLASSIC-MS explored long-term outcomes of patients treated with cladribine tablets.
OBJECTIVE
Assess long-term efficacy in patients previously enrolled in ORACLE-MS, a Phase III parent trial.
METHODS
ORACLE-MS included patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (FCDE or clinically isolated syndrome) who received ⩾1 course of cladribine tablets or placebo. With a median follow-up time of 9.5 years, CLASSIC-MS assessed conversion rates to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), time-to-conversion, relapse rates, long-term mobility/disability status and subsequent disease-modifying therapy (DMT) use.
RESULTS
Of 227 patients from the ORACLE-MS cohort of 616, 68.7% were exposed to cladribine tablets and 31.3% were never exposed. Of the exposed patients at risk, 51.5% converted to CDMS with a median conversion time of 8.4 (95% confidence interval (CI): 5.4-not estimable) years, versus 80.6%, median time 0.8 (95% CI: 0.3-2.4) years, for never exposed. Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.
CONCLUSIONS
Proportionally, more FCDE patients exposed to cladribine tablets experienced delayed conversion to CDMS and fewer relapses and were less likely to use a wheelchair or ambulatory device than never-exposed patients, at 9.5 years (median).

# Bottom line

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) in clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) reduces the risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) compared with delayed treatment, across multiple randomized trials and long‑term follow‑ups. The relative risk reduction is substantial for several agents, and benefits are seen even when treatment is started after a single demyelinating event.

# Evidence from randomized trials and long‑term data

- Interferon beta‑1b (IFNβ‑1b): In the BENEFIT trial, early IFNβ‑1b versus delayed treatment showed a significantly lower conversion to CDMS at 2 years (hazard ratio 0.695, 95% CI 0.547–0.883; p=0.0029; absolute risk difference −30.5%), with sustained long‑term benefits up to 15 years, including lower relapse risk and preserved function in the early‑treated group. <cite id="38730097">In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later... In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group.</cite> <cite id="19901165">The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%... The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention.</cite>

- Glatiramer acetate: In the PreCISe study, early glatiramer acetate reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% versus delayed treatment (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.44–0.80), and delayed conversion by approximately 185% in terms of days (about 972 days), with additional MRI benefits (fewer new T2 lesions and lower lesion volume) and less brain atrophy. <cite id="23234810">Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%) versus delayed treatment.</cite>

- Teriflunomide: In the phase 3 TOPIC trial, both 7 mg and 14 mg doses significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining CDMS compared with placebo (hazard ratios 0.628 and 0.574, respectively), and also reduced the risk of relapse or new MRI lesions; benefits persisted in long‑term extension. <cite id="25192851">Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271)... Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.</cite>

# Reviews and consensus

Reviews conclude that early treatment of CIS—after a single demyelinating event—is beneficial and that multiple DMTs (interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine) have demonstrated efficacy in delaying conversion to CDMS. <cite id="24494633">In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS but have had one attack consistent with MS (CIS), initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS.</cite> <cite id="22206762">All current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome... early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment.</cite> <cite id="31811811">Interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies in patients with the first demyelinating event... All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS.</cite>

Across agents and trial designs, initiating DMT soon after CIS is associated with a lower hazard of conversion to CDMS and improved downstream outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity/lesion burden, and better long‑term function and independence). <snippet id="40654861">Title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
Authors: Zatzman, Matthew, Quintanal-Villalonga, Alvaro, Salehi, Sohrab et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="32676311">Title: EGFR mutation genotypes affect efficacy and resistance mechanisms of osimertinib in T790M-positive NSCLC patients.
Authors: Zheng, Qiufan, Huang, Yan, Zhao, Hongyun et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Translational lung cancer research
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Osimertinib is a potent third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with robust activity in advanced EGFR -mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including those with T790M resistance mutation. However, a broad interpatient variability was observed. This study aimed to evaluate whether EGFR -mutant genotypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms in T790M-positive NSCLC patients receiving osimertinib therapy.
METHODS
All NSCLC patients treated with osimertinib in our institute were screened. We included those with known EGFR -mutant genotypes and T790M positivity. Clinical outcomes including objective response rate (ORR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS), were evaluated and compared between different EGFR genotypes. Patients with next-generation sequencing testing or tumor rebiopsy after osimertinib treatment were analyzed for resistance mechanisms.
RESULTS

Abstract: INTRODUCTION
NSCLC transformation to SCLC has been best characterized with EGFR -mutant NSCLC, with emerging case reports seen in ALK , RET , and KRAS -altered NSCLC. Previous reports revealed transformed SCLC from EGFR -mutant NSCLC portends very poor prognosis and lack effective treatment. Genomic analyses revealed TP53 and RB1 loss of function increase the risk of SCLC transformation. Little has been reported on the detailed clinicogenomic characteristics and potential therapeutic targets for this patient population.
METHODS
In this study, we conducted a single-center retrospective analysis of clinical and genomic characteristics of patients with EGFR -mutant NSCLC transformed to SCLC. Demographic data, treatment course, and clinical molecular testing reports were extracted from electronic medical records. Kaplan-Meier analyses were used to estimate survival outcomes. Next generation sequencing-based assays was used to identify EGFR and co-occurring genetic alterations in tissue or plasma before and after SCLC transformation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on a patient-derived-xenograft model generated from a patient with EGFR-NSCLC transformed SCLC tumor.
RESULTS
A total of 34 patients were identified in our study. Median age at initial diagnosis was 58, and median time to SCLC transformation was 24.2 months. 68% were female and 82% were never smokers. 79% of patients were diagnosed as stage IV disease, and over half had brain metastases at baseline. Median overall survival of the entire cohort was 38.3 months from initial diagnoses and 12.4 months from time of SCLC transformation. Most patients harbored EGFR exon19 deletions as opposed to exon21 L858R alteration. Continuing EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor post-transformation did not improve overall survival compared with those patients where tyrosine kinase inhibitor was stopped in our cohort. In the 20 paired pretransformed and post-transformed patient samples, statistically significant enrichment was seen with PIK3CA alterations (p = 0.04) post-transformation. Profiling of longitudinal liquid biopsy samples suggest emergence of SCLC genetic alterations before biopsy-proven SCLC, as shown by increasing variant allele frequency of TP53, RB1, PIK3CA alterations. # Summary

In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors (notably osimertinib) most commonly arises through EGFR-dependent mechanisms (T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation) and a spectrum of EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, with MET amplification, PIK3CA and FGFR pathway alterations, and RET fusions among the most frequent non‑EGFR dependencies. Lineage plasticity and MAPK pathway reactivation also contribute, with histologic transformation (often to squamous or neuroendocrine features) observed in a subset. Reported frequencies vary by cohort and clinical setting, but integrated analyses suggest EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at resistance, and continuation of osimertinib beyond progression can extend survival in selected patients.

# EGFR-Dependent Mechanisms

- T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation: In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations (interpreted as C797S in clinical practice) accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases, indicating a substantial EGFR‑dependent resistance fraction, particularly in T790M‑positive disease. <cite id="30228210">In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases</cite>. In a large T790M‑positive cohort, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, with exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes showing higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, supporting variability by EGFR genotype. <cite id="32676311">In T790M‑positive patients, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, and exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R</cite>.

# EGFR-Independent Mechanisms

- MET amplification: In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies validated MET as a key driver of osimertinib resistance. <cite id="30228210">In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies confirmed MET as a resistance driver</cite>.

- PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET alterations: Recurrent non‑EGFR pathway alterations included PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET, consistent with activation of RTK‑PI3K and related signaling as resistance mechanisms. <cite id="30228210">Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- EMT and lineage plasticity: Integrated single‑nuclei RNA sequencing in an osimertinib‑treated cohort (n=62) showed that MAPK‑low tumors at progression were more likely to undergo histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages, while those maintaining MAPK activity (e.g., with EGFR or MET amplification) tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity; pre‑existing poorly differentiated/neuroendocrine or squamous‑like populations expanded at progression, implicating lineage plasticity as a complementary resistance mechanism. <cite id="40654861">In an osimertinib cohort (n=62), PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (EGFR or MET amplifications) retained adenocarcinoma identity, whereas MAPK‑low tumors were more likely to transform to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre‑existing poorly differentiated populations expanded at progression, indicating lineage plasticity as a resistance substrate</cite>.

- SCLC transformation: Clinicogenomic profiling of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) identified additional resistance/escape routes; paired and longitudinal analyses showed enrichment for TP53/RB1 loss and PIK3CA alterations post‑transformation, with potential targets such as DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7 expressed in transformed SCLC. <cite id="38357092">In 34 EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to SCLC, post‑transformation samples showed enrichment for PIK3CA alterations and TP53/RB1 loss; scRNA‑seq highlighted potential targets DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7</cite>.

# Clinical Frequency and Cohort Observations

- Predominant EGFR‑independent alterations: Across cohorts with molecular profiling at progression, EGFR‑independent genomic alterations were the dominant resistance mechanisms, with MET amplification (≈14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET alterations, and broader pathway changes recurrently observed. <cite id="30228210">Osimertinib resistance was associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, including MET amplification (14%), PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- Genotype‑specific differences: In T790M‑positive patients receiving osimertinib, EGFR genotype influenced outcomes and resistance profiles; exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some comparisons, though results varied across subsets. <cite id="32676311">Exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some analyses</cite>.

- Additional clinicopathologic context: SCLC transformation from EGFR‑mutant disease portends poor prognosis and may represent a resistance pathway; in one series, median overall survival from SCLC transformation was 12.4 months, and continuation of EGFR TKIs post‑transformation did not improve outcomes, reinforcing that transformation often necessitates alternative strategies. <cite id="38357092">In EGFR‑mutant NSCLC transforming to SCLC, median overall survival from transformation was 12.4 months and continuing EGFR TKI post‑transformation did not improve overall survival</cite>.

# Management Implications

- Overcoming resistance: Given the high frequency of EGFR‑independent alterations, combination strategies (e.g., osimertinib plus EGFR‑directed antibodies or MET/PI3K/FGFR/RET inhibitors) and adaptive use (e.g., continuation of osimertinib beyond progression or with local consolidation) may prolong benefit. In the GEMINI/Moffitt cohorts, continuation of osimertinib after progression was associated with longer overall survival, and radiotherapy consolidation yielded median PFS of 15.5 months. <cite id="30228210">Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with longer overall survival (11.2 vs. 6.1 months), and radiotherapy consolidation provided median PFS of 15.5 months</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Most frequent molecular mechanisms of acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors in EGFR‑mutant NSCLC include EGFR‑dependent re‑acquisition (T790M and C797S) and EGFR‑independent alterations, with MET amplification (~14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET pathway changes, and EMT/lineage plasticity commonly observed; SCLC transformation represents a less common but clinically significant resistance route. data.title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
data.abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors (notably osimertinib) most commonly arises through EGFR-dependent mechanisms (T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation) and a spectrum of EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, with MET amplification, PIK3CA and FGFR pathway alterations, and RET fusions among the most frequent non‑EGFR dependencies. Lineage plasticity and MAPK pathway reactivation also contribute, with histologic transformation (often to squamous or neuroendocrine features) observed in a subset. Reported frequencies vary by cohort and clinical setting, but integrated analyses suggest EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at resistance, and continuation of osimertinib beyond progression can extend survival in selected patients.

# EGFR-Dependent Mechanisms

- T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation: In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations (interpreted as C797S in clinical practice) accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases, indicating a substantial EGFR‑dependent resistance fraction, particularly in T790M‑positive disease. <cite id="30228210">In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases</cite>. In a large T790M‑positive cohort, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, with exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes showing higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, supporting variability by EGFR genotype. <cite id="32676311">In T790M‑positive patients, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, and exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R</cite>.

# EGFR-Independent Mechanisms

- MET amplification: In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies validated MET as a key driver of osimertinib resistance. <cite id="30228210">In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies confirmed MET as a resistance driver</cite>.

- PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET alterations: Recurrent non‑EGFR pathway alterations included PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET, consistent with activation of RTK‑PI3K and related signaling as resistance mechanisms. <cite id="30228210">Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- EMT and lineage plasticity: Integrated single‑nuclei RNA sequencing in an osimertinib‑treated cohort (n=62) showed that MAPK‑low tumors at progression were more likely to undergo histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages, while those maintaining MAPK activity (e.g., with EGFR or MET amplification) tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity; pre‑existing poorly differentiated/neuroendocrine or squamous‑like populations expanded at progression, implicating lineage plasticity as a complementary resistance mechanism. <cite id="40654861">In an osimertinib cohort (n=62), PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (EGFR or MET amplifications) retained adenocarcinoma identity, whereas MAPK‑low tumors were more likely to transform to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre‑existing poorly differentiated populations expanded at progression, indicating lineage plasticity as a resistance substrate</cite>.

- SCLC transformation: Clinicogenomic profiling of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) identified additional resistance/escape routes; paired and longitudinal analyses showed enrichment for TP53/RB1 loss and PIK3CA alterations post‑transformation, with potential targets such as DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7 expressed in transformed SCLC. <cite id="38357092">In 34 EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to SCLC, post‑transformation samples showed enrichment for PIK3CA alterations and TP53/RB1 loss; scRNA‑seq highlighted potential targets DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7</cite>.

# Clinical Frequency and Cohort Observations

- Predominant EGFR‑independent alterations: Across cohorts with molecular profiling at progression, EGFR‑independent genomic alterations were the dominant resistance mechanisms, with MET amplification (≈14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET alterations, and broader pathway changes recurrently observed. <cite id="30228210">Osimertinib resistance was associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, including MET amplification (14%), PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- Genotype‑specific differences: In T790M‑positive patients receiving osimertinib, EGFR genotype influenced outcomes and resistance profiles; exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some comparisons, though results varied across subsets. <cite id="32676311">Exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some analyses</cite>.

- Additional clinicopathologic context: SCLC transformation from EGFR‑mutant disease portends poor prognosis and may represent a resistance pathway; in one series, median overall survival from SCLC transformation was 12.4 months, and continuation of EGFR TKIs post‑transformation did not improve outcomes, reinforcing that transformation often necessitates alternative strategies. <cite id="38357092">In EGFR‑mutant NSCLC transforming to SCLC, median overall survival from transformation was 12.4 months and continuing EGFR TKI post‑transformation did not improve overall survival</cite>.

# Management Implications

- Overcoming resistance: Given the high frequency of EGFR‑independent alterations, combination strategies (e.g., osimertinib plus EGFR‑directed antibodies or MET/PI3K/FGFR/RET inhibitors) and adaptive use (e.g., continuation of osimertinib beyond progression or with local consolidation) may prolong benefit. In the GEMINI/Moffitt cohorts, continuation of osimertinib after progression was associated with longer overall survival, and radiotherapy consolidation yielded median PFS of 15.5 months. <cite id="30228210">Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with longer overall survival (11.2 vs. 6.1 months), and radiotherapy consolidation provided median PFS of 15.5 months</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Most frequent molecular mechanisms of acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors in EGFR‑mutant NSCLC include EGFR‑dependent re‑acquisition (T790M and C797S) and EGFR‑independent alterations, with MET amplification (~14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET pathway changes, and EMT/lineage plasticity commonly observed; SCLC transformation represents a less common but clinically significant resistance route. Frequencies vary by cohort and genotype, but EGFR‑independent alterations predominate when molecular profiling is performed at progression, and targeted continuation strategies can extend outcomes in selected patients. <cite id="30228210,32676311,40654861,38357092">Most frequent mechanisms include EGFR‑dependent (T790M/C797S) and EGFR‑independent alterations (MET amplification ~14%, PIK3CA/FGFR/RET), with lineage plasticity and SCLC transformation as additional routes; EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at progression and continuation strategies can extend outcomes</cite>.

<snippet id="39290529">Title: Hemorrhagic complications after stroke treatment with intravenous thrombolysis despite use of direct oral anticoagulants: an observational study.
Authors: Kleeberg, Antonia, Ringleb, Peter A, Huber, Ioana et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Therapeutic advances in neurological disorders
Abstract: BACKGROUND
For patients experiencing ischemic stroke despite receiving therapy with direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) and without endovascular treatment options, therapeutic prospects are currently dismal. Current guidelines recommend intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) only for patients who have received DOAC in very restricted settings, as an increased risk of bleeding is suspected. However, recent retrospective observational studies suggest that IVT is safe despite DOAC pretreatment.
OBJECTIVES
To provide further evidence that IVT despite previous DOAC treatment is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding.
DESIGN
Observational retrospective study.
METHODS
Demographic, clinical, and radiological data of patients who received IVT (+/- endovascular thrombectomy) despite DOAC pretreatment between June 2021 and January 2024 were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including DOAC plasma concentration at admission. Secondary intracranial hemorrhages and functional outcomes at 3 months were assessed. Since 2023, patients have been treated according to a modified local standard operating procedure at our hospital, allowing for IVT despite DOAC pretreatment regardless of DOAC plasma levels or the use of reversal agents.
RESULTS
Of 1821 patients treated with acute recanalization procedures during the study period, N = 35 had received IVT with (18) or without (17) additional endovascular therapy. Among these patients with a wide age range (42-97 years) and DOAC plasma concentrations up to 369 ng/ml, only one developed symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage. A favorable outcome (modified Rankin scale score 0-2) after 3 months was observed in 57% (20) of the patients.
CONCLUSION
IVT despite direct oral anticoagulation seems to be safe, even at advanced age and high DOAC plasma levels.</snippet>

Authors: Matusevicius, Marius, Säflund, Malin, Balestrino, Maurizio et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Annals of neurology
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) is contraindicated for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients taking direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) within 48 hours before index stroke. Limited data exist on off-label use of IVT for these patients. We compared the safety and outcomes of IVT in AIS patients with DOAC treatment and patients with no OAC before index stroke.
METHODS
We analyzed data from the Safe Implementations of Treatments in Stroke (SITS) International Stroke Thrombolysis Registry during 2013-2024. Outcomes were symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (SICH) by the SITS Monitoring Study and European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study II definitions, functional independency (modified Rankin Scale score 0-2), and death by 3 months. Propensity score matching with a nearest neighbor matching algorithm with a ratio of 1:2 was used for relevant clinical variables. We also analyzed the time from last DOAC dose to IVT treatment.
RESULTS
A total of 1,311 DOAC and 129,384 no OAC patients were included. We matched 894 patients with DOAC to 1,788 with no OAC. INTERPRETATION

Authors: Okada, Takashi, Yoshimoto, Takeshi, Wada, Shinichi et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
Abstract: Background We elucidated the safety of treatment with alteplase at 0.6 mg/kg within 24 hours for patients on direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) before ischemic stroke onset. Methods and Results Consecutive patients with acute ischemic stroke who underwent intravenous thrombolysis using alteplase at 0.6 mg/kg from 2011 to 2021 were enrolled from our single-center prospective stroke registry. We compared outcomes between patients taking DOACs and those not taking oral anticoagulants within 48 hours of stroke onset. No significant differences showed in any intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours or mortality at 3 months. Conclusions Intravenous thrombolysis would be safely performed for patients on DOACs following the recommendations of the Japanese guidelines. Registration URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT02251665.</snippet>

Abstract: The introduction of direct oral anticoagulants (DOA) in the early stage of cerebral infarction after thrombolysis may reduce the recurrence rate but raises safety concern. # Bottom line

Across observational cohorts and trial-adjacent registries, prior exposure to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) does not show a consistent increase in symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (SICH) with intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) compared with no anticoagulant exposure, although absolute rates are low and results depend on definitions and selection.

# Observational evidence

- A single-center observational study (2021–2024) of 35 IVT patients with prior DOAC exposure (within a policy allowing IVT regardless of DOAC level or reversal) found only one SICH overall and a 57% favorable 3‑month outcome, suggesting IVT despite DOAC can be safe even at older age and detectable DOAC levels. However, sample size is small and context-specific policies may limit generalizability. <cite id="39290529">A retrospective observational study of 35 patients receiving IVT despite prior DOAC exposure reported only one symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 57% favorable 3‑month outcomes, concluding IVT despite DOAC seems safe across a wide age range and up to high DOAC plasma levels</cite>.

- The SITS International Stroke Registry (2013–2024) compared 1,311 DOAC patients with 129,384 no-OAC patients using propensity matching. SICH was similar under two definitions (1.1% vs 1.5% for SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% for ECASS-II), as were parenchymal hematoma and functional independence at 3 months; mortality also was comparable. This large, matched observational analysis does not show elevated SICH risk among DOAC users treated with IVT. <cite id="39902556">In a matched analysis of 1,311 DOAC and 129,384 no-OAC patients, SICH rates were similar (1.1% vs 1.5% by SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% by ECASS-II), with comparable functional independence and mortality at 3 months, and no effect of time from last DOAC dose to IVT</cite>.

- A single-center JAMA Network Open study (2022) of IVT with alteplase 0.6 mg/kg in patients within 24 hours of stroke onset reported SICH rates of 2.5% in DOAC users versus 2.4% in non-anticoagulated patients, with no significant differences in SICH, any intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours, or 3‑month mortality. Efficacy (favorable outcomes) was similar despite higher admission NIH Stroke Scale scores in DOAC patients. <cite id="36129032">In a single-center registry of 915 IVT patients, SICH occurred in 2.5% of DOAC users vs 2.4% of non-anticoagulated patients (P=0.95), with similar favorable outcomes (59.4% vs 58.2%) and no difference in 36‑hour hemorrhage or 3‑month mortality</cite>.

# Trial-adjacent and post-thrombolysis anticoagulation studies

- A prospective cohort of patients receiving rt-PA IVT within two weeks of DOAC initiation (rivaroxaban or dabigatran) for non-valvular AF reported no symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia with close clinical and radiological monitoring, supporting feasibility of early DOAC resumption after IVT without increased hemorrhage risk in this selected setting. <cite id="25857461">In 34 patients who received rivaroxaban or dabigatran within two weeks after IVT with rt-PA, none experienced symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia under a structured monitoring protocol</cite>.

# Interpretation and caveats

- Definitions differ: SICH criteria vary (SITS-Monitoring vs ECASS-II), and some registries report broader hemorrhagic outcomes (e.g., any parenchymal hematoma). The SITS/ECASS definitions showed no excess SICH in DOAC users, but broader hemorrhage measures may yield different relative risks depending on baseline rates. <cite id="39902556">Analyses used both SITS-Monitoring and ECASS-II SICH definitions and showed no significant differences between DOAC and no-OAC groups</cite>.

- Timing and drug-specific factors matter: Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not materially affect outcomes in SITS, but DOAC pharmacokinetics (e.g., apixaban’s long half-life) and agent-specific bleeding profiles could influence risk in practice. <cite id="39902556">Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not affect SICH, SICH-ECASS, functional independence, or death</cite>.

- Guidelines remain cautious: Despite observational data showing no clear excess SICH, many guidelines still restrict IVT in recent DOAC exposure due to theoretical bleeding risk and limited randomized evidence; thus, risk-benefit decisions often require individualized assessment, antiplatelet bridging consideration, and readiness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39290529">Guidelines have historically discouraged IVT in patients with recent DOAC exposure due to suspected increased bleeding risk, but recent observational data suggest IVT despite DOAC may be safe in selected cases</cite>.

# Conclusion

Observational and trial-adjacent evidence indicates that prior DOAC use is not consistently associated with higher SICH risk after IVT compared with no anticoagulant exposure, with some studies showing numerically similar SICH rates and no difference in functional outcomes or mortality. However, absolute SICH remains uncommon, and heterogeneity in DOAC types, timing, definitions, and patient selection limits broad generalization; thus, IVT in DOAC-exposed patients should be individualized with careful monitoring and preparedness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39902556,36129032,39290529">Observational and registry data show no consistent increase in SICH with IVT among DOAC users compared with no anticoagulation, though practice policies and definitions vary and careful case selection remains essential</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Intravenous Thrombolysis With Alteplase at 0.6 mg/kg in Patients With Ischemic Stroke Taking Direct Oral Anticoagulants.
data.abstract: Background We elucidated the safety of treatment with alteplase at 0.6 mg/kg within 24 hours for patients on direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) before ischemic stroke onset. Methods and Results Consecutive patients with acute ischemic stroke who underwent intravenous thrombolysis using alteplase at 0.6 mg/kg from 2011 to 2021 were enrolled from our single-center prospective stroke registry. We compared outcomes between patients taking DOACs and those not taking oral anticoagulants within 48 hours of stroke onset. The primary safety outcome was the rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage with a ≥4-point increase on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score from baseline. The efficacy outcome was defined as 3-month modified Rankin Scale score of 0 to 2 after stroke onset. Of 915 patients with acute ischemic stroke who received intravenous thrombolysis (358 women; median age, 76 years; median National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score, 10), 40 patients took DOACs (6 took dabigatran, 8 took rivaroxaban, 16 took apixaban, and 10 took edoxaban) within 24 hours of onset and 753 patients did not take any oral anticoagulants. The rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was comparable between patients on DOACs and those not on oral anticoagulants (2.5% versus 2.4%, P =0.95). The rate of favorable outcomes was comparable between the 2 groups (59.4% versus 58.2%, P =0.46), although the admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was higher in patients on DOACs. No significant differences showed in any intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours or mortality at 3 months. Conclusions Intravenous thrombolysis would be safely performed for patients on DOACs following the recommendations of the Japanese guidelines. # Bottom line

Across observational cohorts and trial-adjacent registries, prior exposure to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) does not show a consistent increase in symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (SICH) with intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) compared with no anticoagulant exposure, although absolute rates are low and results depend on definitions and selection.

# Observational evidence

- A single-center observational study (2021–2024) of 35 IVT patients with prior DOAC exposure (within a policy allowing IVT regardless of DOAC level or reversal) found only one SICH overall and a 57% favorable 3‑month outcome, suggesting IVT despite DOAC can be safe even at older age and detectable DOAC levels. However, sample size is small and context-specific policies may limit generalizability. <cite id="39290529">A retrospective observational study of 35 patients receiving IVT despite prior DOAC exposure reported only one symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 57% favorable 3‑month outcomes, concluding IVT despite DOAC seems safe across a wide age range and up to high DOAC plasma levels</cite>.

- The SITS International Stroke Registry (2013–2024) compared 1,311 DOAC patients with 129,384 no-OAC patients using propensity matching. SICH was similar under two definitions (1.1% vs 1.5% for SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% for ECASS-II), as were parenchymal hematoma and functional independence at 3 months; mortality also was comparable. This large, matched observational analysis does not show elevated SICH risk among DOAC users treated with IVT. <cite id="39902556">In a matched analysis of 1,311 DOAC and 129,384 no-OAC patients, SICH rates were similar (1.1% vs 1.5% by SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% by ECASS-II), with comparable functional independence and mortality at 3 months, and no effect of time from last DOAC dose to IVT</cite>.

- A single-center JAMA Network Open study (2022) of IVT with alteplase 0.6 mg/kg in patients within 24 hours of stroke onset reported SICH rates of 2.5% in DOAC users versus 2.4% in non-anticoagulated patients, with no significant differences in SICH, any intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours, or 3‑month mortality. Efficacy (favorable outcomes) was similar despite higher admission NIH Stroke Scale scores in DOAC patients. <cite id="36129032">In a single-center registry of 915 IVT patients, SICH occurred in 2.5% of DOAC users vs 2.4% of non-anticoagulated patients (P=0.95), with similar favorable outcomes (59.4% vs 58.2%) and no difference in 36‑hour hemorrhage or 3‑month mortality</cite>.

# Trial-adjacent and post-thrombolysis anticoagulation studies

- A prospective cohort of patients receiving rt-PA IVT within two weeks of DOAC initiation (rivaroxaban or dabigatran) for non-valvular AF reported no symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia with close clinical and radiological monitoring, supporting feasibility of early DOAC resumption after IVT without increased hemorrhage risk in this selected setting. <cite id="25857461">In 34 patients who received rivaroxaban or dabigatran within two weeks after IVT with rt-PA, none experienced symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia under a structured monitoring protocol</cite>.

# Interpretation and caveats

- Definitions differ: SICH criteria vary (SITS-Monitoring vs ECASS-II), and some registries report broader hemorrhagic outcomes (e.g., any parenchymal hematoma). The SITS/ECASS definitions showed no excess SICH in DOAC users, but broader hemorrhage measures may yield different relative risks depending on baseline rates. <cite id="39902556">Analyses used both SITS-Monitoring and ECASS-II SICH definitions and showed no significant differences between DOAC and no-OAC groups</cite>.

- Timing and drug-specific factors matter: Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not materially affect outcomes in SITS, but DOAC pharmacokinetics (e.g., apixaban’s long half-life) and agent-specific bleeding profiles could influence risk in practice. <cite id="39902556">Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not affect SICH, SICH-ECASS, functional independence, or death</cite>.

- Guidelines remain cautious: Despite observational data showing no clear excess SICH, many guidelines still restrict IVT in recent DOAC exposure due to theoretical bleeding risk and limited randomized evidence; thus, risk-benefit decisions often require individualized assessment, antiplatelet bridging consideration, and readiness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39290529">Guidelines have historically discouraged IVT in patients with recent DOAC exposure due to suspected increased bleeding risk, but recent observational data suggest IVT despite DOAC may be safe in selected cases</cite>.

# Conclusion

Observational and trial-adjacent evidence indicates that prior DOAC use is not consistently associated with higher SICH risk after IVT compared with no anticoagulant exposure, with some studies showing numerically similar SICH rates and no difference in functional outcomes or mortality. However, absolute SICH remains uncommon, and heterogeneity in DOAC types, timing, definitions, and patient selection limits broad generalization; thus, IVT in DOAC-exposed patients should be individualized with careful monitoring and preparedness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39902556,36129032,39290529">Observational and registry data show no consistent increase in SICH with IVT among DOAC users compared with no anticoagulation, though practice policies and definitions vary and careful case selection remains essential</cite>.

# Summary of Evidence Linking EBV Exposure/Reactivation to MS Onset and Progression

## Epidemiologic Associations
Multiple cross-sectional and case-control studies report that seropositivity to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is far more common in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) than in matched controls, with seronegativity at conception strongly protective against MS risk. These associations are strongest for seroreactivity to latent EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1), less consistent for early-life varicella-zoster virus exposure, and typically weaker for other herpesviruses, suggesting a specific role for EBV rather than ubiquitous viral exposures. Twin and family studies further indicate that the MS-risk association is greater when one monozygotic twin is EBV-seronegative while the other is seropositive, consistent with a mechanistic, rather than purely genetic, link. Population-based studies also show a temporal association: EBV-specific IgG seroconversion occurs after symptom onset in most seronegative-at-birth MS patients, arguing against a strict pre-onset deterministic causation for all cases.

## Cohort and Longitudinal Observations
Prospective cohort data suggest that EBV seropositivity is linked to disease activity in relapse-onset MS, with higher EBNA1 seroreactivity associated with greater relapse burden and MRI lesion load in some cohorts. In primary progressive MS (PPMS), a subset with delayed or absent adolescent EBV seroconversion shows distinct immune signatures and, in at least one cohort, faster disability progression over an 8-year follow-up compared to EBV-seropositive PPMS and controls. These findings support a model in which EBV exposure contributes to disease initiation and may differentially influence progressive disease courses depending on timing and immunologic context.

## Mechanistic and Biomarker Data
Latent EBV proteins, particularly EBNA1, are repeatedly detected in MS lesions and associated with activated B cells in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid, implicating latent infection and reactivation in the CNS microenvironment. EBNA1-specific T-cell and antibody responses correlate with inflammatory activity on MRI and clinical relapses in relapse-onset MS, and elevated EBNA1 responses are selectively increased in PPMS, suggesting a distinct pathogenic role for EBV in progressive forms. In contrast, neutralizing antibodies to the lytic VCA antigen do not show the same association, pointing to latent, rather than lytic, viral phases as more relevant to MS pathology.

## Strengths and Limitations of the Evidence
- Strengths: Consistent seroepidemiology across diverse populations, temporal sequence in seronegative-at-birth MS, twin discordance patterns, and longitudinal correlations between EBNA1-specific immunity and disease activity provide converging support for a causal or contributory role of EBV in MS. The specificity for EBNA1 and the link to CNS-infiltrating B cells/latent EBV in lesions strengthen biological plausibility.
- Limitations: Observational designs limit causal inference; not all MS cases are seronegative at birth, and EBV exposure does not uniformly accelerate progression or predict severe disability. Heterogeneity in assays (EBNA1 vs VCA), variable timing of exposure, and confounding by shared environmental risk factors remain important caveats.

## Bottom Line
Collectively, epidemiologic, temporal, and longitudinal data—especially the strong association with EBNA1-specific immune responses, the protective effect of EBV seronegativity at conception, and the observation that EBV-specific immunity tracks with MRI and clinical activity—support EBV exposure or reactivation as a causal or contributing factor in MS onset and, in some cohorts, faster progression. The weight of evidence favors a contributory, context-dependent role rather than a single-gene, deterministic cause, with latent EBV in B cells within the CNS as a plausible mechanistic driver. <cite id="39666032">Elevated EBNA1-specific antibody responses are selectively increased in primary progressive MS and correlate with progressive disease, and EBV seroprevalence patterns and twin discordance support a contributory role of EBV in both relapse-onset and progressive forms</cite>.
</answer>

Authors: Hooper, Robert G, Ramaswamy, Viraraghavan Vadakkencherry, Wahid, Rachael M et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Developmental medicine and child neurology
Abstract: AIM
To assess the effectiveness and safety of levetiracetam when used as first-line treatment of neonatal seizures.
METHOD
Four electronic databases, Medline, Embase, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov were systematically searched from inception until 20th November 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies that included neonates born preterm and term were eligible for inclusion. The primary outcome measure was levetiracetam effectiveness, defined as seizure cessation within 24 hours of starting treatment. Secondary outcomes included short-term adverse events, mortality before discharge, and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
RESULTS
Fourteen studies assessing 1188 neonates were included: four RCTs, three observational trials with phenobarbital as the control arm, and seven observational studies of levetiracetam with no control arm. Pooled efficacy of levetiracetam from observational studies was 45% (95% confidence interval [CI] 34-57%) (GRADE - very low). Meta-analysis of RCTs evaluating levetiracetam versus phenobarbital showed that both were equally effective (risk ratio [95% CI] 0.6 [0.30-1.20]) (GRADE - very low). Levetiracetam resulted in a lower risk of short-term adverse events compared to phenobarbital (risk ratio [95% CI] 0.24 [0.06-0.92]) (GRADE - moderate).

Very low certainty of evidence suggests levetiracetam might not be more effective than phenobarbital. Moderate certainty of evidence indicates levetiracetam is associated with a lower risk of adverse events. Future trials on neonatal antiseizure medication therapy should include continuous electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring as standard of care and enrol a homogenous population with similar seizure aetiology. What this paper adds Levetiracetam is effective in 45% of neonatal seizures. Levetiracetam might not be more effective than phenobarbital. Levetiracetam is likely to be safer than phenobarbital. Evidence available is limited and of very low certainty.</snippet>

# Summary

- Evidence from a recent Cochrane systematic review indicates that, in neonates with electrographic seizures, phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control after the first loading dose (RR 2.32, 95% CI 1.63–3.30) and after maximal loading dose (RR 2.83, 95% CI 1.78–4.50), based on a single randomized trial focused on EEG-confirmed seizures; however, certainty for these comparative effectiveness estimates is moderate, and the same trial provided very low-certainty evidence for differences in short-term safety outcomes such as mortality before discharge, mechanical ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and post-discharge epilepsy; longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in that trial and thus remain uncertain. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control after first loading dose and after maximal loading dose in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures, but evidence for mortality, ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and epilepsy is very low certainty, and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported</cite>.

- A systematic review and meta-analysis focused on levetiracetam as first-line therapy reported that, in randomized trials comparing levetiracetam versus phenobarbital, both drugs were equally effective (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.30–1.20), while observational data suggested lower efficacy (45%, 95% CI 34–57%); importantly, levetiracetam was associated with a lower risk of short-term adverse events compared to phenobarbital (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06–0.92), with overall certainty of evidence characterized as very low to moderate for safety. <cite id="34124790">In randomized trials, levetiracetam and phenobarbital were similarly effective, but levetiracetam had a lower risk of short-term adverse events; pooled observational efficacy for levetiracetam was 45%, and the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate</cite>.

# Interpretation for Electrographic Seizure Control

- Head-to-head randomized data are limited, but the Cochrane review synthesizes one RCT in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures showing higher odds of seizure control with phenobarbital at both first and maximal loading doses. This suggests phenobarbital may have superior acute electrographic control in this context, though the trial's small sample and limited outcomes warrant caution. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital showed higher effectiveness for seizure control than levetiracetam after first and maximal loading doses in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures, based on a single trial</cite>.

- Conversely, the meta-analysis of levetiracetam including randomized comparisons found no efficacy advantage over phenobarbital, which may reflect differences in study populations, dosing regimens, or the inclusion of observational trials with lower certainty. <cite id="34124790">Randomized trials found no efficacy difference between levetiracetam and phenobarbital as first-line treatments</cite>.

# Short-Term Safety

- The Cochrane review reported very low-certainty evidence for phenobarbital versus levetiracetam regarding mortality before discharge, need for ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and post-discharge epilepsy in the single relevant trial; thus, no firm conclusion can be drawn about relative short-term safety from that comparison alone. <cite id="37873971">Evidence comparing phenobarbital and levetiracetam on short-term safety outcomes (mortality, ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, epilepsy) was very low certainty, precluding firm conclusions</cite>.

- The levetiracetam-focused review reported a lower risk of short-term adverse events with levetiracetam compared to phenobarbital (RR 0.24), with moderate certainty, suggesting a potential safety advantage for levetiracetam in the acute phase of neonatal seizure management. <cite id="34124790">Levetiracetam was associated with a lower risk of short-term adverse events than phenobarbital (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06–0.92)</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Gaps

- For neonatal seizures managed with continuous EEG, phenobarbital appears more likely to achieve rapid electrographic control, particularly after initial loading doses, but high-quality head-to-head trials with standardized EEG endpoints and longer follow-up are needed to confirm superiority and to clarify neurodevelopmental outcomes. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital may be more effective for electrographic control, but better trials with standardized EEG endpoints and long-term follow-up are needed</cite>.

- If minimizing acute adverse effects is a priority, levetiracetam may be considered safer based on the meta-analysis, although randomized evidence for efficacy equivalence must be weighed against phenobarbital's higher likelihood of early control. <cite id="34124790">Levetiracetam may have fewer short-term adverse events than phenobarbital, while randomized trials show similar efficacy</cite>.

- Both reviews emphasize that evidence for longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes is limited and of low to very low certainty, and that future trials should standardize EEG-based diagnosis and reporting of short- and long-term outcomes. <cite id="37873971">Long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in key trials, and future RCTs with EEG-based endpoints and adequate power are needed</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In neonatal seizures with electrographic confirmation, phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam for achieving early seizure control, particularly after initial loading doses, but the comparative short-term safety signal favors levetiracetam, and high-certainty evidence on neurodevelopmental outcomes is lacking. Clinician choice should balance the need for rapid EEG control against the potential for fewer acute adverse effects with levetiracetam, within the context of local expertise, availability, and continuous EEG monitoring. <cite id="37873971,34124790">Phenobarbital may offer superior early electrographic control, while levetiracetam may carry fewer short-term adverse effects; robust evidence on neurodevelopmental outcomes is limited, and decisions should consider local resources and continuous EEG monitoring</cite>.
