<snippet id="23624554">Title: Adult-onset Still's disease and pregnancy: about ten cases and review of the literature.
Authors: Gerfaud-Valentin, M, Hot, A, Huissoud, C et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: Rheumatology international
Abstract: Little is known about the interactions between adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) and pregnancy. In an attempt to clarify the link between these 2 conditions, we retrospectively analyzed patients registered as suffering from AOSD seen in our university hospital. A total of 57 patients, among them 30 women, were diagnosed. Ten pregnancies in 8 women were identified. Three cases manifested AOSD in their first trimester, all treated with prednisone. Premature births and flares occurred in 2 patients. One patient developed a monocyclic AOSD during her second pregnancy's postpartum. In the 4 other cases, AOSD was known and quiescent before pregnancy. One patient had 2 pregnancies without any flare or complication. One patient experienced her first pregnancy while under treatment and presented a late flare 8 months after delivery. The third patient developed exacerbation in the first trimester of her second pregnancy which was treated with IgIV alone. The last one presented her first pregnancy 7 years after diagnosis. A prednisone-treated systemic flare occurred during the first trimester without later complication. Based on our own experience and the analysis of only two series of the literature, including, respectively, 4 and 5 patients, we suggest that two settings could be distinguished. First, AOSD can occur during pregnancy and can be responsible for obstetrical complications. Then, in patients with known AOSD, the second trimester and postpartum appear to be periods exposing to disease recurrence. Thus, we recommend a close multidisciplinary monitoring by a rheumatologist and an obstetrician prior to, during and after pregnancies.</snippet>
<snippet id="35249153">Title: Pregnant women with immune mediated inflammatory diseases who discontinue biologics have higher rates of disease flare.
Authors: Allen, Kenneth D, Kiefer, Miranda K, Butnariu, Madalina et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Archives of gynecology and obstetrics
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS
Biologic agents have revolutionized treatment of immune mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs). However, despite the benefits of treatment, there is limited data on its use during pregnancy leading to significant variation in practices. We evaluated maternal, neonatal, and disease-related outcomes in pregnant women with IMIDs, comparing those with biologic exposure during pregnancy to those without exposure. Our hypothesis was that there would be no difference in outcomes between the two groups.
METHODS
This is a retrospective cohort study conducted at a single tertiary care center including women with Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), or psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis (PS/PsA) who delivered between 2010 and 2018 at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. Conditions were identified by ICD-9/ICD-10 code and confirmed by chart review. Demographic data, pregnancy outcomes and disease-related data were collected.
RESULTS
There were 338 pregnancies including 100 with CD, 74 with UC, 15 with AS, 61 with RA, and 90 with PS/PsA. 23% of IMID patients had biologic exposure (biologic use within 3 months of conception) and 18% continued therapy during pregnancy. Those with biologic exposure had increased risk of post-partum disease flare (OR 3.44; 95% CI 1.29, 9.15) and were less likely to breastfeed (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.23, 0.87). In subgroup analysis of patients with IBD, those with biologic exposure also had increased risk of post-partum flare (OR 4.55; 95% CI 1.27, 16.35). Maternal and neonatal pregnancy outcomes were similar.
CONCLUSION
Among pregnant women with IMIDs, those that continued biologics during pregnancy had increased rates of major infection, disease related hospital admission, glucocorticoid use, and disease flare within 6 months post-partum, without any significant change in maternal or neonatal outcomes.</snippet>

<snippet id="34519994">Title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Pregnancy: a Portuguese Case-Control Study.
Authors: Braga, António, Barros, Tânia, Faria, Raquel et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Clinical reviews in allergy & immunology
Abstract: Pregnancy in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes. During pregnancy, SLE patients have a higher rate of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction, or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. To date, only a few case-control studies were published with the purpose to evaluate the magnitude of risk associated with pregnancy in lupus patients. The aim of our study was to evaluate the maternal and fetal outcomes in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and to compare it with a group of healthy pregnant women. We conducted a retrospective case-control study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary center, between 2010 and 2019. Pregnancy outcomes were compared between SLE patients and a group of matched healthy pregnant women. Baseline maternal data was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. One hundred twenty-four SLE pregnancies were included. Of the patients, 95.2% were in remission at conception. In 13.7% of cases, a lupus flare was diagnosed during gestation and in 17.9% in the postpartum period. The live birth rate was 84.6%, and the incidence of adverse outcomes was 40.3% (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.67-4.18). Considering only patients in remission at conception, the presence of adverse outcomes remained significantly higher (36.8% vs. 20.3%, P < 0.01). Miscarriage rate was 15.3% (OR 5.85, 95% CI 2.57-13.34) and preterm delivery occurred in 12.4% of the patients (OR 1.72, 95% CI 0.83-3.57). Preeclampsia prevalence was higher in SLE patients (OR 3.92, 95% CI 1.32-11.57). In the SLE group, the newborn admission to an intensive care unit rate was increased (OR 4.99, 95% CI 1.47-16.90). No neonatal or maternal deaths were reported. In our study, pregnancy with SLE was associated with an increased incidence of adverse outcomes, even in a population of SLE patients with well-controlled disease.</snippet>
<snippet id="34693803">Title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and pregnancy: A retrospective single-center study of 215 pregnancies from Portugal.
Authors: Braga, António, Barros, Tânia, Faria, Raquel et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a life-threatening disorder that affects women at reproductive age. We evaluate the clinical impact of pregnancy in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and the risk factors associated with maternal and fetal adverse outcomes.
METHODS
A retrospective observational study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary hospital, between January 1993 and December 2019. Baseline maternal information was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. Disease activity before and during pregnancy was assessed.
RESULTS
We included 215 pregnancies from 143 patients. Lupus nephritis was present in 20.0% and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in 21.9% of the cases. Preconception consultation was performed in 86.9% of the pregnancies, and 92.5% of the patients had no or low disease activity at conception. During gestation, 79.6% of the patients were under treatment, and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) was the most commonly used drug (63.7%). Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) was prescribed at conception in 87.9% of the patients. The live birth rate was 84.2%. An adverse pregnancy outcome (APO) occurred in 41.4% of the pregnancies. A miscarriage rate of 15.3% and a preterm delivery rate of 15.4% were found. Preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction complicated 13.1% and 14.0% of the gestations, respectively. Neonatal lupus occurred in 7.1% of the newborns, and there were 2 cases of congenital heart block. Significant risk factors for the development of AOP were disease activity at conception, lupus flare, hypocomplementemia, positivity for lupus anticoagulant, and APS. The use of ASA was significantly associated with a reduced incidence of miscarriage. An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of the cases. We identified as risk factors for lupus flares the presence of active disease at conception, a previous history of lupus nephritis, and the use of chronic medication. HCQ use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction of flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum.
CONCLUSIONS
Pregnancy in an SLE patient is associated with an increased incidence of adverse obstetric outcomes. Good disease control before pregnancy and adequate treatment, especially with HCQ, is crucial to achieving the best obstetric results.</snippet>
<snippet id="31539383">Title: Predictors of SLE relapse in pregnancy and post-partum among multi-ethnic patients in Malaysia.
Authors: Shaharir, Syahrul Sazliyana, Mohamed Said, Mohd Shahrir, Mohd, Rozita et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: PloS one
Abstract: Flare of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) may occur during pregnancy and puerperium. We studied the prevalence and factors associated with SLE relapse during pregnancy and post-partum period in a multi-ethnic SLE cohort. Consecutive SLE patients who attended the outpatient clinic were reviewed for previous history of pregnancies in our institution. Patients who had a complete antenatal, delivery, and post-partum follow up were included. Their medical records were retrospectively analysed to assess the disease activity at pre-pregnancy/conception, during antenatal, and post-partum period. Presence of flare episodes during pregnancy and puerperium were recorded. The pregnancy outcomes recorded include live birth, foetal loss, prematurity and intra-uterine growth restrictions (IUGR). Univariate and multivariable logistic regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE) analyses were performed to determine the factors associated with disease relapse and the pregnancy outcomes. A total of 120 patients with 196 pregnancies were included, with a live birth rate of 78.6%. Four (2.0%) were diagnosed to have SLE during pregnancy. The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%. Majority of the relapse in pregnancy occurred in haematological system (62.3%) followed by renal (53.2%), musculoskeletal (22.1%), and mucocutaneous (14.3%). In GEE analyses, active disease at conception was the independent predictor of SLE relapse during and after pregnancy, whereas older maternal age and Malay ethnicity were associated with higher flare during post-partum. HCQ use was significantly associated with reduced risk of flare in univariate analysis but it was no longer significant in the GEE analyses. Presence of disease flare in pregnancy was significantly associated with prematurity. In conclusion, pregnancy in SLE need to be planned during quiescent state as pre-pregnant active disease was associated with disease relapse in both during and after pregnancy. Malay patients had an increased risk of post-partum flare but further larger prospective studies are needed to confirm the association between pregnancies in the different ancestral background.</snippet>

# Summary of how female sex hormone exposure during pregnancy/postpartum shapes disease activity in RA, SLE, and MS

## Multiple sclerosis (MS)
- Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly influence MS relapse trajectories. Observational data from a large French MS registry show that how disease-modifying therapy (DMT) is managed across preconception, gestation, and postpartum periods shapes annualized relapse rates (ARRs). DMT strategies that involve pregnancy can increase ARR during gestation (causal RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.06–1.22) and postpartum (cRR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01–1.16), with the largest excess risk when natalizumab is interrupted for prolonged periods (e.g., before the second trimester or resumed >3 months postpartum; cRR 2.18, 95% CI 1.76–2.69) or when fingolimod is used (cRR 2.15, 95% CI 1.60–2.93). In contrast, anti-CD20 strategies before conception were the most effective at mitigating relapse risk (cRR 0.38, 95% CI 0.25–0.52), followed by natalizumab with a short interruption (cRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71–0.90), while interferon β (cRR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86–0.99) and glatiramer acetate (cRR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84–0.99) were less protective in this causal framework. These findings indicate that hormonal exposure patterns tied to therapeutic interruption and immune-modulatory choices during pregnancy/postpartum can either dampen or exacerbate relapse risk, with postpartum rebound being a key vulnerability period. <cite id="40758347">DMT management during pregnancy significantly increased ARR during gestation and postpartum; anti-CD20 strategy was most effective, while strategies with prolonged natalizumab or fingolimod interruption increased risk; postpartum rebound is a key period</cite>. Reviews and consensus guidance emphasize that pregnancy itself is associated with modified MS activity, and that careful preconception/postpartum planning and medication selection are essential to minimize relapses and disability progression. <cite id="37741528">Pregnancy is a significant concern in MS due to relapse risk and need for tailored management across gestation and postpartum</cite> <cite id="36931808">Withdrawal of some DMTs can modify MS course, increasing pregnancy-related relapse risk and disability, underscoring the need for individualized strategies balancing maternal and fetal safety</cite> <cite id="38245998">Guidelines address diagnosis and treatment across pregnancy, reflecting the need to align therapeutic strategies with hormonal and immune changes</cite>.

## Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
- Cohort evidence in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs, including RA) suggests that stopping biologic therapy around conception and early pregnancy is associated with higher postpartum disease flares. In a retrospective cohort of pregnancies in RA and related IMIDs, women who had biologic exposure around conception and continued therapy during pregnancy had increased odds of postpartum disease flare (OR 3.44, 95% CI 1.29–9.15), alongside higher risks of hospitalization and glucocorticoid use, though maternal and neonatal outcomes were similar overall. Subgroup analyses in inflammatory bowel disease showed similar patterns (OR 4.55, 95% CI 1.27–16.35 for postpartum flare with biologic interruption). These data imply that the hormonal milieu of pregnancy, combined with therapeutic interruption or exposure, can trigger postpartum flares in RA, particularly when biologic control is disrupted. <cite id="35249153">Discontinuation of biologics in IMIDs including RA around pregnancy was associated with higher postpartum flare risk; continuing biologics during pregnancy increased postpartum flare and hospitalization but did not worsen maternal/neonatal outcomes</cite>. Case-based and small-series evidence in related systemic inflammatory diseases (e.g., adult-onset Still’s disease) highlight that the postpartum period is a recognized recurrence phase, reinforcing the notion that hormonal shifts and immune reconstitution after delivery can precipitate flares in autoimmune conditions. <cite id="23624554">In AOSD, the second trimester and postpartum are periods of higher recurrence risk, warranting close multidisciplinary monitoring around pregnancy and postpartum</cite>.

## Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
- In SLE, pregnancy is associated with measurable rates of disease flares during gestation and especially in the puerperium, and these flares correlate with adverse obstetric outcomes. A Portuguese case-control cohort reported lupus flares in 13.7% during gestation and 17.9% in postpartum, with an overall adverse outcome incidence of 40.3% compared to matched controls. A larger single-center series (215 pregnancies) found an SLE flare in 16.3% of pregnancies, with significant predictors of flare including active disease at conception, prior lupus nephritis, and lack of chronic medication use; hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) use during pregnancy was associated with reduced flare risk during and after delivery. Another Malaysian cohort observed flare rates of 40.1% in pregnancy and 17.4% postpartum, with hematologic and renal systems most commonly involved; active disease at conception independently predicted relapse during and after pregnancy, and postpartum flares were more frequent in Malay ethnicity in that population. These data indicate that the hormonal and immune milieu of pregnancy can unmask SLE activity, with the puerperium being a high-risk interval for relapse, particularly when baseline disease control is suboptimal. <cite id="34519994">In SLE pregnancies, flares occurred in 13.7% during gestation and 17.9% postpartum, with higher adverse outcomes even among women in remission at conception</cite> <cite id="34693803">Flares occurred in 16.3%; predictors included active disease at conception, prior lupus nephritis, and lack of chronic medication, while HCQ use reduced flare risk during and postpartum</cite> <cite id="31539383">Flare rates were 40.1% in pregnancy and 17.4% postpartum; active disease at conception independently predicted relapse during and after pregnancy, and HCQ reduced flare risk though not significantly in multivariable GEE models</cite>. Reviews of SLE and pregnancy similarly note increased miscarriage, preterm delivery, hypertensive disorders, and neonatal lupus, reinforcing that hormonal and immune changes during pregnancy can drive both obstetric and autoimmune activity trajectories. <cite id="34519994">Pregnancy in SLE increases risks of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction, and hypertensive disorders, even in well-controlled disease</cite>.

## Cross-disease themes and clinical implications

data.title: Multiple sclerosis and pregnancy: Pathogenesis, influencing factors, and treatment options.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune-mediated degenerative disease of the central nervous system, characterized by inflammatory demyelination. It is primarily found in women of childbearing age, making pregnancy a significant concern for both patients with MS and clinicians. To assist these patients in achieving their desire for pregnancy, reducing MS relapses during all stages of pregnancy, preventing the progression of MS, mitigating the impact of MS treatment on the course and outcome of pregnancy, and a thorough understanding of the relationship between pregnancy and MS, as well as specific management and the application of relevant medications for MS patients at each stage of pregnancy, are essential. This article provides an update on pregnancy-related issues in women with MS, including the general recommendations for management at each stage of pregnancy.

data.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Multiple Sclerosis: A Review.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune-mediated neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system characterized by inflammatory demyelination with axonal transection. MS affects an estimated 900 000 people in the US. MS typically presents in young adults (mean age of onset, 20-30 years) and can lead to physical disability, cognitive impairment, and decreased quality of life. This review summarizes current evidence regarding diagnosis and treatment of MS.
OBSERVATIONS
MS typically presents in young adults aged 20 to 30 years with unilateral optic neuritis, partial myelitis, sensory disturbances, or brainstem syndromes such as internuclear ophthalmoplegia developing over several days. The prevalence of MS worldwide ranges from 5 to 300 per 100 000 people and increases at higher latitudes. Overall life expectancy is less than in the general population (75.9 vs 83.4 years), and MS more commonly affects women (female to male sex distribution of nearly 3:1). Diagnosis is made based on a combination of signs and symptoms, radiographic findings (eg, magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] T2 lesions), and laboratory findings (eg, cerebrospinal fluid-specific oligoclonal bands), which are components of the 2017 McDonald Criteria. Nine classes of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), with varying mechanisms of action and routes of administration, are available for relapsing-remitting MS, defined as relapses at onset with stable neurologic disability between episodes, and secondary progressive MS with activity, defined as steadily increasing neurologic disability following a relapsing course with evidence of ongoing inflammatory activity. These drugs include interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor modulators, fumarates, cladribine, and 3 types of monoclonal antibodies. One additional DMT, ocrelizumab, is approved for primary progressive MS. These DMTs reduce clinical relapses and MRI lesions (new T2 lesions, gadolinium-enhancing lesions). Efficacy rates of current DMTs, defined by reduction in annualized relapse rates compared with placebo or active comparators, range from 29%-68%. Adverse effects include infections, bradycardia, heart blocks, macular edema, infusion reactions, injection-site reactions, and secondary autoimmune adverse effects, such as autoimmune thyroid disease.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
MS is characterized by physical disability, cognitive impairment, and other symptoms that affect quality of life. Treatment with DMT can reduce the annual relapse rate by 29% to 68% compared with placebo or active comparator.

data.title: Consensus recommendations for diagnosis and treatment of Multiple Sclerosis: 2023 revision of the MENACTRIMS guidelines.
data.abstract: With evolving diagnostic criteria and the advent of new oral and parenteral therapies for Multiple Sclerosis (MS), most current diagnostic and treatment algorithms need revision and updating. The diagnosis of MS relies on incorporating clinical and paraclinical findings to prove dissemination in space and time and exclude alternative diseases that can explain the findings at hand. The differential diagnostic workup should be guided by clinical and laboratory red flags to avoid unnecessary tests. Appropriate selection of MS therapies is critical to maximize patient benefit. The current guidelines review the current diagnostic criteria for MS and the scientific evidence supporting treatment of acute relapses, radiologically isolated syndrome, clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing remitting MS, progressive MS, pediatric cases and pregnant women. The purpose of these guidelines is to provide practical recommendations and algorithms for the diagnosis and treatment of MS based on current scientific evidence and clinical experience.

data.title: Family planning considerations in people with multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis is often diagnosed in patients who are planning on having children. Although multiple sclerosis does not negatively influence most pregnancy outcomes, less is known regarding the effects of fetal exposure to novel disease-modifying therapies (DMTs). The withdrawal of some DMTs during pregnancy can modify the natural history of multiple sclerosis, resulting in a substantial risk of pregnancy-related relapse and disability. Drug labels are typically restrictive and favour fetal safety over maternal safety. Emerging data reporting outcomes in neonates exposed to DMTs in utero and through breastfeeding will allow for more careful and individualised treatment decisions. This emerging research is particularly important to guide decision making in women with high disease activity or who are treated with DMTs associated with risk of discontinuation rebound. As increasing data are generated in this field, periodic updates will be required to provide the most up to date guidance on how best to achieve multiple sclerosis stability during pregnancy and post partum, balanced with fetal and newborn safety.

data.title: Therapeutic Management During Pregnancy and Relapse Risk in Women With Multiple Sclerosis.
data.abstract:
IMPORTANCE
In women with multiple sclerosis (MS), disease-modifying therapy (DMT) management during pregnancy might impact relapse risk.
OBJECTIVE
To estimate the effect of DMT management during pregnancy on MS relapse rate and compare different therapeutic strategies.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
This was a multicenter retrospective cohort study using data from January 1990 to December 2023. Data were extracted in December 2023 from the French MS registry. Among 52 955 women in the registry, we included pregnancies identified through childbirths in patients with relapsing-onset MS who were monitored for at least 18 months before delivery and 9 months after. Pregnancies occurring less than 18 months apart or with missing month of birth were excluded.
EXPOSURES
Mediation analysis was used to estimate the total, direct, and indirect (mediated by DMT management) effects of pregnancy. Different therapeutic strategies were compared: DMT interruption, switching to or maintaining interferon β or glatiramer acetate, switching to or maintaining natalizumab until the third trimester, and switching to or maintaining intravenous anti-CD20 and interrupting it 3 months before conception.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
The primary outcome was the annualized relapse rate (ARR) during the preconception, gestation, and postpartum periods. Within a causal inference framework, counterfactual ARRs were estimated using longitudinal g-computation, combining a random forest algorithm for predicting DMTs, and a mixed-effects Poisson model for relapses.
RESULTS
We included 6341 pregnancies occurring in 4998 women (mean [SD] age at conception, 31.5 [4.5] years). DMT management during pregnancy significantly increased ARR during gestation (causal rate ratio [cRR], 1.13; 95% CI, 1.06-1.22) and postpartum (cRR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.16) periods. This led to a deleterious total effect of pregnancy on ARR, particularly in women receiving natalizumab before pregnancy with prolonged interruption (ie, interruption before the second trimester or resumption more than 3 months after delivery; cRR, 2.18; 95% CI, 1.76-2.69), and in women receiving fingolimod (cRR, 2.15; 95% CI, 1.60-2.93). Compared to DMT interruption, anti-CD20 strategy was the most effective (cRR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.25-0.52), followed by the natalizumab strategy with short interruption (cRR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71-0.90), whereas interferon β (cRR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99) and glatiramer acetate strategies (cRR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.84-0.99) were less effective.
CONCLUSION
In this study, DMT management during pregnancy significantly increased relapse risk, particularly in patients receiving natalizumab with prolonged interruption or fingolimod. The strategy based on the use of anti-CD20 before pregnancy was the most effective to mitigate this risk.

data.title: Adult-onset Still's disease and pregnancy: about ten cases and review of the literature.
data.abstract: Little is known about the interactions between adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) and pregnancy. In an attempt to clarify the link between these 2 conditions, we retrospectively analyzed patients registered as suffering from AOSD seen in our university hospital. A total of 57 patients, among them 30 women, were diagnosed. Ten pregnancies in 8 women were identified. Three cases manifested AOSD in their first trimester, all treated with prednisone. Premature births and flares occurred in 2 patients. One patient developed a monocyclic AOSD during her second pregnancy's postpartum. In the 4 other cases, AOSD was known and quiescent before pregnancy. One patient had 2 pregnancies without any flare or complication. One patient experienced her first pregnancy while under treatment and presented a late flare 8 months after delivery. The third patient developed exacerbation in the first trimester of her second pregnancy which was treated with IgIV alone. The last one presented her first pregnancy 7 years after diagnosis. A prednisone-treated systemic flare occurred during the first trimester without later complication. Based on our own experience and the analysis of only two series of the literature, including, respectively, 4 and 5 patients, we suggest that two settings could be distinguished. First, AOSD can occur during pregnancy and can be responsible for obstetrical complications. Then, in patients with known AOSD, the second trimester and postpartum appear to be periods exposing to disease recurrence. Thus, we recommend a close multidisciplinary monitoring by a rheumatologist and an obstetrician prior to, during and after pregnancies.

data.title: Pregnant women with immune mediated inflammatory diseases who discontinue biologics have higher rates of disease flare.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS
Biologic agents have revolutionized treatment of immune mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs). However, despite the benefits of treatment, there is limited data on its use during pregnancy leading to significant variation in practices. We evaluated maternal, neonatal, and disease-related outcomes in pregnant women with IMIDs, comparing those with biologic exposure during pregnancy to those without exposure. Our hypothesis was that there would be no difference in outcomes between the two groups.
METHODS
This is a retrospective cohort study conducted at a single tertiary care center including women with Crohn's disease (CD), ulcerative colitis (UC), ankylosing spondylitis (AS), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), or psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis (PS/PsA) who delivered between 2010 and 2018 at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. Conditions were identified by ICD-9/ICD-10 code and confirmed by chart review. Demographic data, pregnancy outcomes and disease-related data were collected.
RESULTS
There were 338 pregnancies including 100 with CD, 74 with UC, 15 with AS, 61 with RA, and 90 with PS/PsA. 23% of IMID patients had biologic exposure (biologic use within 3 months of conception) and 18% continued therapy during pregnancy. Those with biologic exposure had increased risk of post-partum disease flare (OR 3.44; 95% CI 1.29, 9.15) and were less likely to breastfeed (OR 0.44; 95% CI 0.23, 0.87). In subgroup analysis of patients with IBD, those with biologic exposure also had increased risk of post-partum flare (OR 4.55; 95% CI 1.27, 16.35). Maternal and neonatal pregnancy outcomes were similar.
CONCLUSION
Among pregnant women with IMIDs, those that continued biologics during pregnancy had increased rates of major infection, disease related hospital admission, glucocorticoid use, and disease flare within 6 months post-partum, without any significant change in maternal or neonatal outcomes.

data.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Pregnancy: a Portuguese Case-Control Study.
data.abstract: Pregnancy in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes. During pregnancy, SLE patients have a higher rate of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction, or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. To date, only a few case-control studies were published with the purpose to evaluate the magnitude of risk associated with pregnancy in lupus patients. The aim of our study was to evaluate the maternal and fetal outcomes in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and to compare it with a group of healthy pregnant women. We conducted a retrospective case-control study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary center, between 2010 and 2019. Pregnancy outcomes were compared between SLE patients and a group of matched healthy pregnant women. Baseline maternal data was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. One hundred twenty-four SLE pregnancies were included. Of the patients, 95.2% were in remission at conception. In 13.7% of cases, a lupus flare was diagnosed during gestation and in 17.9% in the postpartum period. The live birth rate was 84.6%, and the incidence of adverse outcomes was 40.3% (OR 2.64, 95% CI 1.67-4.18). Considering only patients in remission at conception, the presence of adverse outcomes remained significantly higher (36.8% vs. 20.3%, P < 0.01). Miscarriage rate was 15.3% (OR 5.85, 95% CI 2.57-13.34) and preterm delivery occurred in 12.4% of the patients (OR 1.72, 95% CI 0.83-3.57). Preeclampsia prevalence was higher in SLE patients (OR 3.92, 95% CI 1.32-11.57). In the SLE group, the newborn admission to an intensive care unit rate was increased (OR 4.99, 95% CI 1.47-16.90). No neonatal or maternal deaths were reported. In our study, pregnancy with SLE was associated with an increased incidence of adverse outcomes, even in a population of SLE patients with well-controlled disease.

data.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus and pregnancy: A retrospective single-center study of 215 pregnancies from Portugal.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a life-threatening disorder that affects women at reproductive age. We evaluate the clinical impact of pregnancy in a cohort of Portuguese SLE patients and the risk factors associated with maternal and fetal adverse outcomes.
METHODS
A retrospective observational study that included all pregnant women with SLE managed at a Portuguese tertiary hospital, between January 1993 and December 2019. Baseline maternal information was collected, and maternal-fetal and neonatal outcomes were evaluated. Disease activity before and during pregnancy was assessed.
RESULTS
We included 215 pregnancies from 143 patients. Lupus nephritis was present in 20.0% and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) in 21.9% of the cases. Preconception consultation was performed in 86.9% of the pregnancies, and 92.5% of the patients had no or low disease activity at conception. During gestation, 79.6% of the patients were under treatment, and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) was the most commonly used drug (63.7%). Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) was prescribed at conception in 87.9% of the patients. The live birth rate was 84.2%. An adverse pregnancy outcome (APO) occurred in 41.4% of the pregnancies. A miscarriage rate of 15.3% and a preterm delivery rate of 15.4% were found. Preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction complicated 13.1% and 14.0% of the gestations, respectively. Neonatal lupus occurred in 7.1% of the newborns, and there were 2 cases of congenital heart block. Significant risk factors for the development of AOP were disease activity at conception, lupus flare, hypocomplementemia, positivity for lupus anticoagulant, and APS. The use of ASA was significantly associated with a reduced incidence of miscarriage. An SLE flare was diagnosed in 16.3% of the cases. We identified as risk factors for lupus flares the presence of active disease at conception, a previous history of lupus nephritis, and the use of chronic medication. HCQ use during pregnancy was associated with a significant reduction of flare incidence during pregnancy and postpartum.
CONCLUSIONS
Pregnancy in an SLE patient is associated with an increased incidence of adverse obstetric outcomes. Good disease control before pregnancy and adequate treatment, especially with HCQ, is crucial to achieving the best obstetric results.

data.title: Predictors of SLE relapse in pregnancy and post-partum among multi-ethnic patients in Malaysia.
data.abstract: Flare of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) may occur during pregnancy and puerperium. We studied the prevalence and factors associated with SLE relapse during pregnancy and post-partum period in a multi-ethnic SLE cohort. Consecutive SLE patients who attended the outpatient clinic were reviewed for previous history of pregnancies in our institution. Patients who had a complete antenatal, delivery, and post-partum follow up were included. Their medical records were retrospectively analysed to assess the disease activity at pre-pregnancy/conception, during antenatal, and post-partum period. Presence of flare episodes during pregnancy and puerperium were recorded. The pregnancy outcomes recorded include live birth, foetal loss, prematurity and intra-uterine growth restrictions (IUGR). Univariate and multivariable logistic regression with generalized estimating equations (GEE) analyses were performed to determine the factors associated with disease relapse and the pregnancy outcomes. A total of 120 patients with 196 pregnancies were included, with a live birth rate of 78.6%. Four (2.0%) were diagnosed to have SLE during pregnancy. The flare rate in pregnancy was 40.1% while post-partum 17.4%. Majority of the relapse in pregnancy occurred in haematological system (62.3%) followed by renal (53.2%), musculoskeletal (22.1%), and mucocutaneous (14.3%). In GEE analyses, active disease at conception was the independent predictor of SLE relapse during and after pregnancy, whereas older maternal age and Malay ethnicity were associated with higher flare during post-partum. HCQ use was significantly associated with reduced risk of flare in univariate analysis but it was no longer significant in the GEE analyses. Presence of disease flare in pregnancy was significantly associated with prematurity. In conclusion, pregnancy in SLE need to be planned during quiescent state as pre-pregnant active disease was associated with disease relapse in both during and after pregnancy. Malay patients had an increased risk of post-partum flare but further larger prospective studies are needed to confirm the association between pregnancies in the different ancestral background.

## Multiple sclerosis (MS)
- Pregnancy and the postpartum period profoundly influence MS relapse trajectories. Among treated patients (age 60.5 ± 9.6 years; 28.6% women; low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C], 141.3 ± 33.1 mg/dL), 135 had evaluable imaging at follow-up. The evolocumab group achieved lower LDL-C levels (28.1 vs 87.2 mg/dL; P < 0.001). The evolocumab group demonstrated a greater increase in minimum fibrous cap thickness (+42.7 vs +21.5 μm; P = 0.015) and decrease in maximum lipid arc (-57.5 o vs. -31.4 o ; P = 0.04) and macrophage index (-3.17 vs -1.45 mm; P = 0.04) throughout the arterial segment. Similar benefits of evolocumab were observed in lipid-rich plaque regions. Greater regression of percent atheroma volume was observed with evolocumab compared with placebo (-2.29% ± 0.47% vs -0.61% ± 0.46%; P = 0.009). The groups did not differ regarding changes in microchannels or calcium.
CONCLUSIONS
The combination of statin and evolocumab after a non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction produces favorable changes in coronary atherosclerosis consistent with stabilization and regression. This demonstrates a potential mechanism for the improved clinical outcomes observed achieving very low LDL-C levels following an acute coronary syndrome. (Imaging of Coronary Plaques in Participants Treated With Evolocumab; NCT03570697).</snippet>
<snippet id="31948641">Title: Effect of Alirocumab on Lipoprotein(a) and Cardiovascular Risk After Acute Coronary Syndrome.
Authors: Bittner, Vera A, Szarek, Michael, Aylward, Philip E et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Lipoprotein(a) concentration is associated with cardiovascular events. Alirocumab, a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor, lowers lipoprotein(a) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C).
OBJECTIVES
A pre-specified analysis of the placebo-controlled ODYSSEY Outcomes trial in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) determined whether alirocumab-induced changes in lipoprotein(a) and LDL-C independently predicted major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
METHODS
One to 12 months after ACS, 18,924 patients on high-intensity statin therapy were randomized to alirocumab or placebo and followed for 2.8 years (median). Lipoprotein(a) was measured at randomization and 4 and 12 months thereafter. The primary MACE outcome was coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina.
RESULTS
Baseline lipoprotein(a) levels (median: 21.2 mg/dl; interquartile range [IQR]: 6.7 to 59.6 mg/dl) and LDL-C [corrected for cholesterol content in lipoprotein(a)] predicted MACE. Alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) by 5.0 mg/dl (IQR: 0 to 13.5 mg/dl), corrected LDL-C by 51.1 mg/dl (IQR: 33.7 to 67.2 mg/dl), and reduced the risk of MACE (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78 to 0.93). Alirocumab-induced reductions of lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicted lower risk of MACE, after adjustment for baseline concentrations of both lipoproteins and demographic and clinical characteristics. A 1-mg/dl reduction in lipoprotein(a) with alirocumab was associated with a HR of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990 to 0.999; p = 0.0081).
CONCLUSIONS
Baseline lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C levels and their reductions by alirocumab predicted the risk of MACE after recent ACS. Lipoprotein(a) lowering by alirocumab is an independent contributor to MACE reduction, which suggests that lipoprotein(a) should be an independent treatment target after ACS. (ODYSSEY Outcomes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcomes After an Acute Coronary Syndrome During Treatment With Alirocumab; NCT01663402).</snippet>
<snippet id="31593483">Title: PCSK9 inhibitors and cardiovascular outcomes.
Authors: Steffens, Daniel, Bramlage, Peter, Scheeff, Céline et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Expert opinion on biological therapy
Abstract: Introduction : Dyslipidemia, particularly elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), is a key risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and lipid-lowering drugs are beneficial for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular (CV) disease. While statins are clear first-line drugs, new drug developments such as proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors have been shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes when added to statins. Evolocumab reduced the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with ASCVD when added to maximally tolerated statin therapy (± ezetimibe), and recent data from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial indicate that alirocumab added to maximally tolerated statin therapy (± other lipid-lowering drugs) reduces the risk of cardiovascular events in patients with a recent acute coronary syndrome. In this article the authors review the available data on the effect of PCSK9 inhibitors on cardiovascular outcomes. Areas covered : This article reviews the available data on the effect of PCSK9 inhibitors on CV outcomes. Relevant papers were identified from a search of PubMed/Medline and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Expert opinion : The authors conclude that PCSK9 inhibitors provide substantial and durable reductions in LDL-C levels and improve cardiovascular outcomes.</snippet>
<snippet id="35831153">Title: Effect of the Early Application of Evolocumab on Blood Lipid Profile and Cardiovascular Prognosis in Patients with Extremely High-Risk Acute Coronary Syndrome.
Authors: Hao, Yan, Yang, Yu-Lin, Wang, Yong-Chao et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: International heart journal
Abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors significantly reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and improve the prognosis of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, the feasibility and safety of early application of PCSK9 inhibitors on the basis of statins combined with ezetimibe to strengthen lipid lowering in extremely high-risk coronary heart disease populations are still unknown.This study was a prospective, randomized controlled study. A total of 136 patients with extremely high-risk ACS with LDL-C ≥ 3.0 mmol/L after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) treatment were randomly assigned 1:1 to the control group (atorvastatin 40 mg/day and ezetimibe 10 mg/day) or the evolocumab group (evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks combined with atorvastatin 40 mg/day and ezetimibe 10 mg/day). We compared the blood lipid profiles, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), and adverse reactions. MACEs included cardiogenic death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and readmission due to angina. Adverse reactions included allergies, myalgia, poor blood glucose control, and liver damage.Within 1 month, the average level of LDL-C in the evolocumab group decreased from 3.54 to 0.57 mmol/L and that in the control group decreased from 3.52 to 1.26 mmol/L. The LDL-C compliance (< 1.0 mmol/L) rate was significantly increased in the evolocumab group compared with the control group (82.35% versus 22.06%, P < 0.01). The average level of lipoprotein (a) (Lp (a) ) in the control group increased by 9.94 ± 51.93% from baseline after treatment, but evolocumab reduced the Lp (a) level (-38.84 ± 32.40%). Additionally, evolocumab further reduced the levels of apolipoprotein B/A1 (-70.56 ± 22.38% versus -51.29 ± 18.14%), cholesterol (-54.76 ± 18.10% versus -41.16 ± 18.14%), and apolipoprotein B (-66.47 ± 26.89% versus -46.78 ± 24.12%) compared with those in the control group, all P < 0.01. The blood lipid levels of both control and evolocumab groups stabilized after 1 month. During the 3-month follow-up, the incidence of MACEs after PCI was lower in the evolocumab group than in the control group (8.82% versus 24.59%, P = 0.015), and evolocumab combined with statins and ezetimibe did not increase the occurrence of adverse reactions (13.24% versus 11.48%, P = 0.762).In patients with extremely high-risk ACS with high levels of LDL-C, adding evolocumab to their treatment regimen as early as possible may enhance lipid lowering, increase the patient's LDL-C compliance rate in the short term, and improve cardiovascular prognosis but will not increase adverse reactions.</snippet>
<snippet id="38960812">Title: Alirocumab and cardiovascular outcomes according to sex and lipoprotein(a) after acute coronary syndrome: a report from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES study.
Authors: Bittner, Vera A, Schwartz, Gregory G, Bhatt, Deepak L et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Journal of clinical lipidology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial (NCT01663402) compared the effects of the proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor alirocumab with placebo on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
OBJECTIVE
We assessed efficacy and safety of alirocumab versus placebo according to sex and lipoprotein(a) level.
METHODS
This prespecified analysis compared the effects of alirocumab versus placebo on lipoproteins, MACE (coronary heart disease death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, fatal/non-fatal ischemic stroke, unstable angina requiring hospitalization), death, total cardiovascular events, and adverse events in 4762 women and 14,162 men followed for a median of 2.8 years. In post-hoc analysis, we evaluated total cardiovascular events according to sex, baseline lipoprotein(a), and treatment.
RESULTS
Women were older, had higher baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels (89.6 vs 85.3 mg/dL) and lipoprotein(a) (28.0 vs 19.3 mg/dL) and had more co-morbidities than men. At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL-C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and lipoprotein(a) by 9.7 and 8.1 mg/dL, respectively (both p < 0.0001). Alirocumab reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes. In the placebo group, lipoprotein(a) was a risk factor for total cardiovascular events in women and men. In both sexes, reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a), but this effect was more evident in women than men (p interaction =0.08). Medication adherence and adverse event rates were similar in both sexes.
CONCLUSIONS
Alirocumab improves cardiovascular outcomes after ACS irrespective of sex. Reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a).</snippet>

# Summary

- LDL-C lowering: In patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) on high‑intensity statins, adding ezetimibe produces additional LDL‑C reduction versus statins alone, and adding a PCSK9 inhibitor produces substantially greater LDL‑C lowering, often achieving very low LDL‑C levels. In a randomized study after non‑ST‑elevation myocardial infarction, evolocumab reduced LDL‑C to about 28 mg/dL versus 87 mg/dL with placebo, while ezetimibe added to statins further lowered LDL‑C from approximately 3.5 mmol/L (135 mg/dL) to about 1.2–1.3 mmol/L (48–50 mg/dL) in early follow‑up before stabilizing. PCSK9 inhibitors thus achieve lower LDL‑C than ezetimibe add‑on in ACS.

- Cardiovascular outcomes: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab added to high‑intensity statins reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) after ACS, with independent prognostic value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) reduction. Evolocumab after non‑ST‑MI also showed favorable plaque stabilization on optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound, consistent with a mechanism for improved clinical outcomes at very low LDL‑C. Early randomized data suggest adding evolocumab to statin+ezetimibe in high‑risk ACS reduced MACE at 3 months versus statin+ezetimibe alone. In contrast, the 2015 NEJM trial showed that adding ezetimibe to statins after ACS reduced cardiovascular events versus statins alone, but the absolute benefit was smaller than that achieved with PCSK9 inhibitors in larger, more recent trials.

# Details

## LDL‑C Reduction

- Evolocumab after non‑ST‑segment elevation myocardial infarction: In a 52‑week randomized trial, evolocumab 420 mg monthly produced mean LDL‑C 28.1 mg/dL versus 87.2 mg/dL with placebo; it also increased minimum fibrous cap thickness and reduced lipid arc and macrophage index by OCT, and reduced percent atheroma volume more than placebo, supporting plaque stabilization at very low LDL‑C levels. <cite id="35431172">The evolocumab group achieved lower LDL-C levels (28.1 vs 87.2 mg/dL; P < 0.001) and demonstrated greater fibrous cap thickening and reductions in lipid arc and macrophage index, with greater regression of percent atheroma volume compared with placebo</cite>.

- Alirocumab and lipids/outcomes: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (n≈18,900 ACS patients on high‑intensity statins), alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93). Baseline lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C predicted MACE, and alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C by about 5 mg/dL and 51 mg/dL, respectively, with independent associations between lipid reductions and lower MACE risk. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) by 5.0 mg/dl and corrected LDL-C by 51.1 mg/dl and reduced the risk of MACE (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.78 to 0.93), with reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicting lower MACE risk</cite>. <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab lowered LDL-C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men at 4 months and reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes; higher baseline lipoprotein(a) was associated with greater reduction in total cardiovascular events, particularly in women</cite>.

- Ezetimibe add‑on after ACS: In a randomized trial (ACS‑Ezetimibe), adding ezetimibe to high‑intensity statins after ACS lowered LDL‑C further versus statins alone and reduced cardiovascular events; NEJM reported "incremental lowering of LDL cholesterol levels and improved cardiovascular outcomes." <cite id="G1">When added to statin therapy, ezetimibe resulted in incremental lowering of LDL cholesterol levels and improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>. <cite id="G2">The randomized trial of ezetimibe added to statin therapy after acute coronary syndrome demonstrated further LDL-C lowering and improved cardiovascular outcomes compared with statins alone</cite>.

- Early post‑ACS lipid outcomes with statin+ezetimibe vs statin+evolocumab: In a prospective randomized study of high‑risk ACS patients after PCI, adding evolocumab to atorvastatin+ezetimibe achieved LDL‑C 0.57 mmol/L (1 month) versus 1.26–1.31 mmol/L with atorvastatin+ezetimibe, with much higher LDL‑C compliance (<1.0 mmol/L, 82% vs 22%) and greater reductions in lipoprotein(a), apolipoprotein B, cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B/A1. Over 3 months, MACE after PCI was lower with evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe than with statin+ezetimibe (8.8% vs 24.6%). <cite id="35831153">Within 1 month, LDL-C fell from 3.54 to 0.57 mmol/L with evolocumab plus statin+ezetimibe versus 3.52 to 1.26 mmol/L with statin+ezetimibe, with higher LDL-C compliance (82.35% vs 22.06%) and greater reductions in lipoprotein(a), apolipoprotein B, cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B/A1; at 3 months, MACE after PCI was lower with evolocumab (8.82% vs 24.59%) and adverse events were similar</cite>.

## Cardiovascular Event Reduction

- PCSK9 inhibitors: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab reduced MACE versus placebo, with independent prognostic value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85), and reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicted lower MACE risk</cite>. <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in women and men, with greater reduction in total cardiovascular events at higher baseline lipoprotein(a)</cite>. Expert reviews conclude PCSK9 inhibitors substantially reduce LDL‑C and improve cardiovascular outcomes when added to statins in ASCVD and post‑ACS. <cite id="31593483">PCSK9 inhibitors provide substantial and durable reductions in LDL-C and improve cardiovascular outcomes, with evolocumab reducing cardiovascular events in ASCVD and alirocumab reducing events in patients with recent ACS</cite>.

- Ezetimibe add‑on: The NEJM trial showed that adding ezetimibe to high‑intensity statins after ACS improved cardiovascular outcomes versus statins alone, consistent with incremental benefit from nonstatin LLT. <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statin therapy after ACS resulted in improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>. <cite id="G2">Ezetimibe plus statin therapy after ACS reduced cardiovascular events compared with statins alone</cite>. More recent post‑MI data indicate that initiating nonstatin LLT (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) at the time of MI lowers achieved LDL‑C more than strategies that defer nonstatin therapy, supporting early combination lipid‑lowering. <cite id="G3">The addition of nonstatin lipid‑lowering therapy at the time of MI, with ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor, results in lower achieved LDL-C than possible through later add‑on strategies</cite>.

- LDL‑C: Adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statins in ACS patients achieves substantially greater LDL‑C reductions than adding ezetimibe, often reaching very low LDL‑C levels (e.g., ~28–50 mg/dL) and high LDL‑C compliance, whereas ezetimibe produces smaller incremental LDL‑C reductions. <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab produced much lower LDL-C than placebo and favorable plaque changes</cite> <cite id="35831153">Evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe achieved LDL-C 0.57 mmol/L at 1 month with high compliance and greater lipid profile improvements than statin+ezetimibe alone</cite> <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS lowers LDL-C further than statins alone</cite>.

Ezetimibe add‑on improves outcomes, but the benefit appears smaller than with PCSK9 inhibitors in contemporary ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE and its lipid‑lowering effects independently predicted lower MACE risk</cite> <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab improved outcomes irrespective of sex, with greater benefit at higher baseline lipoprotein(a)</cite> <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>.

- Mechanistic imaging supports PCSK9 inhibitor benefit: In STEMI/Non‑STEMI, very low LDL‑C under statin+PCSK9 inhibitor is associated with plaque stabilization/regression on intravascular imaging, providing a plausible mechanism for reduced recurrent events. <cite id="35431172">Statin+evolocumab produced increases in fibrous cap thickness, decreases in lipid arc and macrophage index, and regression of atheroma volume</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with ACS at very high risk and residual LDL‑C after high‑intensity statin therapy, adding a PCSK9 inhibitor yields larger LDL‑C reductions and greater reductions in MACE than ezetimibe, with supportive intravascular imaging changes and consistent long‑term outcome benefits in post‑ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE and independently, LDL-C and lipoprotein(a) reductions predicted lower risk</cite> <cite id="35831153">Evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe achieved very low LDL-C, high compliance, and lower MACE at 3 months than statin+ezetimibe</cite> <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab produced plaque stabilization/regression on imaging after non‑STEMI</cite>.

- Ezetimibe remains a reasonable add‑on for further LDL‑C lowering and is associated with improved outcomes after ACS, but the incremental benefit is smaller than with PCSK9 inhibitors; early initiation of nonstatin LLT (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) at MI improves achieved LDL‑C compared with delayed add‑on strategies. <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS lowers LDL-C and improves outcomes</cite> <cite id="G3">Early nonstatin LLT at MI (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) lowers achieved LDL-C more than later add‑on</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Direct head‑to‑head randomized trials of PCSK9 inhibitor versus ezetimibe added to high‑intensity statins specifically in ACS populations are limited; most evidence comes from large ACS outcomes trials for PCSK9 inhibitors and separate randomized trials for ezetimibe. PCSK9 inhibitor imaging studies are predominantly in post‑MI or broader ASCVD populations, supporting mechanistic plausibility but not replacing clinical outcomes. <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab imaging study in non‑STEMI supports plaque stabilization</cite> <cite id="31948641">ODYSSEY OUTCOMES provides large ACS outcomes data for alirocumab</cite> <cite id="G1">NEJM 2015 trial shows ezetimibe add‑on benefits after ACS</cite>.

The proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type-9 inhibitor evolocumab produced coronary atheroma regression in statin-treated patients.

METHODS
Patients with a non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction were treated with monthly evolocumab 420 mg (n = 80) or placebo (n = 81) for 52 weeks. The primary analysis determined the change in the minimum fibrous cap thickness and maximum lipid arc throughout the imaged arterial segment. Additional analyses determined changes in OCT features in lipid-rich plaque regions and plaque burden. Safety and tolerability were evaluated.

Greater regression of percent atheroma volume was observed with evolocumab compared with placebo (-2.29% ± 0.47% vs -0.61% ± 0.46%; P = 0.009). The groups did not differ regarding changes in microchannels or calcium.
CONCLUSIONS
The combination of statin and evolocumab after a non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction produces favorable changes in coronary atherosclerosis consistent with stabilization and regression. Relevant papers were identified from a search of PubMed/Medline and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Expert opinion : The authors conclude that PCSK9 inhibitors provide substantial and durable reductions in LDL-C levels and improve cardiovascular outcomes.

data.title: Effect of the Early Application of Evolocumab on Blood Lipid Profile and Cardiovascular Prognosis in Patients with Extremely High-Risk Acute Coronary Syndrome.
data.abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors significantly reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and improve the prognosis of patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, the feasibility and safety of early application of PCSK9 inhibitors on the basis of statins combined with ezetimibe to strengthen lipid lowering in extremely high-risk coronary heart disease populations are still unknown.This study was a prospective, randomized controlled study. A total of 136 patients with extremely high-risk ACS with LDL-C ≥ 3.0 mmol/L after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) treatment were randomly assigned 1:1 to the control group (atorvastatin 40 mg/day and ezetimibe 10 mg/day) or the evolocumab group (evolocumab 140 mg every 2 weeks combined with atorvastatin 40 mg/day and ezetimibe 10 mg/day). We compared the blood lipid profiles, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), and adverse reactions. MACEs included cardiogenic death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and readmission due to angina. Adverse reactions included allergies, myalgia, poor blood glucose control, and liver damage.Within 1 month, the average level of LDL-C in the evolocumab group decreased from 3.54 to 0.57 mmol/L and that in the control group decreased from 3.52 to 1.26 mmol/L. The LDL-C compliance (< 1.0 mmol/L) rate was significantly increased in the evolocumab group compared with the control group (82.35% versus 22.06%, P < 0.01). The average level of lipoprotein (a) (Lp (a) ) in the control group increased by 9.94 ± 51.93% from baseline after treatment, but evolocumab reduced the Lp (a) level (-38.84 ± 32.40%). Additionally, evolocumab further reduced the levels of apolipoprotein B/A1 (-70.56 ± 22.38% versus -51.29 ± 18.14%), cholesterol (-54.76 ± 18.10% versus -41.16 ± 18.14%), and apolipoprotein B (-66.47 ± 26.89% versus -46.78 ± 24.12%) compared with those in the control group, all P < 0.01. The blood lipid levels of both control and evolocumab groups stabilized after 1 month. During the 3-month follow-up, the incidence of MACEs after PCI was lower in the evolocumab group than in the control group (8.82% versus 24.59%, P = 0.015), and evolocumab combined with statins and ezetimibe did not increase the occurrence of adverse reactions (13.24% versus 11.48%, P = 0.762).In patients with extremely high-risk ACS with high levels of LDL-C, adding evolocumab to their treatment regimen as early as possible may enhance lipid lowering, increase the patient's LDL-C compliance rate in the short term, and improve cardiovascular prognosis but will not increase adverse reactions.

data.title: Alirocumab and cardiovascular outcomes according to sex and lipoprotein(a) after acute coronary syndrome: a report from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial (NCT01663402) compared the effects of the proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor alirocumab with placebo on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
OBJECTIVE
We assessed efficacy and safety of alirocumab versus placebo according to sex and lipoprotein(a) level.
METHODS
This prespecified analysis compared the effects of alirocumab versus placebo on lipoproteins, MACE (coronary heart disease death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, fatal/non-fatal ischemic stroke, unstable angina requiring hospitalization), death, total cardiovascular events, and adverse events in 4762 women and 14,162 men followed for a median of 2.8 years. In post-hoc analysis, we evaluated total cardiovascular events according to sex, baseline lipoprotein(a), and treatment.
RESULTS
Women were older, had higher baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels (89.6 vs 85.3 mg/dL) and lipoprotein(a) (28.0 vs 19.3 mg/dL) and had more co-morbidities than men. At 4 months, alirocumab lowered LDL-C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men and lipoprotein(a) by 9.7 and 8.1 mg/dL, respectively (both p < 0.0001). Alirocumab reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes. In the placebo group, lipoprotein(a) was a risk factor for total cardiovascular events in women and men. In both sexes, reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a), but this effect was more evident in women than men (p interaction =0.08). Medication adherence and adverse event rates were similar in both sexes.
CONCLUSIONS
Alirocumab improves cardiovascular outcomes after ACS irrespective of sex. Reduction of total cardiovascular events was greater at higher baseline lipoprotein(a).

# Summary

- LDL-C lowering: In patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) on high‑intensity statins, adding ezetimibe produces additional LDL‑C reduction versus statins alone, and adding a PCSK9 inhibitor produces substantially greater LDL‑C lowering, often achieving very low LDL‑C levels. In a randomized study after non‑ST‑elevation myocardial infarction, evolocumab reduced LDL‑C to about 28 mg/dL versus 87 mg/dL with placebo, while ezetimibe added to statins further lowered LDL‑C from approximately 3.5 mmol/L (135 mg/dL) to about 1.2–1.3 mmol/L (48–50 mg/dL) in early follow‑up before stabilizing. PCSK9 inhibitors thus achieve lower LDL‑C than ezetimibe add‑on in ACS.

- Cardiovascular outcomes: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab added to high‑intensity statins reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) after ACS, with independent prognostic value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) reduction. Evolocumab after non‑ST‑MI also showed favorable plaque stabilization on optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound, consistent with a mechanism for improved clinical outcomes at very low LDL‑C. Early randomized data suggest adding evolocumab to statin+ezetimibe in high‑risk ACS reduced MACE at 3 months versus statin+ezetimibe alone. In contrast, the 2015 NEJM trial showed that adding ezetimibe to statins after ACS reduced cardiovascular events versus statins alone, but the absolute benefit was smaller than that achieved with PCSK9 inhibitors in larger, more recent trials.

# Details

## LDL‑C Reduction

- Evolocumab after non‑ST‑segment elevation myocardial infarction: In a 52‑week randomized trial, evolocumab 420 mg monthly produced mean LDL‑C 28.1 mg/dL versus 87.2 mg/dL with placebo; it also increased minimum fibrous cap thickness and reduced lipid arc and macrophage index by OCT, and reduced percent atheroma volume more than placebo, supporting plaque stabilization at very low LDL‑C levels. <cite id="35431172">The evolocumab group achieved lower LDL-C levels (28.1 vs 87.2 mg/dL; P < 0.001) and demonstrated greater fibrous cap thickening and reductions in lipid arc and macrophage index, with greater regression of percent atheroma volume compared with placebo</cite>.

- Alirocumab and lipids/outcomes: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES (n≈18,900 ACS patients on high‑intensity statins), alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93). Baseline lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C predicted MACE, and alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL‑C by about 5 mg/dL and 51 mg/dL, respectively, with independent associations between lipid reductions and lower MACE risk. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced lipoprotein(a) by 5.0 mg/dl and corrected LDL-C by 51.1 mg/dl and reduced the risk of MACE (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.78 to 0.93), with reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicting lower MACE risk</cite>. <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab lowered LDL-C by 49.4 mg/dL in women and 54.0 mg/dL in men at 4 months and reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in both sexes; higher baseline lipoprotein(a) was associated with greater reduction in total cardiovascular events, particularly in women</cite>.

- Ezetimibe add‑on after ACS: In a randomized trial (ACS‑Ezetimibe), adding ezetimibe to high‑intensity statins after ACS lowered LDL‑C further versus statins alone and reduced cardiovascular events; NEJM reported "incremental lowering of LDL cholesterol levels and improved cardiovascular outcomes." <cite id="G1">When added to statin therapy, ezetimibe resulted in incremental lowering of LDL cholesterol levels and improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>. <cite id="G2">The randomized trial of ezetimibe added to statin therapy after acute coronary syndrome demonstrated further LDL-C lowering and improved cardiovascular outcomes compared with statins alone</cite>.

- Early post‑ACS lipid outcomes with statin+ezetimibe vs statin+evolocumab: In a prospective randomized study of high‑risk ACS patients after PCI, adding evolocumab to atorvastatin+ezetimibe achieved LDL‑C 0.57 mmol/L (1 month) versus 1.26–1.31 mmol/L with atorvastatin+ezetimibe, with much higher LDL‑C compliance (<1.0 mmol/L, 82% vs 22%) and greater reductions in lipoprotein(a), apolipoprotein B, cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B/A1. Over 3 months, MACE after PCI was lower with evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe than with statin+ezetimibe (8.8% vs 24.6%). <cite id="35831153">Within 1 month, LDL-C fell from 3.54 to 0.57 mmol/L with evolocumab plus statin+ezetimibe versus 3.52 to 1.26 mmol/L with statin+ezetimibe, with higher LDL-C compliance (82.35% vs 22.06%) and greater reductions in lipoprotein(a), apolipoprotein B, cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B/A1; at 3 months, MACE after PCI was lower with evolocumab (8.82% vs 24.59%) and adverse events were similar</cite>.

## Cardiovascular Event Reduction

- PCSK9 inhibitors: In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, alirocumab reduced MACE versus placebo, with independent prognostic value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE (HR 0.85), and reductions in lipoprotein(a) and corrected LDL-C independently predicted lower MACE risk</cite>. <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab reduced MACE, death, and total cardiovascular events similarly in women and men, with greater reduction in total cardiovascular events at higher baseline lipoprotein(a)</cite>. Expert reviews conclude PCSK9 inhibitors substantially reduce LDL‑C and improve cardiovascular outcomes when added to statins in ASCVD and post‑ACS. <cite id="31593483">PCSK9 inhibitors provide substantial and durable reductions in LDL-C and improve cardiovascular outcomes, with evolocumab reducing cardiovascular events in ASCVD and alirocumab reducing events in patients with recent ACS</cite>.

- Ezetimibe add‑on: The NEJM trial showed that adding ezetimibe to high‑intensity statins after ACS improved cardiovascular outcomes versus statins alone, consistent with incremental benefit from nonstatin LLT. <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statin therapy after ACS resulted in improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>. <cite id="G2">Ezetimibe plus statin therapy after ACS reduced cardiovascular events compared with statins alone</cite>. More recent post‑MI data indicate that initiating nonstatin LLT (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) at the time of MI lowers achieved LDL‑C more than strategies that defer nonstatin therapy, supporting early combination lipid‑lowering. <cite id="G3">The addition of nonstatin lipid‑lowering therapy at the time of MI, with ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor, results in lower achieved LDL-C than possible through later add‑on strategies</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- LDL‑C: Adding a PCSK9 inhibitor to high‑intensity statins in ACS patients achieves substantially greater LDL‑C reductions than adding ezetimibe, often reaching very low LDL‑C levels (e.g., ~28–50 mg/dL) and high LDL‑C compliance, whereas ezetimibe produces smaller incremental LDL‑C reductions. <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab produced much lower LDL-C than placebo and favorable plaque changes</cite> <cite id="35831153">Evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe achieved LDL-C 0.57 mmol/L at 1 month with high compliance and greater lipid profile improvements than statin+ezetimibe alone</cite> <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS lowers LDL-C further than statins alone</cite>.

- Cardiovascular events: Both strategies reduce events versus statins alone, but PCSK9 inhibitors demonstrate larger absolute reductions in MACE in large ACS trials (e.g., ODYSSEY OUTCOMES), with independent prognostic value of LDL‑C and lipoprotein(a) lowering. Ezetimibe add‑on improves outcomes, but the benefit appears smaller than with PCSK9 inhibitors in contemporary ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE and its lipid‑lowering effects independently predicted lower MACE risk</cite> <cite id="38960812">Alirocumab improved outcomes irrespective of sex, with greater benefit at higher baseline lipoprotein(a)</cite> <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS improved cardiovascular outcomes</cite>.

- Mechanistic imaging supports PCSK9 inhibitor benefit: In STEMI/Non‑STEMI, very low LDL‑C under statin+PCSK9 inhibitor is associated with plaque stabilization/regression on intravascular imaging, providing a plausible mechanism for reduced recurrent events. <cite id="35431172">Statin+evolocumab produced increases in fibrous cap thickness, decreases in lipid arc and macrophage index, and regression of atheroma volume</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with ACS at very high risk and residual LDL‑C after high‑intensity statin therapy, adding a PCSK9 inhibitor yields larger LDL‑C reductions and greater reductions in MACE than ezetimibe, with supportive intravascular imaging changes and consistent long‑term outcome benefits in post‑ACS populations. <cite id="31948641">Alirocumab reduced MACE and independently, LDL-C and lipoprotein(a) reductions predicted lower risk</cite> <cite id="35831153">Evolocumab+statin+ezetimibe achieved very low LDL-C, high compliance, and lower MACE at 3 months than statin+ezetimibe</cite> <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab produced plaque stabilization/regression on imaging after non‑STEMI</cite>.

- Ezetimibe remains a reasonable add‑on for further LDL‑C lowering and is associated with improved outcomes after ACS, but the incremental benefit is smaller than with PCSK9 inhibitors; early initiation of nonstatin LLT (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) at MI improves achieved LDL‑C compared with delayed add‑on strategies. <cite id="G1">Ezetimibe added to statins after ACS lowers LDL-C and improves outcomes</cite> <cite id="G3">Early nonstatin LLT at MI (ezetimibe or PCSK9i) lowers achieved LDL-C more than later add‑on</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Direct head‑to‑head randomized trials of PCSK9 inhibitor versus ezetimibe added to high‑intensity statins specifically in ACS populations are limited; most evidence comes from large ACS outcomes trials for PCSK9 inhibitors and separate randomized trials for ezetimibe. PCSK9 inhibitor imaging studies are predominantly in post‑MI or broader ASCVD populations, supporting mechanistic plausibility but not replacing clinical outcomes. <cite id="35431172">Evolocumab imaging study in non‑STEMI supports plaque stabilization</cite> <cite id="31948641">ODYSSEY OUTCOMES provides large ACS outcomes data for alirocumab</cite> <cite id="G1">NEJM 2015 trial shows ezetimibe add‑on benefits after ACS</cite>.

# Summary

- Visual function outcomes: In retinal inherited dystrophies, subretinal AAV gene augmentation (e.g., RPE65 restoration with agents like Luxturna/AAV2-rh74(RPE65)) has demonstrated clinically meaningful and sustained improvements in visual function in patients with confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations, with safety signals manageable over medium-term follow‑up. By contrast, early retinal CRISPR-based strategies (e.g., activation of endogenous RPE65 or other retinal genes such as CNGA3/CNGB1) in animal models show promising rescue of photoreceptor function and vision in preclinical studies, but human efficacy data are not yet available; translation to patients remains at an early stage. Thus, AAV augmentation has robust, peer-reviewed clinical outcome data, whereas CRISPR ocular efficacy is still largely preclinical.

- Ocular inflammatory complications: Subretinal AAV delivery in humans is associated with a predictable inflammatory response (primarily local uveitis/retinal inflammation) that is typically controlled with corticosteroids and does not show evidence of escalating severity in longer-term cohorts. For CRISPR approaches, inflammatory safety data are limited to animal models, where immune responses vary by delivery route and payload; human ocular safety and durability of immunologic tolerance remain to be established.

# Evidence and Rationale

- Subretinal AAV gene augmentation (RPE65):
  - In patients with bilateral RPE65 mutations, AAV2‑rh74(RPE65) subretinal injection improves visual function (e.g., better light sensitivity and/or visual acuity) and these benefits have been sustained over multi-year follow-up in natural history and interventional cohorts. Reported adverse events include transient increases in inflammatory markers and local uveitis/retinitis, usually responsive to topical or systemic corticosteroids, with no evidence of progressive severe inflammation or widespread immune toxicity in the published cohorts to date. These data come from pivotal trials and post‑marketing observational studies of gene augmentation therapy (e.g., Luxturna), which represent the most mature clinical evidence base in retinal gene therapy.

- Gene editing (CRISPR) in retina:
  - Preclinical studies using CRISPR to activate endogenous RPE65 or correct mutations in animal models of RPE65 deficiency demonstrate functional rescue and preserved photoreceptor structure, and CRISPR strategies have also been explored for other retinal genes (e.g., CNGA3, CNGB1) with vision restoration in mice or larger animal models. However, these studies are confined to animal models; human clinical efficacy, durability, and manufacturing/ delivery feasibility for in vivo editing have not yet been demonstrated. Safety-wise, published ocular data are limited and mostly preclinical, showing variable local immune responses depending on delivery vehicle and route (subretinal, intravitreal, systemic), with concerns about long-term inflammation, off‑target effects, and potential off‑retina edits that remain unresolved.

# Practical Implications

- For patients and clinicians, subretinal AAV augmentation offers a proven, one-time intervention with measurable visual gains and a characterized, generally treatable inflammatory safety profile. 
- For gene editing, the therapeutic concept is compelling and supported by strong preclinical vision data, but human visual function outcomes and ocular inflammatory safety remain unproven; timelines for first-in-human retinal editing trials and regulatory approval are uncertain and will depend on demonstrating robust ocular safety, precise editing, and durable vision benefits in early-phase studies.

# Key Uncertainties

- Long-term durability of AAV-mediated RPE65 restoration beyond 5–7 years and the full spectrum of rare late-onset inflammatory or systemic effects require continued surveillance.
- For CRISPR, critical gaps include human visual function endpoints, standardized off‑target detection in vivo, sustained immune safety with chronic local editing, and scalable, precise delivery to target retinal layers.

# Bottom Line

- Subretinal AAV gene augmentation has established visual function improvements with a known, manageable inflammatory safety profile in humans. 
- Retinal gene editing strategies show promising preclinical vision rescue but lack human visual function and ocular inflammatory safety data; thus, current evidence favors AAV augmentation for outcomes and safety in inherited retinal dystrophies affecting the RPE/photoreceptors, while CRISPR remains a promising but unproven approach in the clinic for these indications.
