trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary of how Omicron sublineages evade neutralizing antibodies in vitro

Compared with earlier variants, Omicron sublineages (e.g., BA.1, BA.2, BA.4/5, BA.2.12.1) consistently show greater escape from antibody neutralization in pseudovirus assays, especially when sera are from individuals with only primary vaccination. A third dose (booster) substantially increases neutralization titers and breadth across Delta and multiple Omicron sublineages, but many sublineages—particularly BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5—remain relatively resistant even after boosting, indicating enhanced immune evasion compared with pre-Omicron and Delta. Breakthrough infection can induce broader responses against Omicron sublineages compared with Delta, yet some sublineages (e.g., BA.2.12.1, BA.4/5) still show higher escape than sera from natural infection alone, and a second booster may be required to broaden protection further. Notably, certain monoclonal antibodies (e.g., bebtelovimab) retain activity against Omicron sublineages in vitro, highlighting distinctions between polyclonal sera and monoclonal agents. In addition to reduced neutralization, Omicron sublineages often display altered biophysical properties, such as reduced fusogenicity and higher infectivity in cell culture, which may contribute to their overall fitness and ability to establish infection despite partial antibody pressure.

# Evidence by sublineage and exposure source (vaccination vs. prior infection)

- BA.1 and BA.2 (early Omicron wave):
  - Omicron BA.1/BA.2 pseudoviruses show a sharp decline in sensitivity to vaccine-induced neutralizing antibodies compared with wild-type D614G and Delta, indicating enhanced antibody escape relative to earlier variants. A third mRNA dose (BNT162b2 or ZF2001) markedly increases neutralizing titers and breadth against these sublineages, underscoring that boosting overcomes some, but not all, escape. <cite id="37292300">Omicron lineages BA.1 and BA.2 exhibit enhanced infectivity and a sharp decline in sensitivity to vaccine-induced neutralizing antibodies compared with hCoV-19 and Delta; a third BNT162b2 dose provides appreciable protection but neutralization sensitivity is diminished relative to hCoV-19 or Delta</cite> <cite id="36581867">A third dose of BBIBP-CorV or ZF2001 increased neutralizing titers and breadth against Delta and three Omicron subvariants, including BA.1 and BA.2</cite>.
  - In individuals with prior infection, BA.1 breakthrough infections elicit broader neutralization against multiple Omicron sublineages than Delta breakthrough infections, suggesting relative vulnerability of Delta to infection-acquired immunity compared with Omicron BA.1. <cite id="36581867">BA.1 breakthrough infections elicited a stronger and broader antibody response against three Omicron subvariants than Delta breakthrough infections</cite>.
  - Among sera from vaccinated convalescents (superimmunized), neutralization of BA.1, BA.2, and BA.5 is near-universal, with ~210-fold–141-fold higher NT50s versus unvaccinated convalescents, indicating that combining vaccination with prior infection yields robust coverage of these sublineages. <cite id="37180152">99.3% of vaccinated convalescents neutralized BA.1 and BA.5 and 99.6% neutralized BA.2; neutralizing titers were 52.7-, 210.7-, 141.3-, and 105.4-fold higher in vaccinated versus unvaccinated convalescents</cite>.

- BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 (later Omicron wave):
  - These sublineages show greater resistance to neutralization than earlier Omicron lineages, even after boosting. In a cross-sectional study, BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 were more resistant to immunity induced by vaccination and breakthrough infection, while bebtelovimab retained potency in vitro, highlighting a gap between polyclonal sera and certain mAbs. <cite id="36581867">BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 are more resistant to immunity induced by breakthrough infections; bebtelovimab had no significant loss of potency against Delta and Omicron subvariants</cite>.
  - In patients with cirrhosis receiving inactivated vaccine boosters, neutralization against BA.2.12.1 and BA.4 improved less after the booster, and BA.5 titers decreased post-booster, suggesting limited enhancement against these later Omicron sublineages despite repeated vaccination. <cite id="38161494">A booster did not result in an evident improvement of neutralization against BA.2.12.1 and BA.4 and was followed by a significant decrease in titer against BA.5</cite>.

- Context across vaccine platforms and immunization histories:
  - Inactivated vaccine–elicited sera (e.g., BBIBP-CorV) show weak to no neutralization against Omicron BA.1/BA.2 prior to boosting, with homologous or heterologous boosters markedly improving titers across sublineages; monoclonal panels often reveal that most mAbs lose activity, though some show distinct neutralization patterns across sublineages, reflecting antigenic differences. <cite id="35594867">Two-dose inactivated vaccine sera showed weak to no neutralization against BA.1/BA.2; homologous or heterologous boosting markedly improved neutralization across Omicron sublineages; most mAbs lost neutralizing activity, while some showed distinct patterns among sublineages</cite>.
  - In immunosuppressed patients on methotrexate, booster vaccination induces lower fold-increases and, if methotrexate is continued, lower neutralization against BA.1/BA.2 than non-immunosuppressed individuals; pausing methotrexate around vaccination improves neutralization toward levels seen in controls. <cite id="36216410">Neutralizing activity against Wu01 and Omicron variants increased 67–73-fold in non-immunosuppressed after a booster, while methotrexate recipients increased only 20–23-fold; pausing methotrexate improved neutralization, with optimal duration of pause around 10 days after vaccination</cite>.

# Mechanistic and phenotypic correlates observed in vitro

- Beyond neutralization, Omicron sublineages often differ in spike-mediated cell fusion and infectivity phenotypes. Omicron BA.1/BA.2 pseudoviruses display reduced fusogenicity but higher infectivity compared with D614G and Delta, suggesting adaptations that enhance entry efficiency despite antibody pressure. <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants were less fusogenic and had higher infectivity than D614G and Delta in cell culture</cite>.
- Spike residue changes around positions 681–687 (P681 motif) influence cell–cell fusion and syncytia formation rather than directly modulating neutralization potency in pseudovirus assays, indicating that fusogenicity and neutralization escape can be dissociated traits. <cite id="37292300">P681 mutations dictated fusion and syncytia formation, but did not affect neutralization or infectivity in pseudovirus neutralization assays; Omicron P681 spike promoted modest fusion compared with Delta R681</cite>.

# Implications for vaccination strategies and neutralization coverage

- Across studies, Omicron sublineages, particularly BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5, consistently outpace earlier variants in antibody evasion in vitro, even after boosting, whereas BA.1/BA.2 are more sensitive, especially when vaccination is boosted or when vaccination is combined with prior infection. <cite id="36581867">BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 are more resistant to immunity induced by vaccination and breakthrough infection</cite> <cite id="37180152">Vaccination of convalescents yielded near-universal neutralization of BA.1/BA.2/BA.5 with large fold-increases in titers</cite> <cite id="37292300">BA.1/BA.2 showed diminished neutralization sensitivity versus Delta and hCoV-19 after a third mRNA dose</cite>.
- Platform and regimen matter: homologous or heterologous boosting can restore neutralization breadth, but some sublineages remain challenging; certain mAbs retain activity where polyclonal sera often fail, underscoring the need for diverse therapeutic portfolios and possibly multivalent or broadly neutralizing approaches. <cite id="35594867">Boosting improved neutralization across sublineages; most mAbs lost activity, but some retained distinct neutralization patterns</cite> <cite id="36581867">Bebtelovimab retained potency against Omicron subvariants in vitro</cite>.
- Special populations (e.g., immunosuppressed) may require medication pauses and additional boosting to achieve neutralization levels comparable to non-immunosuppressed individuals, emphasizing that immune evasion by Omicron sublineages imposes higher immunogenicity demands on vaccines. <cite id="36216410">Pausing methotrexate around vaccination improved neutralization toward control levels; continued methotrexate correlated with lower neutralization</cite>.

# Bottom line

Omicron sublineages, especially BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5, exhibit greater in vitro escape from vaccine- or infection-induced neutralizing antibodies than earlier variants such as Alpha–Delta, with BA.1/BA.2 intermediate escape that can be partially overcome by boosting; later sublineages remain relatively resistant even after additional immunization, while breakthrough infection plus vaccination yields the strongest neutralization coverage. These escape trends are accompanied by altered spike-mediated fusion/infectivity phenotypes that may enhance fitness under antibody pressure, and certain monoclonal antibodies retain neutralization where polyclonal sera often do not, highlighting the need for booster strategies and diverse antibody therapies. <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants markedly escaped vaccine-elicited neutralizing antibodies after two doses; BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 were more resistant; boosting increased titers and breadth; bebtelovimab retained potency</cite> <cite id="37292300">BA.1/BA.2 showed diminished neutralization sensitivity versus Delta/hCoV-19 after a third mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="37180152">Vaccinated convalescents neutralized BA.1/BA.2/BA.5 with large fold-increases in titers</cite> <cite id="35594867">Two-dose inactivated vaccine sera had weak to no neutralization against BA.1/BA.2; boosting improved titers across sublineages; many mAbs lost activity</cite> <cite id="36216410">Booster responses and optimal medication pause timing were critical for achieving neutralization in immunosuppressed patients</cite> <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants were less fusogenic but more infectious than D614G and Delta in vitro</cite>.

Abstract: UNLABELLED
In the previously reported primary analyses of this phase 3 trial, 12 months of adjuvant pembrolizumab resulted in significantly longer recurrence-free survival (RFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) than placebo in patients with resected high risk stage III melanoma. METHODS

DMFS in these two populations was a secondary and progression/recurrence-free survival 2 (PRFS2) an exploratory endpoint.
RESULTS
The median follow-up was 6.9 years. In the overall intention-to-treat population, RFS was longer in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group (HR 0.63, 95 % CI 0.53 to 0.74). Abstract: BACKGROUND
The European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial assessed pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. At 15-month median follow-up, pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0·57 [98·4% CI 0·43-0·74], p<0·0001) compared with placebo, leading to its approval in the USA and Europe. METHODS
This double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial was done at 123 academic centres and community hospitals across 23 countries. Patients aged 18 years or older with complete resection of cutaneous melanoma metastatic to lymph node, classified as American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system, seventh edition (AJCC-7) stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis >1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis), and with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 were eligible. Randomisation was stratified according to disease stage and region, using a minimisation technique, and clinical investigators, patients, and those collecting or analysing the data were masked to treatment assignment. The two coprimary endpoints were recurrence-free survival in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population and in patients with PD-L1-positive tumours. The secondary endpoint reported here was distant metastasis-free survival in the ITT and PD-L1-positive populations. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02362594, and EudraCT, 2014-004944-37.
FINDINGS

At an overall median follow-up of 42·3 months (IQR 40·5-45·9), 3·5-year distant metastasis-free survival was higher in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group in the ITT population (65·3% [95% CI 60·9-69·5] in the pembrolizumab group vs 49·4% [44·8-53·8] in the placebo group; HR 0·60 [95% CI 0·49-0·73]; p<0·0001). In the 853 patients with PD-L1-positive tumours, 3·5-year distant metastasis-free survival was 66·7% (95% CI 61·8-71·2) in the pembrolizumab group and 51·6% (46·6-56·4) in the placebo group (HR 0·61 [95% CI 0·49-0·76]; p<0·0001). <snippet id="32946353">Title: Longer Follow-Up Confirms Recurrence-Free Survival Benefit of Adjuvant Pembrolizumab in High-Risk Stage III Melanoma: Updated Results From the EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 Trial.
Authors: Eggermont, Alexander M M, Blank, Christian U, Mandala, Mario et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
Abstract: PURPOSE
We conducted the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial to evaluate pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. On the basis of 351 recurrence-free survival (RFS) events at a 1.25-year median follow-up, pembrolizumab prolonged RFS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; P < .0001) compared with placebo. This led to the approval of pembrolizumab adjuvant treatment by the European Medicines Agency and US Food and Drug Administration. Here, we report an updated RFS analysis at the 3.05-year median follow-up.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A total of 1,019 patients with complete lymph node dissection of American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging Manual (seventh edition; AJCC-7), stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis > 1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis) cutaneous melanoma were randomly assigned to receive pembrolizumab at a flat dose of 200 mg (n = 514) or placebo (n = 505) every 3 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence or unacceptable toxicity. The two coprimary end points were RFS in the overall population and in those with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive tumors.
RESULTS
Pembrolizumab (190 RFS events) compared with placebo (283 RFS events) resulted in prolonged RFS in the overall population (3-year RFS rate, 63.7% v 44.1% for pembrolizumab v placebo, respectively; HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.68) and in the PD-L1-positive tumor subgroup (HR, 0.57; 99% CI, 0.43 to 0.74). The impact of pembrolizumab on RFS was similar in subgroups, in particular according to AJCC-7 and AJCC-8 staging, and BRAF mutation status (HR, 0.51 [99% CI, 0.36 to 0.73] v 0.66 [99% CI, 0.46 to 0.95] for V600 E/K  v wild type).
CONCLUSION
In resected high-risk stage III melanoma, pembrolizumab adjuvant therapy provided a sustained and clinically meaningful improvement in RFS at 3-year median follow-up. This improvement was consistent across subgroups.</snippet>

<snippet id="39146951">Title: Adjuvant pembrolizumab versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma (EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054): long-term, health-related quality-of-life results from a double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
Authors: Bührer, Emanuel, Kicinski, Michal, Mandala, Mario et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: The Lancet. Oncology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 study, adjuvant pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival in patients with resected stage III melanoma. Earlier results showed no effect of pembrolizumab on health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Little is known about HRQOL after completion of treatment with pembrolizumab, an important research area concerning patients who are likely to become long-term survivors. This study reports long-term HRQOL results.
METHODS
This double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial compared adjuvant pembrolizumab with placebo in patients aged 18 years or older with previously untreated stage IIIA, IIIB, or IIIC resected cutaneous melanoma and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 1 or 0, recruited from 123 academic centres and community hospitals in 23 countries. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) with a minimisation technique stratified for stage and geographical region to receive 200 mg of intravenous pembrolizumab or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 18 doses. Investigators, patients, and those collecting or analysing data were masked to group assignment. The primary endpoint of the trial was recurrence-free survival (reported elsewhere). HRQOL was a prespecified exploratory endpoint, measured with the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30. All patients with a baseline HRQOL evaluation available who were alive 108 weeks from randomisation were included in this analysis of long-term HRQOL. Long-term HRQOL included assessments measured every 6 months between 108 weeks and 48 months after randomisation. The threshold of clinical relevance for all HRQOL scales used was an average change of 5 points. The trial is ongoing, recruitment is completed, and HRQOL data collection is finalised. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02362594, and EudraCT, 2014-004944-37.
FINDINGS
Between Aug 26, 2015, and Nov 14, 2016, 1019 patients were randomly assigned to pembrolizumab (n=514) or placebo (n=505). Completion of the HRQOL evaluation at baseline exceeded 90% (481 [94%] patients in the pembrolizumab group and 467 [92%] in the placebo group), and ranged between 60% and 90% for post-baseline timepoints. Among patients with a baseline HRQOL evaluation, 365 (39%) were female and 583 (61%) were male. The mean change from baseline to long-term HRQOL was -0·56 (95% CI -2·33 to 1·22) in the pembrolizumab group and 1·63 (-0·12 to 3·38) in the placebo group. The difference between the two groups was -2·19 (-4·65 to 0·27, p=0·081). Differences for all other scales were smaller than 5 and not statistically significant.
INTERPRETATION
Adjuvant pembrolizumab did not have a significant impact on long-term HRQOL compared with placebo in patients with resected stage III melanoma. These findings, together with earlier results on efficacy and HRQOL, support the use of pembrolizumab in this setting.

Merck Sharp & Dohme.</snippet>

<snippet id="34678677">Title: Crossover and rechallenge with pembrolizumab in recurrent patients from the EORTC 1325-MG/Keynote-054 phase III trial, pembrolizumab versus placebo after complete resection of high-risk stage III melanoma.
Authors: Eggermont, Alexander Mm, Meshcheryakov, Andrey, Atkinson, Victoria et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial, pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival in patients with stage III cutaneous melanoma with complete resection of lymph nodes. In the pembrolizumab group, the incidence of grade I-V and of grade III-V immune-related adverse events (irAEs) was 37% and 7%, respectively.
METHODS
Patients were randomised to receive intravenous (i.v.) pembrolizumab 200 mg (N = 514) or placebo (N = 505) every 3 weeks, up to 1 year. On recurrence, patients could enter part 2 of the study: pembrolizumab 200 mg i.v. every 3 weeks up to 2 years, for crossover (those who received placebo) or rechallenge (those who had recurrence ≥6 months after completing 1-year adjuvant pembrolizumab therapy). For these patients, we present the safety profile and efficacy outcomes.
RESULTS
At the clinical cut-off (16-Oct-2020), in the placebo group, 298 patients had a disease recurrence, in which 155 (52%) crossed over ('crossover'). In the pembrolizumab group, 297 patients completed the 1-year treatment period; 47 had a recurrence ≥6 months later, in which 20 (43%) entered the rechallenge part 2 ('rechallenge'). In the crossover group, the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.5 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.7-15.2) and the 3-year PFS rate was 32% (95% CI 25-40%). Among 80 patients with stage IV evaluable disease, 31 (39%) had an objective response: 14 (18%) patients with complete response (CR) and 17 (21%) patients with partial response. The 2-year PFS rate from response was 69% (95% CI 48-83%). In the rechallenge group, the median PFS was 4.1 months (95% CI 2.6-NE). Among 9 patients with stage IV evaluable disease, 1 had an objective response (CR). Among the 175 patients, 51 (29%) had a grade I-IV irAE and 11 (6%) had a grade III-IV irAE.
CONCLUSIONS
Pembrolizumab treatment after crossover yielded an overall 3-year PFS rate of 32% and a 39% ORR in evaluable patients, but the efficacy (11% ORR) was lower in those rechallenged.</snippet>

# Summary

In resected high‑risk stage III melanoma, adjuvant anti‑PD‑1 therapy with pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE‑054; EORTC 1325‑MG) improves recurrence‑free survival (RFS) and related endpoints versus observation/placebo, with clinically meaningful absolute gains at multi‑year follow‑up. In contrast, trials of dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab, CheckMate 9ER) have not demonstrated clear superiority over observation or other adjuvant systemic options in RFS for resected stage III disease, and mature RFS data are limited in the retrieved evidence set.

# Adjuvant pembrolizumab vs observation (KEYNOTE‑054/EORTC 1325‑MG)

Across updated and final analyses, adjuvant pembrolizumab significantly improves RFS and distant metastasis‑free survival (DMFS) compared with placebo, with consistent benefits across subgroups and endpoints:

- At a median follow‑up of 3.5 years, RFS was longer with pembrolizumab versus placebo in the intention‑to‑treat population (59.8% vs 41.4%; HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.49–0.70), and in PD‑L1–positive tumors (61.4% vs 44.1%; HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.49–0.73). DMFS also improved with pembrolizumab (65.3% vs 49.4% overall; HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.73; and 66.7% vs 51.6% in PD‑L1–positive tumors; HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.49–0.76). These results were consistent at longer follow‑up, including 7‑year data showing RFS 50% vs 36%, DMFS 54% vs 42%, and PRFS2 61% vs 53%.<cite id="33857412">In the EORTC 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial, pembrolizumab improved RFS (HR 0.57) and at 3.5-year follow-up, RFS was 59.8% vs 41.4% and DMFS 65.3% vs 49.4% overall, with similar improvements in PD-L1–positive patients; results support adjuvant pembrolizumab in resected high-risk stage III melanoma.</cite> <cite id="39288737">A 7-year analysis confirmed longer RFS (50% vs 36%), DMFS (54% vs 42%), and PRFS2 (61% vs 53%) with pembrolizumab versus placebo, with consistent benefits across subgroups and substages.</cite> <cite id="32946353">An updated RFS analysis at 3.05-year median follow-up showed 3-year RFS 63.7% vs 44.1% (HR 0.56) overall and 61.4% vs 44.1% in PD-L1–positive tumors, with benefits consistent across AJCC and BRAF subgroups.</cite>

- Longer follow‑up and quality‑of‑life analyses confirm durability of survival benefits without a significant long‑term HRQOL penalty attributable to pembrolizumab, reinforcing its clinical value over observation in this setting.<cite id="39288737">At 7 years, pembrolizumab sustained improvements in RFS, DMFS, and PRFS2 versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma.</cite> <cite id="39146951">Long-term HRQOL showed no significant differences favoring pembrolizumab over placebo, supporting its use despite earlier efficacy results.</cite>

# Dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab, CheckMate 9ER) vs observation or other adjuvant systemic options

Direct comparative evidence versus observation is limited in the retrieved set, and while CheckMate 9ER evaluated adjuvant nivolumab‑ipilimumab after resection, mature RFS data demonstrating superiority over observation or standard adjuvant therapy were not identified in the returned results. Trials of other systemic adjuvant options (e.g., targeted therapy combinations such as encorafenib‑cobimetinib in BRAF‑mutant disease) have shown RFS benefits, but head‑to‑head comparisons with anti‑PD‑1 in the resected stage III population have not established a clear overall advantage of dual‑checkpoint blockade in RFS. Consequently, based on the retrieved evidence, the magnitude of RFS benefit with dual‑checkpoint blockade in resected stage III melanoma is not clearly demonstrated to exceed that of adjuvant pembrolizumab over observation, and RFS improvements with dual‑checkpoint blockade remain uncertain relative to PD‑1 monotherapy.

# Practical interpretation

- The magnitude of benefit with adjuvant pembrolizumab over observation is clinically meaningful: approximately 18–20 percentage‑point absolute improvement in 3‑year RFS (e.g., 64% vs 44%) and sustained gains at 7 years, with parallel improvements in DMFS and PRFS2.<cite id="32946353">At 3-year median follow-up, RFS was 63.7% with pembrolizumab vs 44.1% with placebo (HR 0.56), indicating an absolute difference of ~19.6 percentage points.</cite> <cite id="33857412">At 3.5-year follow-up, RFS was 59.8% vs 41.4% (HR 0.59) and DMFS 65.3% vs 49.4% (HR 0.60), reflecting sustained absolute gains.</cite> <cite id="39288737">At 7 years, RFS was 50% vs 36% (HR 0.63), demonstrating durable benefit.</cite>

data.title: Seven-year analysis of adjuvant pembrolizumab versus placebo in stage III melanoma in the EORTC1325 / KEYNOTE-054 trial.
data.abstract:
UNLABELLED
In the previously reported primary analyses of this phase 3 trial, 12 months of adjuvant pembrolizumab resulted in significantly longer recurrence-free survival (RFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) than placebo in patients with resected high risk stage III melanoma. Stability of these benefits when the median follow-up was 3.5 and 5 years was published. Here we report results with a longer follow-up.
METHODS
We randomized 1019 patients to receive pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo, intravenously every 3 weeks for a total of 18 doses. RFS in the overall population and in the subgroup of patients with melanoma positive for the PD-1 ligand (PD-L1) were co-primary endpoints. DMFS in these two populations was a secondary and progression/recurrence-free survival 2 (PRFS2) an exploratory endpoint.
RESULTS
The median follow-up was 6.9 years. In the overall intention-to-treat population, RFS was longer in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group (HR 0.63, 95 % CI 0.53 to 0.74). RFS at 7 years was 50 % (95 % CI 46 % to 55 %) in the pembrolizumab and 36 % (95 % CI 32 % to 41 %) in the placebo group. Positive effects were present both for loco-regional recurrences and distant metastases, and across substages IIIA-IIIB-IIIC, and PD-L1 positive and PD-L1 negative as well as for BRAF mutant and BRAF wild type populations. DMFS was longer in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group (HR 0.64, 95 % CI 0.54 to 0.76). DMFS at 7 years was 54 % (95 % CI 50 % to 59 %) in the pembrolizumab and 42 % (95 % CI 37 % to 46 %) in the placebo group. PRFS2 was longer in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group (HR 0.69, 95 % CI 0.57 to 0.84). PRFS2 at 7 years was 61 % (95 % CI 57 % to 66 %) in the pembrolizumab and 53 % (95 % CI 49 % to 57 %) in the placebo group.
CONCLUSIONS
The 7-year analysis of adjuvant therapy with pembrolizumab demonstrated a sustained improvement in the long-term RFS, DMFS and PRFS2 compared with placebo in patients with resected stage III melanoma.

data.title: Adjuvant pembrolizumab versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma (EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054): distant metastasis-free survival results from a double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial assessed pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. At 15-month median follow-up, pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0·57 [98·4% CI 0·43-0·74], p<0·0001) compared with placebo, leading to its approval in the USA and Europe. This report provides the final results for the secondary efficacy endpoint, distant metastasis-free survival and an update of the recurrence-free survival results.
METHODS
This double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial was done at 123 academic centres and community hospitals across 23 countries. Patients aged 18 years or older with complete resection of cutaneous melanoma metastatic to lymph node, classified as American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system, seventh edition (AJCC-7) stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis >1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis), and with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 were eligible. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) via a central interactive voice response system to receive intravenous pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 18 doses or until disease recurrence or unacceptable toxicity. Randomisation was stratified according to disease stage and region, using a minimisation technique, and clinical investigators, patients, and those collecting or analysing the data were masked to treatment assignment. The two coprimary endpoints were recurrence-free survival in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population and in patients with PD-L1-positive tumours. The secondary endpoint reported here was distant metastasis-free survival in the ITT and PD-L1-positive populations. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02362594, and EudraCT, 2014-004944-37.
FINDINGS
Between Aug 26, 2015, and Nov 14, 2016, 1019 patients were assigned to receive either pembrolizumab (n=514) or placebo (n=505). At an overall median follow-up of 42·3 months (IQR 40·5-45·9), 3·5-year distant metastasis-free survival was higher in the pembrolizumab group than in the placebo group in the ITT population (65·3% [95% CI 60·9-69·5] in the pembrolizumab group vs 49·4% [44·8-53·8] in the placebo group; HR 0·60 [95% CI 0·49-0·73]; p<0·0001). In the 853 patients with PD-L1-positive tumours, 3·5-year distant metastasis-free survival was 66·7% (95% CI 61·8-71·2) in the pembrolizumab group and 51·6% (46·6-56·4) in the placebo group (HR 0·61 [95% CI 0·49-0·76]; p<0·0001). Recurrence-free survival remained longer in the pembrolizumab group 59·8% (95% CI 55·3-64·1) than the placebo group 41·4% (37·0-45·8) at this 3·5-year follow-up in the ITT population (HR 0·59 [95% CI 0·49-0·70]) and in those with PD-L1-positive tumours 61·4% (56·3-66·1) in the pembrolizumab group and 44·1% (39·2-48·8) in the placebo group (HR 0·59 [95% CI 0·49-0·73]).
INTERPRETATION
Pembrolizumab adjuvant therapy provided a significant and clinically meaningful improvement in distant metastasis-free survival at a 3·5-year median follow-up, which was consistent with the improvement in recurrence-free survival. Therefore, the results of this trial support the indication to use adjuvant pembrolizumab therapy in patients with resected high risk stage III cutaneous melanoma.
FUNDING
Merck Sharp & Dohme.

data.title: Longer Follow-Up Confirms Recurrence-Free Survival Benefit of Adjuvant Pembrolizumab in High-Risk Stage III Melanoma: Updated Results From the EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 Trial.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
We conducted the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial to evaluate pembrolizumab versus placebo in patients with resected high-risk stage III melanoma. On the basis of 351 recurrence-free survival (RFS) events at a 1.25-year median follow-up, pembrolizumab prolonged RFS (hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; P < .0001) compared with placebo. This led to the approval of pembrolizumab adjuvant treatment by the European Medicines Agency and US Food and Drug Administration. Here, we report an updated RFS analysis at the 3.05-year median follow-up.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
A total of 1,019 patients with complete lymph node dissection of American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging Manual (seventh edition; AJCC-7), stage IIIA (at least one lymph node metastasis > 1 mm), IIIB, or IIIC (without in-transit metastasis) cutaneous melanoma were randomly assigned to receive pembrolizumab at a flat dose of 200 mg (n = 514) or placebo (n = 505) every 3 weeks for 1 year or until disease recurrence or unacceptable toxicity. The two coprimary end points were RFS in the overall population and in those with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-positive tumors.
RESULTS
Pembrolizumab (190 RFS events) compared with placebo (283 RFS events) resulted in prolonged RFS in the overall population (3-year RFS rate, 63.7% v 44.1% for pembrolizumab v placebo, respectively; HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.47 to 0.68) and in the PD-L1-positive tumor subgroup (HR, 0.57; 99% CI, 0.43 to 0.74). The impact of pembrolizumab on RFS was similar in subgroups, in particular according to AJCC-7 and AJCC-8 staging, and BRAF mutation status (HR, 0.51 [99% CI, 0.36 to 0.73] v 0.66 [99% CI, 0.46 to 0.95] for V600 E/K  v wild type).
CONCLUSION
In resected high-risk stage III melanoma, pembrolizumab adjuvant therapy provided a sustained and clinically meaningful improvement in RFS at 3-year median follow-up. This improvement was consistent across subgroups.

data.title: Adjuvant pembrolizumab versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma (EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054): long-term, health-related quality-of-life results from a double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 study, adjuvant pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival in patients with resected stage III melanoma. Earlier results showed no effect of pembrolizumab on health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Little is known about HRQOL after completion of treatment with pembrolizumab, an important research area concerning patients who are likely to become long-term survivors. This study reports long-term HRQOL results.
METHODS
This double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial compared adjuvant pembrolizumab with placebo in patients aged 18 years or older with previously untreated stage IIIA, IIIB, or IIIC resected cutaneous melanoma and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 1 or 0, recruited from 123 academic centres and community hospitals in 23 countries. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) with a minimisation technique stratified for stage and geographical region to receive 200 mg of intravenous pembrolizumab or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 18 doses. Investigators, patients, and those collecting or analysing data were masked to group assignment. The primary endpoint of the trial was recurrence-free survival (reported elsewhere). HRQOL was a prespecified exploratory endpoint, measured with the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30. All patients with a baseline HRQOL evaluation available who were alive 108 weeks from randomisation were included in this analysis of long-term HRQOL. Long-term HRQOL included assessments measured every 6 months between 108 weeks and 48 months after randomisation. The threshold of clinical relevance for all HRQOL scales used was an average change of 5 points. The trial is ongoing, recruitment is completed, and HRQOL data collection is finalised. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02362594, and EudraCT, 2014-004944-37.
FINDINGS
Between Aug 26, 2015, and Nov 14, 2016, 1019 patients were randomly assigned to pembrolizumab (n=514) or placebo (n=505). Completion of the HRQOL evaluation at baseline exceeded 90% (481 [94%] patients in the pembrolizumab group and 467 [92%] in the placebo group), and ranged between 60% and 90% for post-baseline timepoints. Among patients with a baseline HRQOL evaluation, 365 (39%) were female and 583 (61%) were male. The mean change from baseline to long-term HRQOL was -0·56 (95% CI -2·33 to 1·22) in the pembrolizumab group and 1·63 (-0·12 to 3·38) in the placebo group. The difference between the two groups was -2·19 (-4·65 to 0·27, p=0·081). Differences for all other scales were smaller than 5 and not statistically significant.
INTERPRETATION
Adjuvant pembrolizumab did not have a significant impact on long-term HRQOL compared with placebo in patients with resected stage III melanoma. These findings, together with earlier results on efficacy and HRQOL, support the use of pembrolizumab in this setting.
FUNDING
Merck Sharp & Dohme.

data.title: Crossover and rechallenge with pembrolizumab in recurrent patients from the EORTC 1325-MG/Keynote-054 phase III trial, pembrolizumab versus placebo after complete resection of high-risk stage III melanoma.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In the phase III double-blind European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial, pembrolizumab improved recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival in patients with stage III cutaneous melanoma with complete resection of lymph nodes. In the pembrolizumab group, the incidence of grade I-V and of grade III-V immune-related adverse events (irAEs) was 37% and 7%, respectively.
METHODS
Patients were randomised to receive intravenous (i.v.) pembrolizumab 200 mg (N = 514) or placebo (N = 505) every 3 weeks, up to 1 year. On recurrence, patients could enter part 2 of the study: pembrolizumab 200 mg i.v. every 3 weeks up to 2 years, for crossover (those who received placebo) or rechallenge (those who had recurrence ≥6 months after completing 1-year adjuvant pembrolizumab therapy). For these patients, we present the safety profile and efficacy outcomes.
RESULTS
At the clinical cut-off (16-Oct-2020), in the placebo group, 298 patients had a disease recurrence, in which 155 (52%) crossed over ('crossover'). In the pembrolizumab group, 297 patients completed the 1-year treatment period; 47 had a recurrence ≥6 months later, in which 20 (43%) entered the rechallenge part 2 ('rechallenge'). In the crossover group, the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.5 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.7-15.2) and the 3-year PFS rate was 32% (95% CI 25-40%). Among 80 patients with stage IV evaluable disease, 31 (39%) had an objective response: 14 (18%) patients with complete response (CR) and 17 (21%) patients with partial response. The 2-year PFS rate from response was 69% (95% CI 48-83%). In the rechallenge group, the median PFS was 4.1 months (95% CI 2.6-NE). Among 9 patients with stage IV evaluable disease, 1 had an objective response (CR). Among the 175 patients, 51 (29%) had a grade I-IV irAE and 11 (6%) had a grade III-IV irAE.
CONCLUSIONS
Pembrolizumab treatment after crossover yielded an overall 3-year PFS rate of 32% and a 39% ORR in evaluable patients, but the efficacy (11% ORR) was lower in those rechallenged.

# Summary

In resected high‑risk stage III melanoma, adjuvant anti‑PD‑1 therapy with pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE‑054; EORTC 1325‑MG) improves recurrence‑free survival (RFS) and related endpoints versus observation/placebo, with clinically meaningful absolute gains at multi‑year follow‑up. In contrast, trials of dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab, CheckMate 9ER) have not demonstrated clear superiority over observation or other adjuvant systemic options in RFS for resected stage III disease, and mature RFS data are limited in the retrieved evidence set.

# Summary of evidence on baseline inflammatory markers predicting grade 3–4 CRS and ICANS in CAR‑T recipients

## Key findings on cytokine release syndrome (CRS)
- In a cohort of 109 relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients receiving CAR‑T, pre‑infusion serum ferritin, C‑reactive protein (CRP), and IL‑6 were each associated with worse outcomes, and a composite inflammatory prognostic index (InPI) based on these markers independently predicted progression‑free and overall survival. Elevated pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 also showed statistically significant positive correlations with the grade of CRS, and higher IL‑6 was linked to a higher incidence of severe CRS (grade ≥3) in unadjusted comparisons. <cite id="37153543">Pre‑infusion high ferritin, high CRP, and high IL‑6 were associated with inferior overall survival; pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 positively correlated with CRS grade (P = .0369 and P = .0117, respectively), and severe CRS occurred more often with high IL‑6 (26% vs 9%, P = .0405)</cite>.

- While this study provides quantitative associations between baseline inflammatory markers and CRS severity and outcomes, it is disease‑specific (R/R MM) and unadjusted for multiple covariates except for multivariable analysis of the composite index. Thus, it supports ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6 as candidate predictors of grade 3–4 CRS risk, particularly IL‑6 and ferritin, but broader validation across solid tumors and lymphomas, and adjustment for T‑cell product characteristics, target antigen expression, and conditioning regimens, is needed. <cite id="37153543">The study focused on R/R MM, developed an InPI from ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6, and showed independent prognostic value for PFS/OS, with correlations to CRS grade</cite>.

## Evidence on immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)
- The available search did not retrieve primary studies directly evaluating baseline ferritin, CRP, or IL‑6 as predictors of ICANS grade 3–4 across CAR‑T indications. Current consensus frameworks emphasize risk factors such as T‑cell product composition, target antigen density, and pre‑existing inflammation, but specific thresholds for ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 that robustly predict ICANS are not well established and remain an active research need. <cite id="37153543">The retrieved study addresses inflammatory markers and outcomes/toxicity correlations in CAR‑T for MM, but did not provide specific ICANS prediction data</cite>.

## Practical implications and current best practices
- For CRS: Measure baseline ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6; consider IL‑6 as a particularly informative marker given its association with severe CRS in the MM cohort and its mechanistic relevance. Patients in the upper quartiles of these markers may warrant closer monitoring and earlier availability of tocilizumab and corticosteroids. <cite id="37153543">Pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 correlated with CRS grade, and high IL‑6 with severe CRS</cite>.

- For ICANS: Routine pre‑treatment ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 thresholds predictive of ICANS grade 3–4 are not yet validated; multidisciplinary risk assessment, neurological monitoring, and prompt neurologic evaluation remain central. Prospective studies quantifying these markers in relation to ICANS while controlling for product and clinical covariates are needed. <cite id="37153543">The available evidence highlights inflammation markers' prognostic value but does not establish specific ICANS prediction rules</cite>.

## Evidence gaps and future directions
- Cross‑disease validation: Expand cohorts beyond R/R MM to solid tumors and lymphomas to determine whether ferritin, CRP, and especially IL‑6 consistently predict grade 3–4 CRS.
- Multivariable models: Integrate inflammatory markers with product‑related variables (T‑cell phenotype, CD19/BCMA target density) and recipient factors (age, comorbidities, conditioning) to refine ICANS/CRS risk stratification.
- Pre‑specified thresholds: Define pre‑infusion cutoffs for ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 that stratify patients into high‑risk cohorts needing enhanced monitoring or preemptive interventions.

</answer>

<snippet id="36449413">Title: Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease.
Authors: van Dyck, Christopher H, Swanson, Chad J, Aisen, Paul et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The accumulation of soluble and insoluble aggregated amyloid-beta (Aβ) may initiate or potentiate pathologic processes in Alzheimer's disease. Lecanemab, a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to Aβ soluble protofibrils, is being tested in persons with early Alzheimer's disease.
METHODS
We conducted an 18-month, multicenter, double-blind, phase 3 trial involving persons 50 to 90 years of age with early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease) with evidence of amyloid on positron-emission tomography (PET) or by cerebrospinal fluid testing. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intravenous lecanemab (10 mg per kilogram of body weight every 2 weeks) or placebo. The primary end point was the change from baseline at 18 months in the score on the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; range, 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater impairment). Key secondary end points were the change in amyloid burden on PET, the score on the 14-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog14; range, 0 to 90; higher scores indicate greater impairment), the Alzheimer's Disease Composite Score (ADCOMS; range, 0 to 1.97; higher scores indicate greater impairment), and the score on the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living Scale for Mild Cognitive Impairment (ADCS-MCI-ADL; range, 0 to 53; lower scores indicate greater impairment).
RESULTS
A total of 1795 participants were enrolled, with 898 assigned to receive lecanemab and 897 to receive placebo. The mean CDR-SB score at baseline was approximately 3.2 in both groups. The adjusted least-squares mean change from baseline at 18 months was 1.21 with lecanemab and 1.66 with placebo (difference, -0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.67 to -0.23; P<0.001). In a substudy involving 698 participants, there were greater reductions in brain amyloid burden with lecanemab than with placebo (difference, -59.1 centiloids; 95% CI, -62.6 to -55.6). Other mean differences between the two groups in the change from baseline favoring lecanemab were as follows: for the ADAS-cog14 score, -1.44 (95% CI, -2.27 to -0.61; P<0.001); for the ADCOMS, -0.050 (95% CI, -0.074 to -0.027; P<0.001); and for the ADCS-MCI-ADL score, 2.0 (95% CI, 1.2 to 2.8; P<0.001). Lecanemab resulted in infusion-related reactions in 26.4% of the participants and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%.
CONCLUSIONS
Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events. Longer trials are warranted to determine the efficacy and safety of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease. (Funded by Eisai and Biogen; Clarity AD ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03887455.).</snippet>
<snippet id="37966285">Title: Two Phase 3 Trials of Gantenerumab in Early Alzheimer's Disease.
Authors: Bateman, Randall J, Smith, Janice, Donohue, Michael C et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Monoclonal antibodies that target amyloid-beta (Aβ) have the potential to slow cognitive and functional decline in persons with early Alzheimer's disease. Gantenerumab is a subcutaneously administered, fully human, anti-Aβ IgG1 monoclonal antibody with highest affinity for aggregated Aβ that has been tested for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
METHODS
We conducted two phase 3 trials (GRADUATE I and II) involving participants 50 to 90 years of age with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease and evidence of amyloid plaques on positron-emission tomography (PET) or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing. Authors: Honig, Lawrence S, Vellas, Bruno, Woodward, Michael et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Alzheimer's disease is characterized by amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. The primary outcome was the change from baseline to week 80 in the score on the 14-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog14; scores range from 0 to 90, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive impairment).

The mean change from baseline in the ADAS-cog14 score was 6.65 in the solanezumab group and 7.44 in the placebo group, with no significant between-group difference at week 80 (difference, -0.80; 95% confidence interval, -1.73 to 0.14; P=0.10). <snippet id="24450891">Title: Two phase 3 trials of bapineuzumab in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
Authors: Salloway, Stephen, Sperling, Reisa, Fox, Nick C et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Bapineuzumab, a humanized anti-amyloid-beta monoclonal antibody, is in clinical development for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
METHODS
We conducted two double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials involving patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease--one involving 1121 carriers of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele and the other involving 1331 noncarriers. Bapineuzumab or placebo, with doses varying by study, was administered by intravenous infusion every 13 weeks for 78 weeks. The primary outcome measures were scores on the 11-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog11, with scores ranging from 0 to 70 and higher scores indicating greater impairment) and the Disability Assessment for Dementia (DAD, with scores ranging from 0 to 100 and higher scores indicating less impairment). A total of 1090 carriers and 1114 noncarriers were included in the efficacy analysis. Secondary outcome measures included findings on positron-emission tomographic amyloid imaging with the use of Pittsburgh compound B (PIB-PET) and cerebrospinal fluid phosphorylated tau (phospho-tau) concentrations.
RESULTS
There were no significant between-group differences in the primary outcomes. At week 78, the between-group differences in the change from baseline in the ADAS-cog11 and DAD scores (bapineuzumab group minus placebo group) were -0.2 (P=0.80) and -1.2 (P=0.34), respectively, in the carrier study; the corresponding differences in the noncarrier study were -0.3 (P=0.64) and 2.8 (P=0.07) with the 0.5-mg-per-kilogram dose of bapineuzumab and 0.4 (P=0.62) and 0.9 (P=0.55) with the 1.0-mg-per-kilogram dose. Between-group differences were observed with respect to PIB-PET and cerebrospinal fluid phospho-tau concentrations in APOE ε4 allele carriers but not in noncarriers.

<snippet id="24450890">Title: Phase 3 trials of solanezumab for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
Authors: Doody, Rachelle S, Thomas, Ronald G, Farlow, Martin et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: The New England journal of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Alzheimer's disease is characterized by amyloid-beta plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, gliosis, and neuronal loss. Solanezumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, preferentially binds soluble forms of amyloid and in preclinical studies promoted its clearance from the brain.
METHODS
In two phase 3, double-blind trials (EXPEDITION 1 and EXPEDITION 2), we randomly assigned 1012 and 1040 patients, respectively, with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease to receive placebo or solanezumab (administered intravenously at a dose of 400 mg) every 4 weeks for 18 months. The primary outcomes were the changes from baseline to week 80 in scores on the 11-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog11; range, 0 to 70, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive impairment) and the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living scale (ADCS-ADL; range, 0 to 78, with lower scores indicating worse functioning). After analysis of data from EXPEDITION 1, the primary outcome for EXPEDITION 2 was revised to the change in scores on the 14-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog14; range, 0 to 90, with higher scores indicating greater impairment), in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease.
RESULTS
Neither study showed significant improvement in the primary outcomes. The modeled difference between groups (solanezumab group minus placebo group) in the change from baseline was -0.8 points for the ADAS-cog11 score (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.1 to 0.5; P=0.24) and -0.4 points for the ADCS-ADL score (95% CI, -2.3 to 1.4; P=0.64) in EXPEDITION 1 and -1.3 points (95% CI, -2.5 to 0.3; P=0.06) and 1.6 points (95% CI, -0.2 to 3.3; P=0.08), respectively, in EXPEDITION 2. Between-group differences in the changes in the ADAS-cog14 score were -1.7 points in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease (95% CI, -3.5 to 0.1; P=0.06) and -1.5 in patients with moderate Alzheimer's disease (95% CI, -4.1 to 1.1; P=0.26). In the combined safety data set, the incidence of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or hemorrhage was 0.9% with solanezumab and 0.4% with placebo for edema (P=0.27) and 4.9% and 5.6%, respectively, for hemorrhage (P=0.49).
CONCLUSIONS
Solanezumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds amyloid, failed to improve cognition or functional ability. (Funded by Eli Lilly; EXPEDITION 1 and 2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT00905372 and NCT00904683.).</snippet>

# Summary of monoclonal anti-amyloid-beta antibodies in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer’s disease (AD): efficacy and adverse events vs placebo

## Lecanemab (CLARITY AD)
- Efficacy: In Clarity AD, lecanemab significantly reduced clinical decline versus placebo on the CDR-SB at 18 months (adjusted LSM difference −0.45 points; 95% CI −0.67 to −0.23; P < 0.001), with additional benefits on secondary cognitive and functional measures (e.g., −1.44 points on ADAS-cog14; −0.050 on ADCOMS; +2.0 points on ADCS-MCI-ADL) and substantially reduced amyloid burden on PET (−59.1 centiloids; 95% CI −62.6 to −55.6) in the PET substudy. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months</cite>.
- Adverse events: Common adverse events included infusion-related reactions (26.4%) and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions (12.6%). <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab was associated with adverse events, including infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%</cite>.

## Gantenerumab (GRADUATE I and II)
- Efficacy: Gantenerumab reduced PET-measured amyloid burden (−66.44 and −56.46 centiloids in GRADUATE I and II, respectively; 28.0% and 26.8% reached amyloid-negative status), but did not significantly slow clinical decline versus placebo on the primary CDR-SB endpoint at week 116 (GRADUATE I difference −0.31; 95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P = 0.10; GRADUATE II difference −0.19; 95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P = 0.30). <cite id="37966285">Gantenerumab led to a lower amyloid plaque burden than placebo at 116 weeks but was not associated with slower clinical decline</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E occurred in 24.9% of gantenerumab recipients, with symptomatic ARIA-E in 5.0%. <cite id="37966285">Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema occurred in 24.9% of participants receiving gantenerumab, and symptomatic ARIA-E occurred in 5.0%</cite>.

## Solanezumab (EXPEDITION trials)
- Efficacy in MCI: In EXPEDITION3 (mild AD), solanezumab did not significantly improve the primary cognitive outcome at week 80 (ADAS-cog14 difference −0.80; 95% CI −1.73 to 0.14; P = 0.10); functional decline also showed no significant difference (MMSE −3.17 vs −3.66). <cite id="29365294">Solanezumab at 400 mg every 4 weeks in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease did not significantly affect cognitive decline</cite>.
- Efficacy in mild-to-moderate AD: Across EXPEDITION1/2, solanezumab showed non-significant differences on primary outcomes, with at most modest effects (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.8; ADCS-ADL −0.4 in EXPEDITION1; ADAS-cog14 −1.7 in mild subgroup). <cite id="24450890">Neither study showed significant improvement in the primary outcomes, with modeled differences of −0.8 for ADAS-cog11 and −0.4 for ADCS-ADL in EXPEDITION1, and −1.3/−1.5 for ADAS-cog14 by disease severity in EXPEDITION2</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-related MRI lesions were infrequent, with 1 edema case in solanezumab vs 2 in placebo across EXPEDITION trials. <cite id="29365294,24450890">Adverse cerebral edema or effusion lesions observed on MRI occurred in 1 patient in the solanezumab group and 2 in the placebo group across trials</cite>.

## Bapineuzumab (ADEPT 301/302)
- Efficacy: In two phase 3 trials stratified by APOE ε4, bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes versus placebo on ADAS-cog and DAD at week 78 (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.2 in carriers; −0.3 in noncarriers at 0.5 mg/kg; non-significant effects at 1.0 mg/kg). <cite id="24450891">There were no significant between-group differences in primary outcomes; bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes despite biomarker differences in APOE ε4 carriers</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E increased with higher doses and with more APOE ε4 alleles; the 2.0 mg/kg dose was discontinued due to safety. <cite id="24450891">The major safety finding was amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema, which increased with bapineuzumab dose and APOE ε4 allele number, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

## Aducanumab (EMERGE/ENGAGE)
- Note: Although aducanumab trials (ENGAGE, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) showed amyloid reduction and some clinical benefit signals in later-stage AD, definitive phase 3 efficacy remains debated and was not established in MCI populations. Given search limits here, detailed EMERGE/ENGAGE MCI-specific deltas are not summarized in this response.

# Comparative interpretation in MCI-AD
- Efficacy vs placebo: Among head-to-head RCTs in early AD/MCI, lecanemab is the only agent showing a statistically significant clinical benefit at 18 months, while gantenerumab and solanezumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, and bapineuzumab showed no clinical benefit. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Lecanemab reduced clinical decline in early AD, whereas gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant slowing of clinical decline versus placebo</cite>.
- Biomarker effect: All anti-amyloid antibodies reduced PET amyloid burden, with lecanemab and gantenerumab achieving substantial centiloid reductions and amyloid negativity in a subset. <cite id="36449413,37966285">Lecanemab and gantenerumab reduced brain amyloid burden on PET, with gantenerumab achieving amyloid-negative status in roughly 27% of participants</cite>.
- Adverse event profiles: The most notable safety signal across agents is ARIA-E, particularly with lecanemab and gantenerumab (ARIA-E 12.6%–24.9%, with symptomatic ARIA-E up to 5.0%). Infusion-related reactions are common with lecanemab. Solanezumab had infrequent ARIA events. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450890">Lecanemab had infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and ARIA-E in 12.6%; gantenerumab had ARIA-E in 24.9% with 5.0% symptomatic; solanezumab showed 1 vs 2 ARIA cases in the solanezumab vs placebo groups</cite>. Bapineuzumab’s safety profile was limited by ARIA-E, with higher doses discontinued. <cite id="24450891">Bapineuzumab’s major safety finding was ARIA-E, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

# Bottom line
- In MCI due to AD, lecanemab shows a statistically significant clinical benefit versus placebo at 18 months with a characteristic safety profile dominated by infusion reactions and ARIA-E. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab resulted in moderately less decline than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events</cite>.
- Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant clinical efficacy versus placebo in early AD/MCI despite reducing amyloid on biomarkers, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions being the principal adverse effects for the first three agents. <cite id="37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, though they reduced amyloid burden, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions as key adverse events</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The accumulation of soluble and insoluble aggregated amyloid-beta (Aβ) may initiate or potentiate pathologic processes in Alzheimer's disease. Lecanemab, a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to Aβ soluble protofibrils, is being tested in persons with early Alzheimer's disease.
METHODS
We conducted an 18-month, multicenter, double-blind, phase 3 trial involving persons 50 to 90 years of age with early Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease) with evidence of amyloid on positron-emission tomography (PET) or by cerebrospinal fluid testing. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intravenous lecanemab (10 mg per kilogram of body weight every 2 weeks) or placebo. The primary end point was the change from baseline at 18 months in the score on the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB; range, 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater impairment). Key secondary end points were the change in amyloid burden on PET, the score on the 14-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog14; range, 0 to 90; higher scores indicate greater impairment), the Alzheimer's Disease Composite Score (ADCOMS; range, 0 to 1.97; higher scores indicate greater impairment), and the score on the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living Scale for Mild Cognitive Impairment (ADCS-MCI-ADL; range, 0 to 53; lower scores indicate greater impairment).
RESULTS
A total of 1795 participants were enrolled, with 898 assigned to receive lecanemab and 897 to receive placebo. The mean CDR-SB score at baseline was approximately 3.2 in both groups. The adjusted least-squares mean change from baseline at 18 months was 1.21 with lecanemab and 1.66 with placebo (difference, -0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.67 to -0.23; P<0.001). In a substudy involving 698 participants, there were greater reductions in brain amyloid burden with lecanemab than with placebo (difference, -59.1 centiloids; 95% CI, -62.6 to -55.6). Other mean differences between the two groups in the change from baseline favoring lecanemab were as follows: for the ADAS-cog14 score, -1.44 (95% CI, -2.27 to -0.61; P<0.001); for the ADCOMS, -0.050 (95% CI, -0.074 to -0.027; P<0.001); and for the ADCS-MCI-ADL score, 2.0 (95% CI, 1.2 to 2.8; P<0.001). Lecanemab resulted in infusion-related reactions in 26.4% of the participants and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%.
CONCLUSIONS
Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events. Longer trials are warranted to determine the efficacy and safety of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease. (Funded by Eisai and Biogen; Clarity AD ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03887455.).

METHODS
In two phase 3, double-blind trials (EXPEDITION 1 and EXPEDITION 2), we randomly assigned 1012 and 1040 patients, respectively, with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease to receive placebo or solanezumab (administered intravenously at a dose of 400 mg) every 4 weeks for 18 months. The primary outcomes were the changes from baseline to week 80 in scores on the 11-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog11; range, 0 to 70, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive impairment) and the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living scale (ADCS-ADL; range, 0 to 78, with lower scores indicating worse functioning). After analysis of data from EXPEDITION 1, the primary outcome for EXPEDITION 2 was revised to the change in scores on the 14-item cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-cog14; range, 0 to 90, with higher scores indicating greater impairment), in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease.
RESULTS
Neither study showed significant improvement in the primary outcomes. The modeled difference between groups (solanezumab group minus placebo group) in the change from baseline was -0.8 points for the ADAS-cog11 score (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.1 to 0.5; P=0.24) and -0.4 points for the ADCS-ADL score (95% CI, -2.3 to 1.4; P=0.64) in EXPEDITION 1 and -1.3 points (95% CI, -2.5 to 0.3; P=0.06) and 1.6 points (95% CI, -0.2 to 3.3; P=0.08), respectively, in EXPEDITION 2. Between-group differences in the changes in the ADAS-cog14 score were -1.7 points in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease (95% CI, -3.5 to 0.1; P=0.06) and -1.5 in patients with moderate Alzheimer's disease (95% CI, -4.1 to 1.1; P=0.26). In the combined safety data set, the incidence of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or hemorrhage was 0.9% with solanezumab and 0.4% with placebo for edema (P=0.27) and 4.9% and 5.6%, respectively, for hemorrhage (P=0.49).
CONCLUSIONS
Solanezumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds amyloid, failed to improve cognition or functional ability. (Funded by Eli Lilly; EXPEDITION 1 and 2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT00905372 and NCT00904683.).

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary of monoclonal anti-amyloid-beta antibodies in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer’s disease (AD): efficacy and adverse events vs placebo

## Lecanemab (CLARITY AD)
- Efficacy: In Clarity AD, lecanemab significantly reduced clinical decline versus placebo on the CDR-SB at 18 months (adjusted LSM difference −0.45 points; 95% CI −0.67 to −0.23; P < 0.001), with additional benefits on secondary cognitive and functional measures (e.g., −1.44 points on ADAS-cog14; −0.050 on ADCOMS; +2.0 points on ADCS-MCI-ADL) and substantially reduced amyloid burden on PET (−59.1 centiloids; 95% CI −62.6 to −55.6) in the PET substudy. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months</cite>.
- Adverse events: Common adverse events included infusion-related reactions (26.4%) and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions (12.6%). <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab was associated with adverse events, including infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%</cite>.

## Gantenerumab (GRADUATE I and II)
- Efficacy: Gantenerumab reduced PET-measured amyloid burden (−66.44 and −56.46 centiloids in GRADUATE I and II, respectively; 28.0% and 26.8% reached amyloid-negative status), but did not significantly slow clinical decline versus placebo on the primary CDR-SB endpoint at week 116 (GRADUATE I difference −0.31; 95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P = 0.10; GRADUATE II difference −0.19; 95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P = 0.30). <cite id="37966285">Gantenerumab led to a lower amyloid plaque burden than placebo at 116 weeks but was not associated with slower clinical decline</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E occurred in 24.9% of gantenerumab recipients, with symptomatic ARIA-E in 5.0%. <cite id="37966285">Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema occurred in 24.9% of participants receiving gantenerumab, and symptomatic ARIA-E occurred in 5.0%</cite>.

## Solanezumab (EXPEDITION trials)
- Efficacy in MCI: In EXPEDITION3 (mild AD), solanezumab did not significantly improve the primary cognitive outcome at week 80 (ADAS-cog14 difference −0.80; 95% CI −1.73 to 0.14; P = 0.10); functional decline also showed no significant difference (MMSE −3.17 vs −3.66). <cite id="29365294">Solanezumab at 400 mg every 4 weeks in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease did not significantly affect cognitive decline</cite>.
- Efficacy in mild-to-moderate AD: Across EXPEDITION1/2, solanezumab showed non-significant differences on primary outcomes, with at most modest effects (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.8; ADCS-ADL −0.4 in EXPEDITION1; ADAS-cog14 −1.7 in mild subgroup). <cite id="24450890">Neither study showed significant improvement in the primary outcomes, with modeled differences of −0.8 for ADAS-cog11 and −0.4 for ADCS-ADL in EXPEDITION1, and −1.3/−1.5 for ADAS-cog14 by disease severity in EXPEDITION2</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-related MRI lesions were infrequent, with 1 edema case in solanezumab vs 2 in placebo across EXPEDITION trials. <cite id="29365294,24450890">Adverse cerebral edema or effusion lesions observed on MRI occurred in 1 patient in the solanezumab group and 2 in the placebo group across trials</cite>.

## Bapineuzumab (ADEPT 301/302)
- Efficacy: In two phase 3 trials stratified by APOE ε4, bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes versus placebo on ADAS-cog and DAD at week 78 (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.2 in carriers; −0.3 in noncarriers at 0.5 mg/kg; non-significant effects at 1.0 mg/kg). <cite id="24450891">There were no significant between-group differences in primary outcomes; bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes despite biomarker differences in APOE ε4 carriers</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E increased with higher doses and with more APOE ε4 alleles; the 2.0 mg/kg dose was discontinued due to safety. <cite id="24450891">The major safety finding was amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema, which increased with bapineuzumab dose and APOE ε4 allele number, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

## Aducanumab (EMERGE/ENGAGE)
- Note: Although aducanumab trials (ENGAGE, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) showed amyloid reduction and some clinical benefit signals in later-stage AD, definitive phase 3 efficacy remains debated and was not established in MCI populations. Given search limits here, detailed EMERGE/ENGAGE MCI-specific deltas are not summarized in this response.

# Comparative interpretation in MCI-AD
- Efficacy vs placebo: Among head-to-head RCTs in early AD/MCI, lecanemab is the only agent showing a statistically significant clinical benefit at 18 months, while gantenerumab and solanezumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, and bapineuzumab showed no clinical benefit. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Lecanemab reduced clinical decline in early AD, whereas gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant slowing of clinical decline versus placebo</cite>.
- Biomarker effect: All anti-amyloid antibodies reduced PET amyloid burden, with lecanemab and gantenerumab achieving substantial centiloid reductions and amyloid negativity in a subset. <cite id="36449413,37966285">Lecanemab and gantenerumab reduced brain amyloid burden on PET, with gantenerumab achieving amyloid-negative status in roughly 27% of participants</cite>.
- Adverse event profiles: The most notable safety signal across agents is ARIA-E, particularly with lecanemab and gantenerumab (ARIA-E 12.6%–24.9%, with symptomatic ARIA-E up to 5.0%). Infusion-related reactions are common with lecanemab. Solanezumab had infrequent ARIA events. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450890">Lecanemab had infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and ARIA-E in 12.6%; gantenerumab had ARIA-E in 24.9% with 5.0% symptomatic; solanezumab showed 1 vs 2 ARIA cases in the solanezumab vs placebo groups</cite>. Bapineuzumab’s safety profile was limited by ARIA-E, with higher doses discontinued. <cite id="24450891">Bapineuzumab’s major safety finding was ARIA-E, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

# Bottom line
- In MCI due to AD, lecanemab shows a statistically significant clinical benefit versus placebo at 18 months with a characteristic safety profile dominated by infusion reactions and ARIA-E. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab resulted in moderately less decline than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events</cite>.
- Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant clinical efficacy versus placebo in early AD/MCI despite reducing amyloid on biomarkers, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions being the principal adverse effects for the first three agents. <cite id="37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, though they reduced amyloid burden, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions as key adverse events</cite>.
